rule_text: If you possess biometric identifiers or biometric information, you must develop and make publicly available a written policy establishing a retention schedule and guidelines for permanently destroying that data when the initial collection purpose is satisfied or within 3 years of the individual's last interaction, whichever occurs first.

rule_text: Individuals aggrieved by a violation of this Act have the right to bring a private action in State circuit court or as a supplemental claim in federal district court, and may recover liquidated damages of $1,000 (or actual damages, whichever is greater) for negligent violations and $5,000 (or actual damages, whichever is greater) for intentional or reckless violations, plus reasonable attorneys' fees, costs, and other relief including injunctions.

rule_text: You cannot recover more than once for a single pattern of biometric data collection by the same entity using the same method, even if that violation occurred multiple times.
rule_text_technical: For purposes of subsection (b) of Section 15, a private entity that, in more than one instance, collects, captures, purchases, receives through trade, or otherwise obtains the same biometric identifier or biometric information from the same person using the same method of collection in violation of subsection (b) of Section 15 has committed a single violation of subsection (b) of Section 15 for which the aggrieved person is entitled to, at most, one recovery under this Section.

Both recognize rights to access and delete personal data, but this Argentine soft-law rule also includes update/rectification rights grounded in Law 25,326, covers AI-system processing specifically, and is a non-binding recommendation rather than a binding mandate.

Alabama H 283 — Data Privacy (Alabama) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Arkansas S 258 — Digital Responsibility Safety and Trust (Arkansas) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Similar to the CCPA right to access/disclosure of personal information, but limited to CCPA-excluded pupil covered information disclosed upon disenrollment request by parents/guardians or adult former pupils.

Both grant consumers the right to access their personal information, but this rule extends the right to contextual data and social graph data specific to social media platforms, and is a voluntary/soft-law bill rather than a binding statute.

Both establish a right to access/disclosure of personal information, but this rule is specific to CCPA-excluded covered pupil information held by educational operators, with requests made by parents/guardians or adult former pupils rather than consumers generally.

Both rules concern the right of data subjects to access their personal information, but the new rule specifically requires maintaining the *source* of personal information in a readily accessible form for inspection, a more granular record-keeping obligation not expressly stated in the CCPA's general right-to-know provision.

This bill (soft law) grants rights to confirm, access (including inferences and profiling), correct, and delete personal data, which parallels CCPA/CPRA access and deletion rights but is a voluntary instrument with different scope and adds profiling/inference access explicitly.
Florida S 2 — Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both provide a right to access personal/covered data including categories and recipients, but this bill specifies a 24-month lookback window and human-readable format, which are meaningful differences from CCPA's access right.

Both grant individuals the right to confirm/know whether a controller is processing their personal data, though Maine's phrasing is more concise and uses 'controller' terminology consistent with state privacy act frameworks rather than CCPA's 'business' terminology.
Maryland H 1261 — Artificial Intelligence Toy Safety Act (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both grant consumers a right to know about data collection and sharing, but this rule is scoped specifically to consumer health data under a Massachusetts proposed bill, whereas the CCPA rule covers all personal information as binding law.
Both grant a right to confirm collection and access personal data, but MA H78 is a proposed bill (soft law/voluntary instrument) with different drafting and scope compared to the binding CCPA/CPRA.

Both grant consumers a right to know about collection and sharing of their data, but this rule is narrowly scoped to Consumer Health Data under a Massachusetts bill, while CCPA covers all personal information with broader disclosure requirements.

Both grant consumers a right to know about data collection and sharing, but this rule is narrower in scope, limited to consumer health data, whereas the CCPA covers broad categories of personal information including categories, sources, and purposes.
New Mexico H 410 — Consumer Info and Data Protection Act (New Mexico) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both provide a right to access personal/health information held about the individual, but the NY bill specifies a 30-day response window (extendable once) and is scoped to regulated health information, while CCPA covers broader personal information and is a binding law.

Both establish a consumer right to access data collected about them, but this New York rule is sector-specific (auto insurance telematics), targets insurers and third-party telematics vendors specifically, and is a state insurance bill rather than a broad general privacy law like CCPA.

Both grant consumers the right to confirm processing and access personal data, but this NY bill is a voluntary/proposed instrument with a 45-day response window and verified-request mechanism, whereas CCPA is a binding law with different procedural specifics.

Both grant consumers the right to access personal data collected about them, but NY S 5486 is narrowly scoped to telematics system data in the automobile insurance context and specifies a 'readable format' requirement, whereas CCPA broadly covers all personal information collected by a business across categories.

Both grant individuals the right to access their personal/covered data, but this NY bill is a soft-law recommendation covering a 24-month lookback window, while the CCPA is a binding law with different scope and framing.

Both require disclosure of categories of personal information collected, sources, and business purposes upon consumer request, but this is a voluntary/soft-law bill targeting social media platforms specifically rather than a binding broadly applicable privacy law.

Both establish a right to access personal data held by a covered entity, but the NC bill applies specifically to AI chatbot licensees and is a proposed state bill rather than the binding CCPA framework with its detailed disclosure requirements.

Both provide a right to access personal data records, but this rule is a voluntary/bill instrument scoped to parents accessing their child's educational data with a 30-day response requirement, whereas CCPA applies broadly to consumers and businesses.

Both rules address providing individuals access to their personal information in portable form, but this rule is a voluntary recommendation specific to certified instructional technology providers in an educational context (covering students and caregivers), whereas the CCPA provision is a binding right applicable to businesses generally.
Both grant access/confirmation rights over personal data, but this is a Vermont bill (voluntary/proposed) with slightly different scope language compared to CCPA's binding California law.
Virginia S 85 — Consumer Data Protection Act (Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Virginia H 2250 — Consumer Data Protection Act (Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both grant rights to confirm processing and access personal data, but this is a voluntary/soft-law bill covering access and confirmation of data sharing, while CCPA is a binding law with different structural requirements.

Both grant a right to access/confirmation of personal information held, but POPIA requires adequate proof of identity as a precondition and does not include the CCPA's additional disclosure of categories and sources.

Both grant individuals the right to obtain confirmation of processing and access to their personal data including origins and purposes, but Senegal's Art. 62 is a broader GDPR-style access right while CCPA focuses on categories and specific pieces collected by businesses.

Both grant individuals the right to access their personal information including sources, recipients, and processing details, but the Philippine law is broader in scope (covering all processors) and lacks the CCPA's business-size thresholds and commercial-context framing.

Both require disclosure of third parties with whom data has been shared; LGPD frames this as a data subject right to information about public and private entities, while CCPA focuses on categories of recipients.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request that a business delete personal information collected from them, and the business must direct its service providers to do the same, subject to statutory exceptions.
rule_text_technical: A consumer has the right to request deletion of personal information collected from them by a business; the business shall delete and direct any service provider or contractor to delete the information from its records, subject to exceptions enumerated in Civil Code § 1798.105(d).

Florida S 2 — Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Kentucky H 559 — Data Privacy and Interoperability (Kentucky) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

New Mexico H 410 — Consumer Info and Data Protection Act (New Mexico) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both establish a right to deletion of personal data, but this New York bill is a voluntary/soft-law instrument covering electronic health products with immediate deletion upon deactivation, while CCPA is a binding law with different scope and procedural requirements.

Both establish a right to request deletion of personal data, but the NC bill applies narrowly to AI chatbot licensees without specifying service provider obligations or exceptions, and is a proposed bill rather than binding law.

Both provide rights to request correction or deletion of personal data, but this rule is a voluntary/bill instrument scoped to parents acting on behalf of children in an educational context, whereas CCPA applies broadly to consumers.

Both establish a right to deletion of personal/health data and require directing affiliates or service providers to also delete, but RI S 2129 is scoped specifically to consumer health data rather than general personal information.

Both require deletion of personal/health data from all systems including service providers, but this rule is scoped to consumer health data in the reproductive/gender-affirming care context rather than general personal information under CCPA.

Both rules address the right to deletion of personal information, but this rule is a voluntary recommendation specific to certified instructional technology providers in an educational context requiring full deletion (not mere anonymization), whereas the CCPA provision is a binding right applicable to businesses generally.
Both grant a right to delete personal data; Vermont H208 explicitly includes derived data and is a proposed bill, while CCPA is binding and requires directing service providers to delete as well.
Virginia S 85 — Consumer Data Protection Act (Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Virginia H 2250 — Consumer Data Protection Act (Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

instances.notes: Both establish a right to deletion of personal data, but the AIGE rule is a soft-law voluntary guideline framed as a general AI governance principle without enforcement mechanisms, whereas the CCPA/CPRA rule is binding law with specific procedural and business-obligation requirements.

Both provide a right to deletion of personal data, but Uganda's Act limits the trigger to data that is 'no longer necessary' while CCPA's deletion right is broader and includes a service-provider directive obligation.

Both provide a right to request cessation of use or deletion of personal data and cessation of third-party provision, but APPI Art. 35 is triggered by prescribed statutory grounds rather than a broad consumer right, reflecting a meaningfully different threshold and scope.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to direct a business not to sell or share their personal information, including via a user-enabled global privacy control.
rule_text_technical: A consumer has the right, at any time, to direct a business that sells or shares personal information about the consumer to third parties not to sell or share the consumer's personal information; this opt-out may be exercised through a clear and conspicuous link or via a user-enabled global privacy control such as the GPC.

Kentucky H 641 — Mental Health Chatbots (Kentucky) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

New Mexico H 410 — Consumer Info and Data Protection Act (New Mexico) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request that a business correct inaccurate personal information that the business maintains about them.
rule_text_technical: A consumer has the right to request a business that maintains inaccurate personal information about the consumer to correct such inaccurate personal information, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of the processing.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to direct a business to limit the use and disclosure of their sensitive personal information to purposes necessary to perform the requested services or other limited purposes specified in the regulations.
rule_text_technical: A consumer has the right, at any time, to direct a business that collects sensitive personal information to limit its use of that information to that use which is necessary to perform the services or provide the goods reasonably expected by an average consumer, or for other purposes authorized under § 1798.121(a) and implementing regulations.

rule_text: You must not sell or share the personal information of a consumer known to be under 16 years of age without affirmative authorization (opt-in consent) from the minor (ages 13–15) or from a parent/guardian (under 13).
rule_text_technical: A business shall not sell or share the personal information of consumers if the business has actual knowledge that the consumer is less than 16 years of age, unless the consumer, in the case of consumers at least 13 and less than 16, or the consumer's parent or guardian, in the case of consumers less than 13 years of age, has affirmatively authorized the sale or sharing of the consumer's personal information.

rule_text: Sensitive personal information includes government identifiers, account credentials, precise geolocation, contents of communications, genetic data, biometric information processed for identification, health/sex life data, and racial/ethnic origin or religious beliefs.

rule_text: Before filing a private action for statutory damages under applicable data protection law, the claimant must provide the business with 30 days' written notice identifying the allegedly violated provisions.

Both address the obligation to use AI in compliance with laws and with awareness of potential harms, but the new rule is a binding citizen-level obligation specific to legal compliance and awareness of harmful outcomes, whereas the OECD rule is a design-level recommendation for AI actors.

Both articulate multi-principle AI ethics frameworks including human-centricity, fairness, transparency, and accountability, but Thailand's framework is a developing national instrument with six specific named principles, while the OECD rule is an international recommendation with broader scope.

Both recommend that AI deployment respect democratic values and human rights, but Sweden's rule specifically frames public administration as a model actor, while the OECD principle addresses AI system design broadly across all actors.

Both address non-discrimination and fairness in AI, but the OECD rule is broader (rule of law, human rights, democratic values, diversity) whereas this rule focuses narrowly on non-discrimination and fair decisions.

Both require AI systems to comply with existing laws including civil rights and privacy protections, but the Oklahoma bill is a voluntary recommendation while the OECD principle is a broader recommendation covering rule of law and human rights more generally.

Both rules recommend AI development according to ethical principles including fundamental rights and responsible innovation, but this Colombian draft law is a voluntary instrument with broader framing while the OECD rule is more specific about rule of law, human rights, democratic values, and non-discrimination safeguards.

Both address accessibility, fairness, and protection of fundamental rights in AI systems, but the Chilean draft is a voluntary recommendation with specific focus on societal groups, while the OECD rule is a broader recommendation covering rule of law, democratic values, and diversity with safeguards.

Both recommend that developers and designers of systems account for data protection and human rights from the outset, but the GDPR recital focuses specifically on personal data rights whereas the OECD principle is broader in scope.

Both require AI research efforts to address ethical, societal, and safety issues, but this rule specifically mandates a component within sector-focused AI Research Institutes rather than general AI system design principles.

Both require adherence to the OECD AI principles including human-centred values and inclusive growth; Colombia's rule explicitly mandates all five OECD principles as binding national policy rather than a recommendation.

Both recommend considering ethical dimensions when developing and adopting AI, but the Mauritius rule is narrower in scope (focused on Mauritius context) while the OECD rule encompasses rule of law, human rights, democratic values, and diversity with explicit safeguards.

Both require transparency and safeguards in AI systems, but Japan's rule is a binding statutory obligation specifically linking transparency to misuse/crime prevention, while the OECD principle is a broader recommendation covering rule of law, human rights, and democratic values.

rule_text: AI systems should be robust, secure, and safe throughout their lifecycle so that under normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety or security risks (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that, in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety and/or security risks.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).

Both rules address lifecycle-based risk management for AI systems, but the G20 rule explicitly emphasizes a 'systematic' and 'continuous' approach across all phases, while the OECD rule focuses on robustness, security, and safety outcomes; additionally, as a voluntary G20 instrument compared to the OECD binding principles, the obligation level and scope differ.

Both are voluntary instruments requiring safety mechanisms for AI systems, but the Saudi rule specifically mandates fail-safe mechanisms scoped to high-risk applications, whereas the OECD principle addresses robustness, security, and safety broadly across all AI systems throughout their lifecycle.

Both address AI safety under adverse or unintended conditions protecting life, health, property, and environment, but the NIST RMF is a voluntary framework with an operational safety definition, while the OECD rule is a broader robustness/security/safety principle across the full lifecycle.

Both address cybersecurity risk assessment and robustness of AI systems, but this voluntary Canadian code specifically focuses on cybersecurity risk assessment and proportionate mitigation including data-related risks, while the OECD principle is broader, covering robustness, security, and safety across the full AI lifecycle.

Both voluntary instruments call for identifying and understanding AI safety risks, but the Bletchley Declaration specifically focuses on frontier AI and building shared international scientific understanding, whereas the OECD principle addresses robustness and safety across the AI lifecycle more broadly.

instances.citation: Recommendation 2(e) - Reliability, robustness, security and safety
instances.notes: Both recommend that organizations take measures to ensure AI safety, robustness, and cybersecurity risk mitigation, but the Israel policy references 'generally accepted professional risk management standards' as the benchmark while the OECD principle covers the full AI lifecycle under normal and adverse conditions.

Both address robustness and safety of AI systems to prevent societal harm, but this Saudi voluntary guideline focuses specifically on generative AI operating within predetermined specifications, while the OECD rule is a broader binding-adjacent principle covering the full AI lifecycle under various adverse conditions.

Both recommend AI systems be safe and minimize risks throughout their lifecycle, but the Qatar NCSA guideline focuses specifically on human safety assessments whereas the OECD principle encompasses robustness, security, and safety more broadly; both are voluntary instruments.

Both recommend designing AI systems to be safe and prevent harms throughout their lifecycle, but the Japanese guideline specifies concrete harm categories (life, health, property, social infrastructure) and is a voluntary instrument, while the OECD principle is broader in scope covering robustness, security, and safety under various use conditions.

Both voluntary instruments address maintaining awareness of AI failure states and ensuring robustness across the system lifecycle, but the DHS rule specifically targets new failure modes and process redundancy introduced when AI is integrated into safety and incident response systems.

Both are voluntary instruments addressing harm avoidance from AI systems, but Tanzania's rule explicitly enumerates social, cultural, economic, natural, and political harms to individuals and collectives, whereas the OECD rule focuses on robustness, security, and safety across the lifecycle.

Both address safety risks arising from AI systems that evolve or change over their lifecycle, but the EU directive frames this as a binding defectiveness assessment factor for product liability while the OECD principle is a voluntary recommendation about robustness and safety throughout the lifecycle.

Both require AI systems to be safe and prevent harm to individuals and society, but this Bahrain voluntary guideline focuses on physical/psychological harm prevention while the OECD principle also covers robustness, security, and lifecycle considerations under normal use and misuse scenarios.

Both rules call for addressing AI safety across multiple dimensions throughout the lifecycle, but this voluntary Chinese framework specifies distinct risk dimensions (data security, system security, cognitive-domain attacks, real-world threats) not enumerated in the OECD principles.

Both address safety and quality requirements for AI/robotic systems, but this Bahraini proposal is narrower in scope (robots in services, manufacturing, and medical intervention) and framed as a proposed law rather than a binding mandate, whereas the OECD principle applies broadly to all AI systems throughout their lifecycle.

Both address balancing multiple trustworthy AI attributes (robustness, safety, etc.) but NIST AI 100-2 specifically frames this as managing trade-offs among attributes including adversarial robustness in the AML context, whereas the OECD principle is a broader lifecycle safety/robustness requirement.

rule_text: Where technically feasible, mechanisms should be in place to bolster information integrity while ensuring respect for freedom of expression (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Mechanisms should also, where technically feasible, be in place to bolster information integrity while ensuring respect for freedom of expression.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).

Both rules address bolstering information integrity through technical mechanisms (AI-based detection tools), but the UAE guide is a voluntary instrument focused narrowly on deepfake detection tooling, whereas the OECD principle is a broader binding-equivalent recommendation about information integrity and freedom of expression.

Both address information integrity in the context of algorithmically generated/synthetic content, but China's rule imposes specific binding obligations (feature pools, conspicuous labeling) on service providers, whereas the OECD principle is a voluntary, high-level recommendation about mechanisms to bolster information integrity.

Both address mechanisms to preserve information integrity regarding synthetic media, but China's rule is a binding legal obligation requiring specific technical watermarking/labeling measures, whereas the OECD principle is a voluntary recommendation and lacks the specificity of mandatory identifying marks on AI-generated content.

Both recommend mechanisms to support information integrity around synthetic/AI-generated content, but the ASEAN rule specifically targets synthetic media and proposes concrete technical measures (content provenance, digital watermarking), while the OECD rule is broader and framed around freedom of expression; both are voluntary instruments with differing specificity and scope.

Both recommend mechanisms to bolster information integrity (watermarking/provenance vs. general mechanisms), but the G7 rule is a voluntary code targeting AI developers specifically and adds concrete examples like watermarking, while the OECD rule is broader and less technology-specific.

Both are voluntary recommendations addressing AI-generated deceptive/manipulated content and information integrity, but the Bletchley Declaration focuses broadly on frontier AI manipulation risks while the OECD rule specifically ties information integrity to freedom of expression and technical feasibility.

Both are voluntary instruments recommending safeguards for information integrity against AI-generated false content, but the Saudi guideline is narrower in scope (government communications only) and explicitly names misinformation, hallucinations, and deepfakes, while the OECD principle is broader and also addresses freedom of expression.

Both are voluntary/recommendation-level instruments addressing synthetic media integrity risks in AI adoption, but the Qatar NCSA rule is narrower and more operationally focused on organizational risk management of deepfakes, while the OECD rule more broadly addresses information integrity and freedom of expression.

Both recommend frameworks to protect information integrity against misuse of technology, but this AU rule specifically targets Member State legal frameworks and digital platforms in an African context, while the OECD rule is a broader voluntary principle focused on balancing information integrity with freedom of expression.

Both address mechanisms to support information integrity in the context of AI-generated/synthetic media, but the India MeitY advisory specifically targets software/platforms that permit synthetic creation of text, audio, visual, or audiovisual content and is a non-binding advisory note, whereas the OECD principle is a broader voluntary recommendation about bolstering information integrity while respecting freedom of expression.

Both address protecting information integrity and democratic values in AI contexts, but Uruguay's strategy explicitly names electoral integrity and public debate, while the OECD principle focuses on freedom of expression; both are soft-law/voluntary instruments with comparable obligation levels.

Both are soft-law recommendations against AI-generated misinformation/misleading content, but the Qatar rule is narrower (focused on publishing misleading AI-generated content) while the OECD rule addresses broader information integrity with a freedom-of-expression carve-out.

Both address protecting information integrity involving synthetic/AI media, but this NC rule focuses specifically on detecting and deterring false attribution of synthetic media to public officials and government entities, while the OECD principle is a broader recommendation about bolstering information integrity generally.

rule_text: You should cooperate with other actors—including suppliers, users, and stakeholders—to manage AI risks effectively (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: AI actors should work with other actors, including suppliers, users, and stakeholders, to manage risks effectively.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).

Both address accountability and cooperative responsibility among AI actors for managing AI risks and trustworthy AI principles, but the G20 rule focuses more explicitly on role-based accountability while the OECD rule emphasizes inter-actor cooperation; both are voluntary instruments.

Both rules address managing relationships and risks associated with third-party AI actors, but the IOSCO rule is more specific, requiring firms to actively monitor and manage third-party AI/ML providers in a financial services regulatory context.

Both recommend multi-stakeholder cooperation in AI governance including government, private sector, and end users, but the Benin rule explicitly extends participation to design, implementation, and ongoing monitoring phases, whereas the OECD rule focuses on risk management cooperation.

Both require collecting and integrating external feedback to manage AI risks, but the OECD rule broadly recommends cooperation with external actors, while NIST GOVERN 5.1 specifies organizational policies and practices for systematically collecting, prioritizing, and integrating external feedback.

Both recommend cooperation and information sharing among actors in the AI ecosystem to manage risks, but this Canadian voluntary code specifically targets complementary firms and best practice sharing, while the OECD principle is broader in scope and actor coverage.

Both are voluntary instruments encouraging cooperation with external actors to manage AI risks, but the G7 rule specifically focuses on facilitating third-party and user discovery and reporting of vulnerabilities after deployment, which is more specific than the OECD's general cooperation recommendation.

Both address multi-stakeholder cooperation on AI governance values including transparency, accountability, and safety, but the Bletchley Declaration explicitly lists a broader cluster of principles (human rights, explainability, fairness, human oversight) and is a voluntary inter-governmental declaration rather than an OECD recommendation.

Both recommend stakeholder engagement and cooperation throughout the AI lifecycle, but the GCC rule specifies advance consultation and post-launch engagement, while the OECD rule focuses on cooperating with other actors to manage AI risks.

Both require cooperation with suppliers and other actors to manage AI risks; ISO 42001 Annex A.10.3 requires establishing formal processes to ensure supplier alignment with the organization's AI approach, which is more operationally specific than the OECD recommendation.

Both address shared responsibility among AI stakeholders for managing outcomes, but this Saudi guideline is voluntary and specifically emphasizes ethical and legal accountability for generative AI data handling, while the OECD principle focuses on cooperative risk management more broadly.

Both rules require cooperation among actors to support AI governance, but the Abu Dhabi law is a binding statutory obligation specifically requiring concerned entities to provide information, data, and documents to the AIATC regulator, whereas the OECD principle is a voluntary recommendation for multi-stakeholder risk cooperation.

Both recommend cooperation with external actors to promote responsible AI, but the Tanzania guideline specifically recommends partnering with ethical AI providers who prioritize diversity, inclusion, and transparency, which is more prescriptive about partner selection criteria.

Both recommend collaboration with third parties to promote responsible AI practices, but this rule specifically addresses joint educational activities and events with third parties to promote GAI risk management best practices, while the OECD rule focuses broadly on cooperating with other actors to manage AI risks effectively.

Both recommend that AI actors cooperate with other stakeholders to ensure appropriate and responsible AI use, but the OECD rule covers broader multi-actor cooperation for risk management while the Oman rule focuses specifically on provider-deployer engagement.

Both promote multi-stakeholder public engagement on AI questions, but Art. 19 is a treaty obligation on state parties to enable public discussion and multistakeholder consultation, while the OECD rule is a voluntary cooperation recommendation directed at AI actors.

Both call for multi-stakeholder cooperation in AI governance, but this rule adds the requirements of universality, networked structure, and adaptive collaboration, going beyond the OECD's narrower risk-management cooperation recommendation.

Both recommend cooperation among AI ecosystem stakeholders to manage AI risks, but the new rule is specifically targeted at security knowledge-sharing on adversarial tactics and techniques within the ASEAN regional context for Gen AI.

Both recommend multi-stakeholder cooperation in AI governance including government, industry, and civil society, but the ASEAN rule is a voluntary regional strategy with an explicit emphasis on open discussion forums, while the OECD rule is a binding-leaning principle focused on risk management cooperation.

Both recommend proactive and continuous measures to protect individuals from AI-related harms, but this rule is a state-level soft-law bill recommendation explicitly covering communities, while the OECD principle focuses on cooperative risk management among actors.

Both address cooperative engagement with external stakeholders for responsible AI, but this SC resolution focuses specifically on university/research/nonprofit partnerships for ethical AI development, while the OECD principle broadly covers multi-actor risk cooperation; additionally, this is a non-binding whereas clause.

Both require cooperation among AI value chain actors to manage AI-related responsibilities, but the OECD rule addresses risk management broadly while this voluntary Code of Practice specifically targets cooperation for marking and labelling of AI-generated content.

Both require outreach and cooperation with diverse stakeholders including civil society, but this rule specifically mandates outreach to civil rights and disability organizations as part of the National AI Initiative.

Both recommend advocating for responsible AI practices through cooperative agreements, but Malaysia's rule specifically targets contractual clauses while the OECD principle addresses broader stakeholder risk management cooperation.

Both address due diligence and oversight to manage AI impacts on human rights and rule of law through cooperation among actors; UNESCO's scope explicitly includes human rights and international law while the OECD rule focuses on cooperative risk management.

rule_text: Governments should facilitate public and private investment in research and development—including long-horizon basic research and interdisciplinary work addressing technical, social, legal, and ethical issues—to spur innovation in trustworthy AI (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Governments should facilitate public and private investment in research and development to spur innovation in trustworthy AI, evaluating sustained public funding and stimulating private sector investment in research, development, and open science—particularly interdisciplinary initiatives addressing both technical challenges and AI-related social, legal and ethical implications and policy issues.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).

The G20 text is a near-verbatim adoption of the OECD Recommendation 2.1 on public and private investment in R&D for trustworthy AI, consistent with the G20's explicit endorsement of the OECD AI Principles.

Both address government-level encouragement of AI adoption and investment, but Qatar's rule specifically targets financial incentives for local businesses and countering labor substitution, whereas the OECD rule broadly covers public and private R&D investment.

Both address institutionalizing AI research and strategy execution at the national level, but the NCAI is a formally designated government center for AI execution and research, whereas the OECD recommendation is a voluntary call for governments to facilitate investment in R&D more broadly.

Both concern government funding of AI research, but this rule is a binding statutory mandate for a specific competitive grant program for National AI Research Institutes, whereas the OECD rule is a non-binding recommendation to facilitate public and private R&D investment broadly.

Both encourage integrating AI into national development and investment frameworks, but the UN resolution focuses on incorporating AI into national development plans in the context of developing countries, while the OECD rule focuses on R&D investment broadly.

Both rules concern fostering public-private collaboration to advance AI, but the NJ rule is a binding tax-credit eligibility requirement mandating university partnerships, while the OECD rule is a non-binding government recommendation to facilitate investment in AI R&D broadly.

Both encourage government-led AI investment and development across economic sectors; Nigeria's rule specifies 'lighthouse projects' in named sectors to showcase feasibility, differing in specificity and voluntary framing.

Both recommend government/institutional support for AI research capabilities, but the Algerian rule is narrowly focused on universities and research centers while the OECD rule broadly covers public and private R&D investment.

Both call for public investment in AI R&D, but the OAS rule specifically emphasizes local and regional innovation in a development context as a voluntary recommendation, while the OECD rule addresses both public and private investment including long-horizon basic research.

Both recommend government investment in AI education, research and workforce development, but OECD's rule emphasizes R&D investment broadly while Namibia's targets curriculum integration at school/university level and training for government officials.

Both recommend government investment in AI research infrastructure, but the Philippine rule is more specific in mandating a quantified 26-fold HPC increase by 2028 with global connectivity, whereas the OECD recommendation is a general facilitation of public and private R&D investment.

Both recommend government investment in AI R&D to foster innovation, but Nepal's rule adds a domestic ecosystem focus tailored to national needs, and is a voluntary strategy rather than a binding OECD recommendation.

Both require governments to actively promote and lead AI development and deployment, but the Japan rule specifically emphasizes government as a direct implementer providing demonstration opportunities, while the OECD rule focuses on facilitating investment in R&D broadly.

Both recommend government support for AI development and investment, but the Morocco rule specifically targets AI companies, startups in high value-added sectors, and international stakeholder attraction, whereas the OECD rule focuses on R&D investment more broadly.

Both address government/institutional support for workforce development and upskilling in emerging technologies including AI, but the Hawaii rule is narrowly focused on content creators in the film/creative industries via a state Film Commission, whereas the OECD rule broadly recommends government investment in AI R&D and education across all sectors.
Both require governments to facilitate public and private investment in AI R&D&I, with CONPES 3.1 adding sectoral focus across different contexts.

Both require R&D institutions to conduct AI research and disseminate results, but the OECD rule is addressed to governments facilitating investment while Japan's Art. 6(1) directly obligates R&D institutions themselves.

rule_text: Governments should foster the development of and access to an inclusive, dynamic, sustainable, and interoperable digital ecosystem for trustworthy AI, including data, technologies, computational and connectivity infrastructure, and knowledge-sharing mechanisms, and should consider promoting data trusts to enable safe, fair, legal, and ethical data sharing (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Governments should foster the development of, and access to, an inclusive, dynamic, sustainable, and interoperable digital ecosystem for trustworthy AI, encompassing data, AI technologies, computational and connectivity infrastructure, and mechanisms for sharing AI knowledge, and should consider promoting data trusts and similar mechanisms to support safe, fair, legal, and ethical data sharing.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).
The G20 text mirrors the OECD Recommendation 2.2 on fostering a digital ecosystem for trustworthy AI, reflecting direct adoption of the OECD language by the G20.

Both recommend developing digital/computing infrastructure for AI, but Qatar's rule specifically emphasizes resilience of computing and connectivity infrastructure, while the OECD rule focuses on an inclusive and interoperable digital ecosystem.

Both address building a digital/data ecosystem to support AI, but the Shenzhen rule is city-specific and focuses on public data resource opening from government agencies, whereas the OECD rule is a broad governmental recommendation for an inclusive, interoperable digital ecosystem.

Both address government investment in digital/AI infrastructure and ecosystem enablement, but the Ethiopian rule is more specific to physical computing infrastructure (National Computing Grid near GERD) with subsidised access, whereas the OECD rule broadly covers digital ecosystem development including interoperability and trustworthy AI.

Chile's focus on accelerating connectivity infrastructure including fiber optic and 5G relates to OECD's recommendation on fostering an interoperable digital ecosystem, but Chile's rule is more specific to physical infrastructure deployment and is a voluntary strategy recommendation.

Both call for a fair, open, and inclusive environment for AI development and deployment, but the UN resolution frames this as a cross-border business environment recommendation across the AI lifecycle, while the OECD rule focuses on a digital ecosystem for trustworthy AI.

Both promote multi-stakeholder collaboration (academia, business, public sector) to foster AI innovation, but Romania's rule is a soft-law strategy recommendation focused on national investment while the OECD rule is a broader binding recommendation about a digital ecosystem.

Both address fostering AI infrastructure and digital ecosystem access, but Nigeria's rule is more specific about national HPC centres and researcher access, while the OECD rule is broader and binding in framing.

Both address fostering digital/data infrastructure for AI development, but the OAS rule specifically focuses on scalable public digital infrastructures as digital transformation drivers, while the OECD rule covers a broader interoperable digital ecosystem.

Both address fostering digital/AI infrastructure and data ecosystems, but OECD's rule is broader and government-facing across member states while Namibia's is a country-specific soft law recommendation focused on connectivity and data center development.

Both promote conditions for AI innovation and an inclusive ecosystem, but the Paris statement adds a specific concern about avoiding market concentration and supporting industrial recovery, which goes beyond the OECD's interoperability and access focus.

instances.citation: Priority 1: Central AI capacity — Common infrastructure
instances.notes: Both rules address the need for shared, interoperable digital and computing infrastructure to support AI deployment, but Canada's rule is specifically scoped to federal government organizations requiring secure, scalable HPC and cloud infrastructure, whereas the OECD recommendation is a broader government policy directive toward an inclusive AI ecosystem.

Both address building government/institutional AI capacity and digital ecosystem development, but the ASEAN rule is a voluntary recommendation focused specifically on public-sector skills across member states, whereas the OECD rule is broader and covers private sector and interoperability.

Both address interoperability and cooperation among entities on AI initiatives including infrastructure sharing, but the Bahrain rule is narrower in scope (government entities only) and voluntary, whereas the OECD rule targets governments fostering broader digital ecosystems.

Both recommend frameworks to foster AI integration with digital ecosystems for inclusive outcomes, but this rule is specific to integrating AI with Digital Public Infrastructure in the financial sector context, whereas the OECD rule is a general cross-sector recommendation.

Both call for developing a digital ecosystem for trustworthy AI including infrastructure, data governance, and ethical adoption, but Nepal's rule additionally specifies public digital platforms and is a voluntary national strategy rather than an OECD binding recommendation.

instances.citation: Axis 1 — Digitalization of Public Services, Lever: Methodology & Tools
instances.notes: Both address fostering a digital ecosystem through shared/interoperable platforms, but the Morocco rule specifies concrete tools (e-Id, e-signature, interoperability platforms) for public administrations, whereas the OECD rule is broader and covers the private sector as well.

instances.citation: Pillar 2: Hardware Localization and Manufacturing - National Public Digital Infrastructure
instances.notes: Both recommend establishing shared digital infrastructure for data sharing and AI deployment, but Zimbabwe's rule is more specific to a national public digital infrastructure for government service delivery while the OECD rule addresses a broader interoperable digital ecosystem.
Both address fostering digital/connectivity ecosystems for AI, but CONPES 2.1 specifically targets national and regional Internet connectivity strengthening for the AI ecosystem.

Both recommend adopting AI and new technologies for improved public services, but the Mauritius rule is more narrowly focused on public service delivery rather than the broader digital ecosystem concept in the OECD recommendation.

Art. 14 requires the national government to secure and train AI human resources in cooperation with local governments, R&D institutions, and businesses, which overlaps with the OECD's digital ecosystem recommendation but is more specifically focused on workforce development.

rule_text: Policymakers should prioritise SME access to data, AI technologies, connectivity, computing capacity, and cloud platforms to foster digital entrepreneurship and innovation (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Policymakers should prioritize small and medium-sized enterprise access to data, AI technologies, connectivity, computing capacity, and cloud platforms to foster digital entrepreneurship and innovation.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).

Both rules prioritize local/domestic actors in AI development and deployment, but the Benin rule is a soft-law recommendation specifically prioritizing local companies in AI solution scaling, while the OECD rule focuses on SME access to data and technologies for digital entrepreneurship.

Both address supporting AI entrepreneurship and SME/start-up ecosystems, but the ASEAN rule is region-specific and voluntary, while the OECD rule focuses on SME access to data, technology, and computing capacity.

Both address expanding AI access to SMEs and regional actors, but the Philippine rule specifically assigns DOST regional offices as delivery agents for MSMEs and local industries, while the OECD recommendation is a general policy directive for policymakers.

Both address enabling smaller entities' access to AI, but this rule focuses on financial sector incentives and infrastructure from the RBI specifically for smaller regulated entities including co-operatives, while the OECD rule is a broader cross-sector SME access recommendation.

Both address prioritising SME access to AI infrastructure, but Malta's rule is a binding legal obligation granting SMEs and start-ups a right to priority access to the national AI regulatory sandbox, whereas the OECD provision is a non-binding policy recommendation about broader digital access.

Both address SME access to AI technologies and fostering digital entrepreneurship, but the OECD rule is a broad international recommendation while this Connecticut bill assigns a specific state agency (DECD) to develop a targeted small business AI program, making the scope and obligation level meaningfully different.

Both address prioritizing underrepresented or smaller entities in AI development, but the NJ rule focuses on underrepresented emerging AI businesses while the OECD rule focuses on SME access to data and technology.

Both address priority access for smaller enterprises to AI-related resources and ecosystems, but Chile's rule focuses specifically on regulatory sandbox access and promotion for SMEs, while the OECD recommendation addresses broader data, technology, and infrastructure access; Chile's rule is also from a voluntary/draft instrument.
Both address facilitating access to AI innovation instruments for companies, but CONPES 3.4 specifically targets Colombian companies adapting AI-based solutions.

rule_text: Governments should ensure policy and regulatory frameworks are appropriate to foster innovation and deployment of trustworthy AI while ensuring effective protection of the public interest, including by reviewing and adapting frameworks and assessment mechanisms as they apply to AI systems (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Governments should ensure that policy and regulatory frameworks are appropriate to foster innovation and the deployment of trustworthy AI, while ensuring effective protection of the public interest; governments must review and adapt, as appropriate, their policy and regulatory frameworks and assessment mechanisms as they apply to AI systems to encourage innovation and competition for trustworthy AI.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).
The G20 text mirrors the OECD Recommendation 2.3 on reviewing and adapting policy and regulatory frameworks to encourage innovation while ensuring safety, reflecting direct adoption.

Both address building regulatory and incentive frameworks conducive to AI-driven business ecosystems, but Qatar's rule emphasizes attractiveness for incorporation while the OECD rule focuses on balancing innovation with effective protection.

Both rules address interagency or governmental coordination to advance AI implementation principles, but the EO is a voluntary/soft-law instrument focused on U.S. federal agency participation in interagency bodies, while the OECD rule is a broader policy recommendation about regulatory frameworks for trustworthy AI.

Both require developing a legal/regulatory framework for AI, but Tajikistan specifically mandates drafting a dedicated AI law defining state regulation principles, which is more concrete and binding than the OECD's general recommendation to ensure appropriate policy and regulatory frameworks.

Both address strengthening AI policy and regulatory frameworks aligned with global standards, but Rwanda's rule is a voluntary national policy recommendation focused on regulatory capacity-building, whereas the OECD rule is a broader intergovernmental recommendation for fostering innovation while ensuring effectiveness.

Both address ensuring policy and regulatory frameworks remain fit for purpose for AI, but the OECD rule is a general governance principle while Tunisia's is a specific recommendation to review and update existing legislation on data protection, cybersecurity, and digital economy.

Both address sector-specific regulatory frameworks for AI, but the Israel rule focuses on empowering existing sectoral regulators to assess concrete needs, while the OECD recommendation speaks more broadly to governments ensuring regulatory frameworks foster innovation and trustworthy AI; Israel's is a soft-law recommendation vs. OECD's non-binding principle.

Chile's recommendation to design an agile institutional framework for responsible AI development mirrors OECD's recommendation for appropriate policy and regulatory frameworks, but Chile's rule is a voluntary national strategy recommendation rather than a binding government obligation.

Both call for appropriate regulatory/policy frameworks for AI, but the WHO guidance is narrower (healthcare/LMMs specifically) and is a soft-law recommendation rather than a binding government obligation.

Both concern establishing a regulatory framework for AI, but the OECD rule is a recommendation to governments about appropriate policy and regulatory frameworks for trustworthy AI, while the Russian decree frames it as a binding primary state objective with no detail on content or approach.

Both address appropriate regulatory frameworks for AI oversight and compliance, but the AU rule specifically requires independent oversight institutions with enforcement and redress mechanisms, while the OECD rule more broadly recommends appropriate policy and regulatory frameworks for trustworthy AI; the AU instrument is also voluntary/soft law like the OECD principles.

Both address enabling fair competition and an innovation environment for AI, but the UN resolution also promotes digital public goods, while the OECD rule focuses on policy and regulatory frameworks for innovation and trustworthy AI deployment.

Both call for multi-stakeholder public engagement in AI governance frameworks, but the CoE Convention focuses specifically on public discussion of important AI questions while the OECD recommendation addresses broader policy and regulatory framework agility.

Both call for national policy/regulatory frameworks to address AI risks and foster trustworthy AI, but the Seoul declaration is a non-binding political commitment specifically focused on AI safety frameworks, while the OECD recommendation is broader and covers innovation and deployment.

Both call for appropriate regulatory frameworks to foster trustworthy AI innovation, but Romania's rule is a voluntary strategy recommendation specifically tied to EU AI Act alignment, while the OECD rule is a binding government recommendation with broader scope.

Both address sector-specific AI policy guidance to foster deployment; Nigeria's rule specifies publishing sector-specific roadmaps, while the OECD rule is a broader principle about appropriate regulatory frameworks.

Both call for appropriate governance/regulatory frameworks for trustworthy AI, but the Moldova White Paper is a voluntary soft-law instrument focused on establishing a governance framework with resilient infrastructure, while the OECD rule is a binding recommendation emphasizing innovation and effective protection.

Both rules call for developing appropriate AI policy and regulatory frameworks, but Zambia's rule is a specific implementation action (finalizing a National AI Policy with consultations and approval) while the OECD rule is a broader governance principle about fostering innovation while ensuring effective protection.

Both recommend developing legal, regulatory, and infrastructure foundations for AI, but the Algerian rule is specific to domestic authorities and enabling environment while the OECD rule addresses broader policy and regulatory frameworks for trustworthy AI.

Both call for appropriate regulatory frameworks covering AI lifecycle, but the OAS rule specifically emphasizes updating data governance/privacy frameworks; as soft law matching a binding recommendation, 'similar' is appropriate.

Both recommend reviewing and adapting legal and regulatory frameworks to address AI-specific issues and ensure trustworthy deployment, but Namibia's rule is a country-specific soft law recommendation explicitly listing data protection, liability, and sector-specific uses.

Both address balancing innovation with public interest and mitigating AI risks in regulatory frameworks, but the OECD rule is a binding international recommendation while this is a state-level voluntary task force mandate with narrower geographic scope.

Both call for periodic review of policy and regulatory frameworks to enable AI innovation while addressing risks, but this rule is specific to financial sector regulators in India, whereas the OECD rule is a general government-level recommendation.

Both require appropriate legal/regulatory frameworks for AI development, but China's rule is narrower and more prescriptive, mandating refinement of specific AI-related laws, regulations, and ethics codes, whereas the OECD recommendation broadly fosters innovation and trustworthy AI deployment.

Both call for governance/regulatory frameworks to ensure trustworthy and accountable AI, but Bhutan's rule is a soft-law recommendation focused on establishing comprehensive regulatory and monitoring frameworks for transparency, fairness, and accountability, while the OECD rule is a broader policy principle about fostering innovation alongside effective protections.

instances.citation: India AI Governance Guidelines 2025, Regulatory Approach
instances.notes: Both recommend that existing regulatory frameworks be used before introducing new AI-specific rules, but the OECD rule focuses on ensuring innovation and effective protection rather than explicitly preferring existing legislation over new AI-specific laws; this is a voluntary guideline matching a binding-leaning recommendation with meaningful framing differences.

instances.citation: Axis 1 — Digitalization of Public Services, Lever: Regulation
instances.notes: Both call for appropriate policy and regulatory frameworks to support digital/AI deployment, but the Morocco rule focuses specifically on public administration digitization legal frameworks, while the OECD rule is broader and binding in framing.

Both call for government policy frameworks addressing trustworthy/fair AI, but the Malaysia AIGE rule specifically focuses on fairness, unbiased data collection, and algorithmic decision-making guidelines, whereas the OECD recommendation addresses broader innovation-enabling policy and regulatory frameworks.

rule_text: Governments should promote an agile policy environment supporting the transition from R&D to deployment, including the use of controlled testing environments (e.g., regulatory sandboxes) where AI systems can be evaluated and scaled (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Governments should promote an agile policy environment that supports transitioning from the research and development stage to the deployment and operation stage, including using controlled testing environments where AI systems can be evaluated and scaled appropriately.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).
The G20 text closely follows the OECD's agile policy environment recommendation supporting R&D-to-deployment transition, consistent with direct endorsement of OECD principles.

Both support the use of controlled testing environments for AI experimentation, but the Shenzhen rule establishes a formal city-level 'innovation testing zone' mechanism with flexible regulatory application, while the OECD rule is a non-binding governmental recommendation to promote agile policy environments.

Both rules address establishing controlled testing environments for AI innovation, but the Benin rule is a soft-law recommendation tied to specific domestic legal articles, while the OECD rule is a broader policy recommendation about agile regulatory environments including sandboxes.

Both recommend the use of regulatory sandboxes as controlled testing environments for AI development and deployment, but Rwanda's rule is a specific national policy activity while the OECD rule is a broader intergovernmental recommendation for agile policy environments supporting R&D-to-deployment transition.

Both recommend controlled testing environments (sandboxes) to support AI innovation, but the OECD rule is a broader policy agility principle while Tunisia's is a specific recommendation for AI-focused regulatory sandboxes for enterprises; both are voluntary instruments.

Both address regulatory sandboxes/controlled testing environments for AI, but AESIA's mandate is a binding legal obligation focused on user protection and anti-discrimination, while the OECD recommendation is a voluntary policy guidance for governments to promote agile environments.

Both establish controlled testing environments (sandboxes) for AI, but the Beijing rule is a binding local regulation creating a specific sandbox in Zhongguancun for generative AI companies, while the OECD recommendation broadly encourages agile policy environments and controlled testing without binding force or sector specificity.

Both recommend incremental, agile regulatory development including use of sandboxes and pilot/experimental tools for AI, but the Israel rule is a domestic soft-law recommendation while the OECD rule is a non-binding international principle with slightly different framing around R&D-to-deployment transition.

Both promote mechanisms to bridge AI research and deployment through partnerships; Nigeria's rule specifies a named tripartite program linking research institutions, businesses, and government, whereas the OECD rule is broader and includes controlled testing environments.

Both address controlled testing environments (sandboxes) for AI development, but the CoE Convention frames it as a party-level obligation in a binding treaty context while the OECD rule is a government recommendation with broader policy agility framing.

rule_text: Governments should work with stakeholders to promote responsible use of AI at work to enhance worker safety, job and public service quality, and to ensure benefits from AI are broadly and fairly shared (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Governments must work closely with stakeholders to promote the responsible use of AI at work, to enhance the safety of workers, the quality of jobs and of public services, to foster entrepreneurship and productivity, and aim to ensure that the benefits from AI are broadly and fairly shared.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).

Both rules address worker protections in the context of AI/algorithmic systems at work, but China's provision is a binding, specific obligation targeting gig-economy platform operators to protect wages and rest rights, whereas the OECD rule is a non-binding government-level recommendation promoting responsible AI use for worker safety and job quality more broadly.

Both rules address worker safety in AI-enabled workplaces, but the Tajikistan rule is narrower (limited to industrial enterprises) and more directly prescriptive about safe conditions, whereas the OECD principle broadly promotes responsible AI use at work including job quality and public services.

Both address responsible AI use in employment contexts, but this ASEAN voluntary rule focuses specifically on fairness assessments in HR decision-making (recruitment, performance, termination) and candidate/employee notification, while the OECD rule broadly addresses worker safety and job quality; additionally, the ASEAN instrument is non-binding whereas the OECD recommendation is a governmental commitment.

Both address AI in employment contexts, but the new rule from Real Decreto 817/2023 takes a binding regulatory approach by classifying recruitment, performance monitoring, and employment-decision AI systems as high-risk, whereas the OECD rule is a voluntary recommendation promoting responsible AI use at work without imposing classification or compliance obligations.

Both address worker education and responsible AI use in the workplace, but this rule is a voluntary guideline focused specifically on data governance and cybersecurity training workshops, while the OECD principle is a broader government-level recommendation on worker safety and job quality.

Both rules address worker engagement with AI in the workplace, but the Chile policy focuses specifically on mechanisms for reflection and capturing worker expectations/concerns, while the OECD rule emphasizes responsible use, safety, and job quality through stakeholder collaboration; additionally, both are soft law instruments but differ in scope and framing.

Both address governmental/institutional attention to AI's impact on the workforce, but the WV rule is narrower (an assessment mandate by a task force) and more focused on employment levels and worker deployment, while the OECD rule is broader, covering worker safety, job quality, and stakeholder engagement; additionally, the WV rule is a soft-law/voluntary instrument versus the OECD non-binding recommendation, and both differ meaningfully in scope and framing.

Both address stakeholder/employee consultation on AI deployment in work contexts, but the Argentine rule specifies a mandatory consultation obligation for public administration bodies under an executive decree, while the OECD principle is a broader government-level recommendation to work with stakeholders on responsible AI at work.

Both instruments recommend that AI deployment support positive labour market outcomes and worker wellbeing, but this is a voluntary summit statement with broad aspirational framing, while the OECD rule is a more structured recommendation addressing responsible use, safety, and public service quality specifically.

instances.citation: Priority 3: Talent and training — Workforce consultation
instances.notes: Both address preparing workers for AI-driven changes through government-stakeholder collaboration, but Canada's rule specifically focuses on bargaining agents and retraining for public servants, while the OECD principle is broader in scope covering worker safety, job quality, and public services; additionally, the new rule is a soft-law strategy recommendation rather than a binding instrument.

Both address government-level oversight of AI's impact on labor and employment, but the Maryland rule is a binding statutory workgroup mandate to monitor and recommend on deployer/developer obligations covering labor, employment, and privacy, whereas the OECD rule is a non-binding recommendation for governments to promote responsible AI use at work more broadly.

Both address safe and responsible AI use at work with attention to worker wellbeing, but the Italian law is a binding statutory obligation with explicit requirements on transparency, human dignity, and data confidentiality, whereas the OECD rule is a voluntary government recommendation.

Both address responsible AI use in workplaces through stakeholder/worker engagement, but the Australian plan specifically emphasises meaningful consultation in the design phase of AI systems, while the OECD principle is broader in scope covering safety, job quality, and public services.

Both address government responsibility to promote workforce adaptation to AI by bridging skills gaps and ensuring labor participation, but Taiwan's rule is a binding statutory mandate with explicit economic security and decent work obligations, whereas the OECD rule is a non-binding recommendation to governments to work with stakeholders on responsible AI at work.

Both address worker training and responsible AI use at work, but the Singapore guideline is narrower and more operational (focusing on agentic AI-specific employee education such as prompting and agent capabilities), while the OECD recommendation is broader and binding on governments rather than organizations.

Both address workforce development, education, and research in the context of AI, but the Illinois rule is a study mandate proposing policy changes while the OECD rule is a broader government stakeholder engagement recommendation.

Both recommend training workers in responsible and productive use of AI tools, but the Puerto Rico rule is a voluntary programmatic component of a specific retraining program while the OECD recommendation is a broader government-stakeholder principle covering workplace safety and job quality.

rule_text: Governments should encourage the development and use of internationally comparable indicators measuring AI research, development, and deployment to assess implementation progress (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Governments should encourage development and use of internationally comparable indicators measuring AI research, development, and deployment, establishing evidence to evaluate principle implementation progress.

first_instance.law_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in OECD AI Principles (2019/2024) (OECD, 2019-05-22).
The G20 text closely mirrors the OECD Recommendation 2.5 on developing and using internationally comparable metrics for AI research, development, and deployment, reflecting direct adoption.

Both involve benchmarking AI competitiveness through indicators/indices, but Rwanda's rule specifically calls for international partnerships and an annual 'AI Readiness Index', while the OECD rule focuses on internationally comparable indicators for R&D and deployment assessment.

Both address monitoring and information/data gaps in AI, but the FSB rule is finance-sector specific and focuses on cross-jurisdictional coordination among standard-setting bodies and national authorities, while the OECD rule concerns internationally comparable indicators for AI R&D broadly.

Both rules call for developing indicators to measure and monitor AI progress, but the Uruguay rule focuses specifically on evaluating continuous improvement of public-sector processes incorporating AI, while the OECD rule addresses internationally comparable indicators for AI research, development, and deployment more broadly.

Both address monitoring AI development progress, but the OECD rule focuses on internationally comparable indicators for R&D and deployment while the Algerian rule specifically recommends a National AI Observatory to monitor strategy implementation.

Both call for tracking/measuring AI development metrics, but Sweden's rule assigns annual oversight responsibility to specific named agencies (DIGG and PTS), while the OECD recommendation is a broader government-level encouragement to develop internationally comparable AI indicators.

rule_text: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety risks under conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that, in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety risk.

first_instance.law_name: G20 AI Principles (Osaka, June 2019)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in G20 AI Principles (Osaka) (G20, 2019-06-09).

Both address security and risk management for AI systems, but the BCBS rule is domain-specific to banking cybersecurity risks (training datasets, third-party interconnectivity, cloud platforms) while the G20 rule broadly covers safety and security across the AI lifecycle.

Both rules require AI systems to be safe and secure across their deployment, but the Tajikistan rule specifically emphasizes information security, human dignity, state security, and socio-economic sectors, reflecting a broader and more sovereignty-oriented framing than the G20 safety/robustness standard.

Both require AI systems to be secure and robust throughout their lifecycle, but the Shenzhen rule is a binding legal obligation with specific technical requirements (adversarial attacks, data poisoning, incident reporting) whereas the G20 rule is a non-binding principle at a higher level of generality.

Both address operational robustness and risk mitigation for AI systems; the new rule is more operationally specific, requiring fallback plans, threshold-setting, and insurance, while the existing rule sets a general safety and robustness standard across the lifecycle.

Both address security and resilience of AI systems, but the G20 rule covers the full lifecycle and safety broadly, while this NIST rule focuses specifically on confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA triad) protection mechanisms.

Both address security and robustness of AI systems, but the ASEAN rule is more specific to cybersecurity measures calibrated by data sensitivity, while the G20 rule covers broader safety and security across the lifecycle.

Both rules address reliability and continuity of AI service delivery, but this rule is a binding obligation specific to generative AI service providers ensuring stable and sustained services, whereas the G20 rule is a non-binding principle covering AI system robustness and safety more broadly across the lifecycle.

Both are voluntary instruments addressing security and safety of AI systems throughout their lifecycle, but the G7 rule is more specific in enumerating physical security, cybersecurity, and insider threat controls, while the G20 rule addresses robustness and safety more broadly.

Both address security and robustness of AI systems throughout their lifecycle, but the GCC rule specifically focuses on security protection of data, training/operation models, and infrastructure against attacks, while the G20 rule is broader about safety and security.

Both require AI systems to be robust, secure, and accurate throughout their lifecycle, but the Spain sandbox rule adds a specific cybersecurity dimension and is a binding sandbox obligation rather than a G20 non-binding principle.

Both require AI systems to meet high standards of safety and security throughout their lifecycle, but the AU rule is a regional soft-law recommendation specific to Africa with additional emphasis on timely identification and isolation of failures.

Both address security of AI systems, but this rule specifically focuses on cybersecurity measures against unauthorized access and adversarial attacks, while the G20 rule addresses broader robustness, safety, and security throughout the lifecycle.

Both address safety and security throughout the AI lifecycle, but this DHS rule specifically emphasizes secure-by-design practices from design through deployment in critical infrastructure contexts, whereas the G20 rule is a broader robustness and safety principle.

Both require care to protect against AI-related risks, but the Colorado rule is a binding legal duty of care on developers/modifiers of high-risk AI systems specifically, while the G20 principle is a voluntary recommendation covering all AI actors across the full lifecycle.

instances.citation: White Paper, Key Requirements for AI (4)
instances.notes: Both address safety and security of AI systems, but the G20 rule covers the full lifecycle and unreasonable safety risks broadly, while this rule focuses narrowly on cybersecurity protection; both are soft law but differ in scope.

Both address safety and security of AI systems throughout their lifecycle, but the Namibia strategy is a voluntary soft-law instrument whereas the G20 principle addresses robustness, safety, and security with a focus on not posing unreasonable safety risks.

Both require AI systems to be safe and reliable throughout their lifecycle with safeguards against harm, but Oman's rule is framed as a binding obligation ('must') while the G20 principle is a recommendation, and Oman's text explicitly mentions testing.

Both require AI systems to be safe and prevent harm throughout their lifecycle, but this is a voluntary government policy recommendation rather than a binding G20 principle, and focuses on physical/psychological harm to individuals or society.

Both require AI systems to be robust, secure, and safe, but the Peru rule is a binding obligation specifically targeting high-risk AI systems with explicit cybersecurity requirements, while the G20 rule is a non-binding recommendation applicable across the full AI lifecycle without risk-tiering.
