rule_text: These minor-protection rules apply to services established in France or outside the EU, and may be applied to services established in another EU Member State after the Directive 2000/31/EC procedure.
rule_text_technical: Articles 10 and 10-1 apply to services established in France or outside the EU; services established in another EU Member State may be subjected to these rules following the procedure of Article 3(4)–(5) of Directive 2000/31/EC.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you operate a software application distribution platform, you must prevent downloading of non-compliant AI applications within 48 hours of a formal request from the relevant sector-specific regulator or central government oversight body.
rule_text_technical: Software application stores must, on ARCOM request, prevent downloading of apps non-compliant with formal notices regarding minor protection or age verification within 48 hours; non-compliance is punishable by a fine up to 1% of worldwide pre-tax turnover.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both require app distribution service providers to stop distributing or remove non-compliant apps upon regulatory direction, but the Singapore rule is triggered by a Commissioner order under online safety law while the French rule involves ARCOM requests with a 48-hour deadline.

rule_text: If you are a hosting provider receiving a child pornography removal request, you must inform content providers of the removal and their appeal rights, and notify the authority if compliance is impossible due to force majeure.
rule_text_technical: Hosting providers receiving removal requests for child pornography images under Article 227-23 must be informed of procedures at least 12 hours before the first request, must inform the authority where compliance is impossible due to force majeure, and must inform content providers of removals and appeal rights.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both rules require internet/hosting providers to remove or disable access to CSAM, but the Pennsylvania rule explicitly covers AI-generated CSAM and imposes a removal/disabling obligation on ISPs, whereas the French rule focuses on hosting providers receiving removal requests and requires notifying content providers of the removal and their appeal rights.

rule_text: If you host content, you must remove child pornography images within 24 hours of receiving a removal request.
rule_text_technical: Failure by hosting providers to remove child pornography images (Article 227-23 Criminal Code) within 24 hours of a removal request is punishable by 1 year's imprisonment and a €250,000 fine, raised to 4% of worldwide turnover for habitual violations by legal entities.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you receive a child-pornography removal request, you have the right to seek annulment from the President of the Administrative Court within 48 hours.
rule_text_technical: Hosting and content providers may petition the President of the Administrative Court to annul a removal request within 48 hours; the court rules within 72 hours, with appeals filed within 10 days and the appellate court ruling within 1 month.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you host content manifestly depicting torture or barbaric acts (Art. 222-1), you may be ordered to remove it within 24 hours, failing which ISPs may block access.
rule_text_technical: On an experimental 2-year basis, the administrative authority may request removal of content manifestly contravening Article 222-1; absent removal within 24 hours, ISPs may be notified to block access, with regularity overseen by a qualified person within ARCOM.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: You cannot bring to public knowledge or disclose to a third party algorithmically generated visual or sound content (deepfakes) reproducing a person without their consent.
rule_text_technical: Article 226-8 of the Criminal Code is extended to visual or sound content generated by algorithmic processing brought to the knowledge of the public or a third party without consent, with penalties of 2 years' imprisonment and €45,000 fine when committed via an online public communication service.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both rules prohibit the non-consensual disclosure of deepfake/algorithmically generated intimate images of identifiable persons, but Vermont's statute is a criminal prohibition framed around 'knowingly disclosing' with specific focus on nude/sexual-conduct imagery, while France's SREN Art. 15 is broader in covering any deepfake reproducing a person without consent and is framed as a civil/regulatory obligation.

Both prohibit publishing non-consensual deepfake intimate depictions, but the US federal rule specifically targets use of an interactive computer service and requires knowledge, while the French rule covers broader disclosure/publication without specifying platform intermediaries.

Both prohibit creating and distributing AI-generated/deepfake intimate images of real persons without consent, but California's rule specifically targets 'synthetic intimate images' under penal code with criminal liability, while France's rule covers broader audiovisual deepfake content under a different legal framework with different scope and remedies.

Both prohibit dissemination of AI-generated/algorithmically generated intimate depictions of a person without consent, but Pennsylvania's rule requires specific intent to harass/annoy/alarm whereas France's rule focuses on non-consensual disclosure without an intent element, and Pennsylvania's rule covers sexually explicit depictions broadly while France's covers deepfakes reproducing a person's image.

Both rules address non-consensual distribution of synthetic intimate depictions, but Wyoming's rule specifically targets threats to distribute such material as a coercive tool, which is a distinct extortion/coercion angle not present in the French rule.

Both prohibit knowingly disclosing deepfakes without consent, but NJ § 2(c)(2) is narrower in that it requires the deepfake to have been created in violation of subsection b (criminal purpose), while France's rule broadly covers disclosure without consent regardless of creation purpose.

Both prohibit knowingly creating or distributing deepfake visual content of a real identifiable person without consent in a sexual/nudity context, but the French rule focuses on public disclosure and reputational harm more broadly, while the Arkansas rule specifically targets nudity or sexual conduct and adds a 'knowingly' mens rea requirement.

instances.citation: Art. 2 (amending Art. 147-B, sole paragraph, Penal Code)
instances.notes: Both prohibit using AI-generated or algorithmically altered depictions of a real person without consent, but the Brazilian law is narrower in victim scope (women only) and frames the offense as psychological violence within the Penal Code, whereas the French law is broader in subject coverage and framed as a disclosure/dissemination prohibition rather than a violence offense.

Both rules prohibit dissemination of AI-generated or algorithmically altered media depicting identifiable adults without consent in intimate or harmful contexts, but the Kansas rule specifically addresses non-consensual pornographic content while the French rule covers broader deepfake disclosure without consent.

Both prohibit non-consensual disclosure of AI-generated/algorithmically-produced intimate images of real persons, but West Virginia's rule adds a threat-to-disclose element and requires intent to harass, coerce, or harm, while France's rule focuses on public disclosure without consent and does not specify intent beyond the disclosure itself.

Both prohibit non-consensual disclosure of synthetic intimate/explicit media of identifiable persons, but Montana's rule adds a 'knows or reasonably should know' knowledge standard and is framed as criminal law, whereas the French rule is broader in framing and applies to algorithmic content generally without specifying the knowledge threshold.

Both prohibit non-consensual distribution of synthetic/AI-generated sexually explicit images of identifiable persons, but Montana HB 514 explicitly covers both real and AI-generated content and is a criminal statute, whereas the French SREN provision is broader in medium (visual and sound) and framed differently.

Both rules prohibit distributing AI-altered/generated depictions of a person without their consent, but the French rule specifies 'algorithmically generated visual or sound content reproducing a person' while the Italian rule covers AI-falsified or AI-altered images, videos, or voices and is codified as a criminal code provision.

Both prohibit communicating AI-generated/algorithmically altered content that falsely depicts a real person, but Singapore's rule targets inauthentic material that falsely depicts a victim's words or actions (closer to defamation/harassment), while France's rule focuses on deepfakes reproducing a person without consent more broadly.

Both prohibit publishing realistic AI-generated/deepfake imitations of identifiable individuals without consent, but the French rule focuses on visual/sound content reproducing a person's image or voice while Hawaii's rule specifically covers 'digital imitation' used in a broader context; Hawaii's bill is also a proposed state bill rather than enacted law.

Both prohibit recreating or disclosing a person's likeness without consent via AI/algorithmic synthesis, but Iowa H 2082 focuses on audio or visual likeness recreation with intent, while France's SREN Art. 15 targets public disclosure of deepfakes and has different scope, framing, and enforcement context.

Both rules prohibit recreating/disclosing a person's audio or visual likeness without consent, but Iowa H 406 focuses on AI-generated recreations intended to be substantially similar while France's SREN Art. 15 targets public disclosure of algorithmically generated deepfakes reproducing a person, and Iowa's bill is a proposed state statute rather than an enacted law.

Both address digitally altered depictions of real persons (deepfakes), but this Massachusetts provision is a non-binding commission study recommendation while the French rule is a binding prohibition on distributing such content without consent.

Both prohibit non-consensual disclosure of deepfake sexual content depicting real persons, but the New Jersey rule is a criminal statute specifying sexual penetration/contact/nudity while the French rule is broader in scope and framing.

Both prohibit non-consensual disclosure of deepfake sexual content depicting an identifiable person, but the New Jersey bill specifies the criminal code section and particular sexual acts covered, while the French law uses broader 'visual or sound content' framing.

Both prohibit disclosing deepfake intimate images of a person without consent, but NJ A2736 is specifically tied to images created in violation of its subsection b and uses criminal law framing, while FR SREN 2024 is broader in scope and context.

Both prohibit disclosing deepfakes depicting a real person without consent, but NJ A 1892 is narrower, limited to sexual content (penetration, contact, exposed intimate parts), while the French SREN Art. 15 covers any deepfake reproducing a person without consent regardless of sexual nature.

Both prohibit disclosing/distributing deepfake intimate images of persons without consent, but NJ S 3551 ties disclosure liability specifically to images created in violation of its own imaging prohibition, while France's rule covers algorithmic content reproducing a person without their knowledge more broadly.

Both prohibit non-consensual synthetic manipulation of a person's image affecting their standing, but the Bahrain rule focuses on reputational harm from compositing personal images while the French rule specifically addresses algorithmically generated audiovisual deepfakes disclosed to third parties.

Both prohibit unauthorized manipulation of a person's image/likeness using AI/algorithmic tools, but the Puerto Rico rule adds a commercial-purpose element and covers voice and digital representation of physical features, while the French rule focuses on public disclosure of deepfakes without consent.

rule_text: If you operate internet access, domain name resolution, web browser, or search engine services, you must implement warnings, blocking, or delisting against online services identified by relevant government authorities as designed for fraud, identity theft, or phishing.
rule_text_technical: ARCOM agents may identify online services manifestly designed to commit fraud, identity theft or phishing; the administrative authority may order browser providers to display warnings (7-day conservatory), ISPs and DNS providers to block access (up to 3 months), and search engines to cease referencing, with regularity overseen by a CNIL-designated qualified person.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both require internet access service providers to block/disable access to specified online content upon regulatory order, but the Singapore rule is issued by the Commissioner under a specific online safety statute while the French rule involves ARCOM and broader ISP/DNS/browser obligations.

rule_text: If you are a very large online platform, you must adopt a charter for monitoring and supporting your content moderators including training, mental-health support and confidentiality.
rule_text_technical: Very large online platforms (per the DSA) must adopt charters for monitoring and supporting online content moderators, covering comprehensive training, mental health awareness, psychological support programs, task rotation, support groups, wellbeing policies, recognition of moderators' work, and confidentiality of support exchanges.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you provide cloud computing services, you cannot grant cloud credits for more than one year (renewals included) or attach exclusivity conditions to them.
rule_text_technical: Under Article L. 442-12 of the Commercial Code, cloud computing credits may only be granted for a limited duration of maximum 1 year including renewals, with no exclusivity conditions permitted; violations attract administrative fines up to €200,000 (natural person) or €1,000,000 (legal entity), doubled for repeat violations within 2 years.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you provide cloud services, you cannot charge data transfer or switching fees that exceed the actual costs incurred.
rule_text_technical: Cloud providers may not charge data transfer fees in connection with switching providers exceeding costs directly related to the change, nor other switching or multi-cloud transfer fees exceeding actual costs incurred; a ministerial order following ARCEP proposal sets maximum tariffs, with exemptions for custom-developed and limited test/evaluation services.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you provide cloud computing services, you must ensure interoperability with other providers and portability of customer digital assets and exportable data.
rule_text_technical: Cloud computing service providers must ensure their services comply with essential requirements of (1) interoperability with customer services or other cloud providers of the same service type, (2) portability of digital assets and exportable data, and (3) free provision of APIs and documentation necessary for interoperability and portability.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both require cloud providers to ensure portability and interoperability after switching, but the Data Act adds more specific obligations (open interfaces at no cost, data export in structured formats, functional equivalence) compared to the French SREN Art. 28.

rule_text: If you provide cloud services, you must publish and regularly update technical interoperability reference offers in line with ARCEP specifications.
rule_text_technical: Providers must publish and regularly update technical interoperability reference offers per ARCEP specifications distinguishing IaaS from other cloud services; IaaS providers must take reasonable measures to facilitate functional equivalence at destination.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you are a State administration processing data of particular sensitivity on cloud services, you must ensure the cloud implements security criteria protecting that data against access by non-EU public authorities.
rule_text_technical: State administrations processing data of particular sensitivity (statutorily secret data; data necessary for essential State missions including national security, public order, health/life protection) on cloud services must ensure those services implement security criteria protecting data against access by public authorities of third States not authorized by EU law.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: You must store health data on EU/EEA territory with measures preventing unauthorized transfer to or access by non-EU/EEA states.
rule_text_technical: Health data under Article L. 1111-8 of the Public Health Code must be stored on EU/EEA territory with measures against unauthorized transfer to or access by non-EU/EEA states.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both require data residency and contractual protections for cloud services, but the Thailand rule applies to AI cloud services with PDPA compliance and encryption requirements, while the French rule specifically mandates EU/EEA territory storage for health data.

rule_text: If you provide cloud services, you must publish information on competent jurisdictions for your infrastructure, third-State access prevention measures, and the environmental footprint of your services.
rule_text_technical: Cloud computing service providers must publish (1) information on competent jurisdictions for deployed infrastructure, (2) description of measures to prevent unauthorized third-State access to or transfer of non-personal data held in the EU, and (3) environmental footprint information (carbon, water, energy).

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you operate a data intermediation service, you are subject to ARCEP supervision under the Data Governance Act, including investigations and sanctions up to 3% of worldwide turnover.
rule_text_technical: ARCEP is the competent authority for data intermediation services under Article 13 of the Data Governance Act, with powers to collect information, investigate, and impose sanctions including financial penalties up to 3% of worldwide turnover (5% for repeat), service suspension or cessation; ARCEP refers data protection issues to CNIL.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: A designated national research institution may conduct automated data collection from online platforms, including those requiring authentication, for systemic risk research when necessary and approved by the relevant data protection authority, notwithstanding platform terms of service.
rule_text_technical: PEReN is authorized to conduct systemic risk detection research under DSA Article 34 and may implement automated data collection methods including from login-gated services notwithstanding terms of use, subject to strict necessity and CNIL-approved methods, with data retention of 9 months for experimentation and 5 years for public research.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: Central government oversight bodies may use independent technical assistance providers for data analysis, source code review, algorithmic processing, and algorithm audits to support AI regulation and enforcement.
rule_text_technical: The DSA Digital Services Coordinator may rely on PEReN technical assistance for data analysis, source code review, algorithmic processing, and algorithm audits; PEReN operates in complete independence with confidentiality obligations.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you edit an online service, you must publish your name, address, contact details, registration numbers and hosting provider details; non-professional editors may remain anonymous publicly by providing details only to the host.
rule_text_technical: Online service editors must publish identification information (name, address, contact details, registration numbers, hosting provider details); non-professional editors may maintain anonymity by providing details only to the hosting provider; violation is punishable by 1 year's imprisonment and €75,000 fine.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you are a hosting provider, you must cooperate against illegal content and immediately notify authorities of specified serious offenses.
rule_text_technical: Hosting provider obligations include cooperation against illegal content and immediate notification to authorities of specified serious offenses (terrorism, sexual abuse of minors, hate speech, etc.).

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If your platform exceeds specified thresholds, you must preserve content for judicial purposes.
rule_text_technical: Platforms above specified thresholds must preserve content for judicial purposes per Article 6.VI of the amended Law No. 2004-575.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both rules impose obligations on recipients of digital content (including harmful material) to preserve or handle it for judicial/legal purposes, but the Nebraska rule is narrowly scoped to CSAM evidence handling by law enforcement and courts, whereas the French rule addresses platform-level content preservation obligations triggered by platform size thresholds.

rule_text: You cannot send malicious or abusive takedown notices to hosting providers.
rule_text_technical: Submitting malicious takedown notices to hosting providers is punishable by 1 year imprisonment and €15,000 fine.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: Data protection authorities and consumer protection regulators are designated as competent authorities for AI platform governance, with one central government oversight body serving as the coordinating authority.
rule_text_technical: Article 7 designates ARCOM, DGCCRF and CNIL as DSA competent authorities and ARCOM as Coordinator for Digital Services; Article 9-2 enables ARCOM to impose financial penalties up to 6% of worldwide turnover (1% for refusal to cooperate) and periodic penalty payments up to 5% of daily turnover.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you operate an online marketplace, you cannot breach DSA obligations on dark patterns, trader traceability, online interface design or consumer information.
rule_text_technical: Article L. 133-1 of the Consumer Code imposes criminal penalties of 2 years' imprisonment and €300,000 fine (or 6% worldwide turnover) on marketplace providers breaching DSA Articles 25 (dark patterns), 30 (trader traceability), 31 (interface design) or 32 (consumer information).

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both prohibit dark patterns in online services and tie violations to existing consumer/trade practice law, but SC H3431 explicitly classifies dark patterns as unlawful trade practices under the SC Unfair Trade Practices Act, while the French rule references DSA obligations in the context of online marketplaces.

rule_text: If you are a very large online platform or search engine, during the 3 months before general elections you must publish in your ad repository the identity of those paying for public-debate-related content, amounts paid, and aggregated election-content information.
rule_text_technical: Per the Electoral Code amendment, during the 3 months before general elections, very large online platforms and search engines (per DSA Art. 33) must make available in their advertising repository the identity of those paying for promotion of public-debate-related content, amounts paid, and aggregated information on election-related content promoted.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both rules address advertising transparency and sponsored content disclosure on digital/media platforms, but the Trinidad and Tobago rule is a soft-law recommendation covering new media generally, whereas the French rule is a binding obligation targeting very large platforms specifically during election periods.

Both require VLOPs to maintain and publish a searchable ad repository, but the DSA Art. 39 applies year-round to all advertisements on VLOPs/VLOSEs while the French SREN Art. 56 narrows the obligation to a 3-month pre-election window for political ads.

rule_text: If you are a data altruism organization, you are supervised by the applicable data protection authority with investigation and sanction powers consistent with applicable data protection law.
rule_text_technical: CNIL is designated as competent authority for data altruism under the Data Governance Act, with investigation, formal notice, and sanctions powers including administrative fines up to GDPR Article 83(4) ceilings.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: If you are a non-EU controller or processor monitoring behavior of persons in France within the EU, the French Data Protection Act applies to you.
rule_text_technical: The French Data Protection Act applies to processing of personal data of persons in France by non-EU controllers or processors when the processing is linked to monitoring of behavior within the EU.

first_instance.law_name: Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et à réguler l'espace numérique

instances.notes: Rule introduced in France SREN Law 2024 (France, 2024-05-21).

Both rules establish extraterritorial application where foreign operators affect domestic users, but the Korean rule applies to AI broadly while the French rule addresses data controllers/processors under data protection law, and the Korean rule uses a 'domestic market or users' effects test rather than a 'monitoring behavior' framing.

Both extend data protection obligations to non-EU/non-established entities processing data of persons within the EU/France, but GDPR Article 3(2) is the original source provision and the French rule is a downstream implementation referencing it; the GDPR rule is the foundational instrument.

Both rules extend privacy law obligations to overseas entities doing business in the jurisdiction, but the NZ rule also explicitly covers domestic agencies handling personal information and uses 'carrying on business' as the jurisdictional hook for overseas agencies, mirroring GDPR-style extraterritorial scope language.

Both rules establish extraterritorial application of a data protection law to foreign entities whose acts relate to personal data of residents/citizens, though the Philippine law adds a nexus test based on equipment use or maintaining offices while the French rule focuses on monitoring behavior of persons in France.

Both rules establish extraterritorial scope for data protection law covering processing outside the jurisdiction that affects residents within it, but the Saudi PDPL applies broadly to all personal data processing of Saudi residents while the French rule specifically addresses non-EU controllers monitoring behavior of persons in France under GDPR.

Both rules establish extraterritorial application of data protection law to overseas actors handling data relating to persons in the jurisdiction, but China's PIPL applies to all personal information handlers outside China processing data 'for the purpose of providing products or services to natural persons in China' or 'analyzing/assessing the behavior of natural persons in China,' while the French rule focuses on controllers/processors monitoring behavior of persons in France within the EU.

Both rules establish extraterritorial application of data protection law to controllers outside the jurisdiction who process data of persons within the territory, but the UAE law adds explicit exemptions (likely for government/security) and uses 'residing in the UAE' rather than the GDPR-style 'monitoring behavior' framing, reflecting meaningful differences in scope and drafting approach.

Both rules extend data protection obligations to non-established foreign controllers/processors who use means or infrastructure in the regulating jurisdiction, but the Zimbabwe rule requires designation of a local representative while the French rule simply applies the law without that specific designation requirement.

Both rules extend a data protection law's territorial reach to cover processing connected to offering goods/services to persons in the jurisdiction, but India's DPDPA applies specifically to digital personal data and Data Principals located in India, while the French rule addresses non-EU controllers monitoring persons in France under the GDPR framework.

Both rules establish territorial/jurisdictional scope for data protection laws covering controllers/processors established in the jurisdiction or processing data of persons located there, but Pakistan's Act adds explicit coverage regardless of where processing occurs and is a comprehensive national data protection statute rather than a provision extending an existing EU framework.

rule_text: To prevail in a digital impersonation action, you must prove the impersonation was published without consent and that either the publisher failed to reasonably convey it was a digital impersonation/disputed, or it would not be obvious to a reasonable person that it was a digital impersonation.
rule_text_technical: A plaintiff must prove: (1) a digital impersonation of the person was published to one or more other persons without the person's consent; and (2) at the time of publication either the publisher did not reasonably convey to the persons to whom the publication was made that the recording or image was a digital impersonation or that its authenticity was disputed, or it would not be obvious to a reasonable person that the recording or image was a digital impersonation.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).
Maryland S 362 — Forged Digital Likenesses (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: If a digital impersonation appears in a paid advertisement, you can only sue the person or entity that originated, ordered, placed, or paid for the advertisement.
rule_text_technical: If the digital impersonation is or is part of a paid advertisement, a cause of action for digital impersonation may be brought only against the person or entity that originated, ordered, placed or paid for the advertisement.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

Both rules concern civil suits for AI-based impersonation/digital identity abuse with injunctive relief, but Utah's rule targets the person who caused publication broadly while Arizona's limits suit to the originator/payer of paid advertisements specifically.

Both grant civil action rights to individuals depicted in deepfake/digital-impersonation content, but Arkansas uniquely extends liability to providers or developers of image generation technology, whereas Arizona limits suit to the originator/orderer/payer of the advertisement.

Both limit the ability to sue publishers/platforms for identity-related digital content, but Utah's rule applies a 'reasonable person' knowledge standard against publishers of offending advertisements or content, while Arizona's rule restricts plaintiffs to suing only the originator/payer of digital impersonation in paid advertisements.

Both address jurisdictional reach for civil suits over digital/intimate depictions, but Guam B 171 establishes broad personal jurisdiction regardless of defendant or platform location, while the Arizona rule limits who can be sued in paid-advertisement contexts.

Both rules limit liability of downstream parties (deployers/licensees vs. ad publishers) who did not originate the harmful content, but the new rule concerns design defect liability for AI product licensees while the Arizona rule concerns digital impersonation in paid advertisements.

Both rules limit plaintiffs to suing only the originator/orderer/payer of a paid advertisement containing a digital impersonation, but Missouri limits to declaratory judgment actions while Arizona applies more broadly.

rule_text: Providers of interactive computer services cannot be sued for digital impersonation when the content was provided by another information content provider.
rule_text_technical: A provider of an interactive computer service may not be subject to an action for digital impersonation for publishing information that is provided by another information content provider.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

Both rules provide safe harbor from liability for platforms acting in good faith regarding nonconsensual intimate imagery, but the TAKE IT DOWN Act applies to 'covered platforms' disabling/removing content upon notice while the Arizona rule tracks Section 230 immunity for interactive computer services not being the content creator.

Both rules address publisher liability for AI-generated impersonation content, but Utah applies a 'reasonable person' knowledge standard for publisher liability while Arizona broadly immunizes interactive computer service providers under a CDA-style rule.

Both rules provide immunity to platforms for good-faith removal or disabling of nonconsensual intimate depiction content, but the TAKE IT DOWN Act applies specifically to covered platforms acting on removal requests under its own framework, while the Arizona rule tracks Section 230 interactive computer service provider immunity.
Mississippi S 2437 — Prohibition of Exploitation By Deepfakes Act (Mississippi) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: Plaintiffs must make diligent efforts to serve and provide prompt actual notice to all defendants, and publishers have the right to appear, be heard, and present evidence before preliminary declaratory relief is entered.
rule_text_technical: The plaintiff shall make diligent efforts to both serve and provide prompt actual notice to all defendants. The publisher of the alleged digital impersonation has the right to appear, be heard and present evidence before the court's entry of preliminary declaratory relief, but a defendant's failure to appear does not preclude a court from granting preliminary declaratory relief.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

Both rules grant publishers the right to appear, be heard, and present evidence before a court enters preliminary declaratory relief in digital impersonation cases, with similar substance but different drafting.

rule_text: Courts must rule on motions for preliminary declaratory relief within two days (excluding weekends and court holidays) of receipt by the assigned judicial officer.
rule_text_technical: The court shall rule on the motion for preliminary declaratory relief within two days after the date that the complaint and motion are received by the judicial officer who is assigned to the case, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and court holidays.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

Both require expedited judicial handling of election-related AI deepfake claims close to an election, but Arizona mandates a specific two-day ruling window on preliminary relief motions while Nevada more broadly requires expedited proceedings within 30 days before an election.

rule_text: To obtain injunctive relief and damages (beyond declaratory relief), you must additionally prove sexual/nude depiction appealing to prurient interests, that the plaintiff was not a public figure, and that the publisher had actual knowledge or failed to take reasonable corrective action within 21 days.
rule_text_technical: A plaintiff may obtain injunctive relief and damages only if the elements of digital impersonation under subsection A and all of the following are proven: (1) the digital impersonation depicts a sexual act or unclothed breasts/buttocks/genitals, appeals to prurient interests and offends local community standards; (2) the plaintiff was not a public figure (including a limited public figure) when the cause of action accrued; and (3) the publication was made with actual knowledge that the recording or image was a digital impersonation, or the publisher failed to take reasonable corrective action within 21 days after having actual knowledge.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

Both laws create a private right of action for nonconsensual disclosure of intimate/deepfake imagery, but Vermont's statute is a criminal-code civil remedy focused on nonconsensual disclosure of nude or sexual images (including deepfakes) while Arizona's provision specifically conditions injunctive relief and damages on proving prurient-interest appeal and is part of a broader digital impersonation framework with distinct procedural requirements.

Both provide for damages and injunctive relief to prevailing plaintiffs in deepfake civil actions, but Arkansas explicitly includes actual, compensatory, and punitive damages plus attorney fees, while Arizona focuses on additional proof requirements to unlock injunctive relief and damages beyond declaratory relief.
Maryland H 663 — Sexual Deepfake Representations and Revenge Porn (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules condition injunctive relief and damages on proof that the digital impersonation depicts the individual in a sexual act or shows nudity appealing to prurient interests, with substantively identical requirements.

rule_text: Publishers shall take corrective action within 21 days of learning content is a digital impersonation, and must remove or disable access to such content and publish a corrective statement to the same audience.
rule_text_technical: Reasonable corrective action includes removing or disabling access to the digital impersonation and publishing to the same audience a statement that the publication was a digital impersonation, undertaken within twenty-one days after the publisher had actual knowledge that the recording or image was a digital impersonation.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

rule_text: Parents or guardians have the right to seek relief under this section on behalf of a minor child or incapacitated person.
rule_text_technical: A parent or guardian of a minor child or incapacitated person may seek relief under this section on the minor child's or incapacitated person's behalf.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

Both rules grant parents or guardians standing to bring civil actions on behalf of minors, but this rule is specific to AI harms on social media platforms (hosting, promoting, sharing, or facilitating harmful AI content) whereas the Arizona rule concerns digital impersonation in a sexual/nude context.

Both rules allow parents or guardians to assert rights on behalf of minors or incapacitated persons, but Colorado's rule extends this to family members acting for deceased individuals and incompetent persons, covering a broader set of representatives.
Arkansas H 1823 — Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Nonconsensual Edits (Arkansas) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Maine H 153 — Harmful Depictions Generated by Artificial Intelligence (Maine) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Both rules grant parents or guardians the right to seek relief on behalf of a minor child or incapacitated person in digital impersonation cases, with substantively identical scope.

rule_text: The statute must be narrowly construed in favor of free and open discourse on matters of public concern and artistic expression, and cannot abrogate other available causes of action.
rule_text_technical: This section shall be narrowly construed in favor of both free and open discourse on matters of public concern and artistic expression and shall not be construed so as to abrogate any cause of action otherwise available.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona HB 2394 — Digitally Altered Media; Civil Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona HB 2394 (Deepfake Civil Remedies) (Arizona, 2024-05-21).

Both rules exempt news, public affairs, political commentary, and similar expressive activities from liability under AI impersonation/identity laws, but Utah's exemption is structured as a specific statutory carve-out for enumerated broadcast/publication contexts while Arizona's is a general narrow-construction mandate favoring free discourse.

Both carve out news/public affairs/journalism and free expression from likeness-related restrictions, but Montana's rule is more specific to news-gathering organizations and sports reporting while Arizona's focuses on narrow construction favoring public discourse and artistic expression.

Both create exemptions for content that is clearly recognizable as digitally manipulated to a reasonable viewer, but the Arizona H 2133 rule applies to the unlawful disclosure prohibition in a sexual material context (§ 13-1425) while HB2394 concerns narrowly construed free speech and artistic expression exemptions in a different statutory context.

Both rules provide a First Amendment carve-out to a digital/AI-content prohibition, preserving constitutionally protected speech, though Colorado's is a standalone exemption clause while Arizona's also mandates narrow construction in favor of free discourse.

Both rules carve out First Amendment-protected activities including satire, parody, and artistic expression, but Georgia S 354 also explicitly includes journalism, while the Arizona rule focuses on narrow construction in favor of free discourse.

Both limit public-interest or public-concern defenses in intimate/deceptive image contexts, but Hawaii's rule specifically addresses the fact that a depicted individual's public figure status alone cannot establish public concern, while Arizona's rule addresses narrow construction in favor of free discourse more broadly.

Both carve out First Amendment-protected activity from liability, but Hawaii's provision is a blanket liability exemption for any First Amendment activity while Arizona's requires narrow construction favoring free discourse and artistic expression, and Arizona is a binding enacted law versus Hawaii's bill.
Maryland S 362 — Forged Digital Likenesses (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules require narrow construction of the statute in favor of free and open discourse on matters of public concern and artistic expression, with nearly identical substantive purpose, though drafted independently in different jurisdictions.

Both exempt political/social commentary, parody, satire, and artistic expression from fabricated-media prohibitions, but NY A 1280 adds a disclosure condition while AZ HB2394 requires narrow construction in favor of free discourse.
West Virginia S 170 — Intimate Deep Fake Media Act (West Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: Parties to contested actions seeking permanent declaratory relief, permanent injunctive relief, or damages have the right to a jury trial.
rule_text_technical: All parties to a contested action seeking permanent declaratory relief, permanent injunctive relief or damages and that is brought pursuant to this section have the right to trial by jury.

rule_text: Frontier AI companies should define 'red lines' — capability thresholds at which a model would not be deployed without additional safety measures (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Signatory companies commit to identifying and publicly defining capability thresholds ('red lines') beyond which a frontier model will not be deployed absent additional, specified safety mitigations.

first_instance.law_name: Seoul AI Safety Declarations 2024 (Ministerial Statement and Company Commitments)
first_instance.citation: Frontier AI Safety Commitments — Dangerous Capability Thresholds

instances.citation: Frontier AI Safety Commitments — Dangerous Capability Thresholds
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Seoul AI Safety Declarations 2024 (International, 2024-05-21).

Both address pre-deployment evaluation of highly capable/frontier AI models against capability or safety thresholds, but the Seoul commitment focuses on defining 'red lines' for deployment while this NIST rule focuses on maintaining a test plan and response policy to periodically evaluate models.

Both require AI providers to have a dedicated risk management system, but the Qatar rule is a binding obligation on financial institution AI providers while the Seoul commitment is a voluntary frontier-AI safety recommendation with a different scope.

Both address ensuring adverse impacts of AI on fundamental rights and safety are adequately addressed with sufficient safeguards, but Art. 16(3) is a broader human-rights-focused treaty obligation covering all AI systems, while the Seoul commitments are voluntary frontier-AI-specific safety thresholds.

Both address structured identification of systemic risks for frontier/general-purpose AI models, but the Seoul commitment focuses on red-line capability thresholds for deployment decisions while this voluntary CoP measure prescribes a detailed risk-typing and analysis process.

Both rules address compute-based thresholds for identifying high-risk frontier/systemic-risk AI models requiring enhanced obligations, but this guideline sets a specific binding-adjacent FLOPs threshold (10²⁵) under EU law while the Seoul commitment is a voluntary 'red lines' framework without a quantified compute figure; additionally, this is soft law guidance interpreting a binding regulation.

Both rules target frontier AI models and require safeguards against critical/severe harms, but the Seoul commitment is a voluntary instrument recommending 'red lines' for deployment thresholds, whereas New York S 6953 is a binding statute imposing a mandatory obligation to implement safeguards against 'unreasonable risk of critical harm'.
California SB 1047 (California) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules target frontier AI developers and require safety planning including child/harm thresholds, but the Seoul Declaration focuses on defining capability 'red lines' for deployment, while this Illinois bill specifically requires a public safety and child protection plan aimed at preventing unacceptable outcomes; both are soft law but differ in scope and specificity.

Both rules address voluntary/soft-law obligations for frontier AI developers to implement safety measures around high-risk outcomes, but the Seoul commitment focuses on defining capability 'red lines' for deployment, while Illinois H 4705 §15(b) specifically targets public safety and child protection planning.

Both rules require pre-deployment risk/capability assessment for frontier/covered AI models, but the Seoul commitment focuses on defining 'red lines' for capability thresholds while Massachusetts S 37 focuses on assessing whether a model is 'reasonably capable of causing or materially enabling' harm; this is a voluntary Massachusetts bill matching a voluntary international commitment with different framing and scope.

rule_text: National governments shall establish or designate AI safety institutes that coordinate internationally through shared evaluation methodologies, joint risk assessments, and coordinated responses to identified AI risks.
rule_text_technical: The Seoul Summit formally establishes the International AI Safety Institute Network, comprising national AI Safety Institutes (including UK, US, Japan, and others), tasked with conducting joint safety evaluations, developing shared methodologies, and coordinating responses to AI risks.

first_instance.law_name: Seoul AI Safety Declarations 2024 (Ministerial Statement and Company Commitments)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Seoul AI Safety Declarations 2024 (International, 2024-05-21).

Both rules recommend establishing a centre or network to facilitate international AI cooperation and resource mobilization, but Zambia's National Emerging Technologies Centre of Excellence is a domestic institution with an international cooperation mandate, while the Seoul network is a purely international coordination mechanism.

Both create institutional structures dedicated to AI safety research and evaluation, but South Korea's provision establishes a domestic ministerial-level institute focused on risk analysis, policy research, and evaluation criteria, whereas the Seoul declaration establishes an international network of national AI Safety Institutes for cross-border coordination.

Both rules concern coordination among AI Safety Institutes, but the Seoul declaration establishes a binding International AISI Network with joint evaluations and shared methodologies, whereas this ASEAN rule is a voluntary recommendation to establish regional dialogue platforms for sharing safety research.

instances.citation: Action 7 — Establishment of AI Safety Institute
instances.notes: Both establish AI Safety Institute structures for monitoring, testing, and sharing information on AI capabilities and risks, but the Seoul declaration creates an international network of national institutes while Australia's AISI is a single national body; additionally, Australia's rule is a voluntary policy framework recommendation rather than a binding mandate.

Both address AI Safety Institute capacity and evaluation functions, but Japan's rule is a binding domestic obligation to expand a specific national AISI's staffing, whereas the Seoul statement establishes an international network of safety institutes with shared methodologies.

Both concern an AI Safety Institute performing risk analysis and citizen protection functions, but the Korean rule establishes a domestic institute under the Minister of Science and ICT with a specific mandate, while the Seoul commitment establishes an international network of national institutes for joint evaluations.

instances.citation: Key Concrete Measures — Nordic-Baltic AI Centre
instances.notes: Both recommend regional/international AI cooperation hubs, but the Nordic-Baltic AI Centre is a sub-regional geographic cooperation hub focused on positioning, whereas the Seoul AI Safety Institute Network is a global safety-focused coordination network among national institutes.

rule_text: Signatories should undergo follow-up compliance review of Seoul commitments at the Paris 2025 AI Safety Summit (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Compliance with and progress on the Seoul government and company commitments will be reviewed at the subsequent Paris 2025 AI Safety Summit, with public reporting providing reputational accountability.

Both recommend adherence to international AI safety commitments, but this OAS rule specifically references the UN General Assembly Resolution of 21 March 2024 on safe, secure, and reliable AI, while the Seoul rule concerns follow-up compliance review of Summit commitments.

Both require follow-up monitoring/review of AI commitments, but this rule establishes an ongoing domestic institutional monitoring mandate by the AI Strategic Headquarters with benchmarks, whereas the Seoul rule is a one-time international compliance review among signatories.

rule_text: Internet websites and regularly published newspapers, magazines, or other periodicals of general circulation are exempt if the publication clearly states that the deceptive media was generated by artificial intelligence.
rule_text_technical: This section does not apply to an internet website or a regularly published newspaper, magazine or other periodical of general circulation, including an internet or electronic publication, that routinely carries news and commentary of general interest and that publishes materially deceptive audio or visual media prohibited by this section if the publication clearly states that the materially deceptive audio or visual media was generated by artificial intelligence.

first_instance.law_name: Arizona SB 1359 — Synthetic Media; Political Advertising; Disclosure

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Arizona SB 1359 (Synthetic Media Election Disclosure) (Arizona, 2024-05-29).

Both provide a news/journalism exemption from AI election content prohibitions, but Nevada focuses on 'news organizations or journalists reporting on news of public concern' while Arizona's exemption covers internet websites and periodicals of general circulation that clearly state the content is AI-generated, reflecting different scopes and conditions.

Both exempt online newspapers/periodicals and broadcasting stations from deepfake/AI political content requirements when appropriate disclosure is made, but the California law specifies 'qualifying' outlets and 'materially deceptive content' framing while Arizona's exemption is broader and structured differently.

Both exempt broadcasting stations airing deceptive/AI content as part of bona fide news programming, but the California rule adds a requirement that the broadcast clearly acknowledges the deceptive nature of the content, while the Arizona rule focuses on periodicals and online publications stating the content does not represent reality.

Both exempt newspapers, periodicals, and online publications of general circulation from deepfake/AI political content prohibitions when publishing or carrying such content, though SD SB164 adds a 'paid to publish' condition.

Both rules exempt newspapers, television, and radio stations (and other commercial media) from political advertisement/AI-content obligations when they are not the source of the content, but the Arizona rule specifically limits the exemption to publications that clearly state they did not create the content, while the North Dakota rule's exemption criteria may differ in scope and conditions.

Both exempt platform intermediaries (streaming, ISPs, broadcasters, telecoms) from AI election content liability, but Nevada AB73 covers a broader and more detailed list of exempted service categories than Arizona SB1359's narrower press/website exemption.

Both exempt newspapers, magazines, and online publications from AI election content rules when the publication clearly states the synthetic/AI nature of the content, though Rhode Island extends this to news and commentary broadly.

Both exempt internet websites and regularly published periodicals of general circulation that routinely carry news, though RI explicitly includes online publications while AZ's text is similarly structured.

Both exempt broadcast/cable/satellite and newspaper operators from synthetic media or deceptive content obligations under certain conditions, but Maine's exemption is narrowly conditioned on whether the operator knew the content violated the disclosure rule, while Arizona's exemption applies if the publication clearly states the content does not represent the candidate's views.
Alabama H 291 — Crimes and Offenses (Alabama) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Arkansas H 1041 — Deceptive and Fraudulent Deepfakes in Elections (Arkansas) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both exempt regularly published newspapers, magazines, periodicals, and internet/electronic publications carrying news from deceptive-content/AI political advertising prohibitions, with largely equivalent scope.

Both exempt internet websites, broadcasters, newspapers, and periodicals from deceptive AI content requirements, but Guam B 209 is a proposed bill (non-binding status unclear) and adds streaming providers/cable operators while Arizona's rule requires the publication to 'clearly state' the content is not factual.

Both exempt websites, newspapers, magazines, and periodicals of general circulation from deepfake/deceptive media prohibitions, with Illinois H 1860 applying to a deepfake prohibition and Arizona's law applying to a synthetic media election disclosure requirement.
Kentucky S 7 — Property Rights to the Use of an Individuals Image (Kentucky) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both shift liability away from distributors (broadcasters, websites) for paid political deepfake content, but Missouri also explicitly covers cable/satellite operators and frames it as a liability shield rather than a pure exemption.
Missouri H 236 — Civil Liability for Publishing or Distributing Material (Missouri) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both exempt internet websites and regularly published newspapers, magazines, and periodicals from AI political deepfake disclosure requirements when the publication clearly states the content does not represent the subject's actual views.
Nevada A 271 — Elections (Nevada) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
New Hampshire H 630 — Deepfake Materials of Political Candidates (New Hampshire) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Both exempt broadcasters, cable operators, websites, and periodicals from AI election content obligations when acting as distribution platforms rather than originators of the deceptive content.

Both exempt media/advertising distribution channels such as websites, newspapers, and broadcasters, but NJ A3585 covers a broader list including mobile apps, video streaming services, and telecom carriers, while Arizona's exemption is narrower and requires a clear statement of non-endorsement.

Both exempt broadcasting stations, websites, and media platforms from deepfake-related prohibitions, but NJ S 2544 is broader, also covering cable services, telecommunications carriers, mobile apps, and video streaming services.

Both exempt broadcasting stations, cable/satellite operators, and internet websites/news periodicals from deceptive media disclosure requirements, though NJ A3838 also includes sound recordings and frames the exemption slightly differently.

Both exempt news reporting from fabricated-media prohibitions, but NY A 1280 adds the condition that the record not be disseminated with intent to misrepresent authenticity, while AZ SB1359 requires the publication to clearly state the material is not factual.

Both provide exemptions for news/media personnel and interactive computer service providers, but the Ohio rule is a binding statutory exemption while the Arizona rule is narrower in scope, focused on periodicals and websites with specific disclosure conditions.

Both carve out media/expressive works from persona/publicity restrictions, but Ohio's exemption specifically targets literary, dramatic, fictional, historical, audiovisual, and musical works with a deepfake-style carveout exception, while Arizona's exemption covers internet websites and periodicals that clearly state the content is not factual.

Both exempt websites and regularly published periodicals (including electronic publications) that carry news and commentary from AI/synthetic media disclosure requirements, with nearly identical scope and carve-out logic.

Both provide exemptions from liability for news reporting and satire/commentary involving AI-generated/synthetic media, but the Oklahoma rule applies to a criminal liability context and includes 'commentary' alongside satire, while the Arizona rule focuses on newspapers/periodicals and requires a clear statement of fabrication.

Both exempt internet websites, newspapers, magazines, and periodicals of general circulation from AI disclosure requirements when they routinely carry such content, but Oklahoma S 746 is a bill and the Arizona rule applies specifically to synthetic media in elections.

Both exempt media outlets (newspapers, magazines, periodicals, online platforms) from AI-related content prohibitions when they are not the originators of the content, but Oklahoma's rule covers deepfake prohibitions broadly while Arizona's covers AI political ad disclosures.

Both exempt internet websites, newspapers, magazines, and periodicals from deepfake/deceptive media prohibitions when the publication clearly states the content does not represent the depicted individual's actual views.

Both exempt internet websites and regularly published periodicals carrying news and commentary from disclosure requirements, but Vermont S 23 is a voluntary instrument and extends the exemption explicitly to electronic publications, while Arizona's law is binding.
West Virginia S 484 — Synthetic Media and Artificial Intelligence (West Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: You cannot rely on a person's consent to the recording or production of an intimate image as consent to disclose it; disclosure consent must be separately established.
rule_text_technical: Consent to recording or production of the visual image does not, by itself, constitute consent for disclosure of the image.

first_instance.law_name: Vermont Act 161 of 2024 (H.878) — Nonconsensual Deepfake Pornography

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Vermont H.878 / Act 161 (Deepfake Pornography) (Vermont, 2024-06-01).

Both rules establish that consent to creation/recording of intimate or visual material cannot be treated as consent to its distribution, requiring separate disclosure/distribution consent, but the Massachusetts statute uses 'visual material' and 'distribution' while Vermont uses 'intimate image' and 'disclose', reflecting independent drafting in the same substantive requirement.

Both rules establish that consent to creation of an intimate image is legally distinct from consent to its disclosure/publication, but the federal DEFIANCE Act drafts this independently with slightly different framing (adding the 'prior disclosure to one individual' clarification) compared to Vermont's formulation.

Both rules address consent requirements for real persons depicted in AI-generated or synthetic media, but the Vermont rule specifically separates recording consent from disclosure consent, while the Chinese standard focuses on obtaining lawful consent or basis for depicting a real person in AI-generated synthetic content and mandates labelling obligations.

Both rules require separate, specific consent for particular uses of a person's identity/image (Vermont focuses on intimate images and separating recording consent from disclosure consent; Utah focuses on AI-simulated personal identity used for advertising, fundraising, or solicitation), sharing the same underlying principle that general consent does not extend to specific commercial or exploitative uses, but differing significantly in subject matter, context, and scope.

Both rules address consent in the context of intimate images and AI-generated/deepfake content, but North Dakota's rule focuses on the prohibition of surreptitious creation and possession of sexually expressive images (including AI-generated ones), while Vermont's rule specifically addresses the separability of recording/production consent from disclosure consent — meaningfully different scope and operative obligation.

Both rules establish that consent to creation of an intimate image/depiction does not constitute consent to its disclosure, requiring separate disclosure consent, but Tennessee applies this to AI-generated 'intimate digital depictions' while Vermont's law addresses recorded or produced 'intimate images'.

Both rules independently establish that consent to creation of an intimate image does not constitute consent to its dissemination and require separate consent for disclosure, but are drafted in different state statutory frameworks.

Both Nebraska L 371 and Vermont H878 establish that consent to original creation or prior disclosure of an intimate image cannot serve as consent to subsequent disclosure, but they are independently drafted with different phrasing and structure rather than verbatim copies; the South Carolina rule (us-sc-hb3058-2025) addresses a narrower formulation focused only on prior sharing.

Both rules independently establish that consent to creation of an intimate image cannot be treated as consent to its disclosure, but Colorado's rule specifically references 'intimate digital depictions' (AI-generated context) while Vermont's rule addresses recording or production more broadly.

Both rules establish that consent to a sexual act or recording cannot be treated as consent to distribution/disclosure of the resulting image; independently drafted but substantively equivalent principle.

Both rules address consent requirements for intimate/private image reproductions, but the Wisconsin rule focuses on prohibiting reproduction without consent to the reproduction itself, while the Vermont rule specifically addresses the distinct consent required for disclosure separately from consent to recording or production.

Both rules establish that consent to creation/recording of an intimate image is legally distinct from and does not imply consent to its disclosure/publication, and that prior disclosure to one person does not authorize broader distribution, but they are drafted independently under different statutory frameworks.

This Vermont H 626 provision restates the same rule from Vermont H 878 (2024) at 13 V.S.A. § 2606(b) — that consent to recording or production of an intimate/visual image does not constitute consent to disclose it — using functionally identical language in the same statutory location.
Arkansas H 1823 — Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Nonconsensual Edits (Arkansas) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules independently establish that prior consent to creation of an intimate image or prior disclosure to another person cannot serve as consent to subsequent dissemination, though phrased differently.

Both rules establish that prior conduct (recording/production or prior sharing) cannot be used to infer consent to disclosure of an intimate image, but Hawaii's rule focuses on inferring consent from prior conduct generally while Vermont's rule specifically separates recording consent from disclosure consent.
Kentucky H 63 — Privacy Protection (Kentucky) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Kentucky H 21 — Privacy Protection (Kentucky) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Mississippi S 2437 — Artificial Intelligence (Mississippi) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Mississippi S 2437 — Prohibition of Exploitation By Deepfakes Act (Mississippi) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules address what cannot be treated as implied or constructive consent, but Vermont's rule is specific to intimate image disclosure while Missouri's rule broadly covers identity attributes in premises/public space contexts.

Both rules establish that consent to creation/recording of an intimate image is legally separate from and cannot substitute for consent to its disclosure, but are independently drafted with different phrasing.
Missouri H 362 — Disclosure of Intimate Digital Depictions (Missouri) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules restrict disclosure of intimate images without consent, but the New Jersey rule focuses on criminalizing non-consensual disclosure of intimate images (including manipulated depictions), while the Vermont rule specifically addresses that prior consent to recording cannot serve as consent to disclosure.

Both rules establish that consent to being recorded/photographed does not constitute consent to disclose the resulting image, requiring separate disclosure consent; the Vermont rule applies to intimate images generally while this New Jersey rule applies specifically to public office candidates.
New Mexico H 530 — Sensitive Deepfake Images (New Mexico) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules restrict non-consensual dissemination of intimate images, but the Vermont rule specifically addresses the separation of recording consent from disclosure consent, while this New York rule focuses on the prohibition against disseminating or threatening to disseminate intimate or digitally altered images without consent, with a knowledge or reasonable-knowledge standard.

Both rules prohibit non-consensual dissemination of intimate images including digitized/altered versions, but New York S 205 focuses on the act of dissemination without consent (including threats) while Vermont H878 specifically addresses the distinct consent requirement for disclosure versus recording/production.

Both rules address non-consensual dissemination of intimate images including digitally altered versions, but the New York rule focuses on the prohibition of dissemination without consent while the Vermont rule specifically addresses that prior recording consent cannot serve as dissemination consent; they share the same underlying concept with different emphases and scope.

Both rules address the limitations of consent in the context of intimate/sexually explicit images, but this rule specifically bars consent as a defense for offenses involving minors (under 18 cannot consent at all), while the Vermont rule addresses the narrower point that consent to record/produce an image does not constitute consent to disclose it.

Both rules address consent as a defense/exception in the context of synthetic or intimate media depicting real persons, but Vermont's rule specifically prohibits treating recording/production consent as disclosure consent, while New York's rule creates a broader consent exception to a synthetic media prohibition without that same separation requirement.

Both rules address the limits of consent in intimate/explicit imagery contexts, but this rule specifically bars consent as a defense for minors entirely (no adult can consent on their behalf), whereas the Vermont rule addresses the distinct issue that consent to record/produce cannot serve as consent to disclose.

Both rules concern consent as a defense or element in intimate image dissemination, but Vermont's rule specifically separates recording/production consent from disclosure consent, while Pennsylvania's rule more broadly treats consent to dissemination as a complete defense to prosecution without that distinction.

Both rules independently establish that consent to creation or prior consensual disclosure of an intimate image cannot serve as consent to subsequent disclosure, though drafted with different phrasing and structure.

Both rules require that consent to perform or record sex acts cannot serve as consent to distribute the resulting image; this SC soft-law rule mirrors the VT binding law's separability-of-consent principle but applies to platform operators rather than distributors.

Both rules establish that consent to creation of an intimate image/depiction is legally separate from and cannot substitute for consent to its disclosure, though drafted independently with different phrasing and in the context of digital depictions specifically.

rule_text: If you operate a website, online service, or mobile application hosting nonconsensual intimate images, you cannot solicit or accept a fee or other consideration to remove, delete, modify, or refrain from posting the image when requested by the depicted person.
rule_text_technical: A person who maintains an internet website, online service, online application, or mobile application that contains a visual image of an identifiable person who is nude or engaged in sexual conduct shall not solicit or accept a fee or other consideration to remove, delete, correct, modify, or refrain from posting or disclosing the visual image if requested by the depicted person.

rule_text: A digital record electronically registered in a blockchain is self-authenticating in Vermont courts if accompanied by a sworn written declaration from a qualified person stating the record's blockchain timestamps and that it was maintained as part of regularly conducted activity.

rule_text: You cannot use against a child in any proceeding the child's decision not to enter the diversion program, prosecutorial objections to diversion, eligibility assessments, or statements made by the child or family during diversion-related assessments or hearings; such statements also cannot be disclosed to law enforcement.

rule_text: You cannot use facial recognition technology to process facial information where other non-biometric technical means can achieve the same identification or authentication purpose.

rule_text: You cannot use facial recognition technology to infringe upon the personal dignity or reputation of individuals.

rule_text: 'Facial recognition technology' means automatically identifying natural persons by analyzing and comparing facial features in images, video, or other data; 'facial information' means biometric information of natural persons extracted or generated through such technology.
