rule_text: You cannot write, create, or sell a consumer review, consumer testimonial, or celebrity testimonial that materially misrepresents that the reviewer/testimonialist exists, actually used the product or service, or that the review reflects the reviewer's honest opinions or experiences.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of 16 CFR Part 465 for a business to write, create, or sell a consumer review, consumer testimonial, or celebrity testimonial that materially misrepresents that: (1) the reviewer or testimonialist exists; (2) the reviewer or testimonialist used or had actual experience with the product, service, or business being reviewed; or (3) the review or testimonial reflects the honest opinions or experiences of the reviewer or testimonialist.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC Fake Reviews Final Rule (2024) (Federal Trade Commission, 2024-08-14).

rule_text: You must not purchase a consumer review, and you shall not disseminate a consumer or celebrity testimonial, if you knew or reasonably should have known that it materially misrepresents the reviewer's existence, actual experience, or honest opinions.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of this part for a business to purchase a consumer review, or to disseminate a consumer or celebrity testimonial, that the business knew or should have known materially misrepresents that: (1) the reviewer or testimonialist exists; (2) the reviewer or testimonialist used or had actual experience with the product, service, or business; or (3) the review or testimonial reflects the honest opinions or experiences of the reviewer or testimonialist.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC Fake Reviews Final Rule (2024) (Federal Trade Commission, 2024-08-14).

rule_text: You must not procure consumer reviews from your officers, managers, employees, agents, or their immediate relatives for posting on third-party platforms when you knew or reasonably should have known the review materially misrepresents that the reviewer is a member of the general public, used the product, or reflects honest opinions.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of this part for a business to procure from its officers, managers, employees, agents, or their immediate relatives a consumer review for posting on a third-party consumer review platform or any other platform when the business knew or should have known the review materially misrepresents that: (1) the reviewer exists as a member of the general public; (2) the reviewer used or had actual experience with the product, service, or business; or (3) the review reflects the honest opinions or experiences of the reviewer.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC Fake Reviews Final Rule (2024) (Federal Trade Commission, 2024-08-14).

rule_text: You cannot provide compensation or other incentives to any person contingent on writing a consumer review that expresses a particular sentiment (positive or negative), whether expressly or implicitly through context or the nature of the incentive; disclosure does not cure such a violation.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of this part for a business to provide compensation or other incentives (monetary or non-monetary) to any person contingent on the person writing a consumer review that expresses a particular sentiment, whether positive or negative, including by expressly conditioning compensation on a positive review or implicitly doing so through context or the nature of the incentive offered. A disclosure of any incentive does not cure a violation if the review is conditioned on expressing a particular sentiment. This section applies to consumer reviews only.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC Fake Reviews Final Rule (2024) (Federal Trade Commission, 2024-08-14).

rule_text: You cannot disseminate a consumer or celebrity testimonial provided by your officer, manager, employee, agent, or their immediate relative without clearly and conspicuously disclosing the material relationship between the testimonialist and the business.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of this part for a business to disseminate a consumer or celebrity testimonial provided by an officer, manager, employee, or agent of the business, or by the immediate relative of any such person, without clear and conspicuous disclosure of the material relationship between the testimonialist and the business.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

rule_text: You cannot require, request, or instruct your officers, managers, employees, agents, or their immediate relatives to write a consumer review without clearly and conspicuously disclosing the reviewer's material relationship to the business.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of this part for a business to require, request, or instruct an officer, manager, employee, or agent of the business, or the immediate relative of any such person, to write or create a consumer review without clearly and conspicuously disclosing the reviewer's material relationship to the business.

rule_text: As an officer or manager, you cannot write or create a consumer review or testimonial about your business or its products without clearly and conspicuously disclosing that you are an officer or manager.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

rule_text: You cannot use unfounded or groundless legal threats, physical threats, intimidation, or false public accusations to prevent the writing of, or cause the removal of, a consumer review or any portion of one.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of this part for a business or any person acting on its behalf to use an unfounded or groundless legal threat, a physical threat, intimidation, or a false public accusation to: (1) prevent the writing or creation of a consumer review; or (2) cause the removal of a consumer review or any portion of a consumer review.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

rule_text: You cannot knowingly make a false public accusation that a consumer review is fake or fraudulent in order to cause its removal.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of this part for a business or any person acting on its behalf to knowingly make a false public accusation that a consumer review is fake or fraudulent in order to cause its removal.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC Fake Reviews Final Rule (2024) (Federal Trade Commission, 2024-08-14).

rule_text: You cannot materially misrepresent that consumer reviews displayed on your website or platform represent most or all reviews submitted when reviews have been suppressed based on their ratings or negative sentiment.
rule_text_technical: It is an unfair or deceptive act or practice and a violation of this part for a business or any person acting on its behalf to materially misrepresent that consumer reviews displayed in a portion of a website or platform dedicated to receiving and displaying consumer reviews represent most or all reviews submitted, when reviews have been suppressed based on their ratings or negative sentiment. This section does not prohibit removing reviews that are fake, fraudulent, or violate terms of service, provided the criteria are applied consistently regardless of whether the review is positive or negative.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews

rule_text: You shall not sell, distribute, purchase, or otherwise procure fake indicators of social media influence (such as bot-generated followers, views, or likes) that you knew or should have known to be fake and that can be used to materially misrepresent influence or importance for a commercial purpose.

rule_text_technical: 'Artificial intelligence system' means a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that may influence physical or virtual environments. rule_text_technical: Each Party undertakes to adopt or maintain measures aimed at overcoming inequalities to achieve fair, just and equitable outcomes, in line with its applicable domestic and international human rights obligations, in relation to activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Israel — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225) (Israel, 2024-09-05).

Art. 10(1) covers equality and non-discrimination in AI lifecycle activities, overlapping with il-il-coei-2024-art-10-2 but focusing on the prohibition of discrimination rather than overcoming inequalities for equitable outcomes; both derive from the same Convention but address distinct sub-obligations.

rule_text: Parties should assess the need for a moratorium, ban, or other appropriate measures regarding certain uses of AI systems considered incompatible with human rights, democracy, or the rule of law.
rule_text_technical: Each Party shall assess the need for a moratorium or ban or other appropriate measures in respect of certain uses of artificial intelligence systems where it considers such uses incompatible with the respect for human rights, the functioning of democracy or the rule of law.

first_instance.law_name: Israel Signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights (CETS 225)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Israel — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225) (Israel, 2024-09-05).
Uruguay's signature of CETS 225 Art. 16(4) is functionally identical in text and obligation to the existing il-il-coei-2024-art-16-4 rule, both drawn from the same Convention.

Both rules contemplate prospective legal limitations on AI use to protect citizens from harms, but Egypt's rule is a forward-looking compliance expectation referencing a forthcoming national AI law rather than a binding present obligation, and the existing rule concerns assessing moratoriums or bans on incompatible AI uses under an existing convention.

instances.citation: Priority 4: Engagement, transparency, and value to Canadians — No-go areas
instances.notes: Both address identifying and potentially banning certain AI uses incompatible with rights or values, but the CoE Convention provision concerns assessing moratoriums/bans on incompatible AI uses as a binding obligation, while this Canadian strategy recommendation is a soft-law call to identify and publish 'no-go' capability areas without specifying criteria or binding effect.

rule_text: Parties must implement the Convention without discrimination on any ground, in accordance with their international human rights obligations.
rule_text_technical: The implementation of the provisions of this Convention by the Parties shall be secured without discrimination on any ground, in accordance with their international human rights obligations.

first_instance.law_name: Israel Signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights (CETS 225)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Israel — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225) (Israel, 2024-09-05).
Uruguay's signature of CETS 225 Art. 17 is functionally identical in text and obligation to the existing il-il-coei-2024-art-17 rule, both drawn from the same Convention.

rule_text: Each Party must establish or designate one or more effective mechanisms to oversee compliance with the Convention's obligations.
rule_text_technical: Each Party shall establish or designate one or more effective mechanisms to oversee compliance with the obligations in this Convention.

first_instance.law_name: Israel Signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights (CETS 225)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Israel — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225) (Israel, 2024-09-05).

Both rules require Parties to establish or designate oversight mechanisms to oversee compliance with the Convention's obligations, but the Uruguay/CETS 225 version uses 'should' (soft law recommendation) while the existing rule uses 'must' (binding obligation), reflecting a meaningful difference in obligation level.

Both require establishment of independent oversight mechanisms for AI, but the UNICEF guidance is a voluntary recommendation focused specifically on child rights protection, while the CoE Convention article is a binding treaty obligation for Parties to establish effective compliance oversight mechanisms.

rule_text: Parties must ensure oversight mechanisms exercise their duties independently and impartially and have the necessary powers, expertise, and resources to effectively oversee compliance with the Convention.
rule_text_technical: Each Party shall ensure that such mechanisms exercise their duties independently and impartially and that they have the necessary powers, expertise and resources to effectively fulfil their tasks of overseeing compliance with the obligations in this Convention, as given effect by the Parties.

first_instance.law_name: Israel Signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights (CETS 225)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Israel — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225) (Israel, 2024-09-05).

Both rules require oversight mechanisms to operate independently, impartially, and with necessary powers and resources, but the Uruguay/CETS 225 version uses 'should' (soft law) while the existing rule uses 'must' (binding), representing a meaningful difference in obligation level.

Both require that the oversight/supervisory body exercise its duties independently without orders or instructions from outside, though Turkey's provision is specifically about the Personal Data Protection Board and the CoE Convention rule is broader in scope.

Both require the oversight body to exercise its functions independently and impartially without direction, but the Zimbabwe rule applies to a data protection authority rather than an AI oversight mechanism under a convention.

rule_text: Parties should adopt or maintain measures to respect human dignity and individual autonomy in relation to AI lifecycle activities.
rule_text_technical: Each Party shall adopt or maintain measures to respect human dignity and individual autonomy in relation to activities within the lifecycle of AI systems.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights (CETS 225)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225) (Uruguay, 2024-09-05).

Both concern human rights obligations for AI actors in Uruguay's context, but this voluntary strategy specifically targets private sector actors and requires human rights due diligence across the AI lifecycle, whereas the existing rule addresses all parties and focuses on dignity and autonomy.

rule_text: Parties are called upon to enable, as appropriate, the establishment of controlled environments (sandboxes) for developing, experimenting and testing AI systems under the supervision of competent authorities.
rule_text_technical: With a view to fostering innovation while avoiding adverse impacts on human rights, democracy and the rule of law, each Party is called upon to enable, as appropriate, the establishment of controlled environments for developing, experimenting and testing AI systems under the supervision of its competent authorities.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights (CETS 225)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225) (Uruguay, 2024-09-05).

Both rules recommend establishing regulatory sandboxes for testing innovative AI concepts in controlled environments, but Zambia's rule is a voluntary strategy recommendation specifying both regulatory and data sandboxes for companies, while the Council of Europe convention article is a binding treaty provision using softer 'as appropriate' language.

Both rules address regulatory sandboxes and experimentation environments for AI, but the Uruguay ENAI rule is a voluntary recommendation to institutionalize such initiatives including innovation hubs, while the CoE Convention article is a binding international treaty obligation to enable controlled environments.

Both promote sandbox/controlled testing environments for AI, but the OAS rule is a soft-law recommendation also encompassing innovation labs and policy testing spaces, while the CoE Convention article is a binding treaty obligation with narrower scope.

Both enable regulatory sandboxes for testing innovative AI applications, but the Argentine rule assigns the function to the Secretariat of Digital Transformation with sectoral regulators and is a domestic executive order, while the CoE Convention provision is a multilateral treaty recommendation to Parties.

Both rules address establishment of an AI regulatory sandbox, but the Lithuanian rule is a binding statutory mandate assigning responsibility to a specific national institution under the EU AI Act framework, whereas the CoE Convention provision is a non-binding encouragement for Parties to enable controlled testing environments.

Both rules require establishment of a regulatory sandbox for AI development, but the Latvia rule imposes a binding obligation on a specific institutional body (the Centre), whereas the CoE Convention provision is a softer call on Parties to enable such environments 'as appropriate'.

Both rules call for establishing regulatory sandboxes to test AI systems, but Kenya's rule additionally recommends proactive soft-law implementation and framing sandboxes explicitly to inform a future AI regulatory framework, whereas the CoE Convention article is a treaty-level obligation with broader scope.

Both rules address regulatory sandboxes for AI, but Brazil's rule specifically requires notification of the competent authority by sectoral regulators operating sandboxes, adding a coordination/oversight obligation absent from the CoE Convention provision.

Both recommend establishing regulatory sandboxes for AI innovation, but this rule is specifically targeted at the financial sector (regulated entities, FinTechs, innovators), whereas the CoE Convention article is a general cross-sector sandbox provision.

Both rules establish AI regulatory sandboxes for development and testing of AI systems, but Italy's rule is binding and assigns joint responsibility to AgID and ACN, whereas the CoE Convention merely calls upon Parties to enable sandboxes as appropriate.

Both rules concern establishing AI regulatory sandboxes, but the CoE Convention provision is voluntary and general while Malta's rule is a binding designation of MDIA as the specific national authority responsible for operating the sandbox under Article 57 of the EU AI Act.

Both provide for regulatory sandboxes for testing AI systems in controlled environments, but Hungary's provision is a binding statutory obligation establishing a national program operated by NMHH, whereas the CoE Convention provision is a non-binding encouragement to Parties.

instances.citation: India AI Governance Guidelines 2025, Innovation Sandboxes
instances.notes: Both recommend establishing regulatory sandboxes for AI experimentation and risk management, but the India guideline is a soft-law recommendation emphasizing a flexible adaptive ecosystem, while the CoE Convention article is a treaty-level instrument encouraging controlled testing environments with somewhat different framing and legal weight.

Both rules address the establishment of sandbox/controlled environments for AI testing and experimentation; the CoE Convention is a binding instrument calling on Parties to enable sandboxes, while Ghana's rule is a voluntary recommendation to establish AI sandboxing environments.

Both provisions authorize the establishment of regulatory sandbox environments for innovative AI products or services, though Taiwan's rule is sector-specific (delegated to sectoral competent authorities) while the CoE Convention provision is addressed to Parties generally.

Both recommend regulatory sandboxes for controlled AI testing under temporary regulatory flexibility, but Zimbabwe's rule is from a voluntary national strategy while the CoE Convention article is a binding international treaty provision.
Virginia SB 1090 (High-Risk AI Act) (Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was vetoed — negative premise.

Both rules call for regulatory sandboxes enabling controlled AI experimentation under regulatory supervision, but the CoE Convention (binding treaty) frames it as a Party-level obligation with more formal language, while this Colombian draft bill is a voluntary/soft-law recommendation with less specificity on scope and conditions.

Both address liability and conditions within AI regulatory sandboxes, but the Chile bill specifically addresses third-party damages during experimentation while the CoE Convention provision focuses on enabling sandbox environments more broadly; additionally, Chile's rule is from a draft/voluntary instrument.

Both rules establish regulatory sandbox frameworks for testing AI systems in controlled environments, but the Spanish draft specifically places the sandbox under AESIA oversight and targets high-risk AI systems, while the CoE instrument is a general call for parties to enable sandboxes; the Spanish rule is also from a soft law draft rather than a binding treaty.

Both require establishment of AI regulatory sandboxes, but Germany mandates the Federal Network Agency to establish and operate at least one sandbox under the specific Articles 57-58 of the EU AI Regulation, while the CoE Convention provision is a general encouragement to parties.

Both address regulatory sandboxes for innovation, but the Mauritius rule focuses specifically on the Fintech space including bank account and licensing timeframes, while the CoE Convention provision is a general AI sandbox framework.

Both recommend regulatory sandboxes for testing AI laws and regulations in controlled environments, but the UNESCO rule is a voluntary recommendation encompassing both policy prototypes and sandboxes, while the CoE Convention article is a binding obligation on Parties to enable such environments.

rule_text: Organizations should establish service limitations based on user application scenarios, cut features that may be abused, and not provide services beyond the preset scope (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended to establish service limitations according to users' actual application scenarios and cut AI systems' features that might be abused; AI systems should not provide services that go beyond the preset scope.

first_instance.law_name: China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260, 2024)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260) (China, 2024-09-09).

Both rules address preventing misuse/abuse of AI systems (including generative AI), but this FSA Discussion Paper rule is a soft-law, finance-sector-specific recommendation focused on financial crime vectors (phishing, deepfakes), whereas cn-cn-aisafety-2024-4-2-2-a is a broader binding obligation to cut abusable features across sectors.

Both address circumvention of built-in AI safety/control mechanisms, but the Chinese rule is directed at organizations establishing service limitations, while this Russian rule targets users who attempt to bypass security measures.

rule_text: Developers should evaluate the readiness of AI products and services based on the legal and risk management requirements of target markets (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that developers evaluate the readiness of AI products and services based on the legal and risk management requirements of the target markets.

first_instance.law_name: China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260, 2024)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260) (China, 2024-09-09).

Both recommend evaluation/assessment mechanisms to support responsible AI use, but the Morocco roadmap is a high-level voluntary recommendation with no specified methodology, while the Chinese guideline specifies evaluating readiness based on legal and risk management requirements of target markets.

Both address a review/selection process before deploying AI systems, but this rule is a binding obligation specific to health care AI device deployers, while the existing rule is a voluntary recommendation for developers evaluating market readiness.

rule_text: Developers should formulate clear test rules and methods (manual, automated, hybrid) and use technologies such as sandbox simulations to fully test and verify models (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that developers formulate clear test rules and methods, including manual testing, automated testing, and hybrid testing, and utilize technologies such as sandbox simulations to fully test and verify models.

first_instance.law_name: China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260, 2024)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260) (China, 2024-09-09).

Both recommend testing AI systems with defined methods and monitoring, but the Argentine guidance emphasizes validation-stage performance metrics and event logging while the Chinese rule focuses on test rules, methods, and sandbox simulations; both are soft law recommendations but differ in framing and specifics.

Both rules address the need to describe methodology for developing and validating AI modifications/tests, but the FDA guidance specifically targets the PCCP modification protocol for medical device software functions in a regulatory submission context, while the Chinese rule broadly covers test rules and sandbox simulation methods for AI products generally.

Both recommend regular vulnerability/security testing and risk management for AI systems, but this rule targets governments conducting audits on systems and data assets within AI/data governance frameworks, while the existing rule focuses on developers using sandbox simulations and test methods; scope and actor differ.

Both call for developing standardised testing tools and benchmarks for AI systems, but the ASEAN rule is a soft-law recommendation for regionally applicable Gen AI evaluation metrics reflecting linguistic and cultural diversity, while the Chinese rule is a binding requirement for developers to use specific test methods including sandbox simulations.

Both address defining test methods and procedures for AI/ML systems, but this rule is specific to medical device contexts requiring clinical/risk-based justification for performance metrics and acceptance criteria, whereas the existing rule is a general AI safety recommendation about test rules and sandbox simulations.

Both require testing AI systems in realistic or simulated scenarios before deployment, but the existing rule covers developers broadly with sandbox/automated testing methods, while this rule is a voluntary government procurement recommendation focused on agency demonstrations of vendor AI systems.

Both require testing AI systems using defined methods, but the Brazilian rule specifies binding reliability testing (robustness, accuracy, precision, coverage) for high-risk AI by sector, while the Chinese rule recommends formulating test rules and using sandbox simulations more broadly.

Both address security validation and testing of AI systems by external or independent means, but this voluntary EU Code provision specifically focuses on security assurance via independent external validation including network, physical, software, and insider threat mitigations, while the Chinese standard broadly addresses test rules and sandbox simulations.

Both rules require adversarial/comprehensive testing of AI systems, but this new rule is a soft-law guideline clarifying a binding EU AI Act obligation for systemic-risk GPAI models specifically requiring red-teaming per standardized protocols, while the CN rule is a voluntary recommendation for general AI developers using sandbox simulations.

Both address structured testing of AI systems across the lifecycle, but this RBI recommendation specifically mandates red teaming as the testing methodology with risk-proportionate frequency for regulated financial entities, whereas the Chinese guideline recommends broader test rules and sandbox simulations.

Both rules require government/developers to build or formulate systems/methods for evaluating AI safety and security, but the Japanese rule focuses on a government-level institutional capacity for model safety, appropriateness, and security evaluations, whereas the Chinese rule targets developer-level test rules and sandbox simulations for product testing.

Both recommend pre-deployment testing of AI systems with defined methods, but the Singapore guideline is specific to agentic AI risks (task accuracy, policy compliance, tool call correctness) while the Chinese standard addresses broader test rules and sandbox simulations; both are voluntary/recommendation instruments.

Both require pre-deployment testing and ongoing monitoring of AI systems, but the Hawaii rule is sector-specific (insurance) and voluntary, while the Chinese rule is a developer-focused recommendation covering broader testing methods including sandbox simulations.

Both require documented testing, evaluation, and validation of AI systems consistent with best practices, but the Illinois bill is a voluntary/soft-law deployer-facing recommendation while the Chinese rule is a developer-facing recommendation with more specific methodology (sandbox simulations, manual/automated/hybrid methods).

Both require establishing test rules and methods for AI safety, but this rule is a voluntary recommendation from NJ's OIT focused on cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities, while the Chinese standard is also recommendatory but broader in scope and covers sandbox simulations and hybrid testing methods.

Both rules require testing AI system changes in a pre-production or sandbox environment before deployment, but this rule is a binding legal mandate tied to a licensing regime while the Chinese rule is a recommendation.
Washington H 1833 — Artificial Intelligence Grant Program (Washington) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both require testing AI systems against diverse datasets and scenarios to identify potential issues, but Malaysia's guideline emphasizes new data and bias identification while China's rule focuses on test rules/methods and sandbox simulations.

Both require testing AI systems using defined methods, but this rule is specifically focused on watermarking techniques for synthetic content detection accuracy and robustness, while the Chinese rule covers general test rules and sandbox simulations.

Both recommend broad pre-release testing of AI systems including in real-world conditions, but UNESCO's rule is a voluntary international recommendation focused on human rights risk, while the Chinese standard is a technical recommendation about test methods and sandbox simulations.

rule_text: Service providers should assess the impact of AI products on users to prevent harm to users' mental and physical health, life, and property (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that service providers assess the impact of AI products on users, preventing harm to users' mental and physical health, life, and property.

first_instance.law_name: China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260, 2024)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260) (China, 2024-09-09).

Both recommend mechanisms to detect and remediate AI performance issues and unintended harms, but the UAE rule is specific to financial institutions and explicitly adds bias detection and reporting as distinct obligations.

Both recommend ongoing monitoring of AI system performance and rectifying harmful or unacceptable behavior, but this rule is a US government procurement recommendation focused on vendor contractual obligations and performance standards, while the existing rule is a Chinese developer/service-provider recommendation about user harm prevention.

Both rules require assessing AI system impacts on user/patient health and safety, but the Hawaii rule is a binding state healthcare-specific mandate covering biases, data confidentiality, and patient rights through regular performance evaluations, while the Chinese rule is a voluntary recommendation for general service providers to assess user harm.

Both require ongoing monitoring of AI impact on users' health, but Hawaii's rule is narrowly focused on medical necessity and prior authorization decisions in insurance contexts, while the Chinese rule addresses broader user health impacts as a general service-provider recommendation.

Both rules require safety assessment of AI systems to prevent harm to users before deployment/use with humans, but this rule is specific to documented pre-deployment safety testing in a human research participants context under Illinois H 5003, while the Chinese rule is a general recommendation for service providers to assess impact on users' mental and physical health.

Both rules require periodic assessment of AI system impacts on user harm and risk mitigation, but Louisiana H 791 is a binding state law mandating monthly chatbot-specific risk assessments against attorney general metrics, while the Chinese guideline is a voluntary recommendation for general AI service providers to assess user impact.

Both rules address preventing harm from AI systems through safety mechanisms, but Missouri S 1474 is a voluntary/soft-law bill focusing on developers, manufacturers, and owners prioritizing safety to prevent direct harm, while the Chinese rule addresses service providers assessing impact on users' health and property; scope, actor, and framing differ meaningfully.

Both require assessing AI system impacts on users/patients and implementing corrective actions, but this rule is binding and specific to health care AI devices with documentation requirements, while the existing rule is a voluntary recommendation for general service providers.

rule_text: General users should review contracts/service terms before use to understand functions, limitations, and privacy policies, and set reasonable expectations about AI judgments (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that before using an AI product, users carefully review the contract or service terms to understand its functions, limitations, and privacy policies, accurately recognize the limitations of AI in judgments and decisions, and set reasonable expectations.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260) (China, 2024-09-09).

rule_text: General users should enhance awareness of personal information protection and avoid entering sensitive information unnecessarily (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that general users enhance awareness of personal information protection and avoid entering sensitive information unnecessarily.

first_instance.law_name: China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260, 2024)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260) (China, 2024-09-09).

Both place responsibilities on end users to protect personal information when using AI, but the AIGE rule frames this as a compliance obligation with regulations, while the Chinese rule is a narrower awareness-focused recommendation about avoiding entering sensitive information.

rule_text: General users should be informed about data processing practices and avoid using products not in conformity with privacy principles (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that general users be informed about data processing practices and avoid using products that are not in conformity with privacy principles.

first_instance.law_name: China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260, 2024)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260) (China, 2024-09-09).

Both address consumers' right to be informed about how AI uses their personal data, but the AIGE rule is broader, covering algorithmic use of personal data for offers/recommendations, while the Chinese rule focuses on awareness of data processing practices and product conformity with privacy principles.

rule_text: General users should be aware of the potential impact of AI products on minors and take steps to prevent addiction and excessive use (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that general users be aware of the potential impact of AI products on minors and take steps to prevent addiction and excessive use.

rule_text: If you operate a large online platform, you must develop and implement procedures using state-of-the-art techniques to identify and remove materially deceptive content depicting candidates, elections officials, or elected officials when reported and posted within the applicable election time period, where you know or act with reckless disregard that the content meets the statutory criteria.
rule_text_technical: Any large online platform shall develop and implement procedures for the use of state-of-the-art techniques to identify and remove materially deceptive content if: (1) the content is reported pursuant to Section 20515(a); (2) the content portrays a candidate, elections official, or elected official as doing or saying something they did not do or say that is reasonably likely to harm reputation/electoral prospects or undermine confidence in election outcomes; (3) the content is posted during the applicable time period in subdivision (e); and (4) the platform knows or acts with reckless disregard for the fact that the content meets these requirements.

first_instance.law_name: Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2655 (Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act) (California, 2024-09-17).

Both are California 2024 laws targeting materially deceptive AI-generated election content, but AB2655 imposes duties on large online platforms to identify and remove such content, while Elections Code §20012(b)(1) imposes a direct prohibition on distributors who act with malice — different actors, different legal mechanism, and a malice requirement not present in AB2655.
New Mexico H 401 — Synthetic Content Accountability Act (New Mexico) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both require platform operators to implement procedures/measures to detect synthetic media, but RI H 7954 uses a 'commercially reasonable' standard and applies to 'covered platforms' broadly, while CA AB2655 specifies 'state-of-the-art techniques' and targets 'large online platforms' for removal of materially deceptive content near elections.

Both rules require large/high-traffic online platforms to block or remove materially deceptive AI-generated election content, but Vermont H.846 is a voluntary/soft-law recommendation limited to specified pre/post-election periods, whereas California AB 2655 is a binding mandate with specific procedural requirements and timelines.
West Virginia H 4496 — Artificial Intelligence (West Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: If you operate a large online platform and determine reported content qualifies for removal, you must remove the post no later than 72 hours after the report.
rule_text_technical: If a post is determined to meet the requirements for removal pursuant to subdivision (a), any large online platform shall remove the post upon that determination, but no later than 72 hours after a report is made pursuant to Section 20515(a).

first_instance.law_name: Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2655 (Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act) (California, 2024-09-17).

Both rules require platforms to take action (blocking/removal) on reported synthetic/AI-generated content within a defined timeframe, but this rule mandates temporary blocking pending determination of sexually explicit digital identity theft, whereas AB2655 requires full removal within 72 hours of a qualifying determination in the electoral context.

Both require platform removal of reported synthetic/deepfake content, but Texas requires removal immediately upon notice of explicit deep fake material while California sets a 72-hour window after determining content qualifies, and Texas also requires removal of known copies.

Both impose takedown deadlines for synthetic/deepfake content after a complaint, but the Indian rule requires removal within 24 hours for non-consensual deepfakes of identifiable real persons upon complaint by the depicted individual, while the California rule requires removal within 72 hours for materially deceptive content on large platforms.

Both rules require large online platforms to remove synthetic/digital replica content, but this rule is triggered by a qualifying court order or judgment and also requires reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies, whereas AB 2655 requires removal within 72 hours of a platform's own determination following a report.

rule_text: If you operate a large online platform, you must use state-of-the-art techniques to identify and remove identical or substantially similar materially deceptive content that you previously removed, when reposted during the applicable election time period.
rule_text_technical: Any large online platform shall identify, using state-of-the-art techniques, and remove, upon discovering or being alerted to the posting or reposting of, any identical or substantially similar materially deceptive content that the platform had previously removed pursuant to this chapter, provided that this removal occurs during the applicable time period in subdivision (e).

first_instance.law_name: Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2655 (Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act) (California, 2024-09-17).

Both rules require platforms to proactively identify and remove identical or similar AI-generated harmful content that has not been individually reported, though this rule applies to sexually explicit digital identity theft material while AB2655 targets materially deceptive election-related content.

Both rules require platforms to make reasonable efforts to identify and remove identical or substantially similar copies of reported synthetic intimate imagery after a valid removal request, though Florida's rule applies specifically to altered sexual depictions while California's focuses on election-related deepfakes.

Both require platforms to prevent re-upload or redistribution of confirmed synthetic explicit/deepfake content after removal, but Texas frames this as implementing measures against 'the same material' while California specifically uses state-of-the-art techniques to identify and remove 'identical or substantially similar' content.

Both rules require blocking/removing not just the original reported content but also identical or substantially similar versions, but the NC rule applies to any pornographic image removed under the law (broader than political deepfakes) and imposes a proactive blocking/redistribution prevention obligation, while CA AB2655 focuses on large online platforms identifying and removing substantially similar materially deceptive content in an election context.

Both rules require platforms to prevent re-upload of identical or substantially similar removed content, but the existing rule is a binding mandate on large online platforms for materially deceptive political media, whereas this new rule is a voluntary recommendation under a proposed bill targeting nonconsensual intimate images using hash-based or equivalent identifiers.

Both rules require platforms to block re-upload of identical or substantially similar removed content, but the South Carolina bill applies to pornographic images broadly while California's AB 2655 targets materially deceptive synthetic media in political contexts, and the SC bill is a proposed state statute whereas CA AB 2655 is enacted law.

rule_text: If you are a candidate for elective office and you distribute digital content portraying yourself doing or saying something you did not do or say during the regulated election period, you must include a clear disclosure stating 'This [image/audio/video] has been manipulated' in the prescribed format.
rule_text_technical: A candidate for elective office who, during the time period set forth in subdivision (e), portrays themself as doing or saying something the candidate did not do or say must include a disclosure stating 'This _____ has been manipulated' (filled with image, audio, or video), formatted per subdivision (d)(2): for visual media, in size easily readable and no smaller than the largest font in the media (and for video, displayed for the entire duration); for audio-only, clearly spoken at the beginning, end, and at intervals not greater than two minutes if longer than two minutes.

first_instance.law_name: Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2655 (Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act) (California, 2024-09-17).

Both rules require candidates using manipulated/deceptive media portraying themselves to include a disclosure, but this rule specifies the exact disclosure language format ('This [image/audio/video] has been manipu...') under a different Elections Code section from the same jurisdiction.

Both rules create a disclosure-based safe harbor from deepfake prohibitions in election communications, but Montana's rule applies broadly to AI-generated election content while California's AB2655 rule is specifically tied to candidates distributing content portraying themselves.

Both require a disclosure when distributing AI-generated/synthetic election media, but RI's rule is a general safe-harbor condition for all distributors while CA's targets candidates specifically portraying themselves, and the exact disclosure language and scope differ.

Both require a disclosure when distributing AI-manipulated/generated political media, but California's rule applies specifically to candidates distributing content portraying themselves, while Rhode Island's rule applies broadly to any distributor of prohibited synthetic media in elections.

rule_text: If the materially deceptive content is in a non-English language, you must provide the candidate disclosure and platform label in both that language and English.
rule_text_technical: This chapter applies to materially deceptive content regardless of the language used. If the language is not English, the disclosure required by Section 20513(d) and the label required by Section 20514 must appear in the language used as well as in English.

first_instance.law_name: Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2655 (Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act) (California, 2024-09-17).

Both rules require that manipulation disclosures appear in the non-English language used in the advertisement or solicitation, but this rule is sourced from a different Elections Code section and a different statute than the existing AB2655 rule.

Both require disclosures to appear in the language used in the communication for AI-manipulated political content, but this rule applies to all election advertisements while CA AB2655 is specifically about materially deceptive content and also requires both the non-English and English languages.

Both require that deepfake/materially deceptive political content disclosures be provided in the same non-English language as the advertisement, but CA AB2655 is an enacted binding law requiring both that language and English, while NJ A4163 is a proposed bill with a comparable but independently drafted language-matching requirement.

rule_text: A plaintiff alleging a violation of this section must prove the violation by clear and convincing evidence.
rule_text_technical: In any civil action alleging a violation of this section, the plaintiff shall bear the burden of establishing the violation through clear and convincing evidence.

first_instance.law_name: Elections: Deceptive AI Content

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California AB 2839 (Election Deepfakes — Individual Liability) (California, 2024-09-17).
