rule_text: You have a defence to the offence if you can prove on a balance of probabilities that you did not know and had no reason to believe that the candidate did not in fact say or do the thing depicted.
rule_text_technical: In proceedings for an offence under section 61MA(1), it is a defence for the person charged to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the person did not know and had no reason to believe that the candidate did not in fact say or do the thing mentioned in subsection (1)(d) and (e).

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

rule_text: Authorities should implement transparency requirements and volatility control mechanisms (such as circuit breakers) to mitigate AI-driven market correlation vulnerabilities, supported by improved data and surveillance mechanisms (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that regulatory authorities consider enhanced transparency requirements and market exchanges adopt circuit breaker mechanisms to mitigate vulnerabilities associated with AI-driven market correlations, complemented by better data and surveillance mechanisms enabling consistent monitoring to take pre-emptive action against the accumulation of correlation-related imbalances.

first_instance.law_name: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (FSB Report)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FSB — Financial Stability Implications of AI (2024) (Financial Stability Board, 2024-11-14).

rule_text: Financial authorities should invest in skills and resources, including data science and IT capabilities, necessary to critically assess AI developments and financial institutions' use of AI (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that financial authorities make adequate investments in skills and resources necessary to critically assess AI developments and FIs' use of AI, addressing organisational skills deficiencies in data science and essential IT capabilities, since inadequate investment could itself pose risks to the financial system.

first_instance.law_name: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (FSB Report)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FSB — Financial Stability Implications of AI (2024) (Financial Stability Board, 2024-11-14).

Both recommend that financial regulators invest in AI skills, training, and institutional capacity, but this rule also proposes a dedicated AI institute within the RBI, going beyond the FSB's general skills and resources recommendation.

The 2024 FSB rule requires financial authorities to invest in skills and IT capabilities to assess AI, while this 2025 rule recommends fostering data sharing on AI usage across domestic sectoral and non-financial authorities; both are FSB soft-law recommendations addressing financial-authority capacity for AI oversight but with different specific mechanisms.

rule_text: This Directive applies to products, including software and AI systems, placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026.
rule_text_technical: This Directive shall apply to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).
EU AI Liability Directive (withdrawn) (European Union) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules define the material scope of an EU instrument applying to products (including software/digital elements) placed on the market, but CRA 2024/2847 focuses on cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements while PLD 2024 addresses product liability, and their specific scope criteria and thresholds differ meaningfully.

rule_text: This Directive does not apply to free and open-source software developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity.
rule_text_technical: This Directive does not apply to free and open-source software that is developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both exempt free and open-source software/AI from scope unless placed on the market commercially, but the Chilean bill adds a high-risk AI system condition for the market-placement exception and is a voluntary draft, whereas the EU PLD is a binding directive.

rule_text: This principle does not affect the applicability of applicable data protection law, including privacy rights, electronic communications protections, and law enforcement data handling requirements.
rule_text_technical: This Directive does not affect the applicability of Union law on the protection of personal data, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and Directives 2002/58/EC and (EU) 2016/680.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: For the purposes of product liability, 'product' includes software, digital manufacturing files, electricity, and raw materials, whether or not integrated into another movable or immovable.
rule_text_technical: 'product' means all movables, even if integrated into, or inter-connected with, another movable or an immovable; it includes electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and software.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules extend product liability frameworks to software/AI (EU PLD broadly includes software and AI systems as 'products'); Arizona H 2737 specifically classifies chatbots as products under Arizona's product liability statute, a narrower and jurisdiction-specific application of the same underlying concept.

rule_text: A 'related service' is a digital service integrated into or interconnected with a product such that its absence would prevent the product from performing one or more of its functions.
rule_text_technical: 'related service' means a digital service that is integrated into, or inter-connected with, a product in such a way that its absence would prevent the product from performing one or more of its functions.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: A product remains within the manufacturer's control where the manufacturer authorises or consents to integration/modification of components (including software updates), or retains the ability to supply software updates or upgrades directly or via a third party.
rule_text_technical: 'manufacturer's control' means that the manufacturer performs or authorises/consents to integration, inter-connection or supply of a component (including software updates or upgrades) or modification of the product, or has the ability to supply software updates or upgrades themselves or via a third party.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: A modification (including via software update or AI continuous learning) is 'substantial' if it is so designated under product safety law or if it changes the product's performance, purpose or type beyond the initial risk assessment and alters its hazard or risk profile.
rule_text_technical: 'substantial modification' means a modification of a product after placing on the market or putting into service that is considered substantial under relevant Union or national product safety rules, or, absent such rules, changes the product's original performance, purpose or type without being foreseen in the initial risk assessment and changes the nature of the hazard, creates a new hazard or increases the level of risk.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules address what constitutes a 'material change' or modification to an AI/product, but this bill focuses on intended use by the developer as the baseline for misuse determinations in product liability, while the EU PLD rule defines 'substantial modification' for safety/liability purposes.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to compensation for damage caused by a defective product, including software and AI systems.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that any natural person who suffers damage caused by a defective product is entitled to compensation in accordance with this Directive.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both provide individuals a right to compensation for damage caused by data processing contraventions, but the DIFC rule is grounded in data protection law (Controller/Processor liability) rather than product liability for defective products, and operates in a different legal framework (DIFC Court).

Both establish a right to compensation for damages caused by AI/defective products, but the Brazilian rule explicitly covers patrimonial, moral, individual, and collective damages and targets providers/operators, while the EU PLD focuses on defective products and individual compensation without the collective damage dimension.

Both grant individuals the right to damages from courts for harms caused, but the Singapore rule is specific to online harmful activity victims and includes loss of future earnings, while the EU PLD rule covers defective products including AI systems.

Both establish deployer/manufacturer liability for AI-caused damage, but Vietnam's rule imposes strict liability on deployers even when compliant with regulations and includes a right of recourse, whereas the EU PLD focuses on defective products and requires proof of defectiveness.

Both provide individuals a right to compensation for violations causing damage, but Thailand's rule is grounded in data protection law (PDPA) rather than product liability, and explicitly adds court-ordered compliance measures and injunctive relief as remedies alongside compensation.

Both provide a right to compensation for harm caused by AI/defective products, but the Russian rule is grounded in general civil legislation without specifying defectiveness standards, causation presumptions, or damage categories, and adds an 'unlawful use' threshold absent from the EU PLD.

Both establish product liability for AI systems, but the new rule specifically targets high-impact or generative AI developers and conditions liability on failure to exercise reasonable care, while the EU PLD focuses on defective products broadly and strict liability without a negligence standard.
Maryland H 712 — Product Liability and Artificial Intelligence (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules establish liability for harm caused by defective AI systems, but the Missouri bill (a voluntary/soft law instrument) frames liability specifically around design, construction, or instructions defects with a proximate cause standard, while the EU PLD 2024 is a binding instrument providing broader compensation rights for damage caused by defective products including AI systems.

Both establish product liability for harm caused by defective AI/software, but the Ohio rule is from a state bill (non-binding in the sense of being a proposed state law) focusing on design, construction, or instructions defects, while the EU PLD is a binding EU regulation with broader scope covering all defective products including software and AI systems.

Both provide individuals a right to compensation for damages caused by AI systems, but this Bahrain provision is from a proposed (voluntary/unenacted) law and specifies joint liability among programmer, processor, and developer, whereas the EU PLD is a binding instrument with broader product defect framing.

Both grant individuals a civil right to compensation for harm caused by AI systems, but this Chilean draft law (soft law/voluntary instrument) also includes cessation of harmful acts and preventive measures as remedies, and does not limit scope to defective products as the EU PLD does.

instances.citation: Part A, Section A2.3, Consumer Right 6
instances.notes: Both establish a right to compensation/redress for AI-caused damages, but the EU PLD is a binding legal instrument with specific product liability scope while the Malaysian guideline is a soft-law consumer rights formulation with broader, less defined scope.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to compensation for destruction or corruption of data that are not used for professional purposes, including the cost of recovering or restoring such data.
rule_text_technical: The right to compensation shall apply in respect of destruction or corruption of data that are not used for professional purposes.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: Individuals have the right to compensation for death or personal injury, including medically recognised damage to psychological health, caused by a defective product.
rule_text_technical: The right to compensation pursuant to Article 5 shall apply in respect of death or personal injury, including medically recognised damage to psychological health.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: A product is defective if it does not provide the safety that a person is entitled to expect or that is required under EU or national law.
rule_text_technical: A product shall be considered defective where it does not provide the safety that a person is entitled to expect or that is required under Union or national law.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules concern defectiveness/non-defectiveness standards for products based on safety expectations and foreseeable risks, but the Illinois bill introduces a rebuttable presumption mechanism tied to risk mitigation efforts, whereas the EU PLD focuses on the safety a person is entitled to expect; additionally, Illinois S 3590 is a proposed bill (voluntary/soft law context) with different legal framing.

rule_text: When assessing defectiveness, you must take into account relevant product safety requirements, including safety-relevant cybersecurity requirements.
rule_text_technical: In assessing the defectiveness of a product, all circumstances shall be taken into account, including relevant product safety requirements, including safety-relevant cybersecurity requirements.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules require consideration of cybersecurity requirements across a product's lifecycle, but this rule mandates a proactive cybersecurity risk assessment integrated into the development process, while the PLD rule addresses cybersecurity in the context of post-market defectiveness assessment.

rule_text: When assessing defectiveness, you must take into account the reasonably foreseeable effects on the product of other products that can be expected to be used together with it, including by means of interconnection.
rule_text_technical: In assessing the defectiveness of a product, all circumstances shall be taken into account, including the reasonably foreseeable effect on the product of other products that can be expected to be used together with the product, including by means of inter-connection.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: When assessing defectiveness, you must take into account the moment the product was placed on the market or, where the manufacturer retains control over the product (e.g. via updates), the moment it left the manufacturer's control.
rule_text_technical: In assessing defectiveness, all circumstances shall be taken into account, including the moment in time when the product was placed on the market or put into service or, where the manufacturer retains control over the product after that moment, the moment in time when the product left the control of the manufacturer.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You are liable as the manufacturer of a defective product, including where you are a developer or producer of software or an AI system provider.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that the manufacturer of a defective product is liable for damage in accordance with this Directive; a developer or producer of software, including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, shall be treated as a manufacturer.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules establish liability for damage caused by AI/data processing, but this DIFC rule is specific to Controllers and Processors under data protection law (with a carve-out limiting Processor liability to failures of specific obligations), whereas the EU PLD rule addresses product manufacturer liability more broadly.

Both rules impose liability on chatbot/AI system providers as product manufacturers, but this Illinois rule applies strict liability specifically to chatbots causing user injury, whereas the EU PLD applies broader product liability to AI system providers without the strict-liability framing.

Both establish controller/provider liability for damages caused by their processing or products, but the GDPR rule specifically allocates liability between controllers and processors based on GDPR infringement rather than product defect.

Both address liability frameworks for AI outcomes attributed to natural or legal persons; UNESCO recommends developing such frameworks as a policy matter and explicitly rejects legal personhood for AI, while the EU PLD is a binding rule imposing manufacturer liability for defective AI products.

rule_text: You are liable as the manufacturer of a defective component (including software components and related services) that is integrated into or interconnected with a product within the manufacturer's control and causes that product to be defective.
rule_text_technical: The manufacturer of a defective component is liable where that component was integrated into, or inter-connected with, a product within the manufacturer's control and caused that product to be defective, without prejudice to the liability of the product manufacturer.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: If you substantially modify a product (including via software updates or AI continuous learning) outside the original manufacturer's control and then make it available, you are treated as a manufacturer and are liable for the modified product.
rule_text_technical: Any natural or legal person that substantially modifies a product outside the manufacturer's control and thereafter makes it available on the market or puts it into service shall be considered to be a manufacturer of that product for the purposes of paragraph 1.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules impose developer-level liability on parties who make substantial modifications to an AI product, but the Illinois rule applies to deployers who make 'material and substantial changes' while the EU PLD focuses on modifications outside the original manufacturer's control before re-placing on market.

rule_text: As a defendant in a defective-product claim, you must disclose relevant evidence at your disposal when ordered by a national court following a plausible claim by the claimant.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that, at the request of a claimant who has presented facts and evidence sufficient to support the plausibility of the claim, the defendant is required to disclose relevant evidence that is at the defendant's disposal, subject to the conditions set out in this Article.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).
Maryland H 712 — Product Liability and Artificial Intelligence (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: Disclosure of evidence ordered under this Directive must be limited to what is necessary and proportionate.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that the disclosure of evidence pursuant to paragraphs 1 and 2 is limited to what is necessary and proportionate.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules allow refusal or limitation of disclosure to protect against serious harm, but the Data Act targets serious economic damage from trade secret disclosure in data access contexts, while the PLD rule requires proportionality and necessity in court-ordered evidence disclosure.

rule_text: National courts must be empowered to take specific measures to preserve the confidentiality of trade secrets when ordered to be disclosed during product liability proceedings.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that, where a defendant is required to disclose information that is a trade secret or alleged trade secret, national courts are empowered to take the specific measures necessary to preserve the confidentiality of that information when used or referred to in the course of or after the legal proceedings.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules grant courts discretion to impose protective measures for trade secrets during disclosure of AI-related information, but this New York bill applies specifically to expert testimony about AI evidence in criminal proceedings rather than product liability discovery.

Both rules protect trade secrets in the context of mandatory disclosure obligations, but the Data Act rule applies to data access requests and requires proportionate measures and confidentiality agreements, while the PLD rule concerns court-ordered disclosure in product liability litigation.

rule_text: National courts must be empowered to require evidence (including digital/AI-related evidence) to be presented in an easily accessible and easily understandable manner where proportionate.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that, where a party is required to disclose evidence, national courts are empowered to require such evidence to be presented in an easily accessible and easily understandable manner, if such presentation is deemed proportionate by the national court in terms of costs and effort.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: As a claimant, you must prove the defectiveness of the product, the damage suffered, and the causal link between them.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that a claimant is required to prove the defectiveness of the product, the damage suffered and the causal link between that defectiveness and that damage.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).
EU AI Liability Directive (withdrawn) (European Union) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both establish negligence/defect-based liability requiring proof of a causal link, but this rule specifically frames developer liability for failure to exercise reasonable care in design under a negligence standard, while the EU PLD rule establishes a strict product liability framework with the claimant proving defectiveness, damage, and causation.
Maryland H 712 — Product Liability and Artificial Intelligence (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules require the plaintiff to prove defective design by preponderance, but Vermont H 792 is a bill/voluntary instrument specific to AI developers with a 'when the product left the developer's hands' framing, while EU PLD art.10-1 is a binding rule requiring proof of defectiveness, damage, and causal link generally for products.

Both address liability and burden of proof in harm causation, but PIPL Art. 69 places the burden on the handler to prove absence of fault (reversed burden/presumption of liability), whereas the EU PLD requires the claimant to prove defectiveness, damage, and causal link.

rule_text: You cannot avoid liability for a defective product by failing to disclose relevant evidence that you are required to provide.
rule_text_technical: The defectiveness of the product shall be presumed where the defendant fails to disclose relevant evidence pursuant to Article 9(1).

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both shift or reverse the burden of proof in favor of claimants for AI-related harms, but the Brazilian rule applies a general presumption of fault (culpa presumida) for non-high-risk AI systems, while the EU PLD provision presumes defectiveness only when the defendant fails to disclose evidence.
EU AI Liability Directive (withdrawn) (European Union) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: Defectiveness is presumed where the claimant shows the product does not comply with mandatory product safety requirements (including cybersecurity) intended to protect against the risk that materialised.
rule_text_technical: The defectiveness of the product shall be presumed where the claimant demonstrates that the product does not comply with mandatory product safety requirements laid down in Union or national law that are intended to protect against the risk of the damage suffered.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both address the knowledge or discoverability standard for defective design liability, but this rule uses a negligence-based 'knew or should have known' standard at the time of leaving the developer's control, while the EU PLD rule presumes defectiveness upon non-compliance with mandatory safety requirements.

rule_text: National courts must presume defectiveness or causation (or both) where the claimant faces excessive difficulties in proving them due to technical or scientific complexity (e.g. AI systems) and shows it is likely that the product is defective or causally linked to the damage.
rule_text_technical: A national court shall presume the defectiveness of the product or the causal link, or both, where, despite disclosure under Article 9 and considering all circumstances, the claimant faces excessive difficulties (in particular due to technical or scientific complexity) and demonstrates that it is likely that the product is defective or there is a causal link.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both address heightened liability standards for high-risk AI systems, but the Brazilian rule imposes strict (objective) liability proportional to participation for high-risk/excessive-risk AI, whereas the EU PLD rule creates presumptions of defectiveness or causation to ease the claimant's burden rather than imposing outright strict liability.
EU AI Liability Directive (withdrawn) (European Union) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: Defendants have the right to present evidence rebutting presumptions of product defect or causal responsibility.
rule_text_technical: The defendant shall have the right to rebut any of the presumptions referred to in paragraphs 2, 3 and 4.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).
EU AI Liability Directive (withdrawn) (European Union) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules address rebuttable presumptions in AI/product liability civil actions, but the Minnesota bill creates a presumption *against* liability (a safe harbor for defendants), whereas the EU PLD art.10-5 gives defendants the right to rebut presumptions of defectiveness or causation that run *against* them, reflecting opposite directional burdens; additionally, this is a voluntary/bill instrument versus binding EU law.

rule_text: You can avoid liability by proving that the objective state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time the product was placed on the market or while within the manufacturer's control was not such that the defect could be discovered (development risk defence).
rule_text_technical: An economic operator shall not be liable if it proves that the objective state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time the product was placed on the market or put into service or during the period in which the product was within the manufacturer's control was not such that the defectiveness could be discovered.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both provide a liability exemption where the defendant proves it bears no responsibility for the causative event, but the DIFC rule applies to data protection contraventions by Controllers/Processors while the EU PLD rule concerns the state of scientific/technical knowledge for defective products.

Both define defenses that excuse AI/product liability, but the Brazilian rule focuses on whether the agent placed the system in circulation, employed, or profited from it, or whether the damage was caused exclusively by the victim or a third party, while the EU PLD defense centers on the state of scientific and technical knowledge at time of market placement.

Both provide exemptions from liability, but Vietnam's exemption is based on wilful fault of the injured party or force majeure, while the EU PLD defense concerns the state of scientific/technical knowledge at time of market placement.

Both create a defense or limitation on liability where dangers are known or unknowable, but this rule specifically addresses open-and-obvious dangers to ordinary users with a presumption against openness for AI, while the EU PLD addresses state-of-the-art scientific/technical knowledge at the time of market placement.

Both rules address failure-to-warn liability for AI/product developers based on knowledge of dangers, but Vermont H 792 is a bill/voluntary instrument requiring preponderance proof that the developer knew or should have known, while EU PLD art.11-1-e provides a defense based on the state of scientific knowledge at time of market placement.

rule_text: You cannot escape liability by claiming the defect arose after placing on the market if the defect is due to a related service, software (including updates/upgrades), failure to provide necessary safety updates, or a substantial modification within the manufacturer's control.
rule_text_technical: By way of derogation from paragraph 1(c), an economic operator shall not be exempted from liability where the defectiveness of a product is due to a related service, software (including updates/upgrades), a lack of software updates or upgrades necessary to maintain safety, or a substantial modification of the product, provided that it is within the manufacturer's control.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: Where two or more economic operators (e.g. a product manufacturer and an AI/software component manufacturer) are liable for the same damage, they can be held jointly and severally liable.
rule_text_technical: Without prejudice to national law on rights of contribution or recourse, Member States shall ensure that where two or more economic operators are liable for the same damage, they can be held liable jointly and severally.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both rules establish joint and several liability where multiple parties (Controllers/Processors or economic operators) are responsible for the same damage, though the DIFC rule is framed in data protection terms while the EU PLD rule is framed in product liability terms.

rule_text: A product manufacturer integrating software from a microenterprise or small enterprise may contractually waive its right of recourse against that software manufacturer for defects in that software component.
rule_text_technical: A manufacturer that integrates software as a component in a product shall not have a right of recourse against the manufacturer of a defective software component where the software manufacturer was, at the time of placing on the market, a microenterprise or small enterprise and the parties contractually agreed to waive that right.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: An economic operator's liability cannot be reduced or disallowed because a third party (e.g. a hacker exploiting a cybersecurity vulnerability) also contributed to causing the damage.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that the liability of an economic operator is not reduced or disallowed where the damage is caused both by the defectiveness of a product and by an act or omission of a third party.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: An economic operator's liability may be reduced or disallowed where the damage is caused both by the product's defectiveness and the fault of the injured person (e.g. failure to install supplied security updates).
rule_text_technical: The liability of an economic operator may be reduced or disallowed where the damage is caused both by the defectiveness of the product and by the fault of the injured person or any person for whom the injured person is responsible.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You cannot, by contract or under national law, limit or exclude your liability towards an injured person under this Directive.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall ensure that the liability of an economic operator pursuant to this Directive is not, in relation to the injured person, limited or excluded by a contractual provision or by national law.

rule_text: If you supply AI-based products or services, you must review in advance whether the AI qualifies as high-impact AI, and you may request the Minister of Science and ICT to confirm this classification.
rule_text_technical: AI business operators that supply AI-based products or services shall review in advance whether the AI qualifies as high-impact AI and may request the Minister of Science and ICT to confirm; the Minister shall provide guidelines on criteria for and examples of high-impact AI.

Both rules require advance classification review of AI-enabled products against a regulatory framework, but the Health Canada guidance is a voluntary recommendation specific to ML-enabled medical devices referencing Schedule 1 of Canadian Medical Device Regulations, while the Korean rule is a binding obligation for all high-impact AI suppliers to review classification status.

Both address proportionate risk management frameworks for AI (including inventorying high-impact AI), but the FSA paper is a voluntary soft-law recommendation for financial institutions, while the Korean law is a binding mandate requiring advance review of whether AI qualifies as high-impact.

Both require advance review and documentation of high-impact AI compliance within a defined process, but M-25-21 imposes a 365-day documentation deadline and addresses non-compliant use case discontinuation, while the Korean act focuses on pre-supply review and ministerial consultation.

Both rules address oversight of high-impact AI affecting people's life opportunities, but the Maryland rule creates a workgroup advisory/monitoring function rather than a binding pre-supply review obligation, and uses 'livelihood and life opportunities' rather than a formal 'high-impact AI' classification threshold.

Both assign a competent authority a role in maintaining or reviewing high-risk AI classifications, but Brazil's rule specifically mandates dynamic updating of the list based on defined criteria such as scale and impact, whereas Korea's rule focuses on the supplier's duty to pre-check classification and request ministerial confirmation.

Both rules require identifying high-risk AI uses and establishing criteria/thresholds, but the Korean law is a binding mandate requiring advance review and ministerial consultation, while ISO/IEC 42005:2025 is a voluntary recommendation to establish internal thresholds and escalation processes.

Both rules require agencies/suppliers to identify and inventory high-impact or heightened-scrutiny AI systems in advance of or during deployment, but the Texas rule mandates a biennial agency-level review with an inventory as part of a broader report, while the Korean rule requires a pre-supply self-review with an option to request ministerial confirmation.

Both require establishing a system of risk levels and assigning risk classifications to AI systems, but the Korean rule is a binding legal obligation to review whether AI qualifies as high-impact, whereas this is a voluntary recommendation to formulate risk factor systems internally.

Both require assigning risk ratings/classifications to models and reviewing them, but the OSFI rule is specific to internal model risk management in financial institutions with trigger-based reassessment, while the Korean act focuses on advance review of high-impact AI at the product/service level.

Both require providers/suppliers to review or self-classify AI risk before deployment and prepare documentation, but Vietnam mandates a formal classification dossier for medium- and high-risk systems while Korea allows requesting ministerial confirmation of high-impact status.

Both laws establish a government-promoted AI risk classification framework, but Taiwan's rule focuses on international interoperability and delegating framework promotion to a ministry, while Korea's rule places the obligation on AI suppliers to self-assess and query the Minister, representing different actors and mechanisms.

This Enforcement Decree provision implements and mirrors the obligation already captured from the parent AI Basic Act (Art. 33), requiring advance review of high-impact AI status before providing products/services and allowing confirmation requests from the Minister.

Both require a prior risk review of AI systems and mandate special treatment for high-risk AI, but the Korean rule is narrower (focused on suppliers checking for 'high-impact AI' classification and consulting the Minister), while the Turkish rule broadly requires risk assessment during both development and use with special measures for high-risk systems.

Both rules concern identifying/classifying high-risk AI systems that make or assist consequential decisions, but California S 719 provides a statutory definition of 'high-risk automated decision system' focused on legal or similarly significant effects on individuals, while the Korean rule requires advance review and ministerial confirmation of high-impact AI status.

Both define 'high-risk' or 'high-impact' AI systems as those assisting or replacing human discretionary decisions with significant legal or similar effects, but California S 420 is a voluntary instrument with different drafting and scope compared to Korea's binding statutory definition.

Both rules identify categories of high-impact or high-risk AI applications requiring special oversight (including healthcare), but New York A 9219 is a voluntary/soft-law instrument focused on professional expert oversight requirements, while the Korean AI Basic Act imposes a binding obligation to review whether AI qualifies as high-impact AI before supply.

Both rules define or require review of 'high-impact AI systems' used as controlling or significant factors in consequential decisions, but Vermont H 792 is a voluntary/soft-law instrument providing a definition, while the Korean AI Basic Act imposes a binding pre-supply review obligation with a ministerial confirmation mechanism.

Both rules provide a mechanism for entities to seek official guidance on whether an AI system qualifies as high-risk/high-impact, but the German rule limits the assessment to non-binding opinions from the Federal Network Agency on borderline cases for public bodies, whereas the Korean rule allows any supplier to request a ministerial determination.

rule_text: You must establish and operate user-protection measures if you supply high-impact AI.

rule_text: You must appoint a domestic representative in Korea and report the appointment to the Minister of Science and ICT, if you have no address or place of business in Korea and meet user or revenue thresholds set by Presidential Decree.

Both require designation of a domestic/local representative with notification to an authority, but GDPR targets controllers/processors not established in the EU with a written representative requirement, while the Korean rule targets AI entities with no Korean address and requires reporting to the Minister of Science and ICT.

rule_text: You face imprisonment of up to three years or a fine of up to 30 million won if you disclose confidential Committee information or use it for purposes other than your duties.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to be clearly and promptly informed when interacting with AI systems of national public administration bodies, including the purpose of AI use and how to exercise their rights.
rule_text_technical: Individuals interacting with AI systems operated by national public administration bodies, or subject to AI-assisted decisions of such bodies, shall have the right to be clearly and promptly informed that AI is being used, the purpose for which it is used, and how to exercise their rights under this Decree and applicable law.

rule_text: You must comply with the DIFC Data Protection Law if you are a Controller or Processor incorporated in the DIFC, regardless of where the actual Processing of Personal Data takes place.
rule_text_technical: The Law applies to the Processing of Personal Data by a Controller or Processor incorporated in the DIFC, regardless of whether the Processing takes place in the DIFC or not.

rule_text: You must comply with the Law if you (or any of your Sub-processors) Process Personal Data in the DIFC as part of stable arrangements, regardless of where you are incorporated.

rule_text: You must comply with the Law when Processing Personal Data of a Data Subject in the DIFC where the activities relate to offering goods/services to such Data Subjects or monitoring their behaviour in the DIFC, regardless of your place of incorporation.

rule_text: When you receive a request from a public authority to disclose or transfer Personal Data, you must exercise reasonable caution and diligence to determine the validity and proportionality of the request and shall ensure disclosure is made solely for the purposes identified in the request.
rule_text_technical: Where a Controller or Processor receives a request from a public authority (a Requesting Authority) for disclosure and transfer of Personal Data, it should exercise reasonable caution and diligence to determine the validity and proportionality of the request, including ensuring disclosure is made solely for the purpose of meeting the objectives identified in the request.

rule_text: When responding to a public authority data request, you must assess the impact on Data Subjects' rights and implement risk-mitigation measures, including redacting or minimizing the data transferred where appropriate.

rule_text: Liability for compensation is allocated as follows: a Controller is liable for any damage caused by Processing; a Joint Controller is liable only if responsible for the contravened provision; and a Processor is liable only where it breached Processor-specific obligations or acted contrary to the Controller's lawful instructions.

rule_text: The state technology and innovation policy implementing institution serves as Lithuania's national competent authority and notifying authority under Articles 28(1) and 70(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, responsible for assessing, designating, notifying, and monitoring conformity assessment bodies under the AI Act.
rule_text_technical: Pursuant to Article 28(1) and Article 70(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the institution implementing the state technology and innovation policy performs the functions of the national competent authority — notifying authority — in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the procedures established by the Minister of Economy and Innovation for the assessment, designation, notification and monitoring of conformity assessment bodies, and other legal acts regulating conformity assessment.

rule_text: You should describe how Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) has been considered within your organization and implemented throughout the MLMD product lifecycle (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: The evidence provided with an MLMD application should include a description of how the manufacturer has considered GMLP within the organization and implemented it throughout the product lifecycle, as applicable, including quality practices ensuring the PCCP change description will be realized by following the PCCP change protocol.

rule_text: Your PCCP change description should characterize the device baseline and performance envelope, list the specific pre-authorized changes, and detail the motivation, source, effect, scope, responsible party, frequency, and any anticipated labelling/UI modifications for each change (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: The PCCP change description should document the initial baseline device design and performance envelope; list specific changes proposed for pre-authorization that would otherwise be significant changes; and for each change describe the motivation/trigger, cause/source, effect on the device, where the change applies, who will make the change, planned frequency, and any anticipated modifications to the device description, labelling or user interface.

rule_text: Your PCCP impact assessment should outline the benefits and risks of implementing the PCCP, how the change protocol ensures ongoing safety and effectiveness, and the collective impact of all proposed changes on the device and clinical workflow (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: The impact assessment should consider the benefits and risks of implementing the PCCP and risk controls in place; how the change protocol will continue to ensure ongoing safety and effectiveness; and the collective impact of all proposed changes on the MLMD and on other elements of the clinical workflow, including other medical devices.

rule_text: Your risk analysis should consider, as applicable, erroneous outputs, bias, overfitting, underfitting, performance degradation, automation bias, alarm fatigue, and risks associated with the PCCP (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: The risk analysis should consider, as applicable: erroneous outputs (false positives/negatives, incorrect, delusional/confabulated, false or misleading information); bias (systematic differential treatment, including unwanted bias considering identity, technical, contextual, dataset and development factors); overfitting; underfitting; degradation of ML system performance; automation bias; alarm fatigue; risks associated with using a PCCP; and impacts of a PCCP on risk management.

rule_text: Clinical validation study descriptions should include study type/design/statistical methods with rationale, model description (including software version), independent characterization of participants, study results overall and for subgroups, and limitations (recommendation).
rule_text_technical: Clinical validation studies should be described including: type of study; design and statistical methods; rationale (relevance to intended use, comparison to standard of care, retrospective/prospective evaluation); description of the model studied (ML software version, methods, training algorithms); characterization of participants and confirmation that the study population is independent of data used for development/training/tuning; rationale for the study population (intended use, sex/gender/race/age representation, statistical considerations); study results overall and for appropriate subgroups; and limitations.

rule_text: You cannot place on the market, put into service, or use AI systems that deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative techniques exploiting psychological weaknesses, where the objective or effect is to materially distort behaviour in a manner causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm.
rule_text_technical: Article 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems deploying subliminal techniques beyond consciousness or purposefully manipulative techniques exploiting psychological vulnerabilities or biases, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Both elements (manipulative technique + material distortion causing significant harm) must be present.

Both prohibit cognitive/subliminal behavioral manipulation by AI, but the EU rule applies broadly to all actors and covers subliminal techniques and exploitation of vulnerabilities, while Montana's rule is narrowly scoped to government entities and state officers.

Both prohibit AI systems using subliminal/manipulative techniques to distort behavior, but Kazakhstan's rule is broader (no 'beyond consciousness' threshold or 'significant harm' qualifier) and applies to creation/operation rather than market placement.

rule_text: You cannot place on the market, put into service, or use AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities of persons due to age, disability, or social or economic situation in a way that materially distorts their behaviour and causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.
rule_text_technical: Article 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems exploiting vulnerabilities of a specific group of persons due to age, disability, or social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person in that group in a manner causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Exploitation must be targeted using knowledge of the vulnerability.

Both prohibit AI exploiting vulnerabilities such as age or disability to cause harm, but Kazakhstan's formulation omits the EU's additional criteria of social/economic circumstances and significant harm threshold.

Finland's § 21(2) mirrors EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(b) prohibiting exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability, or social/economic circumstances, as a direct national implementation of the EU prohibition.

rule_text: Public authorities cannot use AI systems for general social scoring of natural persons based on social behaviour or personal characteristics where the score leads to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or treatment disproportionate to the behaviour.
rule_text_technical: Article 5(1)(c) prohibits AI systems for evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups over a period of time based on social behaviour or known/inferred/predicted personal or personality characteristics, where the social score leads to (i) detrimental treatment in social contexts unrelated to the original data context, and/or (ii) detrimental treatment unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. Targeted at public authorities.

rule_text: You cannot place on the market, put into service, or use AI systems that categorise individuals based on their biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation.
rule_text_technical: Article 5(1)(e) prohibits AI systems that individually categorise natural persons based on biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Exception: labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets in law enforcement context. Applies regardless of accuracy.

rule_text: You cannot use AI systems for emotion recognition in workplaces or educational institutions, except where deployed for genuine medical or safety reasons.

rule_text: You cannot create or expand facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage.
rule_text_technical: Article 5(1)(g) prohibits AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or from CCTV footage. Targeted collection of identified persons in lawful investigations or with explicit consent is not prohibited.

rule_text: 'High-risk artificial intelligence interaction' means a generative AI interaction involving the collection of sensitive personal information (health, financial, or biometric data), the provision of personalized advice for significant decisions (financial, legal, medical, or mental health), or other applications defined by Division rule.
rule_text_technical: 'High-risk artificial intelligence interaction' means an interaction with generative artificial intelligence that involves: (a) the collection of sensitive personal information, including health data, financial data, or biometric data; (b) the provision of personalized recommendations, advice, or information that could reasonably be relied upon to make significant personal decisions, including financial, legal, medical, or mental health advice or services; or (c) other applications as defined by division rule.

rule_text: You must comply with these Measures if you use AI to generate or synthesize text, images, audio, video, or virtual scenes and provide such content to the public within the territory of the People's Republic of China.
rule_text_technical: These Measures apply to organizations and individuals within PRC territory that use AI technology to generate or synthesize text, images, audio, video, virtual scenes, or other information content and provide such content to the public (service providers); sector-specific labelling rules for news, film/TV, and online audio-visual programs apply additionally.

rule_text: You must place a clear label at the beginning or end of any short-form AI-generated text of 100 Chinese characters or fewer.
rule_text_technical: Short-form text of one hundred Chinese characters or fewer that is entirely AI-generated shall bear a clear label at the beginning or end of the text.

rule_text: You must place a label at the beginning of substantially AI-generated long-form text, and may add section-level labels where appropriate.
rule_text_technical: Long-form text that is substantially AI-generated shall bear a label at the beginning, and may additionally include section-level labels where appropriate.

rule_text: You must label AI-assisted edits that materially alter the meaning or factual content of original human-authored text.

rule_text: Any person or entity shall interpret 'AI-generated content,' 'service provider,' 'platform,' 'explicit label,' and 'implicit label' exclusively according to the definitions set out in Article 30.

rule_text: Health sector organizations must establish and implement policies governing patient access to and use of AI-powered personal assistants during inpatient services, ensuring that such policies protect health information consistent with applicable health privacy law and sector-specific regulations.
rule_text_technical: Regulations promulgated by the Board shall require each hospital, nursing home, and certified nursing facility to establish and implement policies to ensure the permissible access to and use of an intelligent personal assistant provided by a patient while receiving inpatient services; such policies shall ensure protection of health information in accordance with the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, 42 U.S.C. § 1320d et seq. 'Intelligent personal assistant' means a combination of an electronic device and a specialized software application designed to assist users with basic tasks using a combination of natural language processing and artificial intelligence, including 'digital assistants' or 'virtual assistants.'

rule_text: You must provide parents or guardians of minor patients access to the patient's health records through the same secure channels available to the patient, except when doing so would require disclosing information the patient has restricted or information requiring consent that has not been obtained.

rule_text: You cannot falsely utter, speak, write, or publish (including through synthetic digital content) words about another person that are construed as insults tending to violence and breach of the peace, or that impute unchaste acts to a person of chaste character; doing so is a Class 3 misdemeanor.

rule_text: For purposes of insulting words actions, 'synthetic digital content' is defined as digital audio, image, text, or video that realistically but falsely depicts an individual's appearance, speech, or conduct, produced by an AI system based on a foundation model.
rule_text_technical: 'Synthetic digital content' means any digital content, including audio, image, text, or video, that realistically but falsely depicts an individual's appearance, speech, or conduct and is produced by any system or service that (i) incorporates technology that uses data to train statistical models for the purpose of enabling a computer system or service to autonomously perform any task normally associated with human intelligence or perception, including visual perception, natural language processing, and speech recognition, and (ii) is based on a foundation model.

rule_text: Copyright protections under this article apply only to works of human authorship; you cannot reproduce, disseminate, or distribute such human-authored works without prior written authorization from the author or rights holder.
rule_text_technical: Article 217 restricts protection to works, artistic interpretations or performances, phonograms, broadcasts, audiovisual recordings or photographic images 'of human authorship,' and punishes with 2 to 6 years imprisonment and 30 to 90 day-fines anyone who performs unauthorized acts in respect thereof without prior written authorization of the author or rights holder.

rule_text: You cannot commit computer crimes using artificial intelligence or similar/analogous technologies; if you do, the judge will increase the custodial sentence by up to one-third above the maximum legal limit for the offence.
rule_text_technical: Numeral 5 added to Article 11 of Law 30096 (Computer Crimes Law) provides that the judge increases the custodial sentence by up to one-third above the maximum legal limit established for any offence under that Law when the agent commits the offence using artificial intelligence or similar or analogous technologies.

rule_text: You cannot intentionally disclose or threaten to disclose a private intimate image (including computer-generated or digitally manipulated images) of an identifiable individual without their consent; the depicted individual has a private right of action against you if you knew or recklessly disregarded the lack of consent, the private nature of the image, and the individual's identifiability.
rule_text_technical: A depicted individual who is identifiable and who suffers harm from a person's intentional disclosure or threatened disclosure of an intimate image that was private without the depicted individual's consent has a cause of action against the person if the person knew or acted with reckless disregard for whether (1) the depicted individual did not consent, (2) the image was private, and (3) the depicted individual was identifiable.

rule_text: You cannot publish or allow users to publish a pornographic image on your platform unless you have verified that every individual depicted was at least 18 when it was created, gave explicit written consent for each sexual act depicted, and gave explicit written consent for distribution of the specific image.
rule_text_technical: An online entity operator may not publish or allow a user to publish a pornographic image to the online entity unless the operator has verified, for each individual appearing in the image, that: (1) the individual was not less than 18 years of age when the image was created; (2) the individual provided explicit written evidence of consent for each act of sexual activity engaged in during creation; and (3) the individual provided explicit written consent for the distribution of the specific pornographic image.

rule_text: You are civilly liable to a child, the child's parent, or next friend if, as an owner or operator of an AI chatbot, LLM, character AI, or similar generative AI service, you knowingly direct a communication to a child intended to facilitate, encourage, offer, solicit, or recommend that the child imminently engage in sexually explicit conduct, production of visual depictions of such conduct, illegal drug or alcohol use, self-harm or suicide, or violent crimes.
rule_text_technical: Any owner or operator of a computer online service, Internet service, or bulletin board service, including a provider of an AI chat program, LLM AI bot, chat bot, character AI, or other application whose sole purpose is to provide responsive open-ended generative communication through AI, shall be liable to a child, parent, or next friend if the owner or operator knows at the time of directing the communication to the child that it is made with intent to facilitate, encourage, offer, solicit, or recommend that the child imminently engage in: (a) sexually explicit conduct; (b) production or participation in production of a visual depiction of such conduct; (c) illegal use of drugs or alcohol; (d) acts of self-harm or suicide; or (e) any crime of violence against another person.

rule_text: Regulators should adopt a graded AI liability framework whereby regulated entities remain liable for customer losses, but supervisors take an accommodative approach where appropriate safety mechanisms were followed, denied for repeated breaches or gross negligence.
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that regulators adopt a graded liability framework under which REs remain liable for any customer loss, but with an accommodative supervisory approach where the RE has followed appropriate safety mechanisms; this tolerant stance is recommended to be limited to first time/one-off aberrations and denied in the event of repeated breaches or gross negligence.

rule_text: If you are a municipality using an automated speed enforcement system, you must publish the locations of all safety zones where system equipment is installed on the municipality's website.

rule_text: You cannot base compensation paid for an automated speed enforcement system on the number of traffic citations issued or revenue generated; it must be based on the value of the equipment or services provided.

rule_text: You cannot, as a member of the General Assembly or as an officer or employee of a municipality or county, knowingly accept employment, compensation, or fees from a vendor that provides automated speed enforcement equipment or services to municipalities or counties (with a 2-year cooling-off period after leaving office/employment).
rule_text_technical: No member of the General Assembly and no officer or employee of a municipality or county shall knowingly accept employment or receive compensation or fees for services from a vendor that provides automated speed enforcement system equipment or services to municipalities or counties; former members of the General Assembly and former municipal/county officers and employees are subject to a 2-year post-service prohibition.

rule_text: The Department may revoke a permit or authorization for an automated speed enforcement system if an official or employee of the operating county or municipality is charged with bribery, official misconduct, or a similar crime related to the system; revoked entities cannot reapply for 1 year.
rule_text_technical: The Department may revoke any permit, approval, or other authorization granted to a county or municipality for the placement, installation, or operation of an automated speed enforcement system if any official or employee who serves that county or municipality is charged with bribery, official misconduct, or a similar crime related to the placement, installation, or operation of the system; rules shall describe the revocation process, ensure notice, and provide appeal rights, and a revoked county or municipality may not reapply for one year.

rule_text: The University of Illinois Chicago Urban Transportation Center must conduct a study evaluating the effectiveness of cameras powered by artificial intelligence in improving compliance, detecting risky driving, and reducing crashes and fatalities on North and South DuSable Lake Shore Drive.
rule_text_technical: The University of Illinois Chicago Urban Transportation Center shall conduct a study including: (1) review of City of Chicago multi-year crash data on North and South DuSable Lake Shore Drive; (2) available research on potential effectiveness of cameras powered by artificial intelligence in improving compliance and reducing crashes and road fatalities; (3) analysis of driving behavior to detect risky driving patterns; (4) assessment of psychological deterrence in reducing habitual speeding; and (5) assessment of how fatalities can be reduced using AI-powered cameras and other technical options.

rule_text: An 'automated speed enforcement system' is defined as a photographic, radar, laser, or other electrical or mechanical device installed in a safety zone designed to record a vehicle's speed and capture a clear image of the vehicle and registration plate while the driver violates speed laws.
rule_text_technical: 'Automated speed enforcement system' means a photographic device, radar device, laser device, or other electrical or mechanical device or devices installed or utilized in a safety zone and designed to record the speed of a vehicle and obtain a clear photograph or other recorded image of the vehicle and the vehicle's registration plate or digital registration plate while the driver is violating Article VI of Chapter 11 of this Code or a similar provision of a local ordinance; the recorded image must also display the time, date, and location of the violation.

rule_text: The State Superintendent of Education may convene a statewide stakeholder council to advise on AI guidance for schools; the council must include AI experts and at least two currently practicing classroom teachers and reflect the state's diversity.
rule_text_technical: The State Superintendent of Education may convene stakeholders for a statewide council to consult on the further development of guidance, resources, and other support for school districts and educators on the use of artificial intelligence in schools. The council must include individuals with expertise in artificial intelligence and no fewer than 2 currently practicing classroom teachers, and shall represent the ethnic, racial, and geographic diversity of this State across early childhood, elementary, middle, and high school settings.

rule_text: School districts incorporating Internet safety instruction must include recognizing and reporting online harassment and cyber-bullying, including the creation and distribution of false representations of individuals created by AI, such as sexually explicit images and videos (deepfakes).
rule_text_technical: The recommended Internet safety unit of instruction taught at least once each school year to students in grades 3 through 12 shall include recognizing and reporting online harassment and cyber-bullying, including the creation and distribution of false representations of individuals created by artificial intelligence, including, but not limited to, sexually explicit images and videos.

rule_text: You cannot enforce a provision in a personal or professional services agreement that authorizes the creation and use of a digital replica of an individual's voice or likeness for new performances on or after January 1, 2026, if the provision lacks a reasonably specific description of the intended uses and the individual was neither represented by legal counsel who negotiated the digital replica licensing terms in writing nor covered by a labor union collective bargaining agreement expressly addressing digital replica uses.
rule_text_technical: A provision in an agreement between an individual and any other person for the performance of personal or professional services is contrary to public policy and unenforceable, as it relates to a new performance fixed on or after January 1, 2026 by a digital replica, if all the following are met: (1) the provision allows creation/use of a digital replica of the individual's voice or likeness in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person; (2) the provision does not include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses; and (3) the individual was not represented either (A) by legal counsel who negotiated digital replica licensing in a written agreement, or (B) by a labor union whose collective bargaining agreement expressly covers digital replica uses.

rule_text: You may still enforce a digital replica provision that lacks a specific description of intended uses if the actual uses are consistent with the terms of the personal or professional services contract and with the fundamental character of the photography or sound track as recorded or performed.

rule_text: A school's bullying policy must include procedures for promptly reporting bullying (including cyber-bullying via digital replicas), with a designated school email and phone number and an option for anonymous reporting.

rule_text: If you develop a high-risk AI system, you must use reasonable care to protect consumers from any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination arising from the intended and contracted uses of the system, beginning June 30, 2026.
rule_text_technical: On and after June 30, 2026, a developer of a high-risk artificial intelligence system shall use reasonable care to protect consumers from any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination arising from the intended and contracted uses of the high-risk AI system; a rebuttable presumption of reasonable care applies if the developer complied with this section and rules adopted by the attorney general under § 6-1-1707.

rule_text: Organizations that develop high-risk AI systems must notify the national enforcement authority and any known deployers or developers of any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination without unreasonable delay and no later than 90 days after discovery.
rule_text_technical: On and after June 30, 2026, a developer of a high-risk AI system shall disclose to the attorney general, in a form and manner prescribed by the attorney general, and to all known deployers or other developers of the high-risk AI system, any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination arising from the intended uses of the system without unreasonable delay but no later than ninety days after the triggering date specified in the statute.

rule_text: Developers must disclose requested statements or documentation to enforcement authorities within 90 days and may designate such materials as proprietary or trade secret to limit public disclosure.
rule_text_technical: On and after June 30, 2026, the attorney general may require a developer to disclose the statement or documentation described in subsection (2) no later than ninety days after the request, in a form and manner prescribed by the attorney general; such disclosures are not subject to the Colorado Open Records Act, may be designated as proprietary information or trade secret, and disclosure does not waive attorney-client privilege or work-product protection.

rule_text: If you deploy a high-risk AI system, you must use reasonable care to protect consumers from known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination, beginning June 30, 2026.
rule_text_technical: On and after June 30, 2026, a deployer of a high-risk AI system shall use reasonable care to protect consumers from any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination; a rebuttable presumption of reasonable care applies in enforcement actions if the deployer complied with this section and rules adopted by the attorney general under § 6-1-1707.

rule_text: If a high-risk AI system you deployed produces an adverse consequential decision against a consumer, you must provide the consumer with clear disclosure of the decision, its basis, and their right to challenge or appeal it.

rule_text: Organizations must notify the national enforcement authority without unreasonable delay and no later than 90 days after discovering that a deployed high-risk AI system has caused algorithmic discrimination.
rule_text_technical: If a deployer deploys a high-risk AI system on or after June 30, 2026, and subsequently discovers that the system has caused algorithmic discrimination, the deployer shall, without unreasonable delay but no later than ninety days after the date of discovery, send to the attorney general, in a form and manner prescribed by the attorney general, a notice disclosing the discovery.

rule_text: If you deploy or make available an AI system intended to interact with consumers, you must ensure that each consumer is informed they are interacting with an AI system.
rule_text_technical: On and after June 30, 2026, and except as provided in subsection (2), a deployer or other developer that deploys, offers, sells, leases, licenses, gives, or otherwise makes available an artificial intelligence system intended to interact with consumers shall ensure the disclosure to each consumer who interacts with the AI system that the consumer is interacting with an artificial intelligence system.

rule_text: An impact assessment following an intentional and substantial modification must include a statement disclosing the extent to which the system was used consistently with, or varied from, the developer's intended uses.
rule_text_technical: In addition to information required under subsection (3)(b), an impact assessment completed following an intentional and substantial modification to a high-risk AI system on or after June 30, 2026, must include a statement disclosing the extent to which the high-risk AI system was used in a manner consistent with, or varied from, the developer's intended uses.

rule_text: You must classify AI systems into one of four risk categories: prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk, or minimal-risk, as defined in these Regulations.
rule_text_technical: AI systems are classified into prohibited (Art. 8 of Law 31814), high-risk (Art. 5 and Annex I), limited-risk (Art. 6, transparency obligations), and minimal-risk categories for purposes of these Regulations.

rule_text: You must treat AI systems that interact with natural persons and pose a non-negligible risk of deception or influence on user decisions as limited-risk and subject to transparency requirements under Article 20.
rule_text_technical: AI systems interacting with natural persons that are not high-risk but have a non-negligible risk of deceiving users or affecting their decisions are classified as limited-risk and subject to transparency requirements specified in Article 20 of these Regulations.

rule_text: If you are a micro-enterprise, you are entitled to simplified compliance: simplified self-assessment in lieu of full conformity assessments, reduced documentation, and a 12-month grace period from entry into force to achieve compliance.

rule_text: You must apply this guideline if you are a federally regulated financial institution in Canada, including foreign bank and insurance company branches, to the extent consistent with their Canadian business obligations.
