rule_text: You must apply MRM requirements proportionally to your institution's size, strategy, risk profile, complexity of operations, and interconnectedness.
rule_text_technical: This guideline applies on a risk-basis, proportional to the institution's size, strategy, risk profile, nature, scope, and complexity of operations, and interconnectedness such that disruptions could harm other financial institutions, the financial system, or the broader economy.

rule_text: You must maintain an enterprise-level model inventory that is comprehensive, accurate, evergreen, subject to robust controls, and updated in a timely manner including for decommissioned models.
rule_text_technical: An institution's model inventory should be comprehensive (covering models with non-negligible inherent risk), maintained at the enterprise level, accurate, evergreen, subject to robust controls, updated in a timely manner including modifications and changes, and inclusive of decommissioned models for a reasonable period.

rule_text: You must establish a model risk rating approach based on inherent model risk, supported by clear, measurable quantitative and qualitative criteria.
rule_text_technical: A risk rating approach should be implemented based on inherent model risk, supported by clear measurable criteria for each risk dimension, incorporating both quantitative factors (e.g., portfolio size, financial impacts) and qualitative factors (e.g., business use, model complexity, autonomy, data reliability, customer impacts, regulatory risk).

rule_text: You must establish a clear, documented rationale for deploying or modifying a model, articulating purpose, scope, coverage, intended use, and assessing the risk of intended usage.

rule_text: You must have controls to ensure appropriate data cleansing operations, including handling of inaccurate and missing values.

rule_text: You must deploy models in an environment with quality and change control processes that preserve model integrity and reliability.

rule_text: Data processing for research and scientific experimentation in developing AI for healthcare purposes by public entities, non-profit organizations, and qualifying private partners engaged in such research is recognized as a matter of significant public interest under applicable data protection law.
rule_text_technical: Processing of data, including personal data, by public and non-profit private entities, IRCCS, and private healthcare entities participating in research projects with such entities, for research and scientific experimentation in realizing AI systems for prevention/diagnosis/treatment, drug development, rehabilitation, medical devices, public health, and study of human physiology/biomechanics/biology, when necessary for creating data banks and base models, is declared of significant public interest under Articles 32 and 33 of the Constitution and GDPR Article 9(2)(g).

rule_text: You may process personal data, including special categories of personal data, for anonymization, pseudonymization, or synthetic data generation in healthcare research after providing the data subject with an information notice as required by applicable data protection law.

rule_text: The California State Auditor must conduct an audit of the February 2025 bar exam to evaluate its administration and how problems with the exam occurred.

first_instance.law_name: California S 47 — February 2025 Bar Exam: Audit

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California S 47 — February 2025 Bar Exam: Audit (California, 2025-10-01).

rule_text: The audit must evaluate the events that led the State Bar to use artificial intelligence to create multiple choice questions for the February 2025 bar exam, including when and by whom the decision was made, the rationale, when executive leadership became aware of the AI use, the evaluation criteria used to ensure questions were correct and appropriate, and any oversight deficiencies and their remediation.
rule_text_technical: The audit shall evaluate the events that led the State Bar to use artificial intelligence to create multiple choice questions for use on the February 2025 State Bar examination, including: (i) when the decision was made; (ii) who or what department made the decision; (iii) the rationale for making the decision; (iv) when executive leadership at the State Bar knew that artificial intelligence was used to create questions; (v) what evaluation criteria were used to ensure that the questions were correct and appropriate; and (vi) what deficiencies in oversight by executive leadership at the Office of Admissions existed, if any, and how any such deficiencies have been remedied.

rule_text: The audit must itemize the State Bar's costs arising from administration of the February 2025 bar exam (including contract, legal, and remedy costs) and compare projected savings from the new exam format against those itemized costs.
rule_text_technical: The audit shall (i) itemize the State Bar costs arising from administration of the February 2025 State Bar examination, including but not limited to costs from existing contracts, legal representation, remedies provided to takers, and any other associated costs (including money already spent, money legally obligated to be spent going forward, and other anticipated costs); and (ii) identify how much money the State Bar claimed it would save by using the February 2025 examination format and compare that amount to the total itemized costs.

rule_text: A 'photograph' under this section means any still or moving photograph, photographic reproduction, videotape, or live television transmission in which the person is readily identifiable to the naked eye, and individuals appearing only as members of a definable group (e.g., crowds, audiences, teams) generally cannot claim under this section.
rule_text_technical: 'Photograph' means any photograph or photographic reproduction, still or moving, or any videotape or live television transmission, of any person, such that the person is readily identifiable. A person is readily identifiable when a viewer with the naked eye can reasonably determine the person depicted is the complainant. If the photograph includes multiple identifiable persons, complainants must be represented as individuals rather than solely as members of a definable group; persons appearing solely due to presence at the time of the photograph and not singled out are deemed members of a definable group.

rule_text: If you are a real estate broker, salesperson, or someone acting on their behalf and you include a digitally altered image in an advertisement or promotional material for the sale of real property, you must include a reasonably conspicuous statement (on or adjacent to the image) disclosing that the image has been altered, along with a link, URL, or QR code to a publicly accessible website that includes and clearly identifies the original, unaltered image.
rule_text_technical: A real estate broker or salesperson, or person acting on their behalf, who includes a digitally altered image in an advertisement or other promotional material for the sale of real property shall include in the advertisement or promotional material a statement disclosing that the image has been altered and a link to a publicly accessible internet website, URL, or QR code that includes, and clearly identifies, the original, unaltered image. The statement shall be reasonably conspicuous and located on or adjacent to the image and shall include language indicating that the unaltered images can be accessed on the linked internet website, URL, or QR code.

Both rules relate to conformity assessment under the EU AI Act framework, but the Malta rule concerns notified body qualification requirements, while this new rule addresses avoiding duplicate conformity assessment for AI embedded in regulated products like medical devices or machinery.

Both rules concern designating/authorising conformity assessment bodies meeting Article 31 AI Act requirements, but the KI-MIG rule specifically addresses notifying authorities already designated under harmonisation legislation in Annex I Section A, while Malta's rule concerns the MDIA's notification power generally.

Both rules govern the notification/accreditation of conformity assessment bodies under the EU AI Act, but the Finnish rule specifies FINAS as the accreditation body while the Maltese rule references Article 31 of the AI Act requirements without naming a national accreditation body.

rule_text: If you are a provider (or authorised representative) of a high-risk AI system listed in point 2 of Annex III, you must register the system with the MDIA in the manner it prescribes.
rule_text_technical: The provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative shall register high-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 with the Malta Digital Innovation Authority in the manner as may be prescribed from time to time by the MDIA, including by virtue of guidelines or other binding documentation.

first_instance.law_name: Malta Artificial Intelligence Regulations 2025 (Legal Notice 226 of 2025)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malta AI Market Surveillance Regulations (Malta, 2025-10-10).

Both require pre-deployment registration/notification of high-risk AI systems with a competent authority, but Vietnam's rule covers medium-risk systems as well, uses a single-window AI portal, and designates the Ministry of Science and Technology rather than Malta's MDIA.

Both rules require providers/deployers of high-risk AI systems to register in an EU database, but the new rule explicitly simplifies the registration requirements whereas the Malta rule references full compliance with the existing Annex III registration regime without simplification.

Both require registration of high-risk AI systems with a supervisory authority and a conformity assessment, but the Malta rule specifically references Annex III point 2 systems and the MDIA as the registry, while the Turkish bill is broader in scope and does not specify a particular annex or registry body.

Both require registration of high-risk AI systems in a national/official database, but the Spain draft is a voluntary/soft-law instrument while Malta's regulation is binding, and Malta's rule specifically references Annex III point 2 systems with a designated authority (MDIS).

Malta's Regulation 8 requires registration of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III with the MDIA, which mirrors this EU AI Act recital-level obligation but is narrower in scope (only Annex III point 2 systems) and references a national authority rather than the EU database.

rule_text: The MDIA must organise awareness-raising and training activities on the AI Act tailored to SMEs, start-ups, deployers, and local public authorities.
rule_text_technical: The MDIA shall organise specific awareness raising and training activities on the application of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 tailored to the needs of SMEs including start-ups, deployers and, as appropriate, local public authorities.

first_instance.law_name: Malta Artificial Intelligence Regulations 2025 (Legal Notice 226 of 2025)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malta AI Market Surveillance Regulations (Malta, 2025-10-10).

Both rules require outreach and awareness-raising activities on AI use directed at small businesses/SMEs, but A2583 assigns this to California's Small Business Advocate for small business concerns, while Malta's rule assigns it to MDIA under a binding EU AI Act implementation framework.

Both require the designated national AI authority to carry out awareness-raising and advisory activities under the EU AI Act, but Germany additionally mandates advising public bodies on high-risk AI systems and broader innovation-promotion functions.

rule_text: The MDIA must facilitate the participation of SMEs and other relevant stakeholders in the AI standardisation development process.
rule_text_technical: The MDIA shall facilitate the participation of SMEs and other relevant stakeholders in the standardisation development process.

first_instance.law_name: Malta Artificial Intelligence Regulations 2025 (Legal Notice 226 of 2025)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malta AI Market Surveillance Regulations (Malta, 2025-10-10).

rule_text: The MDIA may impose a daily penalty of €12,000 per day on an operator while an infringement persists, in addition to or instead of the main administrative penalty.
rule_text_technical: The MDIA may, instead of, or in addition to the administrative penalty referred to in sub-regulation (1), impose on an operator who commits an infringement a daily penalty of €12,000 for each day during which such infringement persists.

first_instance.law_name: Malta Artificial Intelligence Regulations 2025 (Legal Notice 226 of 2025)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malta AI Market Surveillance Regulations (Malta, 2025-10-10).

Both set administrative fine ceilings for AI regulation infringements, but KI-MIG caps fines at €50,000 for all offences under § 15(1)-(2), while Malta's rule sets a €12,000 daily penalty in addition to a main penalty, making the scope and structure meaningfully different.

rule_text: When deciding whether to impose an administrative penalty and determining its amount, the MDIA must consider all relevant circumstances including nature/gravity/duration of the infringement, prior penalties, operator size, intent, cooperation, and mitigation actions.
rule_text_technical: When deciding whether to impose an administrative penalty and in determining the amount in each case, all relevant circumstances of the specific situation shall be taken into account, having regard to factors including the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement; prior penalties for the same or related conduct; operator size and turnover; aggravating or mitigating factors; degree of cooperation; technical and organisational measures; manner of discovery and self-notification; intent or negligence; and mitigation actions taken.

first_instance.law_name: Malta Artificial Intelligence Regulations 2025 (Legal Notice 226 of 2025)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malta AI Market Surveillance Regulations (Malta, 2025-10-10).

Both rules require the national authority to consider proportionality criteria before imposing fines, with Hungary specifying market position, financial capacity, and prior compliance history, while Malta's rule refers more broadly to 'all relevant circumstances'.

Both require consideration of multiple factors (nature, severity, intent, prior history) when determining penalty amounts, but Ohio's rule is in a voluntary bill targeting AI watermarks, while Malta's is a binding regulation with a broader administrative penalty framework.
Both require decision-makers to consider all relevant circumstances when determining administrative penalty amounts, including nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement.

Both rules require consideration of relevant factors when deciding whether to impose an administrative penalty and determining its amount, but the GDPR Article 83(2) specifies a distinct and more detailed set of factors (nature, gravity, duration, intentionality, mitigation, etc.) in the data protection context, while Malta's reg-11-4 is tailored to its AI regulations.

Both require the regulator to weigh specified factors when setting an administrative penalty, but POPIA's factors are tailored to personal information processing context and its South African regulatory framework.

Norway's Ch. 19.2 discretionary fine assessment factors (nature, gravity, duration, impact, number of affected persons) align with Malta's Reg. 11(4) multi-factor fine determination requirement, though expressed in different phrasing.

rule_text: Where the infringer is a public authority or body, the administrative penalty may not exceed €50,000 per infringement, with an additional daily penalty of up to €50 per day for ongoing infringements.
rule_text_technical: The MDIA may, after giving due regard to the circumstances of the case, impose an administrative penalty on a public authority or body, provided that such penalty shall not exceed €50,000 for each infringement and, additionally, may impose a daily penalty of €50 for each day during which such infringement persists.

first_instance.law_name: Malta Artificial Intelligence Regulations 2025 (Legal Notice 226 of 2025)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malta AI Market Surveillance Regulations (Malta, 2025-10-10).

rule_text: The MDIA must initiate proceedings within 2 years of the date the infringement is alleged to have been committed; otherwise the action is time-barred.
rule_text_technical: The initiation of proceedings by the Malta Digital Innovation Authority under these regulations shall be prescribed by the lapse of two (2) years from the date on which the infringement is alleged to have been committed.

first_instance.law_name: Malta Artificial Intelligence Regulations 2025 (Legal Notice 226 of 2025)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malta AI Market Surveillance Regulations (Malta, 2025-10-10).

Both establish a limitation period for imposing administrative fines (Finland: 5 years from breach/end of continuous breach; Malta: 2 years from alleged commission), with the same underlying concept but different time limits.

rule_text: Authorities should design AI monitoring indicators that capture AI usage across different types of financial institutions, including by financial activity, size, and regulatory status, to provide a holistic view of AI-related vulnerabilities.
rule_text_technical: Recommendation: monitoring indicators that capture AI usage across different types of FIs in terms of financial activity, size, and regulatory status, among other factors, can provide a more holistic view of AI-related vulnerabilities than data limited to individual financial sub-sectors.

first_instance.law_name: Monitoring Adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Related Vulnerabilities in the Financial Sector (FSB Report)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FSB — Monitoring AI Adoption and Vulnerabilities (2025) (Financial Stability Board, 2025-10-10).

rule_text: Authorities should collect AI monitoring data at regular intervals and adopt flexible, forward-looking approaches so data collection adapts to the rapidly evolving AI environment.
rule_text_technical: Recommendation: given the rapid developments in AI, data that are collected at regular intervals will be valuable for surveillance, as snapshots could quickly become outdated; a flexible, forward-looking approach can help ensure that data collection initiatives adapt to the evolving environment.

first_instance.law_name: Monitoring Adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Related Vulnerabilities in the Financial Sector (FSB Report)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FSB — Monitoring AI Adoption and Vulnerabilities (2025) (Financial Stability Board, 2025-10-10).

rule_text: Authorities should track the share of financial institutions adopting AI, segmented by institution size, type of use case, and AI model, to identify adoption trends over time.
rule_text_technical: Recommendation: authorities could track the proportion of FIs adopting AI, segmented by their size and type of use cases and AI models for identifying adoption trends over time.

first_instance.law_name: Monitoring Adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Related Vulnerabilities in the Financial Sector (FSB Report)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FSB — Monitoring AI Adoption and Vulnerabilities (2025) (Financial Stability Board, 2025-10-10).

rule_text: Authorities should develop aggregate metrics on supervisory findings related to AI model risk management and governance, ideally broken down by source of deficiency such as explainability, model validation, outcomes analysis, and data governance.
rule_text_technical: Recommendation: developing aggregate metrics on the number of supervisory findings related to AI model risk management and governance can help authorities monitor evolution of vulnerabilities; ideally broken out by source of deficiency (e.g. explainability, model validation, outcomes analysis, data governance).

first_instance.law_name: Monitoring Adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Related Vulnerabilities in the Financial Sector (FSB Report)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FSB — Monitoring AI Adoption and Vulnerabilities (2025) (Financial Stability Board, 2025-10-10).

rule_text: Authorities should track AI-driven financial fraud, including the number of fraud cases involving generative AI, deepfakes, synthetic identities, or fraudulent claims, and qualitatively evaluate how financial institutions use AI tools for fraud detection and prevention.
rule_text_technical: Recommendation: tracking the number of fraud cases involving GenAI, such as use of deepfakes, synthetic identities, or fraudulent claims; authorities should explore ways to qualitatively evaluate how FIs are prepared, including through leveraging AI tools for fraud detection and prevention.

first_instance.law_name: Monitoring Adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Related Vulnerabilities in the Financial Sector (FSB Report)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FSB — Monitoring AI Adoption and Vulnerabilities (2025) (Financial Stability Board, 2025-10-10).

rule_text: The Public Utilities Commission must submit any assessment of data center-related cost shifts to the relevant policy committees of the Legislature and publicly post a copy on the commission's internet website on or before January 1, 2027.
rule_text_technical: The commission shall submit an assessment completed pursuant to Section 913.22 to the relevant policy committees of the Legislature and publicly post a copy of the assessment on the commission's internet website on or before January 1, 2027.

first_instance.law_name: California S 57 — Electrical Corporations: Data Centers: Report

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California S 57 — Electrical Corporations: Data Centers: Report (California, 2025-10-11).

Both rules require the California Public Utilities Commission to submit a data center cost-shift assessment to legislative policy committees, but this new rule sets a specific January 1, 2027 deadline and uses 'should' (voluntary), whereas the existing rule from S 57 uses a similar reporting obligation with different statutory framing and timing.

rule_text: The Public Utilities Commission is authorized to assess the extent to which electrical corporation costs associated with new loads from data centers (including those supporting AI) result in cost shifts to other electrical corporation customers, including analysis of procurement costs, transmission/distribution asset costs, stranded assets, and mitigation opportunities.
rule_text_technical: The commission may assess the extent to which electrical corporation costs associated with new loads from data centers result in cost shifts to other electrical corporation customers, which assessment may include analysis of utility procurement costs to meet growing data center load demands, costs of new transmission and distribution assets including stranded assets, and identification of opportunities to prevent or mitigate substantial cost shifts.

first_instance.law_name: California S 57 — Electrical Corporations: Data Centers: Report

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California S 57 — Electrical Corporations: Data Centers: Report (California, 2025-10-11).

Both assign oversight roles to the PUC regarding utility AI/data-center energy issues, but the new rule is a soft-law recommendation splitting jurisdiction between PUC and Energy Commission for utility AI safety, while the existing rule is a binding authorization to assess cost allocation for data center loads.

Both rules direct the California PUC to assess cost shifts to other ratepayers from new data center electrical loads, but the existing rule (SB 57) is from a binding law while this rule (A 222) is a voluntary/bill instrument, and the citation and framing differ slightly.

Both involve a Public Utilities Commission role regarding data center energy load, but California's rule authorizes the PUC to assess cost allocation for data center electrical loads, while Colorado's rule establishes a process for regulated utilities to submit targeted resource acquisition applications to meet data center energy and capacity needs.

Both rules involve utility commission authority over electricity costs for large data center/energy users, but Delaware H 233 mandates creation of a separate service classification with its own tariff, while California S 57 authorizes the PUC to assess cost allocation extent without mandating a separate tariff class.

Both rules assign a public utilities regulatory body to monitor and assess energy costs and requirements related to data centers (including AI data centers), but NJ S 680 focuses on the BPU monitoring other PJM-region states for comparable clean-energy requirements and triggering automatic adoption, whereas CA S57 authorizes the PUC to assess cost allocation between data center loads and other ratepayers.

Both rules assign a utility regulatory body to assess data center electricity cost issues, but the New Jersey rule focuses on monitoring other PJM-region states' policies on AI data center electricity cost allocation, whereas the California rule authorizes the PUC to assess the extent to which data center costs are borne by ratepayers.
Tennessee S 1999 — Energy (Tennessee) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules involve a Public Utilities Commission investigating data center energy costs/loads, but Vermont's rule is broader (covering AI data centers generally with input from Department of Public Service) while California's focuses specifically on cost allocation between data center loads and other ratepayers.

rule_text: You must publish details of your suicide and self-harm prevention protocol on your internet website.
rule_text_technical: The operator shall publish details on the protocol required by this subdivision on the operator's internet website.

Both require companion chatbot operators to publish a suicide/self-harm protocol, but Connecticut S 86 is a proposed state bill (potentially not yet enacted) and California SB243 is binding law; the Connecticut rule specifies public accessibility on a website while California's framing is substantively similar but independently drafted.
Florida H 659 — Interactions With Artificial Intelligence (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Maryland H 952 — Companion Chatbots and Regulation (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both require publishing a suicide and self-harm protocol on a publicly accessible website, but Pennsylvania S 1090 is a proposed bill of unknown enactment status while California SB243 is an enacted binding law, and the Pennsylvania bill applies to AI companions specifically.

Both require publishing a safety protocol on a website for AI companion/chatbot services, but California's rule specifically concerns suicide and self-harm prevention while Pennsylvania's rule applies broadly to AI companion safety protocols.

Both require publishing a suicide/self-harm prevention protocol on the operator's website, but Vermont H 804 is a companion chatbot bill context while California SB 243 is a binding law with additional specificity.

rule_text: For users you know are minors, you must provide by default a clear and conspicuous notification at least every three hours during continuing chatbot interactions reminding the user to take a break and that the chatbot is artificially generated and not human.
rule_text_technical: An operator shall, for a user that the operator knows is a minor, provide by default a clear and conspicuous notification to the user at least every three hours for continuing companion chatbot interactions that reminds the user to take a break and that the companion chatbot is artificially generated and not human.

first_instance.law_name: Companion Chatbot Safety and Disclosure Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California SB 243 (Companion Chatbot) (California, 2025-10-13).

Both require AI services to disclose to minor users that they are interacting with AI, but Oregon's rule is a one-time disclosure obligation while California's rule requires a notification at least every three hours during continuing interaction.

Both require periodic AI disclosure to minors during chatbot/conversational AI interactions, but Iowa mandates a persistent visible disclaimer or one appearing every three hours specifically for minor account holders, while California's rule applies to users known to be minors and requires a notification every three hours during continuing chatbot interaction with no persistent disclaimer alternative.
Alabama H 325 — Consumer Protection (Alabama) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules address disclosures to known minor users interacting with chatbots, but this rule specifically requires disclosure that the user is interacting with AI, while the existing SB 243 rule requires a time-based notification every three hours during continuing interaction.

Both require clear and conspicuous periodic notifications (at least every three hours) to known minor users during continuing chatbot interactions, but Connecticut S 86 is a proposed bill while California SB243 is binding enacted law, making this a similar rather than identical match.
Florida S 2 — Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Florida S 482 — Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Florida H 659 — Interactions With Artificial Intelligence (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Florida S 1344 — Companion Artificial Intelligence Chatbots (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Florida H 1395 — Artificial Intelligence (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both require recurring AI chatbot disclosures to minor users during continuing interaction, but Georgia S 540 requires the disclosure every hour while California SB 243 requires it every three hours, and Georgia's trigger is knowing or reasonably knowing the user is a minor.

Both require periodic disclosures during ongoing interactions with minors (every three hours), but this Hawaii bill also requires disclosure at the beginning of each session and is a soft-law instrument, whereas CA SB 243 is a binding mandate focused specifically on chatbot interactions.

Both require AI disclosure to users known to be minors, but Hawaii H 2502 is a voluntary instrument requiring a clear AI disclosure at the outset, while California SB243 is a binding rule requiring recurring conspicuous notifications during chatbot interactions.

Both require periodic AI interaction notifications to minors at intervals during continuous chatbot sessions (this rule sets every three hours, matching California's interval), but this is a voluntary recommendation under Hawaii S 2788 whereas California's rule is a binding mandate.

Both require clear and conspicuous notifications to minor users during chatbot interactions, but the California rule mandates periodic notifications every three hours during continuing interactions while the Iowa rule requires a disclaimer at the beginning of each interaction session.

Both require disclosure that a chatbot is AI at the start of interactions, but Iowa H 2715 adds a 'not licensed' qualifier and applies to public-facing chatbots generally, while California SB 243 targets minor users with a three-hour interval notification requirement; Iowa's rule covers the initial disclosure only.
Kansas H 2671 — State Community Harmed by AI Technology Act (Kansas) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Louisiana H 734 — Commerce (Louisiana) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both require periodic conspicuous notifications to minor users during chatbot interactions, but this rule mandates hourly notifications from the start of each interaction while California SB 243 requires notification every three hours during continuing interactions.

Both require periodic AI reminders during continuing chatbot interactions, but Missouri sets a two-hour interval while California (SB 243) sets three hours and applies only when the user is known to be a minor.

Both require periodic notifications to users during chatbot interactions, but the California rule targets minors specifically with a 3-hour interval while this rule applies broadly at conversation initiation and at 'reasonably regular intervals' for a different disclosure purpose (age-related).

Both require periodic repetition of an AI/non-human notification during continuing interactions (every 3 hours), but the California rule is a binding law specific to minor users of chatbots, while the New Jersey bill applies to all users of AI companion interactions and is a proposed bill.

Both require periodic notifications during continuing chatbot/AI companion interactions (every 3 hours), but the California rule targets minors specifically and is binding, while this New York bill applies to all users of AI companion interactions and its status as a proposed bill with potentially voluntary framing warrants 'similar' rather than 'agrees'.

Both require periodic notifications to users during ongoing AI chatbot/companion interactions (every 3 hours), but California's rule targets minors specifically and is a binding statute, while New York A 6767 applies to all users of AI companions and its enactment status and exact scope may differ.

Both require disclosure to minor users of companion chatbots that they are interacting with AI, but California's rule mandates periodic notifications every three hours during continuing interactions while Oklahoma's rule focuses on initial disclosure; Oklahoma S 2085 is a non-binding bill.

Both require periodic conspicuous notifications to minor users during chatbot interactions, but Oklahoma's rule applies at the start of each individual session as a disclaimer while California's requires a notification at least every three hours during continuing interaction; Oklahoma's is a proposed bill (voluntary instrument) and California's is binding.

Both require a clear and conspicuous notification at regular intervals during continuing chatbot/AI companion interaction for minor users, but Pennsylvania S 1090 is a proposed bill while California SB243 is enacted, and the Pennsylvania provision targets AI companions specifically for known or suspected minors.

Both require periodic notifications during AI companion/chatbot interactions (every three hours), but California's rule applies only to known minors and concerns chatbot identity, while Pennsylvania's rule applies to all users and requires disclosure at session start plus every three hours.

Both require periodic notifications during continuing chatbot interactions reminding users they are interacting with AI, but California's rule applies only to known minors while Rhode Island S 2195 applies to all users; additionally, this is a binding state bill whereas the match is also binding but from a different jurisdiction with a narrower scope.

Both require periodic notifications during continuing chatbot/AI companion interactions (California requires every three hours for known minors; Rhode Island H 7350 applies to all users at the start and every three hours), but Rhode Island's bill is a state legislative proposal covering all users rather than California's enacted law targeting minors specifically.
Utah H 438 — Artificial Intelligence Amendments (Utah) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both require periodic AI interaction reminders for minor users, but Vermont H 804 sets a 30-minute interval while California SB 243 requires at least every three hours, and California's is a binding law whereas Vermont H 804 is a bill.

Both require periodic pop-up notifications during chatbot interactions, but this rule applies to all users (not just minors) and triggers on login, every 30 minutes, and at specific conversational events, whereas the California rule applies only to known minor users and triggers every three hours.

Both require periodic pop-up notifications to users during chatbot interactions, but California's rule targets minor users specifically and requires notification every three hours, while Virginia's rule applies to all users upon login and every 30 minutes of sustained use.
Washington S 5870 — Civil Liability for Suicide (Washington) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Washington S 5984 — Artificial Intelligence Companion Chatbot Regulations (Washington) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
West Virginia H 4770 — Artificial Intelligence Technology (West Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: Beginning July 1, 2027, you must annually report to the Office of Suicide Prevention the number of times you issued a crisis service provider referral notification in the preceding calendar year.
rule_text_technical: Beginning July 1, 2027, an operator shall annually report to the office the number of times the operator has issued a crisis service provider referral notification pursuant to Section 22602 in the preceding calendar year.

first_instance.law_name: Companion Chatbot Safety and Disclosure Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California SB 243 (Companion Chatbot) (California, 2025-10-13).

Both rules require annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention beginning in 2027/2028, but this rule (from a soft-law/voluntary bill) covers companion chatbot crisis expressions and pause durations rather than crisis service provider referrals, and uses 'should' rather than 'must', reflecting a weaker obligation and different subject matter.

Both rules require annual reporting of crisis service provider referral counts to a government body beginning July 1, 2027, but the Colorado rule reports to the Attorney General while the California rule reports to the Office of Suicide Prevention, and Colorado H 1263 is a bill (soft law) while California SB 243 is a binding statute.
Florida H 659 — Interactions With Artificial Intelligence (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules require annual reporting to a state agency on crisis service provider referrals beginning January 1, 2027, but Hawaii H 2502 reports to the Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs while California SB 243 reports to the Office of Suicide Prevention, and this Hawaii bill is a voluntary/soft law instrument rather than binding legislation.

Both rules require annual reporting to a state health authority on AI-related crisis/behavioral health metrics beginning in 2027-2028, but Hawaii S 3001 is a voluntary/soft-law instrument targeting the Behavioral Health Administration starting 2028, while California SB 243 is a binding mandate to the Office of Suicide Prevention starting 2027, with differing scope and recipient agencies.

Both rules require annual reporting to a state attorney general or oversight office on the number of times a crisis intervention/service protocol was triggered, but Illinois S 3262 is a voluntary/companion bill targeting a different state agency (Illinois AG) and likely a different platform context (companion AI) versus California SB 243's suicide prevention focus.

Both rules require annual reporting of crisis referral notifications to a state mental health authority beginning July 1, 2027, but Missouri S 1012 applies specifically to companion chatbot operators and reports to the Department of Mental Health, while California SB 243 targets AI systems more broadly and reports to the Office of Suicide Prevention; additionally, Missouri S 1012 is a bill (soft law) whereas California SB 243 is a binding law.
Utah H 438 — Artificial Intelligence Amendments (Utah) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules require annual reporting to a state attorney general office on the number of times a crisis service provider referral or similar intervention was issued, but Vermont H 804 targets companion chatbot providers and reports to the Attorney General, while California SB 243 targets AI chatbot operators and reports to the Office of Suicide Prevention, with different scopes and recipient agencies.
Washington S 5870 — Civil Liability for Suicide (Washington) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: Beginning July 1, 2027, you must annually report to the Office of Suicide Prevention the protocols you have put in place to detect, remove, and respond to instances of suicidal ideation, and the protocols to prohibit chatbot responses about suicidal ideation or actions.
rule_text_technical: Beginning July 1, 2027, an operator shall annually report to the office the protocols put in place to detect, remove, and respond to instances of suicidal ideation by users, and the protocols put in place to prohibit a companion chatbot response about suicidal ideation or actions with the user.

first_instance.law_name: Companion Chatbot Safety and Disclosure Act

rule_text: You cannot include any identifiers or personal information about users in the annual report to the Office of Suicide Prevention; the report must contain only the listed required information.
rule_text_technical: The report required by this section shall include only the information listed in subdivision (a) and shall not include any identifiers or personal information about users.

Both rules prohibit including user identifiers or personal information in mandatory reports to government bodies, with this rule applying to annual reports on conversational AI services to Colorado's Attorney General and the existing rule applying to reports to California's Office of Suicide Prevention.
Florida H 659 — Interactions With Artificial Intelligence (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Maryland H 952 — Companion Chatbots and Regulation (Maryland) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Utah H 438 — Artificial Intelligence Amendments (Utah) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Washington S 5870 — Civil Liability for Suicide (Washington) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Florida H 659 — Interactions With Artificial Intelligence (Florida) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text_technical: Any out-of-state subpoena, warrant, wiretap order, pen register trap and trace order, legal process, or request from any law enforcement agent or entity shall include an affidavit or declaration under penalty of perjury that the discovery is not in connection with an out-of-state proceeding relating to any legally protected health care activity unless the out-of-state proceeding meets all of the following requirements: is based in tort, contract, or on statute; is actionable in an equivalent or similar manner under California law; was brought by the patient or patient's legal representative.

rule_text: If you are a California corporation providing electronic communication or remote computing services to the general public, you cannot comply with an out-of-state subpoena, warrant, wiretap order, pen register/trap and trace order, other legal process, or law enforcement request seeking customer identity, stored data, usage, communication recipients, or content unless it includes the required affidavit or declaration.
rule_text_technical: A California corporation that provides electronic communication services or remote computing services to the general public shall not comply with an out-of-state subpoena, warrant, wiretap order, pen register trap and trace order, other legal process, or request by a law enforcement agent or entity seeking records that would reveal the identity of customers, data stored by or on behalf of the customer, usage, recipients/destinations of communications, or content of communications, unless the request includes the affidavit or declaration defined in subdivision (d). A corporation subject to this subdivision is entitled to rely on the representations made in the affidavit or declaration.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to apply for an address confidentiality program enabling state and local agencies to respond to public records requests without disclosing the residential location of designated health care providers, employees, volunteers, or patients, or other individuals facing public threats due to public-entity work.

Virginia H 2047 — State Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Washington S 5469 — Rental Housing Market (Washington) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both prohibit landlords from using algorithmic tools to set or coordinate rental prices, but the Washington bill focuses on the landlord's act of subscribing to or contracting with such a service, while the NY rule focuses on knowingly setting/adjusting prices using nonpublic competitor data; additionally, Washington S 5469 is a bill whose status is unclear but is treated here as a soft-law/voluntary instrument.
Wisconsin S 142 — Algorithmic Software for Residential Housing (Wisconsin) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Wisconsin A 142 — Algorithmic Software for Residential Housing (Wisconsin) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both rules prohibit using algorithmic software to set residential rental prices, but Wisconsin S 142 adds a distinct prohibition on the sale/licensing of such software to landlords, and applies only in Wisconsin, while NY S7882 focuses on the landlord's use and also covers lease renewal terms and occupancy levels.

Both prohibit using algorithmic software to set residential rental rates or occupancy levels, but Wisconsin A142 is a voluntary/soft-law bill while the New York rule is a binding prohibition, and New York's rule also covers lease renewal terms and eviction decisions.

rule_text: For purposes of this law, an 'algorithm' is a computational process using a set of rules to define a sequence of operations, and an 'algorithmic device' is any machine, device, computer program, or software that, alone or with human assistance, performs a coordinating function.
rule_text_technical: 'Algorithm' means a computational process that uses a set of rules to define a sequence of operations. 'Algorithmic device' means any machine, device, computer program or computer software that on its own or with human assistance performs a coordinating function.

first_instance.law_name: New York S 7882 — Residential Rental Dwelling Units

instances.notes: Rule introduced in New York S 7882 — Residential Rental Dwelling Units (New York, 2025-10-16).

Both laws define terms related to algorithmic devices used in rental/housing pricing, but NY S7882 defines 'algorithm' and 'algorithmic device' broadly while CA S52's 'nonpublic competitor data' is a distinct, narrower definitional element specific to competitor data inputs in rental pricing algorithms.
Kentucky H 201 — Use of Algorithmic Devices (Kentucky) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

Both define scope for algorithm/platform laws with size thresholds, but the Massachusetts rule specifies 'covered platforms' doing business in Massachusetts with a user/revenue threshold, whereas the New York rule defines 'algorithm' and 'algorithmic device' without a platform-scope provision; this is a voluntary/soft law instrument matching a binding rule, and the coverage criteria differ meaningfully.

Both define 'algorithm' for consumer protection purposes but MN H4454 explicitly includes AI systems and facial-recognition software within the definition, while NY S7882 defines algorithm and algorithmic device more broadly without that specificity.

Both laws define key terms for algorithmic/automated systems in a New York context, but this rule specifically defines 'food delivery platform' and 'delivery worker' for a gig-economy food delivery context, whereas the existing rule defines 'algorithm' and 'algorithmic device' for a broader commercial setting.

Both define algorithmic/computational processes for automated decision-making, but this rule specifically focuses on wage-setting algorithms in an employment context, while the existing rule defines 'algorithm' and 'algorithmic device' more broadly for general pricing contexts.

Both define 'algorithmic device' in the context of New York landlord rent-setting, but NY S 7882 provides a broader combined definition of 'algorithm' and 'algorithmic device' while S 9700 focuses specifically on rent advisory use with explicit mention of local or statewide rent data.

Both define algorithmic/computational systems used in platform-based work contexts, but this rule specifically targets food delivery platforms and covers assignment, scheduling, pay, and access functions, while the existing rule defines 'algorithm' and 'algorithmic device' more broadly without sector specificity.

Both define 'algorithm' in the context of New York AI/algorithmic regulation, but NY S7882 also defines 'algorithmic device' as a separate term while this bill's definition is broader and includes machine learning systems within the algorithm definition itself.

Both rules define 'algorithm' as a computational process, but NY A 4427 adds insurance-specific definitions ('external consumer data and information sources') and is a binding state law addressing a narrower insurance-sector scope, whereas s7882 defines algorithmic devices more broadly for general commerce.

Both rules define 'algorithm' as a computational process using rules to define a sequence of operations for purposes of an algorithmic pricing or device law, though this rule also defines additional terms ('consumer,' etc.) specific to the pricing discrimination context.
Tennessee S 1990 — Trade Regulation (Tennessee) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.
Wisconsin S 1140 — Algorithmic Pricing of Essential Consumer Goods (Wisconsin) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: You must comply with technology export controls and obtain required approvals before transferring core AI security technologies (including large-scale model training and autonomous network security systems) to overseas entities.
rule_text_technical: Article 18 requires that network technology R&D involving AI, including large-scale AI model training and autonomous network security systems, comply with technology export control regulations and obtain necessary approvals before transferring core AI security technologies overseas.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

rule_text: You must maintain logs of significant AI model deployments within your network infrastructure for at least six months.
rule_text_technical: Article 21(3) requires network operators to maintain logs of significant AI model deployments within their network infrastructure for a minimum of six months.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

Both rules impose retention obligations for AI-related records with specific time periods, but the NY rule requires retention for the deployment period plus five years for test results on frontier models, while the CN rule requires six months of deployment logs within network infrastructure.

Both require logging/retention of AI system operational records for security purposes, but this Chilean draft applies specifically to high-risk AI systems with a focus on information and security events during operation, while the Chinese rule mandates logs of significant AI model deployments for at least six months within network infrastructure.

Both require retention of AI system logs, but the Finnish rule applies to providers of high-risk AI systems under EU AI Act Article 19 without specifying a duration, while the Chinese rule mandates at least six months for AI model deployment logs in network infrastructure.

rule_text: The mandatory pre-deployment security assessment must evaluate model robustness against adversarial inputs, data poisoning resistance, output predictability, and alignment with cybersecurity policies.
rule_text_technical: Article 22(2) prescribes the mandatory scope of the pre-deployment security assessment, requiring evaluation of adversarial robustness, data poisoning resistance, output predictability, and cybersecurity policy alignment.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

Both require pre-deployment assessment and ongoing monitoring of AI systems, but Thailand's rule is sector-specific to algorithmic trading and adds unique requirements such as SEC approval, circuit breakers, and market disruption prevention not present in the Chinese cybersecurity rule.

Both require safety and cybersecurity standards for AI systems in critical sectors, but the Zimbabwe rule is a voluntary strategy recommendation covering multiple sectors broadly, whereas the Chinese rule is a binding mandatory pre-deployment security assessment with specific technical evaluation criteria.

Both rules require empirical assessment of AI model privacy/robustness guarantees, but this rule specifies concrete privacy auditing techniques (canary insertion, membership inference) as voluntary guidance, while the Chinese rule mandates a broader pre-deployment security assessment including robustness against adversarial inputs.

rule_text: You cannot develop, deploy, or sell AI tools designed or primarily used to conduct cyberattacks, including offensive automated vulnerability scanners, AI-assisted intrusion tools, or AI-generated phishing/social engineering systems.
rule_text_technical: Article 23(1) prohibits the development, deployment, or sale of AI tools designed or primarily used for cyberattacks, including offensive automated vulnerability scanners, AI-assisted intrusion tools, and AI-generated phishing or social engineering systems.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

Both prohibit using AI to conduct cyberattacks including phishing and hacking, but the PR rule frames it as a criminal aggravating circumstance under an existing penal code, while the CN rule is a direct regulatory prohibition on developing or deploying such tools.

rule_text: As a critical information infrastructure operator, you must segregate AI system deployments from core operational technology networks unless the AI system has passed an enhanced security assessment.
rule_text_technical: Article 27(1) requires CIIOs to segregate AI systems from core OT networks unless the AI system has passed an enhanced security assessment.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

rule_text: You must conduct post-incident reviews specifically evaluating the accuracy and reliability of AI systems used during the incident.
rule_text_technical: Article 34(3) requires post-incident reviews specifically evaluating the accuracy and reliability of AI systems used during cybersecurity incidents.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

Both require post-incident review following a security breach or incident, but CN cybersecurity amendment focuses on evaluating AI system accuracy during incidents, while CA S 468 focuses on documenting responsive actions and improving security measures after a personal data breach.

rule_text: If you process personal information using AI systems, you must protect such information against model inversion attacks, membership inference attacks, and other AI-specific privacy threats through appropriate technical safeguards.
rule_text_technical: Article 40(1) requires network operators processing personal information via AI systems (including profiling, recommendation, and automated decision-making) to protect such information against model inversion, membership inference, and other AI-specific privacy threats with appropriate technical safeguards.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

rule_text: You cannot use AI systems to conduct discriminatory content moderation that systematically disadvantages users based on lawfully expressed political views, subject to compliance with information content management regulations.
rule_text_technical: Article 47 prohibits network operators from using AI systems to conduct discriminatory content moderation that systematically disadvantages users based on political views expressed through lawful means, subject to the overriding obligation to comply with information content management regulations.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

rule_text: You must comply within two hours when competent authorities order temporary suspension of AI systems during a major cybersecurity incident where those systems are exacerbating the incident or operating anomalously.
rule_text_technical: Article 56 empowers competent authorities to order temporary suspension of AI systems during major cybersecurity incidents where the systems are assessed to be exacerbating the incident or operating anomalously, and requires network operators to comply within two hours of receiving such orders.

first_instance.law_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

rule_text: Individuals who violate AI cybersecurity requirements face criminal liability, while organizations face fines of RMB 500,000–10,000,000 and potential business license revocation.
rule_text_technical: Article 63 subjects violations of Article 23 prohibitions to criminal liability under the Criminal Law for individuals, and to fines of RMB 500,000 to 10,000,000 plus revocation of business licenses for organizations.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Cybersecurity Law Amendments 2025 (China, 2025-10-28).

rule_text: The HMAIC must report annually to the Parliament on the state of AI governance in Hungary.
rule_text_technical: The Hungarian Artificial Intelligence Council shall submit annual reports to the National Assembly regarding the state of AI governance in Hungary.

first_instance.law_name: Act LXXV of 2025 on the Domestic Implementation of the EU AI Act (Hungary)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Hungary AI Act Implementation 2025 (Hungary, 2025-10-31).

rule_text: The NMHH must acknowledge receipt of complaints within 15 days and conclude its preliminary assessment within 90 days.
rule_text_technical: Upon receipt of a complaint, the NMHH shall acknowledge receipt within 15 days and complete its preliminary assessment within 90 days.

first_instance.law_name: Act LXXV of 2025 on the Domestic Implementation of the EU AI Act (Hungary)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Hungary AI Act Implementation 2025 (Hungary, 2025-10-31).

rule_text: Sandbox participants are granted limited exemptions from certain conformity assessment requirements during testing periods, which may not exceed 12 months (extendable by 12 months in exceptional cases).
rule_text_technical: Participants in the regulatory sandbox receive limited exemptions from specified conformity assessment requirements during the testing period, subject to NMHH conditions; sandbox periods shall not exceed 12 months, extendable by an additional 12 months in exceptional cases.

first_instance.law_name: Act LXXV of 2025 on the Domestic Implementation of the EU AI Act (Hungary)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Hungary AI Act Implementation 2025 (Hungary, 2025-10-31).

Both rules address conformity assessment requirements for high-risk AI systems, but Vietnam's rule imposes a mandatory pre-use conformity assessment (including re-assessment after significant changes) as a binding obligation, whereas the Hungarian rule addresses sandbox exemptions from such requirements during testing periods.

Both rules provide conformity assessment relief for smaller or testing-phase actors under the EU AI Act framework, but the Hungarian rule concerns sandbox participants with a 12-month time limit, while this rule specifically targets SMEs with extended timescales for high-risk AI conformity assessment.

Both establish time-limited designations or exemptions for conformity/verification bodies (3-year IVO designation vs. 12-month sandbox exemption), but the contexts and mechanisms differ significantly.

Both involve a time-limited pre-full-deployment testing/staging phase with regulatory oversight, but this rule mandates a minimum 18-month staging period in an operational environment for utility AI systems, while the Hungarian rule grants sandbox exemptions up to 12 months for conformity assessment purposes.

rule_text: Sandbox participants must report findings to the NMHH and, where applicable, contribute to NMHH guidance on EU AI Act requirements.
rule_text_technical: Sandbox participants shall report findings to the NMHH and, where applicable, contribute to the development of NMHH guidance on the application of EU AI Act requirements.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Hungary AI Act Implementation 2025 (Hungary, 2025-10-31).

rule_text: The NMHH must publish national implementation guidance within 6 months of the Act's entry into force.
rule_text_technical: The NMHH shall publish national implementation guidance regarding the EU AI Act within 6 months of the entry into force of Act LXXV of 2025.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Hungary AI Act Implementation 2025 (Hungary, 2025-10-31).

rule_text: The responsible government authority must designate a lead regulatory body or officer to administer online safety requirements, investigate complaints from affected parties, and advance online safety protections.
rule_text_technical: Section 5 requires the Minister to appoint a Commissioner of Online Safety to administer Parts 2–9, provide timely redress to persons affected by online harmful activity, and promote online safety; Deputy and Assistant Commissioners may also be appointed and all are deemed public servants.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: You cannot publish identity information (name, address, contact, NRIC, photographs, family/employment details) of a person where a reasonable person would conclude the publication was likely intended to cause the victim harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.
rule_text_technical: Section 10 prohibits publication of identity information of a person — including name, address, email, phone, date of birth, NRIC/passport number, photographs/videos, or family/employment/education information — which a reasonable person would conclude was likely intended to cause the victim harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: You cannot publish private information about a person without consent where a reasonable person would conclude it is likely to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.
rule_text_technical: Section 11 prohibits publication of private information (information not previously widely available to the public) about a person without consent where a reasonable person would conclude it is likely to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

Both rules prohibit publishing or threatening to disclose private information about individuals without consent, but Iowa S 2161 specifically contextualizes this as a form of coercive control in domestic abuse situations and enumerates specific categories (sexual orientation, gender identity, medical information), whereas the Singapore rule is a general online safety prohibition framed around harassment/alarm.

Both rules prohibit sharing private information without consent where it causes harm, but the Singapore rule covers harassment/alarm/distress in a binding online safety context, while this New York school bill targets embarrassment/reputational harm in a bullying/student conduct context and is a school policy instrument rather than a binding civil law.

rule_text: If you receive a Part 5 direction from the Commissioner, you must comply regardless of whether you are inside or outside Singapore.
rule_text_technical: Section 26 empowers the Commissioner, after receiving a report and where there is reason to suspect online harmful activity, to issue Part 5 directions to any individual or entity inside or outside Singapore, requiring acts inside or outside Singapore; for s.17 and s.18 publications, only right-of-reply directions may generally be given.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you receive a stop communication direction, you must cease communicating the relevant material in Singapore.
rule_text_technical: Section 29 authorises the Commissioner to issue a stop communication direction requiring the recipient to stop communicating the relevant material in Singapore.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you are an online service provider receiving an access disabling direction, you must disable end-user access in Singapore to the relevant material.
rule_text_technical: Section 32 authorises the Commissioner to require an online service provider to disable end-user access in Singapore to the relevant material.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you are a prescribed online service provider receiving an access disabling (class) direction, you must disable end-user access in Singapore to all material in the relevant class.
rule_text_technical: Section 33 authorises the Commissioner to require a prescribed online service provider to disable end-user access in Singapore to any material in the relevant class.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you receive a labelling direction, you must label the relevant online material with the specified label.
rule_text_technical: Section 37 authorises the Commissioner to require the communicator or administrator to label the relevant material with a specified label.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you are an online service provider receiving an account restriction direction, you must restrict the specified Singapore account from accessing or using your service or specified functionality for the specified period.
rule_text_technical: Section 39 authorises the Commissioner to require an online service provider to restrict a Singapore account from accessing or using its service or specified functionality for a specified period.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you are a prescribed online service provider receiving an engagement reduction direction, you must reduce the engagement or amplification of the relevant material on your service (e.g., suppressing recommendations or distribution).
rule_text_technical: Section 40 authorises the Commissioner to require a prescribed online service provider to reduce the engagement or amplification of the relevant material on its service, such as suppressing recommendations or distribution.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you are an online service provider, you must retain relevant records for at least one year (or longer) when required by the Commissioner, or face fines of up to $5,000 (individual) or $10,000 (other).
rule_text_technical: Section 48 empowers the Commissioner to require an online service provider to retain relevant records for one year or longer; failure to comply incurs a fine up to $5,000 (individual) or $10,000 (other).

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

rule_text: If you are a prescribed online service provider and the Commissioner suspects an end-user engaged in online harmful activity through your service, you must obtain specified identity information from the end-user as a condition of continued service and provide it to the Commissioner.
rule_text_technical: Section 52 empowers the Commissioner, where there is suspicion that an end-user engaged in online harmful activity via a prescribed online service provider, to require the provider to obtain specified identity information from the end-user as a condition of continued service and provide it to the Commissioner; failure incurs penalties up to $20,000/12 months imprisonment plus $2,000/day continuing (individual) or $500,000 plus $50,000/day continuing (other).

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: Eligible applicants have the right to receive disclosure of end-user identity/contact information from the Commissioner for prescribed purposes, subject to conditions; breaching conditions incurs fines up to $20,000 or 12 months imprisonment (individual) or $50,000 (other).
rule_text_technical: Section 53 empowers the Commissioner to disclose end-user identity/contact information to eligible applicants for prescribed purposes, subject to conditions; breaching conditions incurs a fine up to $20,000 or 12 months imprisonment (individual) or $50,000 (other).

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you have acquired information in the course of administering this Act, you must not disclose it except in performance of duties or as required by law, on penalty of fines up to $20,000 or 12 months imprisonment.
rule_text_technical: Section 54 prohibits specified persons from disclosing information acquired in their capacity except in performance of duties or as required by law; breach incurs a fine up to $20,000 or 12 months imprisonment.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: Eligible persons including victims, direction recipients, and prescribed affected persons have the right to apply to the Commissioner to reconsider decisions, directions, or orders.
rule_text_technical: Sections 56–59 provide that eligible persons (including the victim/report-maker, the direction recipient, and prescribed affected persons) may apply to the Commissioner to reconsider decisions, directions, or orders; the Commissioner may confirm, vary, substitute, or revoke the original decision.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: Individuals have the right to appeal reconsidered decisions to an Appeal Committee drawn from the Online Safety Appeal Panel.
rule_text_technical: Sections 60–67 establish an Online Safety Appeal Panel from which Appeal Committees are drawn to hear appeals against reconsidered decisions; Appeal Committees may confirm, vary, substitute, or revoke directions or orders.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

rule_text: If you fail to comply with an access blocking order, you face fines up to $250,000 plus $20,000/day continuing; for app removal order non-compliance, fines up to $500,000 plus $50,000/day continuing.
rule_text_technical: Section 72 imposes penalties for non-compliance with orders: access blocking order — fine up to $250,000 plus $20,000/day continuing; app removal order — fine up to $500,000 plus $50,000/day continuing.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you are an administrator, you cannot develop, maintain or administer an online location in a manner that facilitates or permits applicable online harmful activity, intending or knowing such activity is likely to occur there.
rule_text_technical: Section 90 creates a tort prohibiting persons from developing, maintaining or administering an online location in a manner that facilitates or permits any applicable online harmful activity, intending or knowing that such activity is likely to be conducted there; defence is that respondent's conduct was reasonable in the circumstances.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

rule_text: If you are an administrator and receive a written online harm notice from a victim, you must assess whether the activity occurred and take reasonable steps to address it within a reasonable time.
rule_text_technical: Section 91 imposes a duty on administrators receiving a written online harm notice to assess whether the activity occurred and, if so, take reasonable steps to address it within a reasonable time; failure is presumed if the material remains accessible after a reasonable period following notice; defence is that notice was not received through no fault of the administrator's.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: If you are an online service provider and receive a written online harm notice, you must assess and take reasonable steps to address the harmful activity within a reasonable time (or prescribed period for prescribed providers).
rule_text_technical: Section 94 mirrors Part 11 obligations for online service providers; for prescribed online service providers, a mandatory prescribed period replaces 'reasonable time' and a provider responding in accordance with prescribed requirements is deemed compliant.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: Victims have the right to enhanced damages where they made a reasonable written request to address the harmful activity and the respondent failed without reasonable excuse to do so within a reasonable time.
rule_text_technical: Section 98 empowers courts to award enhanced damages (additional to general/special damages, distinct from punitive/aggravated damages) where a victim made a reasonable written request to address the harmful activity and the respondent failed without reasonable excuse to do so within a reasonable time.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

rule_text: Courts may order respondents to remove material, stop storing/transmitting it, suspend or delete online locations, restrict Singapore accounts, disable end-user access, and prevent specified persons from creating accounts that interact with Singapore users.
rule_text_technical: Section 99 empowers courts to order respondents to: remove specified material; stop storing/transmitting it; suspend or delete specified online locations; stop the relevant online activity; restrict specified Singapore accounts; disable end-user access; and prevent specified persons from creating accounts interacting with Singapore users.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore, 2025-11-05).

rule_text: Courts may issue orders against third parties (including administrators and online service providers) requiring them to stop communicating offending material or disable Singapore end-user access.
rule_text_technical: Section 100 empowers courts in proceedings involving communication of offending material to order third parties to stop communicating the material, require administrators to stop it from being communicated, and require online service providers to disable access for Singapore end-users.

first_instance.law_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025

rule_text: You can avoid the deception presumption by providing a conspicuous disclaimer in the credits of the audiovisual work and in any related advertisement featuring the digital replica, stating that the use was not authorized by the rights holders.
