rule_text: You cannot report, by word or action including by using AI or generative AI, a fictitious occurrence of child abuse, maltreatment, or abuse/neglect of a vulnerable person to the statewide central register, the vulnerable persons' central register, or to mandated reporters, when you know the information is false or baseless.
rule_text_technical: A person is guilty when, knowing the information to be false or baseless, such person reports, by word or action including using artificial intelligence or generative artificial intelligence as defined by section 1700 of the general business law, an alleged occurrence or condition of child abuse or maltreatment or abuse or neglect of a vulnerable person which did not in fact occur or exist to (a) the statewide central register of child abuse and maltreatment or the vulnerable persons' central register, or (b) any mandated reporter under SSL § 413(1) or § 491, knowing that the person is required to report such cases and with the intent that such alleged occurrence be reported to the applicable register.

rule_text: You must publish a publicly available disclosure at least 90 days before using a new covered AI product, or within 180 days of the effective date for AI products already in use, including the system name/vendor, capabilities and limitations, data inputs and outputs, authorized and unauthorized uses, and internal validation summaries.
rule_text_technical: At least ninety days prior to the use of a new covered AI product, the law enforcement agency shall publish a publicly available disclosure; for covered AI products already in use, the agency shall publish a disclosure within 180 days of the effective date. The disclosure shall include: name of each system (vendor and product name); description of capabilities and limitations; description of data inputs and outputs; description of authorized and unauthorized uses; and copies of all internal validation summaries and internal performance checks.

rule_text: You must post AI inventory information conspicuously on the agency's website in text-searchable format at no cost; agencies with fewer than ten full-time sworn officers without a website may instead provide it upon request at no cost within the response time set by article six of the public officers law.
rule_text_technical: AI system inventory information is publicly available if posted conspicuously on the law enforcement agency's website in a text-searchable format and accessible at no cost. Police agencies with fewer than ten full-time sworn officers and no website satisfy the requirement by making information available upon request, consistent with the disclosure response time established in article six of the public officers law, at no cost.

rule_text_technical: Disclosure of the use of covered AI in a police report shall include, at minimum: the name of the covered AI; and a brief description of the covered AI's role in the investigation, including whether it was used to generate an investigative lead, or identify or aid in the identification of a suspect, witness, or victim.

rule_text: Any police report or law enforcement record created in whole or part using generative AI must include a disclaimer noting AI-generated content, identify the specific AI-generated content where technically feasible, and include a certification by the author that they have reviewed the report for accuracy.
rule_text_technical: A police report or other law enforcement record generated during a criminal investigation that was created in whole or in part by using generative AI shall: include a disclaimer that the report or record contains content generated by artificial intelligence; where technically feasible, identify the specific content in the report that was generated by AI; and include a certification by the author of the report or record that the author has read and reviewed the report or record for accuracy.

rule_text: You must provide all notices, disclosures, forms, and communications to individuals in plain, straightforward language without technical or legal jargon, through an interface the individual regularly uses.
rule_text_technical: All notices, disclosures, forms, and other communications to individuals provided pursuant to this article shall use plain, straightforward language, avoiding technical or legal jargon, and must be provided through an interface the individual regularly uses in connection with the regulated entity's product or service.

rule_text: If you own, license, or operate a visual or audio generative AI system accessible to New York residents, you must implement a reasonable method to prevent users from creating unauthorized realistic depictions of a public official or candidate within 60 days of receiving notice from that person objecting to such depictions.
rule_text_technical: The owner, licensee or operator of a visual or audio generative artificial intelligence system shall implement a reasonable method to prohibit users from creating unauthorized realistic depictions of a covered person within sixty days of being notified by such covered person; reasonableness is assessed by consistency with industry standards, burden on the system, cost-effectiveness, and being up to date.

Both rules require generative AI providers to implement measures (provenance data vs. reasonable method to prevent realistic depictions) for systems accessible to New York residents, but S 6954 specifically mandates provenance data application while A 235 focuses on preventing unauthorized realistic depictions, representing related but meaningfully different obligations.

rule_text: You cannot knowingly or recklessly use algorithms or other automated systems that prioritize content by a method other than solely chronological order to promote content that advocates imminent lawless action, advocates imminent self-harm, or contains false statements of fact or fraudulent medical theories likely to endanger public safety or health.
rule_text_technical: No person, by conduct either unlawful in itself or unreasonable under all the circumstances, shall knowingly or recklessly create, maintain or contribute to a condition in New York state that endangers the safety or health of the public through the promotion of content, including through the use of algorithms or other automated systems that prioritize content by a method other than solely by time and date such content was created, where the person knows or reasonably should know the content: (1) advocates for the use of force, is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action, and is likely to incite or produce such action; (2) advocates for self-harm, is directed to inciting or producing imminent self-harm, and is likely to incite or produce such action; or (3) includes a false statement of fact or fraudulent medical theory that is likely to endanger the safety or health of the public.

rule_text: For purposes of this disclosure law, 'generative artificial intelligence' is defined as the use of machine learning technology, software, automation, and algorithms to perform tasks or make rules/predictions based on existing data sets and instructions, including systems performing tasks under unpredictable circumstances, simulating human-like cognition, or acting rationally as intelligent agents.
rule_text_technical: 'Generative artificial intelligence' means the use of machine learning technology, software, automation, and algorithms to perform tasks, to make rules and/or predictions based on existing data sets and instructions, including: systems performing tasks under varying and unpredictable circumstances without significant human oversight or that learn from experience; systems solving tasks requiring human-like perception, cognition, planning, learning, communication, or physical action; systems designed to think or act like a human including cognitive architectures and neural networks; techniques including machine learning designed to approximate cognitive tasks; and systems designed to act rationally including intelligent software agents or embodied robots.

rule_text_technical: The reliability and accuracy of the specific use of the artificial intelligence in creating or processing the evidence is sufficient where the proponent of the evidence has a qualified expert testify and such testimony is sufficient to prove that: (a) the specific use has been validated through rigorous scientific or technical testing demonstrating it consistently produces accurate and reliable results in varied environments; (b) the AI has been subjected to testing or application in environments similar or analogous to the specific context with accurate and reliable results; and (c) the AI has not been subjected to any variables that, based on scientific or technical testing, have a substantial probability of causing a materially inaccurate or unreliable result, with the court considering the weight of the artificially created evidence relative to other admitted evidence.

rule_text: In civil proceedings, to meet the 'substantially supported by independent and admissible evidence' standard, you must show the independent evidence is separate from and not derived from the AI, is admissible under existing rules, and bears a close and significant corroborating relationship to the AI-created evidence.
rule_text_technical: Evidence is substantially supported by independent and admissible evidence where: (1) the independent evidence is separate from, and not derived from, the artificial intelligence that generated the artificially created evidence; (2) the independent evidence is admissible under the existing rules of evidence; and (3) the independent evidence bears a close and significant relationship to the artificially created evidence in such a manner that it reinforces or corroborates the information created from the artificially created evidence.

rule_text: In civil proceedings, to establish reliability and accuracy of AI-created or AI-processed evidence, you must present qualified expert testimony proving the AI was validated through rigorous scientific/technical testing, has been tested in analogous environments with accurate results, and has not been subjected to variables with substantial probability of causing materially inaccurate or unreliable results.
rule_text_technical: The reliability and accuracy of the specific use of the artificial intelligence in creating or processing the evidence is sufficient where the proponent of the evidence has a qualified expert testify and such testimony is sufficient to prove that: (1) the specific use has been validated through rigorous scientific or technical testing demonstrating it consistently produces accurate and reliable results in varied environments; (2) the AI has been subjected to testing or application in environments similar or analogous to the specific context with accurate and reliable results; and (3) the AI has not been subjected to any variables that, based on scientific or technical testing of the system, have a substantial probability of causing a materially inaccurate or unreliable result, with the court considering the weight of the artificially created evidence relative to other admitted evidence.

rule_text: You cannot represent, directly or indirectly, that your entity is licensed under this law unless you actually hold a high-risk advanced AI system license.
rule_text_technical: No person shall make, directly or indirectly, orally or in writing, or by any method, practice or device, a representation that such entity is licensed under the law except that a licensee may represent licensure as a high-risk advanced AI system under this article.

rule_text: You cannot develop or operate an AI system that engages in unauthorized acquisition, retention, dissemination of, or access to sensitive personal information or non-public data in violation of data privacy, security, or hacking laws.

rule_text: If the Secretary issues a written demand to cease development or operation of a prohibited AI system, you must cease development, operation, and access immediately, with cessation continuing through any petition or appeal until a favorable determination.
rule_text_technical: Upon written demand by the secretary, the person developing or operating a prohibited AI system shall cease development, operation, and access within the time set by the secretary; the demand is finally and irrevocably binding unless the person petitions for a hearing within the prescribed period, and cessation must continue prior to petition until a favorable determination.

rule_text: As a member, officer, director, or employee of an operator, if you knowingly publicly or privately operate a prohibited AI system, you commit a class D felony and incur a civil penalty equal to the amount earned or damages caused, whichever is greater.
rule_text_technical: Any member, officer, director or employee of an operator who knowingly publicly or privately operates any prohibited system shall be guilty of a class D felony and incur a civil penalty of the amount earned from creation of the prohibited system or amount of damages caused, whichever is greater.

rule_text: You must publish a summary of the most recent disparate impact analysis and the tool's distribution date on your website before using the automated decision tool, and make it accessible through any digital housing listing where the tool will be used.
rule_text_technical: A summary of the most recent disparate impact analysis of the automated decision tool, as well as the distribution date of the tool to which the analysis applies, shall be made publicly available on the landlord's website prior to the implementation or use of such tool, and shall also be made accessible through any listing for housing on a digital platform for which the landlord intends to use such tool.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in New York A 3930 — Use of AI in Rental Housing and Loan Decisions (New York, null).

rule_text: You cannot share a tenant's personal data with any third party without the tenant's written consent.

rule_text: You must disclose to each tenant the categories of personal data processed, sources of collection, processing purposes, retention periods, and the identity of each third party with whom data is shared along with details about each third party's processing.
rule_text_technical: A landlord shall disclose to each tenant: (i) the categories of personal data processed by the landlord and any processor; (ii) the sources from which personal data is collected; (iii) the purposes for processing; (iv) the retention period for each category of personal data (or the criteria used to determine such period); and (v) the identity of each third party to whom personal data was disclosed, shared, transferred, or sold, including for each third party the categories shared, purposes, retention periods, and whether the third party uses the data for targeted advertising.

rule_text: The lead government ministries responsible for housing, financial services, and human rights must jointly conduct a study on AI and machine learning's impact on housing discrimination and redlining within one year, and submit a report with findings and recommendations to the head of government and legislature within 90 days of completing the study.
rule_text_technical: The division of housing and community renewal, in conjunction with the department of financial services and the division of human rights, shall conduct a study on the impact of artificial intelligence and machine learning on housing discrimination and how such AI and machine learning may further redlining, to be completed within one year of the effective date; and shall submit a report to the governor and legislature on findings and recommendations for legislative action no later than ninety days after completion of the study.

rule_text: You cannot use algorithms on a third-party food delivery platform that effectively promote deliveries by workers in timeframes only achievable by exceeding 15 mph on an e-bike or e-scooter or by violating traffic laws, including offering incentives for shorter times or penalties for not meeting such times.

rule_text: You cannot adjust any algorithm or equation used to construct actuarial tables or otherwise determine the cost of motor vehicle insurance coverage based on the prohibited factors listed in subdivision (a), including consumer credit information and indicators of socioeconomic status.

first_instance.law_name: New York A 4947 — NY Privacy Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in New York A 4947 — NY Privacy Act (New York, null).

Both prohibit inferring consent from inaction or continued use and prohibit obtaining consent through manipulation; the New York A4947 binding rule addresses these as separate provisions, while this voluntary bill combines them and uses 'should not' rather than a binding prohibition.

Both rules address affirmative consent requirements before charging/processing, but this rule specifically targets automatic renewal and continuous service offer terms in a subscription billing context, while the matched rule broadly prohibits inferring consent from inaction or continued service use.

Both rules address the requirement that consent must be specific and that generic or implied consent (e.g., inaction or blanket authorizations) is insufficient, though drafted differently and in different jurisdictional contexts.

rule_text: When you must process technical data (IP addresses, system configuration, URLs, locale, keystrokes, etc.) to obtain consent, you must process only what is necessary, use it solely to request consent, and promptly delete it if consent is withheld, denied, or withdrawn.
rule_text_technical: To process IP addresses, system configuration, referring URLs, locale and language preferences, keystrokes, or similar data to obtain consent, controllers must process only the necessary data, solely for that purpose, and promptly delete it if consent is withheld, denied, or withdrawn.

rule_text: When purchasing a product or service that is or contains an algorithmic decision system, state units should ensure it adheres to responsible AI standards that avoid harm, including minimizing risks of physical or mental injury, unjustified deletion or disclosure of information, and unwarranted damage to property, reputation, or environment.
rule_text_technical: A state unit shall, when purchasing a product or service that is or contains an algorithmic decision system to be used by the state, purchase one adhering to responsible AI standards including the avoidance of harm: minimization of (A) risks of physical or mental injury; (B) unjustified deletion or disclosure of information; and (C) unwarranted damage to property, reputation, or environment.

rule_text: For purposes of this law, an 'algorithmic decision system' is defined as a computational process — including one derived from machine learning, statistics, or other data processing or AI techniques — that makes or facilitates a decision impacting individuals.
rule_text_technical: 'Algorithmic decision system' means a computational process, including one derived from machine learning, statistics, or other data processing or artificial intelligence techniques, that makes a decision, or facilitates human decision making, in a manner that impacts individuals.

first_instance.law_name: New York A 5216 — State Units

instances.notes: Rule introduced in New York A 5216 — State Units (New York, null).

Both define a computational process using machine learning, statistical methods, or AI techniques, but the NY A5216 rule is framed as an 'algorithmic decision system' while this bill uses 'covered algorithm,' and this is a voluntary/bill instrument vs. a binding law.

Both define an automated/algorithmic decision system as a computational process using machine learning or statistical techniques to make or support decisions, but NY A 8295's definition focuses specifically on government agency use and automation/support of decisions, while A5216's definition is broader in scope and context.

Both rules define terms for automated/algorithmic decision systems in a government/public-interest context, but Vermont H 752 defines a broader set of terms (algorithm, automated decision system, automated final decision system, automated support decision system) for a state digital services agency context, while the NY rule defines 'algorithmic decision system' specifically for employment/consequential decision contexts.
Virginia H 999 — State Human Rights Act (Virginia) proposed this rule but the bill was failed — negative premise.

rule_text: If you are a corporation that terminates or substantially reduces the hours of employees at or above the threshold (e.g., 25+ for employers with 100–250 employees, scaling up to 250+ for employers with 1,001+ employees) due to AI, algorithms, computational models, or robotic hardware automating or replacing human labor, you must pay a worker displacement surcharge of 2% of your business income base.
rule_text_technical: A surcharge is imposed at 2% of the corporation's business income base on corporations that terminate the employment or substantially reduce the hours of at least the threshold number of employees due to any system or process that uses algorithms, computational models, artificial intelligence techniques, robotic hardware, or a combination thereof, to automate, support, or replace human labor. Thresholds: (i) 25+ for 100–250 employees; (ii) 50+ for 251–500; (iii) 100+ for 501–1,000; (iv) 250+ for 1,001+.

All surcharge monies collected shall be paid to the department of labor to be used, in a manner prescribed by the commissioner of the department of labor, for worker retraining programs, workforce development programs, or to be paid to the unemployment insurance fund.

rule_text: You cannot contact a subscriber on the Do Not Call Registry by telephone to obtain their prior express written consent; non-telephonic outreach must be used instead.
rule_text_technical: Nothing prohibits a telephone solicitor from contacting by nontelephonic notice a telephone subscriber whose number appears on the Do Not Call Registry to obtain prior express written consent, but a telephone solicitor shall not contact such a subscriber by telephone to obtain this prior express written consent.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: If consent is disputed, you (the telephone solicitor) bear the burden of proving prior express written consent by producing the original, facsimile, or electronic signed document or other authentication.
rule_text_technical: In any dispute regarding whether a telephone subscriber has provided prior express written consent, the telephone solicitor has the burden of proving consent by producing the original document, a facsimile, or an electronic form signed by the subscriber, or other authentication evidencing consent. The subscriber may subsequently retract consent.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You cannot use an automatic dialing and recorded message player to make a robocall to a telephone number, except under specifically permitted circumstances.
rule_text_technical: Except as provided in this section, no person may use an automatic dialing and recorded message player to make a robocall to a telephone number.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You may make a robocall as a tax-exempt charity, political party/candidate, government official, or polling/broadcast organization only if no part is a solicitation and you clearly identify your name, contact information, and the nature of the call.
rule_text_technical: A robocall is permitted where the caller is a tax-exempt charitable/civic organization, political party/candidate, governmental official, or opinion polling/broadcast/rating organization, provided no part of the robocall is a telephone solicitation and the caller clearly identifies the person's name and contact information and the nature of the robocall.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You may use a robocall only if a live operator first identifies themselves, states the nature and length of the recorded message, and obtains the recipient's prior approval to play it.
rule_text_technical: A robocall is permitted where, prior to playing the robocall, a live operator complies with G.S. 75-102(c), states the nature and length in minutes of the recorded message, and asks for and receives prior approval to play the recorded message from the person receiving the call.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

Both rules require obtaining recipient consent before playing a prerecorded message, but the NC rule requires a live operator to first identify themselves and state the nature and length of the message, while Vermont H 829 requires only asking for consent within the prerecorded announcement itself, and Vermont's instrument is a bill (possibly voluntary/pending) rather than enacted law.

rule_text: You may make a robocall about an existing debt or contract only if no part is a solicitation and you clearly identify your name, contact information, and the nature of the call.
rule_text_technical: A robocall is permitted in connection with an existing debt or contract for which payment or performance has not been completed, provided no part is used to make a telephone solicitation and the caller clearly identifies the person's name, contact information, and nature of the robocall.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You may make a robocall about a scheduled appointment or service outage/restoration only if it conveys solely that information, contains no solicitation, and identifies your name, contact information, and the nature of the call.
rule_text_technical: A robocall is permitted when placed by a person with whom the subscriber made an appointment (conveying only appointment information), or by a utility/telephone/cable/satellite or similar entity for the sole purpose of conveying network outage, repair, service interruption, or service restoration information, provided no part is a telephone solicitation and the caller clearly identifies name, contact information, and nature of the robocall.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You may make a robocall on behalf of a health insurer regarding a subscriber's health care, preventive services, medication, or covered benefits only if no part is a solicitation and you clearly identify your name, contact information, and the nature of the call.
rule_text_technical: A robocall is permitted by or on behalf of a health insurer (as defined in G.S. 58-51-115(a)(2)) conveying information related to the subscriber or family member's health care, preventive services, medication, or covered benefits, provided no part is a telephone solicitation and the caller clearly identifies name, contact information, and nature of the robocall.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You may use automated calling systems solely to protect public health, safety, or welfare (such as product or drug recalls and unfilled prescriptions) only if the call contains no commercial solicitation, identifies your contact information and the nature of the call, and complies with applicable health data protection regulations where applicable.
rule_text_technical: A robocall is permitted where no part is a telephone solicitation, the caller clearly identifies contact information and the nature of the robocall, and the sole purpose is to protect public health, safety, or welfare by informing the subscriber of (a) a recalled product, (b) a recalled prescription/OTC medication (with HIPAA compliance), or (c) an unpicked-up filled prescription (with HIPAA compliance), subject to specified conditions.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You cannot, as a telephone solicitor or robocaller, transmit misleading caller-ID information or otherwise block or misrepresent the origin of a telephone solicitation or robocall (i.e., no spoofing).
rule_text_technical: No telephone solicitor or robocaller shall cause misleading information to be transmitted to users of caller identification technologies or otherwise block or misrepresent the origin of a telephone solicitation or robocall. It is not a violation to use the name and number of the entity on whose behalf the solicitation is made rather than the solicitor's.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You cannot, as a telephone solicitor or robocaller, impersonate a federal, state, or local government official, law enforcement professional, or government agency to defraud, confuse, harm, or extract personal information from a telephone subscriber.
rule_text_technical: No telephone solicitor or robocaller shall impersonate any federal, State, or local government official, law enforcement professional, or government agency in order to defraud, confuse, or financially or otherwise injure the telephone subscriber, or to obtain personal information that may be used fraudulently or unlawfully.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: There is a rebuttable presumption that a telephone subscriber with a North Carolina area code is a North Carolina resident or located in North Carolina at the time of a telephone solicitation or robocall.
rule_text_technical: There is a rebuttable presumption that a telephone subscriber with a North Carolina area code is a North Carolina resident or in North Carolina at the time a telephone solicitation or robocall is made.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: Individuals who receive a robocall or telephone solicitation in violation of this Article have the right to sue in civil court for an injunction and statutory damages of $500/$1,000/$5,000 per violation.
rule_text_technical: A telephone subscriber who has received a robocall or telephone solicitation from or on behalf of a telephone solicitor or robocaller in violation of this Article may bring a civil action to enjoin further violations and to recover $500 for the first violation, $1,000 for the second, and $5,000 for the third or subsequent within two years; penalties are assessed for each provision violated by a single call.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 936 — Robocall Solicitation Modifications (North Carolina, null).

Both laws grant individuals a private right of action for receiving unlawful telemarketing/robocall solicitations, but Pennsylvania H 2255 applies specifically to AI-related violations under the Telemarketer Registration Act in a court of common pleas, while North Carolina H936 covers robocalls and telephone solicitations more broadly with injunctive relief and statutory damages.

Both grant individuals a private right of action for robocall violations, but Vermont H 829 specifies Superior Court jurisdiction and a $500 civil penalty cap, while North Carolina H 936 references civil court with injunctive relief and statutory damages under a different damages framework.

rule_text: If you are a public utility, you may charge rates designed to recover data-center-related costs only if those rates are incurred solely from commercial data centers or are prorated based on electric demand.
rule_text_technical: Public utilities may charge rates or charges designed to recover costs associated with subsection (b) if the rates or charges are incurred solely from commercial data centers or are prorated based on electric demand.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: For purposes of this law, a 'commercial data center' is defined as a facility, campus, or array of interconnected facilities in North Carolina used to operate computing hardware/software primarily for processing, storing, retrieving, or transmitting data, with peak demand of 100 megawatts or greater.
rule_text_technical: 'Commercial data center' means a facility, campus of facilities, or array of interconnected facilities in this State that is used by an entity or other business enterprise to operate, manage, or maintain a computer, group of computers, or other organized assembly of hardware and software for the primary purpose of processing, storing, retrieving, or transmitting data and has a peak demand of 100 megawatts or greater.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act (North Carolina, null).

Both laws define a 'commercial data center' or similar AI/data facility for regulatory purposes, but Oklahoma H 2992 focuses on ratepayer protection by setting a 75 MW load threshold that triggers utility cost-allocation obligations, while the North Carolina rule defines a commercial data center for utility rate purposes without that specific threshold or consumer-protection framing.

rule_text: Governments should establish a dedicated multi-stakeholder body composed of representatives from the executive branch, legislative branch, utility regulators, and other relevant sectoral authorities to provide integrated advice on data center planning and infrastructure requirements.
rule_text_technical: There is established a Special Commission for Data Center Planning composed of 14 members appointed as specified by the Governor (3), President Pro Tempore of the Senate (1), Speaker of the House (2), minority leaders of the House and Senate (1 each), the North Carolina Utilities Commission (2), the Secretary of Commerce (2), and the Secretary of Health and Human Services (2).

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: The Special Commission should review existing grid and energy supply, recommend data center locations, recommend grid expansion, consider load management approaches, examine future trends including artificial intelligence and its impact on the electric grid, survey employer perceptions, and propose legislation and budget recommendations.
rule_text_technical: The Commission shall: (1) review existing electric grid and energy supply and make recommendations for data center locations based on such review and consideration of fiber, water, labor, and latency; (2) make recommendations to expand grid capacity where energy for data applications is most needed; (3) make recommendations on energy generation, transmission, and distribution expansion necessary to serve the industry; (4) consider creative approaches to manage usage including variable load, on-site generation, efficiency, and backup generation; (5) examine future trends including artificial intelligence and project impact on the electric grid; (6) survey corporate employers regarding adequacy of data center capacity; and (7) propose related legislation and budget recommendations.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act (North Carolina, null).

Both rules require consideration of energy supply, grid reliability, and environmental factors in reviewing AI/data center infrastructure, but Vermont's rule additionally specifies water consumption and broadens to include grid reliability and environmental impacts as explicit required considerations for the PUC report.

Both direct a legislative/special body to review existing grid and energy supply in relation to data center growth, but the Puerto Rico rule focuses on a standing House Committee investigating each power plant's generation capacity, while the NC rule establishes a special commission to recommend data center locations and grid expansion.

rule_text: The designated supervisory body shall submit a written report of its findings and recommendations to the lead government ministry, legislative leadership, and the relevant sectoral regulator no later than three months following the conclusion of its final meeting.
rule_text_technical: The Commission shall submit a written report of its findings and recommendations to the Governor, the President Pro Tempore of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, the minority leaders of the Senate and the House of Representatives, and the North Carolina Utilities Commission no later than three months after the date of the last meeting of the Commission.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1002 — Rate Payer Protection Act (North Carolina, null).

Both rules require a designated body to submit a written report on data center/AI infrastructure findings and recommendations to legislative leaders, but Vermont's report is directed at House and Senate committees by a Public Utility Commission while North Carolina's goes to the Governor and legislative leaders from a Special Commission.

rule_text: The Board of Governors of The University of North Carolina should select up to eight constituent institutions to serve as Artificial Intelligence Hubs by no later than December 1, 2026, with at least one being a Public Historically Black College/University or the University of North Carolina at Pembroke (recommendation under appropriations bill).
rule_text_technical: No later than December 1, 2026, the Board of Governors of The University of North Carolina shall select up to eight constituent institutions of The University of North Carolina to serve as Artificial Intelligence Hubs (AI Hubs), and at least one AI Hub shall be one of North Carolina's Public Historically Black Colleges and Universities or the University of North Carolina at Pembroke.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: Selected AI Hub constituent institutions should not receive the allocated nonrecurring infrastructure funds until they match ten percent of those funds with non-State funds (recommendation under appropriations bill).
rule_text_technical: Funds appropriated for establishing AI Hubs shall not be made available to a selected constituent institution until that institution matches ten percent (10%) of the funds made available pursuant to this subdivision with non-State funds.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: Each selected AI Hub should establish an expert-in-residence position using the recurring operational support funds appropriated for that purpose.
rule_text_technical: Eight million dollars ($8,000,000) in recurring funds shall be used for operational support and personnel needed for the AI Hubs, including to establish an expert in residence position at each AI Hub.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: To qualify for AI research grant funding from the North Carolina Collaboratory, a research project should involve applied AI research to develop an application in education, workforce development, healthcare, or government (recommendation/eligibility criterion).
rule_text_technical: To qualify for grant funding, a research project must focus on applied AI research to develop an application in one of the following priority areas: Education, Workforce development, Healthcare, or Government.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: Alternatively, to qualify for AI research grant funding, a research project should pertain to AI fundamentals and infrastructure by addressing core AI technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision and how those technologies contribute to advancing AI infrastructure.
rule_text_technical: To qualify for grant funding, a research project must pertain to AI fundamentals and infrastructure by addressing core AI technologies (including, but not limited to, machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision) and how the technologies contribute to advancing AI infrastructure.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina H 1004 — Technology Hubs (North Carolina, null).

rule_text: You must use a geofence system maintained by a licensed location-based technology provider to dynamically monitor the geolocation of persons attempting to access or create an account for obscene or harmful-to-juveniles material.
rule_text_technical: The organization shall utilize a geofence system maintained and monitored by a licensed location-based technology provider to dynamically monitor the geolocation of persons attempting to access or creating an account or subscription to access the material or performance that is obscene or harmful to juveniles, and shall ensure that the location-based technology provider performs a geolocation check.

first_instance.law_name: Ohio H 84 — Innocence Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ohio H 84 — Innocence Act (Ohio, null).

This rule is substantively identical to the existing rule us-oh-h84-2026-1349-10-b-3-a-b, covering the geofence system requirement for monitoring geolocation of persons attempting to access obscene or harmful-to-juveniles material.

rule_text: You must implement a notification mechanism to alert persons attempting to access or create an account for obscene or harmful-to-juveniles material when a geolocation check fails.
rule_text_technical: The organization shall implement a notification mechanism to alert persons attempting to access or creating an account or subscription to access the material or performance that is obscene or harmful to juveniles, of a geolocation check failure.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ohio H 84 — Innocence Act (Ohio, null).

This rule is substantively identical to the existing rule us-oh-h84-2026-1349-10-b-4, covering the notification mechanism requirement for geolocation check failures when users attempt to access or create accounts.

rule_text: You must develop and maintain a data privacy policy compliant with federal and state law and maintain data in a manner that is reasonably secure.
rule_text_technical: The organization shall develop and maintain a data privacy policy compliant with federal and state law and maintain data in a manner that is reasonably secure.

first_instance.law_name: Ohio H 84 — Innocence Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ohio H 84 — Innocence Act (Ohio, null).

The new rule is functionally identical to the existing rule from the same law (us-oh-h84-2026), requiring development and maintenance of a data privacy policy compliant with federal and state law and secure data maintenance.

rule_text: Organizations must immediately delete any identifying information used for age verification (except information needed for account access and billing) after verification is complete, and must provide compliance documentation to the national enforcement authority upon request through official investigation procedures or violation notices.
rule_text_technical: An organization shall immediately delete any identifying information, except the information required for the purpose of granting access to the account or subscription and for billing, that is used for age verification after age verification is completed. In response to any subpoena or notice of violation received pursuant to section 1349.101, the organization shall submit an affidavit to the attorney general stating that the organization has complied with this requirement.

first_instance.law_name: Ohio H 84 — Innocence Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ohio H 84 — Innocence Act (Ohio, null).

The new rule is functionally identical to the existing rule from the same law (us-oh-h84-2026), requiring immediate deletion of identifying information used for age verification except for account access and billing purposes.

rule_text: Records obtained through compulsory legal process and compliance certifications collected during an investigation by the national enforcement authority are exempt from public disclosure requirements.
rule_text_technical: Neither subpoenas issued and records obtained pursuant to a subpoena issued by the attorney general nor an affidavit as described in division (C)(3) of section 1349.10 are public records under section 149.43 of the Revised Code when obtained by the attorney general as part of an investigation.

rule_text: In a prosecution, the trier of fact may infer that a depiction is an artificially generated depiction of a minor if the material represents or depicts the person as such through its title, text, or visual representation.
rule_text_technical: In a prosecution under this section, the trier of fact may infer that a person in the material or performance involved is an artificially generated depiction of a minor if the material or performance, through its title, text, visual representation, or otherwise, represents or depicts the person as an artificially generated depiction of a minor.

first_instance.law_name: Ohio S 393 — Sexually Oriented Offenses Changes

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ohio S 393 — Sexually Oriented Offenses Changes (Ohio, null).

Both rules allow the trier of fact to infer that a depiction is an artificially generated depiction of a minor based on the material's title, text, or other contextual indicators, but Ohio H 786 applies to § 2907.321 while the existing rule (us-oh-s393-2026) covers substantially the same inference provision under the same statutory section with similar drafting.

rule_text: Prosecutors must include a specification in the charging document stating that the material possessed by the offender consisted of 100 or more images, in order to trigger the five-year mandatory prison term; a single film or digital recording counts as 75 images.
rule_text_technical: Imposition of a mandatory five-year prison term under division (B)(12) of section 2929.14 is precluded unless the offender is convicted of a violation of division (C)(3)(c) of section 2907.321 or division (E)(3)(c) of section 2907.322 and the indictment, count, or information specifies that the material possessed consisted of one hundred or more images. A single motion picture film, video, or digital recording shall be deemed equivalent to seventy-five images.

rule_text: The national enforcement authority may, within six months of receiving notice of proposed governance changes, request additional information or deny the changes if found inadequate; if rejected, the affected organization has 30 days to modify its plan and determine whether previously assessed AI systems require reassessment.

rule_text: You cannot bring or cause to be brought into Ohio any obscene material containing an artificially generated depiction of a minor.
rule_text_technical: No person, with knowledge of the character of the material involved, shall bring or cause to be brought into this state any obscene material that has an artificially generated depiction of a minor as one of its participants or portrayed observers.

first_instance.law_name: Ohio H 786 — Artificial Generated Depiction of Minor

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ohio H 786 — Artificial Generated Depiction of Minor (Ohio, null).

Both address protecting minors from harmful AI-generated/deepfake content in Ohio, but the new rule is a broader policy statement from a voluntary/soft-law bill covering deepfake images, video, and audio of minors generally, while the existing binding rule specifically prohibits importing obscene AI-generated depictions of minors into Ohio.
Wisconsin A 105 — Distribution of Certain Material on the Internet (Wisconsin) proposed this rule but the bill was vetoed — negative premise.

Both prohibit distributing obscene material containing artificially generated depictions of minors, but Wisconsin S 130 focuses on internet publication/distribution and includes 'purported child' language, while the Ohio rule specifically addresses bringing such material into the state.

rule_text: Mistake of age is not a defense to a charge of pandering obscenity involving a minor or artificially generated depiction of a minor.
rule_text_technical: Mistake of age is not a defense to a charge under section 2907.321 of the Revised Code.

first_instance.law_name: Ohio H 786 — Artificial Generated Depiction of Minor

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ohio H 786 — Artificial Generated Depiction of Minor (Ohio, null).

Both rules independently bar mistake-of-age as a defense in prosecutions involving minors (including AI-generated depictions), but Ohio H786 covers pandering obscenity/sexually oriented matter while SC H3471 covers first and second degree sexual exploitation of a minor.

Both rules bar a mistake-of-age defense in prosecutions involving depictions of minors (including AI-generated ones), though Washington's rule also allows a reasonable-belief affirmative defense as a partial offset, creating a slight structural difference.

rule_text: You cannot bring or cause to be brought into Ohio any material showing an artificially generated depiction of a minor engaged in sexual activity, masturbation, or bestiality.
rule_text_technical: No person, with knowledge of the character of the material involved, shall bring or cause to be brought into this state any material that shows an artificially generated depiction of a minor participating or engaging in sexual activity, masturbation, or bestiality.

rule_text: Key terms governing surveillance pricing include 'algorithmic price increase' (price above baseline determined or materially influenced by individual personal data via automated algorithm/AI), 'baseline price', 'personal data', 'online retailer', and 'price decrease'.
rule_text_technical: Definitions: 'Algorithmic price increase' means charging a price higher than the seller's baseline price where the seller uses an automated algorithm, AI, or other data processing system and the price is determined or materially influenced by personal data tied to an individual consumer. 'Online retailer' means any person or entity selling goods or services through an internet website, mobile application, or other digital platform. 'Price decrease' means any reduction below the baseline price.

rule_text_technical: Definitions: 'Algorithm' means a computerized procedure consisting of steps to accomplish a task; 'Artificial intelligence systems' means systems capable of (A) perceiving an environment through data acquisition and processing and interpreting derived information to take actions or imitate intelligent behavior given a goal, and (B) learning and adapting behavior by analyzing how the environment is affected by prior actions; 'Automated decision system' means an algorithm, including one incorporating machine learning or other AI techniques, that uses data-based analytics to make or support governmental decisions, judgments, or conclusions; 'Automated final decision system' makes final decisions without human intervention; 'Automated support decision system' provides information to inform a human decision maker's final decision.

rule_text: For AI disclosure purposes, "generative artificial intelligence" means a trained AI system designed to simulate human conversation through text, audio, or visual communication and producing nonscripted human-like outputs with limited or no human oversight. A "high-risk AI interaction" includes interactions involving sensitive personal information (health, financial, biometric), personalized recommendations or advice that could be relied on for significant personal decisions (financial, legal, medical, mental health), or other applications designated by the national enforcement authority through regulatory rule.
rule_text_technical: 'Generative artificial intelligence' means an AI technology system that is trained on data, designed to simulate human conversation with a consumer through text, audio, or visual communication, and generates nonscripted outputs similar to outputs created by a human, with limited or no human oversight. 'High-risk artificial intelligence interaction' means an interaction with generative AI involving the collection of sensitive personal information (health, financial, or biometric data); the provision of personalized recommendations, advice, or information that could reasonably be relied upon to make significant personal decisions, including financial, legal, medical, or mental health advice or services; or any other applications set forth in rules adopted by the Office of the Attorney General.

Both rules require lifecycle-covering risk management for high-risk AI systems, but the Spain Draft AI Law is a voluntary/draft instrument requiring a comprehensive system across the entire lifecycle, while the Virginia law is a binding mandate focusing on annual review and updates of risk management policy for critical AI systems.

Both require development/maintenance of a risk management policy for AI systems, but this Puerto Rico resolution is a voluntary recommendation to study and develop such a policy referencing NIST AI RMF, whereas Virginia's rule is a binding mandate requiring annual review and update of an existing risk management policy for critical AI systems.

Both rules require documentation of risk-related considerations for AI systems by a designated official, but the Kentucky rule focuses on the executive director conducting an upfront assessment covering discrimination avoidance, while the Virginia rule focuses on annual review and update of a risk management policy triggered by material changes.

Both rules require risk management policies for critical AI systems, but Virginia's rule focuses on annual review and update obligations while Montana's rule targets critical infrastructure deployment specifically and mandates developing a risk management plan rather than reviewing an existing one.

rule_text: It is prima facie evidence that a person's death is caused by the wrongful act, neglect, or default of the owner of an AI system if the death is determined to be suicide, the person provided suicide-related inputs, the AI caused or aided the suicide (by providing instructions, encouraging the attempt, or failing to refer to the 988 hotline), and the owner knew or should have known the AI could cause or aid suicide.
rule_text_technical: For purposes of this chapter, it is prima facie evidence that the death of a person is caused by the wrongful act, neglect, or default of the owner of an artificial intelligence system if: (a) the person's cause of death is determined to be suicide; (b) the person provided inputs to the owner's artificial intelligence system related to suicide; (c) the owner's artificial intelligence system caused or aided the person's suicide by providing instructions on how to attempt suicide, encouraging the person to attempt suicide, or failing to refer the person to the 988 national suicide prevention hotline or its successor; and (d) the owner of the artificial intelligence system knew or should have known that the artificial intelligence system could cause or aid a person to attempt suicide.

Both rules impose double fines on legal persons for crimes committed in their name or on their account, with Bahrain's 2024 AI Law containing an identical concept; the PDPL 2018 version applies specifically to Article 58 offences in the data protection context.

Both impose personal liability on de facto managers/legal representatives of juristic persons for violations committed in the entity's name or interest, but Egypt requires knowledge and a causal breach of duties while Bahrain doubles prescribed penalties for the legal person.

Both impose vicarious liability on a principal entity for violations committed by agents/representatives, but Zimbabwe's rule applies specifically to fines incurred by agents/assignees of data controllers, while Bahrain's doubles the prescribed penalty for legal persons.

Both impose liability on legal persons (doubled or separate fines) when a crime is committed in their name or for their benefit by directors or managers, though the Oman provision specifies a fixed range (5,000–100,000 OMR) while Bahrain doubles the prescribed penalty.

Both impose personal liability on responsible officers of a legal person for violations, but Sri Lanka's PDPA applies specifically to directors, partners, and managing officers upon a penalty being imposed on the body, while Bahrain doubles prescribed penalties against the legal person itself.

Both multiply criminal fines for corporate offenders (Bahrain doubles the prescribed penalty; Indonesia multiplies tenfold reaching up to Rp 60 billion), reflecting the same principle of enhanced corporate liability but with different multipliers and caps.

Both impose corporate liability extending to officers who knowingly authorized or permitted the contravention when an offence is committed by a company, independently drafted under different legal systems.

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model meeting the threshold for high-impact capabilities, notify the AI Office no later than two weeks after the requirements are met or are known to be met.
rule_text_technical: Providers of general-purpose AI models meeting the applicable threshold for high-impact capabilities (presumed systemic risk) must notify the AI Office at the latest two weeks after the requirements are met or it becomes known they will be met, with possibility to demonstrate exceptional non-applicability.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, report serious incidents and possible corrective measures without undue delay to the Commission and national competent authorities, and ensure adequate cybersecurity protection.
rule_text_technical: Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must without undue delay track and report serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the Commission and national competent authorities, and ensure adequate cybersecurity protection of the model and its physical infrastructure throughout the lifecycle.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a high-risk AI system that is also a critical product with digital elements, undergo the conformity assessment of the cybersecurity regulation for cybersecurity essential requirements.
rule_text_technical: High-risk AI systems falling within scope of this Regulation that are also qualified as important and critical products with digital elements under the horizontal cybersecurity regulation are subject to that regulation's conformity assessment provisions for cybersecurity essential requirements; for other aspects, this Regulation's internal control conformity assessment applies.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both address the intersection of AI Act high-risk systems and CRA products, requiring the applicable conformity assessment procedure to cover both sets of requirements; the CRA article operationalises the AI Act recital.

rule_text: You must ensure high-risk AI systems comply with accessibility requirements under Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882 by design.
rule_text_technical: Providers must ensure full compliance with accessibility requirements (including Directive (EU) 2016/2102 and Directive (EU) 2019/882) by integrating necessary measures into the design of high-risk AI systems for persons with disabilities.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a former provider, cooperate with new providers and provide necessary information and technical access required for compliance with conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems.
rule_text_technical: Where a third party becomes a provider under Article 25, the former provider must closely cooperate with the new provider, make available necessary information, and provide reasonably expected technical access and other assistance required to fulfil obligations including conformity assessment, unless the change to high-risk was expressly excluded.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a third party supplying AI tools, services, components or processes integrated into a high-risk AI system, provide the provider by written agreement with necessary information, technical access and assistance to enable their compliance.
rule_text_technical: Third parties supplying AI systems, tools, services, components or processes integrated into high-risk AI systems must by written agreement provide the high-risk AI system provider with necessary information, capabilities, technical access and assistance based on the state of the art to enable full compliance with this Regulation, without compromising IP rights or trade secrets.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must subject a high-risk AI system to a new conformity assessment whenever a substantial modification occurs or its intended purpose changes.
rule_text_technical: Whenever a change occurs that may affect compliance of a high-risk AI system with this Regulation (e.g. operating system or software architecture changes), or when intended purpose changes, the AI system shall be considered new and undergo a new conformity assessment; pre-determined learning changes assessed at conformity assessment are not substantial modifications.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: When using real-time remote biometric identification for permitted law enforcement purposes, you must consider the seriousness of the situation and consequences for rights, complete a fundamental rights impact assessment, and register the system in the EU database.
rule_text_technical: Use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement shall consider the nature/seriousness of the situation and consequences for rights and freedoms; deployment is authorised only if the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registered the system in the EU database under Article 49.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Norway's EEA implementation of EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(h) prohibiting real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement mirrors eu-eu-aiact-2024-article-5-2 near-verbatim, consistent with EEA incorporation.

rule_text: You must obtain prior authorisation from a judicial or independent administrative authority before each use of a real-time remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, with limited exceptions for urgency requiring authorisation within 24 hours.
rule_text_technical: Each use of a real-time remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement shall be subject to prior authorisation by a judicial authority or independent administrative authority issued upon reasoned request; in justified urgency, use may begin without authorisation provided it is requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, with rejection requiring immediate cessation and deletion of data.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Norway's Art. 5(2)-(6) requirement for prior judicial or independent administrative authority authorization and fundamental rights impact assessment before real-time remote biometric identification is a near-verbatim EEA transposition of eu-eu-aiact-2024-article-5-3 and eu-eu-aiact-2024-recital-34.

rule_text: You must notify the relevant market surveillance authority and national data protection authority of each use of real-time remote biometric identification systems for law enforcement purposes.
rule_text_technical: Each use of a 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement shall be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and national data protection authority in accordance with national rules; the notification shall not include sensitive operational data.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: Member States and the Commission must publish annual reports on the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems for law enforcement, excluding sensitive operational data.
rule_text_technical: National market surveillance authorities and national data protection authorities shall submit annual reports to the Commission on the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems; the Commission shall publish annual reports based on aggregated data, excluding sensitive operational data.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must classify an AI system as high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product (or is itself a product) covered by listed Union harmonisation legislation, and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment.
rule_text_technical: An AI system shall be considered high-risk where: (a) it is intended for use as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) the product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market or putting into service.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both rules address high-risk AI system classification under EU law, but this rule adds a cybersecurity-specific compliance layer (CRA essential requirements) on top of the AI Act's existing high-risk classification framework.

Norway's KI-loven Art. 6(1)-(2) is a direct EEA implementation of EU AI Act Article 6(1), classifying AI systems as high-risk based on Annex I product safety components or Annex III use cases — near-verbatim transposition.

rule_text: You must ensure datasets take into account characteristics particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural, or functional setting where the high-risk AI system is intended to be used.
rule_text_technical: Data sets shall take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements that are particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting within which the high-risk AI system is intended to be used.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Norway's KI-loven is an EEA implementation of the EU AI Act; this rule mirrors Article 10(2)-(3) quality criteria for training, validation, and testing datasets including relevance and representativeness, which is captured in eu-eu-aiact-2024-article-10-4.

Both address eliminating gender stereotyping and discriminatory biases from AI datasets, but the UNESCO rule is a soft-law recommendation for proactive redress while the EU AI Act provision is a binding obligation tied to high-risk systems and specific contextual characteristics.

rule_text: You may exceptionally process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction in high-risk AI systems, but only with strict safeguards including pseudonymisation, access controls, and deletion once bias is corrected.
rule_text_technical: Providers may exceptionally process special categories of personal data for bias detection/correction subject to: bias correction cannot be effective with other data; technical limits on re-use and state-of-the-art security measures including pseudonymisation; strict access controls; no transmission to other parties; deletion once bias corrected or retention period reached; and recorded justification.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must design high-risk AI systems to technically allow for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system to ensure traceability appropriate to its intended purpose.
rule_text_technical: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risks/substantial modifications, post-market monitoring, and operational monitoring under Article 26(5).

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).
Norway's EEA implementation of the logging/traceability requirement for high-risk AI systems mirrors EU AI Act Article 12 in substance with minor rephrasing.

rule_text: For remote biometric identification high-risk AI systems, logs must record the period of each use, the reference database, input data leading to a match, and identification of natural persons verifying the results.
rule_text_technical: For high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, logging capabilities shall provide recording of: period of each use; reference database against which input was checked; input data leading to a match; and identification of natural persons involved in verification under Article 14(5).

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: For remote biometric identification high-risk AI systems, you must ensure no action is taken by deployers based on the identification unless it has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two competent natural persons.
rule_text_technical: For high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, oversight measures shall ensure no action or decision is taken by the deployer based on identification unless separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with necessary competence, training and authority, except where Union or national law considers application disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control, or asylum.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must design high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after deployment to eliminate or reduce the risk of biased outputs influencing future inputs (feedback loops).
rule_text_technical: High-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service shall be developed in such a way as to eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of possibly biased outputs influencing input for future operations (feedback loops), with appropriate mitigation measures.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both address correcting inaccuracies and mitigating bias in automated/AI processing, but GDPR Recital 71 targets profiling with mathematical/statistical procedures and human oversight rights, while EU AI Act Article 15-4 targets high-risk AI systems that continue learning post-deployment.

rule_text: You must keep automatically generated logs of high-risk AI systems under your control for at least six months, unless other Union or national law requires longer.
rule_text_technical: Providers of high-risk AI systems shall keep logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems, to the extent under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of at least six months unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).
Norway's EEA implementation of the six-month log retention requirement for high-risk AI systems matches EU AI Act Article 19 in substance with minor phrasing differences.

Both require contemporaneous documentation and retention of compliance records, but 45 CFR 92.9(c) specifically mandates retaining employee training completion records for a defined period in health nondiscrimination contexts, while EU AI Act Article 19 focuses on automated logs of high-risk AI systems.

rule_text: As a distributor, you must verify before making a high-risk AI system available that it bears the CE marking, is accompanied by the declaration of conformity and instructions, and that the provider and importer have met their obligations.
rule_text_technical: Before making a high-risk AI system available, distributors shall verify: CE marking is affixed; system is accompanied by EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use; provider and importer have complied with obligations under Article 16(b)(c) and Article 23(3); shall not make available if non-compliant; shall take corrective actions if needed.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: As a deployer, you must monitor operation of the high-risk AI system, suspend use if it presents a risk, and inform providers, distributors, and market surveillance authorities; you must report serious incidents immediately.
rule_text_technical: Deployers shall monitor operation of the high-risk AI system based on instructions; where they have reason to consider use may result in risk under Article 79(1), they shall inform provider/distributor and relevant market surveillance authority and suspend use; on identifying a serious incident, they shall immediately inform provider, then importer/distributor and market surveillance authorities.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both authorize a supervisory authority to order suspension or interruption of processing when it poses risks to rights and freedoms, but Senegal's CDP provision also allows data locking and definitive withdrawal of authorization, and applies specifically to urgent personal data processing violations.

Both require deployers to notify the provider/distributor and market surveillance authority when they believe the AI system presents a risk, but the Finnish rule specifically adds a fine for failure to do so.

rule_text: As a deployer, you must keep automatically generated logs of high-risk AI systems under your control for at least six months, unless other Union or national law requires otherwise.
rule_text_technical: Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep logs automatically generated by the system to the extent under their control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular Union law on the protection of personal data.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: As an employer using a high-risk AI system at the workplace, you must inform workers' representatives and affected workers before putting it into service that they will be subject to its use.
rule_text_technical: Before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system at the workplace, deployers who are employers shall inform workers' representatives and affected workers that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system, in accordance with applicable rules and procedures of Union and national law on worker information.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).
