Both require notifying workers of AI use in the workplace, but the AIGE adds a bias-free requirement while the EU AI Act is narrower (high-risk systems only, with worker representatives), making this a soft-law voluntary analog with broader scope.

Finland's § 18(5) mirrors EU AI Act Article 26(7) nearly verbatim, requiring employer-deployers to inform worker representatives and affected workers before putting a high-risk AI system into service at the workplace.

rule_text: As a public authority deploying a high-risk AI system, you must comply with registration obligations and must not use a high-risk system that has not been registered in the EU database.
rule_text_technical: Deployers of high-risk AI systems that are public authorities or Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies shall comply with registration obligations under Article 49; if they find the high-risk AI system has not been registered in the EU database, they shall not use that system and shall inform the provider or distributor.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: Where applicable, as a deployer you must use the information provided by the provider to comply with your obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment under applicable data protection law.
rule_text_technical: Where applicable, deployers of high-risk AI systems shall use the information provided under Article 13 to comply with their obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: Before using a high-risk AI system for post-remote biometric identification in a targeted criminal investigation, you must request prior or near-immediate (within 48 hours) authorisation from a judicial or administrative authority, with use limited to what is strictly necessary.
rule_text_technical: In the framework of an investigation for the targeted search of a person suspected or convicted of a criminal offence, the deployer of a high-risk AI system for post-remote biometric identification shall request authorisation, ex ante or without undue delay and no later than 48 hours, by a judicial authority or binding administrative authority subject to judicial review; if rejected, use shall stop immediately and personal data shall be deleted.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

The KI-MIG rule implements the same prior/near-immediate authorisation requirement for post-remote biometric identification in targeted criminal investigations as EU AI Act Article 26(10), but specifies that the reviewing body is Germany's independent AI Market Surveillance Chamber, adding a national institutional layer not present in the EU-level rule.

Norway's Art. 26(10) requirement for targeted use of post-remote biometric identification AI systems for specified law enforcement purposes is a near-verbatim EEA transposition of eu-eu-aiact-2024-article-26-10.

rule_text: Each Member State must designate or establish at least one notifying authority responsible for assessment, designation, notification, and monitoring of conformity assessment bodies, ensuring no conflicts of interest.
rule_text_technical: Each Member State shall designate or establish at least one notifying authority responsible for setting up and carrying out procedures for assessment, designation, notification and monitoring of conformity assessment bodies; notifying authorities shall be organised to safeguard objectivity and impartiality, with no conflicts of interest, and shall not provide consultancy services on a commercial basis.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Norway's EEA implementation requires designation of at least one notifying authority and market surveillance authority, mirroring EU AI Act Article 28's requirement for Member States to designate notifying authorities, adapted for EEA incorporation.

rule_text: Notified bodies must be established under national law with legal personality, be independent of the providers they assess, satisfy organisational and cybersecurity requirements, and have permanent availability of competent personnel with relevant expertise.
rule_text_technical: Notified bodies shall be established under national law with legal personality; satisfy organisational, quality management, resource, process, and cybersecurity requirements; be independent of providers and any operator with economic interest in assessed systems; safeguard impartiality; maintain confidentiality; have appropriate liability insurance; have permanent availability of sufficient administrative, technical, legal and scientific personnel with experience in relevant AI systems.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Norway designates its national accreditation body specifically for assessment and monitoring of conformity assessment bodies, which is a more specific institutional assignment than the general notified body requirements in EU AI Act Article 31.

rule_text: Notified bodies subcontracting tasks must ensure subcontractors meet the requirements, take full responsibility for subcontracted work, obtain provider agreement before subcontracting, and make a list of subsidiaries publicly available.
rule_text_technical: Where a notified body subcontracts specific conformity assessment tasks or has recourse to a subsidiary, it shall ensure subcontractor/subsidiary meets Article 31 requirements and inform the notifying authority; notified bodies take full responsibility for tasks performed; activities may be subcontracted only with provider agreement; notified bodies shall make a list of subsidiaries publicly available.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a deployer, cooperate with relevant competent authorities in any actions taken regarding the high-risk AI system to implement this Regulation.
rule_text_technical: Deployers shall cooperate with relevant competent authorities in any action those authorities take in relation to the high-risk AI system to implement this Regulation.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must notify the market surveillance authority of the results of the fundamental rights impact assessment using the provided template.
rule_text_technical: Once the fundamental rights impact assessment has been performed, the deployer shall notify the market surveillance authority of its results, submitting the filled-out template, except in cases referred to in Article 46(1).

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a notified body, ensure confidentiality of information obtained during conformity assessment activities except where disclosure is required by law.
rule_text_technical: Notified bodies shall have documented procedures ensuring that personnel, committees, subsidiaries, subcontractors, and associated bodies maintain confidentiality of information obtained during conformity assessment activities, except where disclosure is required by law.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a notified body planning to cease conformity assessment activities, inform the notifying authority and providers concerned at least one year before cessation.
rule_text_technical: Where a notified body decides to cease conformity assessment activities, it shall inform the notifying authority and providers concerned as soon as possible and at least one year before ceasing activities in case of planned cessation.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of an Annex III point 1 high-risk AI system, follow either the internal control or the notified-body conformity assessment procedure as applicable.
rule_text_technical: For high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III point 1, providers shall opt for conformity assessment based on internal control (Annex VI) where harmonised standards or common specifications are applied, or follow the Annex VII procedure where standards/specifications are absent, partly applied, not applied, or restricted.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both require stricter/notified-body conformity assessment for certain high-risk product categories, but CRA applies to important digital products (Annex III) rather than AI Act Annex III point 1 systems.

Norway's KI-loven Article 43 restates the EU AI Act Article 43 conformity assessment obligation for high-risk AI systems using internal control or notified-body procedures, in EEA implementation language.

Both rules require providers of high-risk AI systems to undergo the conformity assessment procedure under Article 43 before market placement, with Finland implementing this as a national obligation mirroring the EU AI Act requirement.

rule_text: You must, as a provider of high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III points 2-8, follow the internal-control conformity assessment procedure in Annex VI.
rule_text_technical: For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers shall follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control as referred to in Annex VI.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must undergo a new conformity assessment when the high-risk AI system undergoes a substantial modification.
rule_text_technical: High-risk AI systems already subject to conformity assessment shall undergo a new conformity assessment in the event of substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must register any AI system you classify as not high-risk in a designated database before making it available to users or deploying it.
rule_text_technical: Before placing on the market or putting into service an AI system the provider has concluded is not high-risk under Article 6(3), the provider or authorised representative shall register themselves and that system in the EU database.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

The Finnish Act directly implements and cross-references Article 49(1) of the EU AI Act, requiring providers to register high-risk AI systems in the EU database, making it a near-verbatim transposition of the EU AI Act registration obligation.

rule_text: You must, as a public authority deployer, register yourself and the high-risk AI system in use in the EU database before putting it into service or using it.
rule_text_technical: Before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (excluding point 2), public authority deployers, Union institutions/bodies, or persons acting on their behalf shall register themselves, select the system, and register its use in the EU database.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

This rule transposes Articles 79 and 81 EU AI Act notification duties into German law by designating competent market surveillance authorities and adding the procedural requirement to route notifications through the BNetzA.

rule_text: You must process personal data in an AI regulatory sandbox only when developing AI for substantial public interest and meeting all specified conditions.
rule_text_technical: In the AI regulatory sandbox, personal data lawfully collected for other purposes may be processed solely for developing, training and testing AI in the sandbox where conditions are met: substantial public interest in listed areas, necessity (no anonymised/synthetic alternative), monitoring mechanisms for high risks, isolated protected processing environment, restrictions on sharing, no decisions affecting data subjects, technical/organisational safeguards, log retention, full process documentation, and public summary.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must allow subjects of real-world testing to withdraw consent at any time without detriment and request immediate deletion of their personal data.
rule_text_technical: Any subjects of real-world testing or their legally designated representative may, without resulting detriment and without justification, withdraw from testing at any time by revoking informed consent and may request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data; withdrawal does not affect activities already carried out.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must report any serious incident identified during real-world testing to the national market surveillance authority and adopt immediate mitigation measures or suspend testing.
rule_text_technical: Any serious incident identified in the course of real-world testing shall be reported to the national market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 73, and the provider shall adopt immediate mitigation measures or suspend/terminate testing, and establish a procedure for prompt recall.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must register information about high-risk AI systems and systems you determine are non-high-risk in a centralized database accessible to regulators.
rule_text_technical: The Commission, in collaboration with Member States, shall set up and maintain an EU database containing information on Annex III high-risk AI systems registered under Articles 49 and 60 and on AI systems not considered high-risk under Article 6(3) registered under Articles 6(4) and 49.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

This rule implements the EU AI Act's reporting/notification obligations at the German national level by routing them through a designated single point of contact, adding a procedural layer not present in the EU-level rule.
Norway's requirement to register high-risk AI systems in the EU database before market placement is a direct EEA transposition of EU AI Act Articles 49 and 71.

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a high-risk AI system, establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the technology and risks.
rule_text_technical: Providers shall establish and document a post-market monitoring system in a manner proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and risks of the high-risk AI system, based on a post-market monitoring plan that is part of the technical documentation.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).
Norway's EEA implementation of the post-market monitoring system requirement matches EU AI Act Article 72(1) in substance with minor rephrasing.

rule_text: You must report serious incidents involving widespread infringements within two days of becoming aware of them.
rule_text_technical: In the event of a widespread infringement or a serious incident as defined in Article 3(49)(b), the report shall be provided immediately and not later than two days after awareness.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must report serious incidents involving the death of a person within 10 days of awareness.
rule_text_technical: In the event of the death of a person, the report shall be provided immediately after the provider or deployer establishes or suspects a causal relationship between the high-risk AI system and the incident, but not later than 10 days after becoming aware.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, following the report of a serious incident, perform necessary investigations including risk assessment and corrective action without delay.
rule_text_technical: Following the reporting of a serious incident, the provider shall without delay perform necessary investigations including a risk assessment and corrective action, cooperating with competent authorities and not altering the AI system in a way that may affect subsequent evaluation prior to informing competent authorities.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both require providers to report serious incidents and take corrective action including withdrawal/recall, but the Finnish rule adds a fine sanction for failure to do so, while the EU AI Act provision focuses on the obligation itself.

rule_text: You must grant market surveillance authorities access to the source code of a high-risk AI system upon reasoned request when necessary to assess conformity and other testing has been exhausted.
rule_text_technical: Market surveillance authorities shall be granted access to the source code of high-risk AI systems upon reasoned request only when access is necessary to assess conformity with Chapter III Section 2 and testing/auditing procedures based on data and documentation have been exhausted or proved insufficient.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both require providers to supply information to market surveillance authorities upon reasoned request, but the Finnish rule frames this as a sanctionable obligation with fines, whereas the EU AI Act provision focuses on access to source code specifically.

rule_text: You must grant national authorities supervising fundamental rights access to documentation created or maintained under this Regulation when necessary to fulfil their mandate.
rule_text_technical: National public authorities or bodies that supervise or enforce obligations under Union law protecting fundamental rights, including non-discrimination, shall have the power to request and access documentation created or maintained under this Regulation in accessible language and format when necessary for effective fulfilment of their mandates within their jurisdiction.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as an operator, take all appropriate corrective actions to bring a non-compliant AI system into compliance, withdraw it from the market, or recall it within the period prescribed by the market surveillance authority.
rule_text_technical: Where a market surveillance authority finds an AI system non-compliant, it shall require the relevant operator to take all appropriate corrective actions to bring the AI system into compliance, to withdraw or recall it within a prescribed period, in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or as provided by relevant Union harmonisation law.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Norway's KI-loven Art. 20 implementing EU AI Act Art. 79(2) obligation to take corrective actions, withdraw, disable, or recall non-conforming high-risk AI systems is a near-verbatim EEA transposition.

rule_text: You must apply Directive (EU) 2019/1937 to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and to the protection of persons reporting such infringements.
rule_text_technical: Directive (EU) 2019/1937 shall apply to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and the protection of persons reporting such infringements.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You may, as a downstream provider, lodge a duly reasoned complaint with the AI Office alleging an infringement of this Regulation by a general-purpose AI model provider.
rule_text_technical: Downstream providers shall have the right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement of this Regulation, duly reasoned and indicating point of contact of the GPAI provider, description of facts and provisions concerned, reasons, and any other relevant information.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both grant a right to lodge a complaint with an authority regarding AI Regulation infringement, but the EU rule is narrower (downstream providers complaining about GPAI model providers to the AI Office), while the Norwegian EEA implementation grants a broader right for any person to complain to a market surveillance authority about any infringement.

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model, supply documentation and information requested by the Commission to assess compliance with this Regulation.
rule_text_technical: The Commission may request the provider of the general-purpose AI model concerned to provide documentation drawn up under Articles 53 and 55 or any additional information necessary to assess compliance, with fines under Article 101 for incorrect, incomplete or misleading information.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model, provide the Commission with access to the model through APIs or other technical means including source code when an evaluation is conducted.
rule_text_technical: The AI Office may conduct evaluations of general-purpose AI models to assess compliance or investigate systemic risks; for this purpose, the Commission may request access through APIs or other appropriate technical means and tools, including source code, with fines under Article 101 for failure to provide access.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model, comply with Commission requests to take measures including compliance actions, mitigation measures, or restriction/withdrawal/recall of the model.
rule_text_technical: Where necessary and appropriate, the Commission may request providers of general-purpose AI models to take appropriate measures to comply with Articles 53 and 54, implement mitigation measures where evaluation has given rise to serious and substantiated concern of systemic risk, or restrict the making available, withdraw or recall the model.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You may voluntarily adopt codes of conduct that impose stricter requirements on your non-high-risk AI systems than legally required, including enhanced transparency, risk management, and human oversight measures.
rule_text_technical: The AI Office and Member States shall encourage and facilitate codes of conduct for voluntary application to non-high-risk AI systems of some or all Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and concerning specific requirements based on objectives and KPIs including ethical guidelines, environmental sustainability, AI literacy, inclusive design, and prevention of negative impact on vulnerable groups.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: When objections are raised to a national regulatory action on an AI system, you must consult with the affected jurisdiction's market surveillance authority and affected operators within a reasonable timeframe before deciding whether the action is justified, with expedited consultation required for fundamental safety violations.
rule_text_technical: The Commission shall, upon objection by a Member State market surveillance authority or where it considers a measure contrary to Union law, enter into consultation without undue delay and decide within 6 months (60 days for Article 5 violations) whether the national measure is justified.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a Member State, take appropriate restrictive measures (including withdrawal) against an AI system if the Commission deems a national measure justified, or withdraw the measure if deemed unjustified.
rule_text_technical: Where the Commission considers the national measure justified, all Member States shall ensure restrictive measures are taken against the AI system; where unjustified, the Member State shall withdraw the measure.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider or operator, ensure corrective action is taken on all affected AI systems made available on the Union market within the timeline prescribed by the market surveillance authority.
rule_text_technical: The provider or other relevant operator shall ensure corrective action is taken in respect of all AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market within the timeline prescribed by the market surveillance authority.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a market surveillance authority, require providers to end formal non-compliance such as missing CE marking, missing EU declaration of conformity, missing registration, missing authorised representative, or unavailable technical documentation.
rule_text_technical: Where the market surveillance authority finds formal non-compliance (improper or absent CE marking, missing or incorrect EU declaration of conformity, missing EU database registration, missing authorised representative, or unavailable technical documentation), it shall require the provider to put an end to the non-compliance within a prescribed period.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must recognize that the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce obligations on providers of general-purpose AI models under Chapter V, with the AI Office implementing these tasks.
rule_text_technical: The Commission shall have exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, taking into account procedural guarantees under Article 94, and shall entrust implementation to the AI Office.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model, provide documentation drawn up under Articles 53 and 55 or any additional information necessary for compliance assessment when requested by the Commission.
rule_text_technical: The Commission may request the provider of a general-purpose AI model to provide the documentation drawn up in accordance with Articles 53 and 55, or any additional information necessary for assessing compliance.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model, supply requested information through authorised representatives, with clients remaining responsible for incomplete, incorrect or misleading information.
rule_text_technical: Providers of general-purpose AI models or their representatives shall supply the information requested; persons authorised to represent legal entities shall provide information on behalf of the provider, with clients remaining fully responsible for the accuracy of supplied information.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must allow the AI Office, after consulting the Board, to conduct evaluations of general-purpose AI models to assess compliance or investigate systemic risks at Union level.
rule_text_technical: The AI Office, after consulting the Board, may conduct evaluations of general-purpose AI models to assess compliance with obligations or investigate systemic risks at Union level, particularly following a qualified alert from the scientific panel.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Restates the AI Office/Commission supervision and enforcement obligations (Articles 88-93) already captured in eu-eu-aiact-2024-article-92-1 and related rules, with no meaningful substantive difference.

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model, provide the Commission access to the model through APIs or other appropriate technical means, including source code, when requested for evaluation purposes.
rule_text_technical: For the purposes of evaluation, the Commission may request access to the general-purpose AI model concerned through APIs or further appropriate technical means and tools, including source code.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model, comply with Commission requests to take measures to fulfil obligations under Articles 53/54, implement risk mitigation measures, or restrict, withdraw or recall the model.
rule_text_technical: Where necessary and appropriate, the Commission may request providers to take appropriate measures to comply with obligations under Articles 53 and 54, implement mitigation measures where systemic risk is substantiated, or restrict, withdraw or recall the model.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).
Near-verbatim restatement of the Commission's power to require corrective measures under Article 93, already recorded as eu-eu-aiact-2024-article-93-1.

rule_text: You must encourage and facilitate the development of voluntary industry codes of conduct that apply transparency and documentation requirements to AI systems that are not classified as high-risk.
rule_text_technical: The AI Office and Member States shall encourage and facilitate codes of conduct, including governance mechanisms, intended to foster voluntary application of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 to non-high-risk AI systems.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both rules require involvement of civil society and stakeholders in developing codes of conduct, but the KI-MIG rule specifically names trade unions, industry, science/research, and the Länder as required participants in a domestic coordination centre, going beyond the EU AI Act's general facilitation mandate.

rule_text: You must, as a Member State, lay down rules on penalties for infringements of this Regulation that are effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and take SMEs' interests and economic viability into account.
rule_text_technical: Member States shall lay down rules on penalties and other enforcement measures applicable to infringements of this Regulation, ensuring they are effective, proportionate and dissuasive, taking into account the interests of SMEs including start-ups, and their economic viability.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both require Member States/supervisory authorities to ensure penalties are effective, proportionate and dissuasive, but GDPR Article 83(1) applies to administrative fines specifically imposed by supervisory authorities in each individual case, whereas EU AI Act Article 99-1 requires Member States to lay down rules on penalties generally.

Both require that infringements of EU AI Regulation obligations not already covered by Article 99 be subject to administrative penalties, with KI-MIG implementing that Member State obligation at the national level.

Norway's § 5 first paragraph making EU AI Act Art. 99(3)–(7) fines directly applicable domestically implements the same penalty framework as Art. 99(1)'s requirement that Member States lay down effective penalty rules.

Both rules require Member States to establish effective, proportionate, and dissuasive penalties for regulatory infringements, but apply to different EU instruments (DGA vs. AI Act) and are independently drafted.

Both require Member States to establish effective, proportionate, and dissuasive penalties for infringements and to notify the Commission, but NIS2 Art. 36 applies to cybersecurity measures transposing that directive rather than AI Act obligations.

Both the EU AI Act (Art. 99-1) and the Data Act (Chapter IX) require Member States to lay down effective, proportionate, and dissuasive penalties for infringements, but they apply to different regulatory regimes and the Data Act specifies maximum fines for legal persons while the AI Act sets explicit percentage/fixed-amount caps.

rule_text: You must, as an operator or notified body violating obligations (other than Article 5) including provider, deployer, importer, distributor, or transparency obligations, face administrative fines of up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
rule_text_technical: Non-compliance with obligations of providers (Art. 16), authorised representatives (Art. 22), importers (Art. 23), distributors (Art. 24), deployers (Art. 26), notified bodies (Arts. 31, 33, 34), or transparency obligations (Art. 50) shall be subject to fines of up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both impose fines on operators/controllers for breaching specific obligations, but GDPR Article 83(4) sets fines up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover for controller/processor and certification body obligations, whereas EU AI Act Article 99-4 covers different obligations in the AI context with different thresholds.

Norway's Art. 99 transposition of the EUR 7.5 million / 1% turnover fine tier for supplying incorrect or misleading information mirrors EU AI Act Art. 99(4)/(5) in different phrasing as an EEA implementation.

Both the DSA and the EU AI Act impose percentage-of-turnover fines for platform/operator non-compliance, but the DSA sets a 6% cap on total annual worldwide turnover for a broader range of digital service obligations, while the EU AI Act Article 99(4) sets fines up to 3% for operators/notified bodies violating obligations other than Article 5, covering a different regulatory scope.

Both establish tiered EU administrative fines based on turnover percentages and fixed euro amounts, but NIS2 Art. 34(4) targets cybersecurity obligations of essential entities (EUR 10M/2% turnover) while the EU AI Act targets high-risk AI system operators at EUR 15M/3%.

Both impose fines on providers of high-risk AI systems for specific violations, but the Finnish rule specifies particular domestic violations (lacking risk management system, improper testing) while the EU AI Act sets the overarching framework with percentage-based caps.

rule_text: You must, when imposing fines on SMEs including start-ups, apply the lower of the percentage or fixed amount set out in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5.
rule_text_technical: In the case of SMEs, including start-ups, each fine referred to in this Article shall be up to the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever thereof is lower.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Norway's § 5 second paragraph applying maximum fine amounts to public authorities but excluding turnover-based calculation is similar to but meaningfully different from EU AI Act Art. 99(6)'s SME/start-up lower-cap rule.
Both provide for reduced or waived fines in certain circumstances, but the Finnish rule focuses on minor breaches or manifest unreasonableness rather than the EU Act's SME-specific lower-amount rule.

rule_text: Data protection authorities must impose administrative fines on public institutions for violations of core data protection principles (up to EUR 1,500,000) and other regulatory obligations (up to EUR 750,000).
rule_text_technical: The European Data Protection Supervisor may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of up to EUR 1,500,000 for non-compliance with Article 5 prohibitions, and up to EUR 750,000 for non-compliance with other requirements.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: Data protection authorities must provide regulated entities an opportunity to be heard before issuing enforcement decisions, base decisions solely on documented evidence, and respect procedural rights including access to the enforcement file.
rule_text_technical: Before taking decisions under Article 100, the EDPS shall give the Union institution the opportunity of being heard, base decisions only on elements parties could comment on, and fully respect rights of defence including access to the EDPS file subject to data protection and trade secrets.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as the Commission, communicate preliminary findings to the provider of a general-purpose AI model and give it an opportunity to be heard before adopting a fine decision.
rule_text_technical: Before adopting the decision pursuant to Article 101(1), the Commission shall communicate its preliminary findings to the provider of the general-purpose AI model and give it an opportunity to be heard.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as a provider of an AI system that is a component of large-scale IT systems listed in Annex X placed on the market before 2 August 2027, bring it into compliance with this Regulation by 31 December 2030.
rule_text_technical: AI systems which are components of large-scale IT systems established by legal acts listed in Annex X placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 shall be brought into compliance with this Regulation by 31 December 2030.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, as an operator of high-risk AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026, comply with this Regulation only if subject to significant design changes thereafter; public authority high-risk AI systems must comply by 2 August 2030.
rule_text_technical: This Regulation shall apply to operators of high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 only if subject to significant design changes thereafter; providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for use by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both address transitional compliance periods for AI systems already on the market before the Act's entry into force, but the Norwegian rule cross-references EU AI Act transitional periods rather than setting its own, and applies as an EEA implementation measure.

rule_text: You must, as a provider of a general-purpose AI model placed on the market before 2 August 2025, take necessary steps to comply with this Regulation's obligations by 2 August 2027.
rule_text_technical: Providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 shall take necessary steps to comply with the obligations laid down in this Regulation by 2 August 2027.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must comply with this regulation according to a phased implementation schedule: certain prohibitions take effect first, followed by obligations for general-purpose AI systems, with the most stringent requirements for high-risk AI applications taking effect last.
rule_text_technical: This Regulation shall apply from 2 August 2026, with the following exceptions: Chapters I and II from 2 February 2025; Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, VII, XII and Article 78 from 2 August 2025 (except Article 101); Article 6(1) and corresponding obligations from 2 August 2027.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must classify as high-risk the following biometric AI systems: remote biometric identification systems (excluding biometric verification confirming claimed identity), biometric categorization based on sensitive/protected attributes, and emotion recognition systems.
rule_text_technical: High-risk biometric AI systems include: (a) remote biometric identification systems (excluding biometric verification systems for confirming claimed identity); (b) biometric categorization systems classifying based on sensitive or protected attributes inferred from such characteristics; (c) emotion recognition systems, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must classify as high-risk AI systems used for recruitment/selection, work-related decisions affecting promotion/termination, task allocation based on behavior/traits, or monitoring/evaluating performance and behavior in employment relationships.
rule_text_technical: AI systems used in employment, workers' management and access to self-employment are high-risk where intended for: (a) recruitment or selection of natural persons including targeted job advertisements, application analysis and candidate evaluation; (b) decisions affecting work-related terms, promotion or termination, task allocation based on behaviour/traits, or monitoring and evaluating performance and behaviour.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both address discrimination risks in AI-assisted hiring/candidate filtering, but the AIGE frames it as a due-diligence question about training data at a voluntary/soft-law level, while the EU AI Act mandates high-risk classification and compliance obligations.

Both rules address AI use in recruitment, hiring, promotion, and work-related decisions, but the EU AI Act classifies such systems as high-risk requiring conformity obligations, whereas the Illinois rule directly prohibits discriminatory use of AI in those employment decisions under civil rights law with different scope, enforcement mechanism, and burden.

rule_text: As a provider, you must prepare and maintain a declaration of conformity that includes: identification of the AI system, your contact details, a statement of your responsibility for the system's compliance, confirmation that the system conforms to applicable AI regulations and other relevant laws, documentation of data protection and privacy compliance where applicable, references to any AI standards or frameworks applied, details of any third-party conformity assessor involved, and the date and authorized signatory information.
rule_text_technical: The EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 shall contain: AI system identification; provider/representative details; sole responsibility statement; conformity statement with this Regulation and applicable Union law; for personal data processing, compliance statement with Regulations (EU) 2016/679, (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680; references to harmonised standards used; notified body details if applicable; and place/date/signatory of declaration.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).
Both require an EU declaration of conformity with specified content, but CRA applies to products with digital elements and cybersecurity requirements rather than high-risk AI systems.

rule_text: You must verify that your quality management system meets applicable standards, examine your technical documentation for completeness and accuracy, and ensure your product design, development, and post-market monitoring practices align with that documentation.
rule_text_technical: The conformity assessment procedure based on internal control requires the provider to: verify the established quality management system is in compliance with Article 17 requirements; examine information in technical documentation to assess compliance with essential requirements in Chapter III Section 2; and verify that design, development and post-market monitoring under Article 72 is consistent with the technical documentation.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both describe internal control conformity assessment procedures requiring technical documentation and quality/production controls, but CRA Annex VIII Part I adds vulnerability-handling process requirements specific to cybersecurity products.

rule_text: You must, when undergoing third-party conformity assessment, submit application to a notified body for quality management system approval and technical documentation assessment, and allow surveillance, periodic audits, and access to training/validation/test data sets.
rule_text_technical: Conformity assessment based on quality management system and technical documentation requires application to a notified body which examines and approves the QMS, examines technical documentation (with access to training, validation and test datasets via API or technical means), issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate where compliant, conducts ongoing surveillance via periodic audits, and re-assesses changes affecting compliance.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

Both require submission to a notified body with technical documentation for third-party type examination, but CRA Annex VIII Part II applies to products with digital elements and their cybersecurity characteristics rather than AI quality management systems.

rule_text: You must submit and keep current your provider information, system identification, intended purpose, and justification for why your AI system poses minimal risk, along with details about where you plan to distribute it.
rule_text_technical: Providers registering AI systems per Article 49(2) shall submit and keep updated: provider/submitter/representative details; AI system trade name and identification; intended purpose description; condition(s) under Article 6(3) supporting not-high-risk classification; short summary of grounds for not-high-risk assessment; system status; and Member States of placement.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must register high-risk AI systems by submitting and regularly updating information about the deployer and system provider, including a summary of how the system may affect fundamental rights and data protection.
rule_text_technical: Deployers of high-risk AI systems registering per Article 49(3) shall submit and keep updated: deployer name/address/contact; submitter details; URL of system's EU database entry by provider; summary of FRIA conducted under Article 27; summary of DPIA carried out under Article 35 GDPR or Article 27 Directive (EU) 2016/680, as specified in Article 26(8).

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must, when registering testing in real world conditions per Article 60, submit and update: unique Union-wide identification number; provider/deployer details; AI system description and intended purpose; summary of testing plan; and information on suspension/termination.
rule_text_technical: Testing in real world conditions under Article 60 shall be registered with: Union-wide unique identification number; provider/prospective provider/deployer name and contact details; brief AI system description, intended purpose and identification information; summary of main characteristics of testing plan; and information on suspension or termination.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).
Norway's KI-loven EEA implementation mirrors EU AI Act Annex IX on registration and prior approval for real-world condition testing outside regulatory sandboxes.

rule_text: You must, as the Commission, when designating a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, consider criteria including: parameter count; dataset quality/size; training computational resources; input/output modalities; benchmarks and capability evaluations; high impact on internal market (presumed for ≥10,000 registered EU business users); and number of registered end-users.
rule_text_technical: For determining general-purpose AI models with systemic risk under Article 51, the Commission shall consider: (a) parameter count; (b) dataset quality or size measured in tokens; (c) training computation in floating point operations or estimated cost/time/energy consumption; (d) input/output modalities, state-of-the-art thresholds for high-impact capabilities, specific input/output types; (e) capability benchmarks including task adaptability, autonomy, scalability, tool access; (f) high impact on internal market through reach, presumed when made available to ≥10,000 registered EU business users; (g) number of registered end-users.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU AI Act (European Union, 2024-06-13).

rule_text: You must process personal data lawfully, fairly, and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject.
rule_text_technical: Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

POPIA Section 8 requires the responsible party to ensure lawful processing conditions are met, similar to GDPR Article 5(1)(a) but framed as a pre-processing compliance obligation specific to the responsible party role under South African law.
Both require personal data to be processed lawfully and fairly, with Senegal adding 'non-fraudulently' as a distinct element but covering the same substantive principle.

Both require lawful, fair, and transparent processing with purpose limitation, but the Philippine DPA frames it as transparency, legitimate purpose, and proportionality — a slightly different tripartite formulation without the full GDPR lawful bases framework.

Turkey's KVKK Art. 4(2) independently establishes the same core data processing principles (lawfulness, fairness, accuracy, purpose limitation, data minimization) as GDPR Art. 5(1), though drafted differently and in a national context.
Both require lawful and fair processing of personal data, but Qatar's 2016 law is independently drafted under a different legal tradition from the EU GDPR.
Bahrain Art. 3(1) requires fair and lawful processing, substantively identical in principle to GDPR Art. 5(1)(a), though drafted more concisely and without the explicit transparency requirement.

Both require lawful, specific, and transparent processing of personal data, but LGPD Art. 6º, I focuses on purpose limitation and informing the data subject, while GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) addresses lawfulness, fairness, and transparency more broadly.
Both require lawful, fair, and transparent processing of personal data, but the Uganda Act is independently drafted rather than a copy of the GDPR.

Both require processing personal data in accordance with the data subject's right to privacy / lawfully, fairly and transparently, but Kenya frames this as a rights-based obligation while GDPR frames it as a processing principle.

Both require lawful, fair, and transparent processing for specific purposes, but Egypt's rule adds correctness, validity, and security requirements in a single provision, and is a binding statute rather than EU regulation.
Both require lawful processing of personal data, but the Swiss revDSG frames it as a standalone principle without the GDPR's additional 'fairly and transparently' language in the same provision.

Both impose a general lawfulness and appropriateness standard for personal data processing, but Brunei's rule uses a 'reasonable person' standard for appropriateness while GDPR specifies lawful bases and transparency requirements more precisely.

Both require lawful, fair, and principled personal data processing, but PIPL adds 'sincerity' and 'necessity' as explicit principles and prohibits using misleading means, reflecting a distinct Chinese regulatory framing.
Both require that processing of personal data be necessary, fair, and lawful, but Zimbabwe's formulation is more compressed and does not separately enumerate transparency as a standalone requirement.

Both require lawful, fair, transparent processing for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes with no incompatible further processing, but Sri Lanka's PDPA is drafted independently with slightly different phrasing.
Both require lawful, fair, and transparent processing of personal data, but drafted independently under different legal systems.
Nigeria's § 24(1)(a) reproduces the GDPR Article 5(1)(a) lawfulness, fairness, and transparency principle in near-verbatim terms.
Both require that processing have a lawful, specific, and clear purpose, consistent with the principle of purpose limitation and lawfulness, though phrased differently.
Both require purpose limitation for personal data processing, but the Bangladesh ordinance is drafted independently with similar substantive requirements to GDPR Article 5(1)(b).

rule_text: You must ensure that any processing of personal data is supported by at least one of the six lawful bases (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest/official authority, or legitimate interests).
rule_text_technical: Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the conditions in Article 6(1)(a)–(f) applies.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

Both require a lawful basis before processing personal data, but Colombia's Art. 9 specifically requires demonstrable evidence of the data owner's authorization (consent-centric), whereas GDPR Art. 6(1) provides six alternative lawful bases with consent being only one.
Both enumerate the same six lawful bases for processing personal data, independently adopted in Serbian law with equivalent substantive content but different legislative context.
Both require a lawful basis for processing personal data (consent or specified lawful grounds); Kenya independently adopted the same lawfulness requirement with similar enumerated grounds.

Both require a valid legal basis for processing personal data and enumerate similar grounds (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest, legitimate interests), but the ADGM rule adds a documentation requirement and is drafted independently under a different jurisdictional framework.
Rwanda's law independently adopts the same lawful basis requirement for processing personal data as GDPR Article 6(1), using similar enumerated grounds but drafted differently under Rwandan law.

The Kuwait rule closely mirrors GDPR Article 32's CIA triad requirement (confidentiality, integrity, availability, resilience), though the existing database entry cited is Art. 6(1); the requirement for continuous CIA and resilience of processing systems is most directly analogous to GDPR Art. 32 concepts present in the database through other rules.

rule_text: You must not rely on the legitimate interests legal basis if you are a public authority processing personal data in the performance of your tasks.
rule_text_technical: Point (f) of the first subparagraph of Article 6(1) shall not apply to processing carried out by public authorities in the performance of their tasks.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

Both restrict public bodies from processing personal data without a proper legal basis, but the Swiss rule applies to all personal data (requiring a statutory basis) whereas the GDPR provision specifically bars public authorities from relying on legitimate interests.

rule_text: You must, before further processing personal data for a new purpose without consent or specific legal authorisation, assess the compatibility of that purpose with the original purpose using factors such as the link between purposes, context, nature of data, possible consequences, and safeguards.
rule_text_technical: Where further processing is not based on consent or a Union/Member State law safeguarding objectives in Article 23(1), the controller shall, to ascertain compatibility, take into account inter alia: any link between purposes; context of collection; nature of the personal data (including special categories); possible consequences for data subjects; and existence of appropriate safeguards including encryption or pseudonymisation.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

POPIA Section 13(1) requires collection for a specific, explicitly defined, and lawful purpose linked to the responsible party's function, sharing the purpose-limitation concept with GDPR Article 6(4) but focused on the collection stage rather than further processing compatibility.

Both address purpose limitation for personal data collection, but Senegal's rule is broader in framing while GDPR's article 6(4) specifically addresses compatibility assessment for further processing.

Both address purpose limitation for personal data processing, but Colombia's Art. 4 requires processing only for legitimate, specific, and disclosed purposes, while GDPR Art. 6(4) focuses on compatibility assessment for further processing beyond the original purpose.

Both impose purpose limitation on personal data processing, but the GDPR provides a detailed compatibility assessment framework for secondary use while the Côte d'Ivoire law states the principle more simply without that mechanism.
Both require that further processing be compatible/consistent with the original collection purpose; Kenya adopted the same compatibility assessment requirement independently.

Both address purpose limitation and compatible further processing, but the Swiss rule adds the requirement that the purpose be 'recognisable to the data subject,' a somewhat different framing from the GDPR's compatibility assessment.

Both rules restrict repurposing personal data beyond the original collection purpose, but GDPR requires a compatibility assessment while APPI sets a 'reasonably linked' standard without a formal assessment process.

Both require a clear, legitimate purpose with handling limited to what is necessary, but PIPL emphasizes direct relevance and minimal impact, whereas GDPR focuses on compatibility assessment for secondary use.
Both allow secondary use of personal data only under specified conditions including data subject authorisation or legal basis, independently drafted.

Nigeria's purpose limitation principle mirrors GDPR Article 5(1)(b) on specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes, though the existing matched rule covers compatibility assessment for further processing rather than the basic purpose limitation obligation itself; the concept is closely related but the existing rules do not capture the core purpose limitation duty directly.

Both rules restrict further processing of personal data to purposes compatible with the original collection purpose, but India's DPDPA frames it as a flat prohibition on incompatible use while GDPR requires a compatibility assessment before further processing.
Both require that processing be compatible with the original collection purpose, though the GDPR provides a detailed compatibility assessment while Jordan's law states it as a direct obligation.

Both address purpose limitation for personal data use, but the Kuwait rule is a direct prohibition on using data beyond specified collection purposes, while GDPR Art. 6(4) provides a compatibility assessment framework for further processing.

Both require purpose limitation — data collected for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes and not further processed incompatibly — but Ethiopia's Proclamation is independently drafted rather than copied from the GDPR.

rule_text: You must be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing of their personal data where processing is based on consent.
rule_text_technical: Where processing is based on consent, the controller shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to processing of his or her personal data.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

POPIA Section 11(1) establishes a similar lawful-basis framework to GDPR Article 6/7 including consent, but enumerates grounds (legitimate interest, contractual necessity, legal obligation, etc.) in a single provision rather than separately, reflecting South African legislative structure.

Both require a valid legal basis (including consent) for data processing and governance mechanisms, but the UNESCO recommendation is a voluntary soft-law instrument framing this as a multi-stakeholder governance recommendation rather than a binding legal obligation as in the GDPR.

Both require consent as a lawful basis for processing personal data, but Senegal's Art. 33 lists alternative lawful bases (legal obligation, public interest) alongside consent in a single provision, whereas GDPR Art. 7(1) focuses specifically on demonstrating consent when consent is the chosen basis.

Both require documented/demonstrable consent before processing personal data, but Uruguay's Art. 9 adds 'free, prior, express, and informed' qualifiers and predates GDPR by eight years, while GDPR focuses on the accountability/demonstrability aspect.

Both require demonstrable consent before processing personal data, but Costa Rica's law specifically mandates express written (physical or electronic) form and includes an explicit revocation right, whereas GDPR Article 7-1 focuses on the ability to demonstrate consent without mandating a written form.

Both establish consent as one of several lawful bases for processing personal data, but the Philippines DPA (2012) predates the GDPR (2016) and enumerates lawful bases in a single provision covering all personal information, while GDPR Article 7 focuses specifically on demonstrating consent; the overall lawful-basis framework is conceptually aligned but differs in structure, scope, and binding detail.

Both rules establish consent as a lawful basis for processing personal data, but the GDPR rule focuses on the controller's obligation to demonstrate consent was given, whereas the Ivorian rule simply permits processing on the basis of unambiguous consent without the evidentiary/accountability framing.

Both require a lawful basis for processing personal data with consent as the default, but Turkey's KVKK uses 'explicit consent' as the starting point with exceptions listed in Art. 5(2), whereas GDPR Article 7(1) focuses on the demonstrability of consent rather than framing it as a prohibition with exceptions, and GDPR provides a broader set of lawful bases at the same level rather than treating consent as the primary gate.

Both rules require that consent be demonstrable and genuine, but Qatar's Law No. 13 adds explicit invalidity for duress/deception and uses 'clear, specific, free' criteria, while GDPR Article 7(1) focuses on the controller's burden of proof without expressly voiding coerced consent in the same provision.
Both require demonstrable, specific, and explicit consent for processing, but Bahrain's Art. 24(1) adds a legal capacity requirement and a written form requirement not present in GDPR Art. 7(1).

Serbia's Law on Personal Data Protection is a near-verbatim transposition of GDPR Article 4(11)/Article 7, requiring consent to be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and demonstrated through a clear affirmative act.

Both require that consent be demonstrable and serve as a lawful basis for processing, but Panama adds 'prior' and 'unequivocal' qualifiers and also acknowledges alternative legal bases in the same provision, whereas GDPR Article 7(1) focuses solely on demonstrating consent.

Both rules place the burden of proof on the controller to demonstrate consent, but Kenya's § 32(1) frames it as 'burden of proof for a specified purpose' while GDPR Article 7(1) frames it as demonstrating the data subject has consented.

Both require that personal data collection/processing be grounded in the data subject's consent (or alternative lawful basis), but Egypt's rule adds a specific requirement to obtain data from the holder or competent entities, whereas GDPR focuses on demonstrating consent was given.

Both require that consent be voluntary and specific, but the Swiss revDSG explicitly adds 'for one or more specific instances of processing based on appropriate information' while GDPR Article 7(1) focuses on demonstrability of consent; the substantive requirement of free, specific, informed consent is shared but drafted differently.

Both require demonstrable consent as a lawful basis for processing, but Paraguay's rule adds specific form requirements (written, electronic, digital, or other reliable means) and qualifies consent as 'express, unequivocal, free and informed', going beyond GDPR's more flexible approach.

Both rules address consent as a lawful basis for processing personal data, but the ADGM rule goes further by specifying the attributes of valid consent (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, withdrawable), aligning closely with GDPR Article 7 read together with Recital 32/Article 4(11), whereas the existing rule focuses solely on the demonstrability requirement.

Both require demonstrable, informed consent as a lawful basis for processing, but the Saudi PDPL specifies explicit and specific consent requirements while GDPR article 7-1 focuses on the ability to demonstrate consent was given.

Ecuador's rule shares GDPR-style consent requirements (free, specific, informed, unequivocal) and adds a revocation mechanism, but GDPR Art. 7 focuses on demonstrability of consent while Ecuador's Art. 8 focuses on the quality and revocability of consent, reflecting meaningful drafting and scope differences.

Both require prior consent before processing personal data beyond the specified purpose, but APPI frames it as scope-of-purpose limitation with prior consent while GDPR focuses on demonstrating consent as a lawful basis generally.

Both require that consent be voluntary, informed, and demonstrable, but PIPL adds an explicit requirement for separate/individual consent per purpose and uses slightly different framing than GDPR's burden-of-proof focus.

Both require demonstrable, specific, and freely given consent, but Quebec's rule explicitly adds the requirement that consent be presented separately from other information in writing, and covers clarity and purpose-specificity more explicitly than GDPR Article 7-1.

The UAE rule mirrors the GDPR's consent definition (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, affirmative act) but is independently drafted and the GDPR rule focuses on the demonstrability requirement rather than the definition itself, making this an agreement on substance rather than an identical copy.

Rwanda's rule requires explicit consent for sensitive data with narrow exceptions, paralleling GDPR Article 9 in substance, but the existing matched rule covers the general consent demonstration requirement; the sensitive data explicit consent concept is broadly GDPR-aligned but no exact match exists for sensitive data explicit consent in the database.

Both require demonstrable consent before processing personal data, but Oman mandates explicit written consent as the default lawful basis and specifies clarity requirements for the request, whereas GDPR treats consent as one of several legal bases and does not require writing in all cases.

Both require that consent be freely given, specific, informed, and demonstrable, and that consent requests be presented distinctly; the Sri Lanka provision also adds the unambiguous requirement and obligation to inform of withdrawal rights, closely mirroring GDPR Article 7 but independently enacted.

Both require that consent be explicit, free, specific, informed, and documented, and both apply heightened standards for sensitive data, but Indonesia's UU PDP is independently drafted with its own phrasing and structure.

Both require explicit/demonstrable consent for processing sensitive personal data, but the Nigeria rule specifically addresses sensitive data with explicit consent and narrow exceptions, while GDPR Article 7 addresses consent more generally; the closest GDPR analog for sensitive data is Article 9, but the existing rule indexed is Article 7-1.

Both require high-quality consent for personal data processing, but India's DPDPA enumerates specific quality elements (free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, clear affirmative action) more explicitly than GDPR Article 7, which focuses on demonstrability; the GDPR's full consent quality requirements are spread across Recitals and Article 4(11).
Both require demonstrable/documented consent, but Jordan specifies the form (written or electronic) explicitly, while GDPR focuses on demonstrability without mandating a specific form.

Both require demonstrable consent for data processing, but Pakistan's rule adds specific quality requirements (free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous) and explicitly invalidates coerced consent, going beyond GDPR's bare demonstrability requirement.

Both require demonstrable consent before collecting or processing personal data, but Kuwait's rule adds the requirement to ensure the data subject's knowledge of all conditions and obligations, going slightly beyond GDPR's bare demonstration requirement.

Both require explicit consent for sensitive data processing with narrow exceptions, but the Ethiopia rule bundles explicit consent with specific exception categories (employment, medical treatment) in a way that differs from GDPR's more detailed Article 9 framework; the closest existing rule only covers demonstrability of consent generally.

Both require demonstrable consent before processing, but the Mexican rule specifically targets profiling for commercial advertising, adding a purpose-specific and sector-specific threshold not present in GDPR's general consent rule.

Both rules concern consent under GDPR framework, but this UK rule specifically addresses solely automated decision-making involving special category data (a narrower, more specific context than the general consent demonstration requirement in GDPR Article 7), adding the explicit consent plus controller safeguards condition for such automated decisions.

Both require valid consent as a basis for processing personal data, but India's Rule 4 adds specific mechanics (free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, clear affirmative action, no pre-ticked boxes) that go beyond GDPR Article 7(1)'s mere demonstrability requirement, more closely resembling GDPR Recital 32 and Article 7 combined.

rule_text: You must make reasonable efforts, taking available technology into account, to verify that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility for a child.
rule_text_technical: The controller shall make reasonable efforts to verify in such cases that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child, taking into consideration available technology.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

Both address consent for processing children's personal data via a legal representative/parental authority, but Colombia's Art. 7 also requires respecting the best interests of the child as an additional substantive condition, while GDPR Art. 8-2 focuses on verification of parental consent.

Both address consent for persons lacking legal capacity requiring a guardian's authorization, but Bahrain's rule addresses all persons lacking/having limited legal capacity broadly, while GDPR Art. 8(2) focuses specifically on verification of parental consent for children.
LGPD Art. 14 §5º mirrors GDPR Article 8(2) nearly verbatim, requiring reasonable efforts to verify parental consent using available technologies, strongly suggesting direct borrowing from the GDPR.

Both rules require mechanisms to verify age and parental consent for children's data, but Kenya's § 33(2) is a broader obligation to incorporate such mechanisms generally, while GDPR Article 8(2) specifically addresses reasonable technical efforts to verify parental authorization.

Both require reasonable efforts using available technology to verify guardian/parental consent for minors, though Kuwait sets the age threshold at under 18 while GDPR's Article 8 targets younger children, making this a close but independently drafted agreement.

Both require reasonable technical and other measures to verify parental consent before processing a child's data, but India's Rule 10 sets the age threshold at under 18 (versus GDPR's under 16) and is a binding administrative rule specifying verifiable consent from a parent or legal guardian.

rule_text: You must inform the data subject of the existence of profiling and the consequences of such profiling.
rule_text_technical: The data subject shall be informed of the existence of profiling and the consequences of such profiling, as part of the information ensuring fair and transparent processing.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

instances.citation: Part A, Section A2.3, Consumer Right 2
instances.notes: Both require informing individuals when their personal information is used in algorithmic/profiling processes for decisions, but the AIGE rule broadens scope to offers and third-party data sharing beyond GDPR's profiling-specific context.

Both require informing data subjects about automated decision-making and profiling, but Serbia's rule specifies the disclosure must occur at the time of collection, while GDPR recital 60 is framed more broadly as part of the right to be informed.

Both require notifying the data subject when a significant decision is based solely on automated processing, but Tanzania's rule specifies a 'as soon as practicable' timing standard rather than the GDPR's broader transparency framing.

Both require informing data subjects about profiling, but Jordan's Art. 9(F) is a pre-processing disclosure obligation while GDPR recital 60 frames it as informing of the existence and consequences of profiling.
