instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

Both grant individuals the right to access, rectify, or delete their personal data free of charge, though Costa Rica adds the right to consent to assignment and imposes a response obligation on the controller.

Both grant individuals a right to access personal data held about them, but Uruguay's provision specifies free access at six-month intervals and applies to any public or private database, whereas Ghana's Act 843 addresses access to data held by a 'data controller' without specifying frequency or cost conditions.

Both grant individuals a right to access their personal data from public and private databases, but the Uruguayan law specifies a free-of-charge interval mechanism while Colombia's Art. 8(a) grants access at any time without such interval restriction.

Both establish a right to access personal data held by controllers, but Uruguay's rule specifies free access at six-month intervals while Côte d'Ivoire's rule states the right without specifying frequency or cost conditions.

Both grant free periodic access to personal data held in databases, but the Dominican Republic law is specific to credit history/reports via the SIC with a four-times-per-year (quarterly) cadence, whereas Uruguay's rule is a general data access right at six-month intervals.

Both grant individuals the right to access, rectification, deletion, and related rights over their personal data at any time, though Paraguay also explicitly includes opposition and portability rights not enumerated in Uruguay's provision.

rule_text: The recipient of communicated personal data is subject to the same legal obligations as the sender, and the sender remains jointly and severally liable for compliance.
rule_text_technical: El destinatario quedará sujeto a las mismas obligaciones legales y reglamentarias del emisor y éste responderá solidaria y conjuntamente por la observancia ante el organismo de control y el titular.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).
Both impose accountability on the original controller for personal information transferred to third parties for processing, requiring contractual or equivalent safeguards, though drafted differently.
Both impose the same legal obligations on recipients of transferred data as on the sender/controller, establishing downstream accountability.

rule_text: Healthcare establishments and health professionals may collect and process patients' physical and mental health data while respecting professional secrecy and the law.
rule_text_technical: Los establecimientos sanitarios públicos o privados y los profesionales vinculados a las ciencias de la salud pueden recolectar y tratar los datos personales relativos a la salud física o mental de los pacientes, respetando los principios del secreto profesional y la normativa específica.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

rule_text: Telecommunications operators must guarantee personal data protection in their activities and adopt technical and management measures to preserve security; if a particular risk to network security exists, they must inform subscribers.
rule_text_technical: Los operadores de redes públicas o servicios de comunicaciones electrónicas deberán garantizar la protección de datos personales y adoptar medidas técnicas y de gestión adecuadas para preservar la seguridad. En caso de riesgo particular de violación de seguridad, informarán a los abonados sobre el riesgo y medidas a adoptar.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

rule_text: You may process data for advertising profiles only when it appears in publicly accessible documents, has been provided by the data subjects, or obtained with their consent; subjects may exercise free access and request removal or blocking at any time.
rule_text_technical: En recopilación de domicilios, publicidad, prospección comercial y similares, se podrán tratar datos aptos para perfiles promocionales cuando figuren en documentos accesibles al público o sean facilitados por los titulares u obtenidos con consentimiento. El titular podrá ejercer acceso sin cargo y solicitar retiro o bloqueo en cualquier momento.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

rule_text: You may process commercial/credit data of individuals for solvency assessment, but personal commercial obligations may only be registered for five years (renewable once for another five), and cancelled obligations may remain registered up to five years from cancellation.
rule_text_technical: Queda autorizado el tratamiento de datos sobre solvencia patrimonial o crediticia. Los datos relativos a obligaciones comerciales de personas físicas sólo podrán estar registrados por cinco años desde su incorporación, renovable por una vez por otros cinco si la obligación permanece incumplida. Obligaciones canceladas permanecerán registradas máximo cinco años no renovable desde la cancelación.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

Both impose a five-year retention limit on personal credit/commercial data, though Paraguay frames it from the date of registered events while Uruguay frames it from the obligation's original date, with both allowing exceptions.

Both limit retention of credit/financial obligation data to five years, though Ecuador specifically addresses the moment of expiration while Uruguay counts from the last significant information or original expiration.

rule_text: Credit database controllers must process registered information objectively as supplied and must abstain from making subjective valuations.
rule_text_technical: Los responsables de las bases se limitarán a realizar el tratamiento objetivo de la información registrada tal cual fuera suministrada, debiendo abstenerse de efectuar valoraciones subjetivas.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

Both rules require credit-related information to be reported without alteration or subjective modification, though Paraguay's is framed as an obligation on credit information companies and Uruguay's focuses on credit database controllers abstaining from subjective valuations.

rule_text: Once a debt is cancelled, the creditor must communicate this to the database controller within five business days, and the controller has three business days to update the data.
rule_text_technical: Cuando se haga efectiva la cancelación de cualquier obligación incumplida, el acreedor deberá comunicarlo al responsable de la base en plazo máximo de cinco días hábiles, y éste dispondrá de tres días hábiles para proceder a la actualización del dato.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

Both require immediate cessation of processing or disclosure of data on cancelled debts once notified, though Uruguay specifies communication from creditor to controller within five days while Paraguay focuses on the company's immediate duty to stop.

rule_text: Armed forces, police, and intelligence agencies may process personal data without prior consent only for purposes strictly necessary for national defense, public security, or crime suppression, with databases classified by reliability category, and police data must be cancelled when no longer needed.
rule_text_technical: El tratamiento de datos personales con fines de defensa nacional o seguridad pública por parte de las fuerzas armadas, organismos policiales o inteligencia, sin previo consentimiento, queda limitado a los supuestos y categorías necesarios para el estricto cumplimiento de sus misiones legalmente asignadas. Las bases deberán ser específicas y clasificadas por categorías según fiabilidad. Los datos con fines policiales se cancelarán cuando no sean necesarios.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

rule_text: You cannot hold personal data of a different nature than what was declared in the registry.
rule_text_technical: Ningún usuario de datos podrá poseer datos personales de naturaleza distinta a los declarados en el registro.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

rule_text: The Control Body must oversee compliance with the legality, integrity, accuracy, proportionality and security of data, with powers to inspect controllers, demand documents, intervene archives, seize evidence (up to six days), and conduct on-site inspections (with judicial warrant for private homes).
rule_text_technical: El órgano de control controlará la observancia del régimen legal —legalidad, integridad, veracidad, proporcionalidad y seguridad— pudiendo: exigir exhibición de libros y archivos; intervenir documentos; incautar elementos hasta seis días hábiles; practicar inspecciones (con orden judicial para domicilios particulares); requerir información a terceros; solicitar auxilio de fuerza pública.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

Both rules grant the data protection authority investigative powers including inspections and document production upon complaint, but Costa Rica's Prodhab procedure specifies a three-business-day response period for controllers while Uruguay's Control Body has broader ongoing oversight powers.

rule_text: The Control Body may sanction violators with observation, warning, fines up to 500,000 Indexed Units, suspension of the database for five days, or judicial closure of the database, graduated by gravity, repetition, or recidivism.
rule_text_technical: El órgano de control podrá aplicar las siguientes sanciones graduadas por gravedad, reiteración o reincidencia: 1) Observación; 2) Apercibimiento; 3) Multa de hasta 500.000 UI; 4) Suspensión de la base de datos por cinco días; 5) Clausura de la base de datos.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

Both rules establish a tiered fine structure for data protection violations (minor, serious, very serious), but Costa Rica uses base salaries as the unit of measurement with specific bands, while Uruguay uses Indexed Units with different thresholds and also includes database suspension as a sanction.

Both laws establish administrative enforcement penalties for data protection violations including fines and suspension of processing, but the Colombian law specifies fines up to 2,000 monthly minimum legal wages and permanent database closure, while Uruguay's law sets fines up to 500,000 Indexed Units and five-day suspension with different enforcement body powers.

Both grant a data protection supervisory authority powers to issue warnings, compliance orders, and suspension of processing, but the Uruguayan rule also specifies fines and judicial liquidation as sanctions, while the Ivorian rule is limited to warnings, compliance orders, and temporary suspension.

Both grant a supervisory authority power to impose fines on data controllers for violations, but Panama's Art. 36 specifies fines from B/.1,000 upward while Uruguay's Art. 35 sets fines up to 500,000 Indexed Units with additional sanctions like suspension.

Both provide for a graduated enforcement process including warnings, suspension, and cancellation of registrations for data protection violations, but Egypt's rule includes a prior notification step requiring violators to stop before sanctions are applied.

Both rules empower a data protection authority to impose sanctions including warnings and fines on controllers/processors, but Paraguay's law specifies fines up to 15,000 minimum daily wages (doubled for repeats) while Uruguay's law references up to 500,000 Indexed Units and additional measures like database suspension, reflecting the same underlying concept with different thresholds and scope.

Both establish tiered administrative penalties for data protection violations, but Ethiopia's Proclamation is a binding statute with structured fine tiers while Uruguay's rule covers a different jurisdictional and institutional context with different sanction types.

Both establish a tiered fine structure for data protection violations with elevated penalties for more serious infractions (e.g., sensitive data), but the Mexican rule specifies fines in MXN daily wages with a specific range and elevated fines for automated decision-making violations, while the Uruguayan rule uses Indexed Units and focuses on database suspensions rather than algorithmic systems.

rule_text: Habeas data proceedings are summary: the court must convene a hearing within three days of filing, render judgment within 24 hours of the hearing, and order compliance within a maximum of 15 calendar days.
rule_text_technical: Salvo improcedencia manifiesta, se convocará audiencia pública dentro de tres días de presentación de la demanda. La sentencia se dictará en la audiencia o dentro de 24 horas de su celebración. El plazo para cumplimiento no será mayor de quince días corridos desde la notificación.

first_instance.law_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008 (Uruguay, 2008-08-11).

Both establish a habeas data / data access judicial remedy, but the Dominican Republic rule focuses on the right to bring the action and its substantive scope (access, suspension), while Uruguay's rule addresses the procedural mechanics of the summary proceedings (hearing timelines, judgment deadlines).

rule_text: Individuals have the fundamental right to informational self-determination, allowing them to control the flow of information concerning them and prevent discriminatory actions.
rule_text_technical: Every person has the right to informational self-determination, recognized as a fundamental right derived from the right to privacy, encompassing the principles and guarantees relating to the legitimate processing of their personal data and aimed at preventing discriminatory actions.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

instances.citation: Part II — Data subject participation principle
instances.notes: Both recognize individuals' rights over their personal data, but Ghana's Act 843 specifies access and correction rights while Costa Rica's article frames this as a broader fundamental right to informational self-determination; the Ghana provision bundles two distinct rights (access + correction) into a single participation principle.

Both establish a broad right of individuals to control information about themselves, but Paraguay's provision explicitly extends the right to cover persons under parental authority, guardianship, or custody, and their assets, which goes beyond Costa Rica's general informational self-determination framing.

Both establish a broad right of informational self-determination allowing individuals to know, decide on, and limit handling of their personal information, though PIPL is a binding statute with specific legislative exceptions whereas Costa Rica's is framed as a fundamental right.

rule_text: Express consent is not required when collection is ordered by competent judicial authority or a special legislative investigative commission, when the data are of unrestricted access from public sources, or when the data must be delivered by constitutional or legal mandate.
rule_text_technical: Express consent shall not be required when: (a) there is a reasoned order by competent judicial authority or an agreement adopted by a special investigative commission of the Legislative Assembly; (b) the data are of unrestricted access obtained from sources of general public access; or (c) the data must be delivered by constitutional or legal provision.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

Both enumerate exceptions to the consent requirement for personal data processing, including publicly available sources and state/government functions, though the Dominican Republic rule also adds marketing lists and data already known to the recipient as additional exceptions.

Both permit processing without consent in specified exceptional circumstances (legal obligations, vital interests, public interest), but Zimbabwe's rule is specifically limited to non-sensitive data and includes an evidentiary/offence-proving ground not present in the Costa Rica rule.

Both rules permit processing without consent under specified legitimate/public-interest grounds, but India's DPDPA lists distinct categories (voluntary provision, State subsidies, medical emergencies) that differ from Costa Rica's judicial or legislative exceptions.

Both permit processing without consent for public-authority tasks, but Jordan's exception also extends to contracted third parties acting on behalf of public entities, which Costa Rica's rule does not explicitly cover.

rule_text: You may only process restricted-access personal data for public purposes or with the express consent of the data subject.
rule_text_technical: Personal data of restricted access — those forming part of public-access registries that are not of unrestricted access because they are of interest only to the holder or the Public Administration — may be processed only for public purposes or with the express consent of the holder.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

Both rules require specific prior consent (or an enumerated exception) as the default requirement for processing sensitive/restricted personal data, independently drafted but substantively aligned in requiring heightened protection for sensitive categories.

Both require express consent/authorization before processing personal data, but Colombia's Art. 9 adds an 'informed' and 'prior' requirement and includes statutory exceptions, while Costa Rica's rule is narrower, focusing on restricted-access data for public purposes.

Both require explicit/express consent before processing personal data, but the Dominican Republic rule applies generally to all personal data processing and transfer with a written/equivalent consent requirement, while the Costa Rica rule specifically governs restricted-access data for public purposes.

Both restrict sensitive data processing to a limited set of lawful bases including explicit consent, but the Saudi PDPL adds health/medical purposes and requires written consent, while Costa Rica's provision focuses on public purposes or express consent.

Both require express consent for processing sensitive personal information, but Quebec's rule applies in the context of releasing (communicating) sensitive information within a public body framework, while Costa Rica's rule covers processing restricted-access data for public purposes.

rule_text: You may issue a protocol of action governing collection, storage, and handling of personal data, but it must be registered with Prodhab to be valid, and Prodhab may verify compliance at any time.
rule_text_technical: Natural and legal persons, public or private, having functions of collection, storage, or use of personal data may issue a protocol of action establishing procedures for compliance with this law. To be valid, protocols and subsequent modifications must be registered with Prodhab, which may verify compliance at any time. Processing under a registered protocol creates an iuris tantum presumption of compliance with this law for purposes of authorizing data transfers.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

rule_text: Prodhab employees cannot provide services to entities engaged in personal-data processing (extending two years after leaving), cannot have personal interest in matters before the Agency, and cannot reveal personal data accessed in their role.
rule_text_technical: All Prodhab employees are prohibited from: (a) providing services to persons or companies engaged in collection, storage, or handling of personal data, with the prohibition persisting two years after cessation; (b) personally and improperly taking interest in matters before the Agency; (c) revealing or propagating personal data accessed in their role, with the prohibition persisting indefinitely; and (d) for those in professional posts, externally exercising their profession (with limited exceptions). Violation constitutes a most serious fault.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

rule_text: It is a minor offense to collect personal data without providing sufficient information to the data subject under Article 5, or to collect, store, or transmit third-party personal data through insecure mechanisms.
rule_text_technical: Minor offenses include: (a) collecting personal data for use in a database without providing sufficient and ample information to the data subject under Article 5(I); and (b) collecting, storing, and transmitting third-party personal data through insecure mechanisms or mechanisms that do not guarantee security and inalterability.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

Both address civil/minor infractions for refusing data subject rights (review, correction, cancellation), but the Costa Rica law frames it more broadly as failure to inform while DR Law 172-13 specifically targets refusal to honor data holder requests.

Both impose penalties for failing to respect data subject rights or violating collection conditions, but Egypt specifies EGP monetary fine ranges while Costa Rica classifies these as minor offenses with different penalty structures.

rule_text: It is a serious offense to process personal data without informed express consent, transfer data in violation of Chapter III, use data for a purpose other than authorized, or unjustifiably refuse access, deletion, or rectification requests.
rule_text_technical: Serious offenses include: (a) collecting, storing, transmitting, or otherwise using personal data without the informed and express consent of the holder; (b) transferring data to others in contravention of Chapter III; (c) using data for a purpose other than that authorized by the holder; (d) unjustifiably refusing to grant a data subject access to verify quality, collection, storage, and use; and (e) unjustifiably refusing to delete or rectify data when so requested by clear and unequivocal means.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

Both criminalize unauthorized processing of personal data, but the Philippine law specifies imprisonment ranges and peso-denominated fines while Costa Rica's law categorizes it as a 'serious offense' without equivalent criminal penalties.

Both address unauthorized use of personal data beyond the permitted purpose, but DR Law 172-13 is specific to SIC credit report misuse with minimum-wage-based fines, while Costa Rica's law covers broader unauthorized processing with different penalties.

Both classify processing personal data without consent as a serious infraction, but Costa Rica's law provides more detail on additional serious offenses while Panama's Art. 40(1) focuses specifically on the consent violation.

Both impose penalties for collecting/processing/disclosing personal data without legal authorization or consent, but Egypt specifies EGP monetary fines with a commercial-purpose aggravating factor, while Costa Rica uses a tiered offense classification system.

rule_text: It is a very serious offense for private parties to process sensitive data, obtain data through deceit/violence/threat, reveal protected information, provide false data, process without registering with Prodhab, or transfer data abroad without consent.
rule_text_technical: Very serious offenses include: (a) private natural or legal persons collecting, storing, transmitting, or otherwise using sensitive data as defined in Article 3; (b) obtaining personal data through deceit, violence, or threat; (c) revealing information registered in a database whose secrecy is legally obligatory; (d) knowingly providing third parties with false or different information from a data file; (e) processing personal data without proper registration with Prodhab where required by Article 21; and (f) transferring personal information of Costa Ricans or foreign residents to databases in third countries without the holders' consent.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

Both establish criminal penalties (fines and/or imprisonment) for serious personal data violations, but the Ivorian rule specifies a maximum fine of XOF 10,000,000 and up to 5 years imprisonment, while Costa Rica's rule uses a tiered offense classification with different penalty structures.

Both address fraudulent/deceptive access to protected data systems, but DR Law 172-13 is specific to SIC databases with minimum-wage fines or imprisonment, while Costa Rica's very serious offenses cover a broader range of data processing violations.
Both classify fraudulent or deceptive collection of personal data as a very serious infraction, consistent with the tiered infraction frameworks in both laws.

Both impose heightened penalties (including imprisonment) for processing sensitive personal data without consent or legal authorization, but Egypt specifies EGP 500,000–5,000,000 fines with at least 3 months imprisonment while Costa Rica classifies it as a very serious offense with a different penalty structure.

rule_text: You must pay an annual canon of US$200 for the regulation and administration of databases registered with Prodhab.
rule_text_technical: Controllers of databases required to register with Prodhab under Article 21 are subject to an annual canon of two hundred United States dollars (US$200) for regulation and administration of databases, with collection procedures detailed by regulation.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

rule_text: You must pay Prodhab a canon of between US$0.25 and US$1 for each commercial sale of personal data of identifiable individuals from registered databases.
rule_text_technical: The controller must pay Prodhab a canon for each sale of data of files defined in Article 3(b), of individualizable persons legitimately registered, when commercialized for profit, ranging from twenty-five US cents (US$0.25) to one US dollar (US$1), as fixed by regulation; for global contracts of low, medium, or high consumption or online service modalities, the regulation fixes detail of the charge, which shall not exceed ten percent of the contractual price.

first_instance.law_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011 (Costa Rica, 2011-07-05).

rule_text: You must have a lawful basis before processing personal data.
rule_text_technical: Personal data shall only be processed where there exists a lawful basis recognised under the Act.

first_instance.law_name: Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Ghana, 2012-07-16).

rule_text: You must specify a legitimate purpose before collecting personal data.
rule_text_technical: The purposes for which personal data is collected must be specified, explicit, and legitimate at the time of collection.

first_instance.law_name: Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Ghana, 2012-07-16).

rule_text: You cannot process personal data for purposes incompatible with those originally specified.
rule_text_technical: Processing of personal data shall be limited to the specified purposes and may not be further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.

first_instance.law_name: Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Ghana, 2012-07-16).

rule_text: Individuals have the right to lodge complaints with the Data Protection Commission.
rule_text_technical: A data subject may lodge a complaint with the DPC concerning any alleged contravention of the Act by a data controller or processor.

first_instance.law_name: Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843)
first_instance.citation: Part IV — Right to lodge complaint

instances.citation: Part IV — Right to lodge complaint
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Ghana, 2012-07-16).

Both rules grant individuals the right to lodge complaints with a data protection supervisory authority against violators, but the Colombian law specifies the Superintendency of Industry and Commerce as the authority and identifies controllers/processors as the respondents, whereas the Ghana DPA refers to a Data Protection Commission without specifying the respondent parties.

Both grant individuals the right to lodge complaints with a data protection authority, but Bahrain's rule specifies written form, requires a legitimate interest, and allows complaints about unlawful processing, while Ghana's rule is more general.

Both grant individuals the right to lodge complaints with a data protection authority, but the Serbian rule additionally includes judicial review as a remedy, whereas the Ghana DPA rule is limited to administrative complaints only.

Both independently grant individuals the right to lodge complaints with a data protection authority, but the Ugandan Act names a different body (Personal Data Protection Office) versus Ghana's Data Protection Commission.

Both Ghana's DPA 2012 and Kenya's DPA 2019 grant individuals the right to lodge complaints with the data protection authority, but Kenya specifies complaints about 'decisions affecting them under the Act' while Ghana's formulation is broader and less specific.

Both rules grant individuals the right to file complaints with a data protection authority for infringements, but Egypt's rule additionally specifies failure to enable rights and DPO decisions as grounds, and the receiving body is called the 'Center' rather than a 'Data Protection Commission'.

Both grant individuals the right to lodge complaints with a data protection authority, but India's rule adds a precondition (prior grievance to the Data Fiduciary must be unsatisfactorily addressed) before the complaint to the Board is available, whereas Ghana's rule provides a direct right to complain to the Commission without such a prerequisite.

rule_text: The Act does not apply to information about government officers' functions, government-contracted services, journalistic/artistic/literary/research processing, public authority functions, AML compliance by financial institutions, or data originally collected from foreign residents under foreign law.
rule_text_technical: The Act does not apply to: information about government officers/employees relating to their position; information about individuals performing services under government contract; information relating to discretionary financial benefits; personal information processed for journalistic, artistic, literary or research purposes; information necessary for public authority functions including the central monetary authority and law enforcement/regulatory agencies; information necessary for banks and financial institutions to comply with anti-money laundering laws; and personal information originally collected from residents of foreign jurisdictions in accordance with their laws.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

Both laws exclude personal/domestic activity and intelligence/security files from scope, but the Philippine DPA also excludes journalistic, artistic, literary, and research processing, while the Dominican Republic law's exclusions appear limited to personal/domestic records and intelligence files.

Both rules carve out exemptions from personal data protection obligations (Turkey excludes purely personal/household activities, anonymized statistics, artistic/historical/scientific activities; Philippines excludes government functions, journalistic/research activities), but the specific categories and structure of exclusions differ meaningfully.

Both provide exemptions from data protection requirements for personal/household use and law enforcement purposes, but Qatar's law frames these as 'reduced requirements' rather than full exclusions, and the specific exempted categories differ somewhat.

Both provisions carve out journalistic, artistic, academic, and public security purposes from the data protection law's scope, but LGPD Art. 4 also explicitly excludes exclusively private/non-economic processing and adds a specific national security/defense carve-out structure distinct from the Philippine law.

Both laws exempt personal/household activities and national security/defense processing from data protection obligations, but Ethiopia's Proclamation also contemplates modified (rather than full) exemptions for certain categories, and the Philippine DPA additionally exempts journalistic, artistic, literary, and research processing.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to be informed whether their personal information shall be, is being, or has been processed.
rule_text_technical: The data subject is entitled to be informed whether personal information pertaining to them shall be, are being or have been processed.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

Both give individuals the right to be informed about the uses and processing of their personal data, though the Philippine law focuses on whether processing is occurring while Colombia's Art. 8(c) specifically grants a right to request information about uses upon demand.

Both grant individuals the right to be informed whether their personal data is being processed and to obtain information about that processing, though drafted independently and with different structural scope.

Both grant individuals the right to be informed about processing of their personal data, but Kenya's formulation focuses on the 'use to which data will be put' while the Philippine DPA focuses on whether data 'shall be, is being, or has been processed.'

Both require informing data subjects about processing of their personal data, but the Swiss nFADP Art. 19(1) covers both direct and indirect collection, while the Philippine DPA focuses on the right to be informed whether data is/will be processed.

Both concern the right to be informed about processing of personal information, but Zimbabwe's version focuses on purpose of use while the Philippines' rule covers whether data is being or has been processed.

Both establish the right to be informed about processing of personal data, but Bangladesh frames it as a pre-collection/at-collection right while the Philippine law focuses on whether data is being or has been processed.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to be furnished with information before their data enters processing, including its description, purposes, scope, recipients, automated access methods, controller identity, retention period, and their rights.
rule_text_technical: The data subject shall be furnished, before entry of their personal information into the processing system or at the next practical opportunity, with: description of the personal information; purposes of processing; scope and method of processing; recipients or classes of recipients; methods utilized for automated access; identity and contact details of the controller; storage period; and existence of their rights.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

Both require informing individuals about data processing, but the Philippine DPA mandates detailed pre-processing disclosure while Côte d'Ivoire's rule focuses on notification at the time of collection with less specified content.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to be indemnified for damages sustained due to inaccurate, incomplete, outdated, false, unlawfully obtained, or unauthorized use of their personal information.
rule_text_technical: The data subject is entitled to be indemnified for any damages sustained due to inaccurate, incomplete, outdated, false, unlawfully obtained or unauthorized use of personal information.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

Both provide individuals a right to seek damages through courts for data protection violations, but the Philippine provision specifies the nature of the harm (inaccurate, incomplete, unlawfully obtained data) while the Ivorian provision is a broader, general civil damages right without specifying types of violations.

Both POPIA § 99(1) and the Philippine DPA § 16(f) grant individuals a right to civil damages against a responsible party for data protection breaches, but the Philippine provision focuses specifically on damages from inaccurate/unlawfully obtained data while POPIA provides a broader right to sue for breach of any provision of the Act.

Both provide a right to compensation for damages caused by unlawful personal data processing, but the Philippine law specifically enumerates types of data inaccuracies while Turkey's provision is framed more broadly as 'unlawful processing'.

Both grant individuals the right to claim compensation from a data controller for damages caused by processing of personal data, but Bahrain's rule also extends liability to a 'data protection guardian' and does not specify the categories of data violations triggering the right as the Philippines law does.

Both establish a right to compensation for damages caused by unlawful personal data processing, but the LGPD Art. 42 explicitly extends liability to patrimonial, moral, individual, and collective damages and covers any violation of data protection legislation, while the Philippine DPA focuses on inaccurate, incomplete, or unlawfully obtained data.

Both provide individuals with civil redress for damages arising from data protection violations, but the Serbian rule explicitly covers both material and non-material damages before national courts, while the Philippine rule focuses on indemnification for specific data quality failures without that express dual-damages framing.

Both provide individuals a right to sue for damages from unlawful data processing, but the Philippine provision specifies particular causes (inaccurate, incomplete, outdated, false, or unlawfully obtained data) while Uganda's provision broadly covers all unlawful processing by controllers and processors.

Both rules establish a right to indemnification for damages caused by improper/unlawful processing of personal data enforceable through ordinary courts, but Panama's Art. 37 explicitly covers both patrimonial and moral damages and specifies ordinary court jurisdiction, while the Philippine DPA frames it as a data subject right to indemnification for specific categories of data inaccuracy or unauthorized use.

Both Kenya's DPA 2019 and the Philippines' DPA 2012 entitle individuals to compensation for damages caused by violations of the data protection act by the controller or processor, though the Philippines provision specifies particular categories of data inaccuracy while Kenya's formulation covers contraventions generally.

Both grant individuals a private right of action for damages resulting from personal data protection violations by organisations, but Brunei's rule ties the right specifically to contraventions of Parts 4-7 of the Order, while the Philippines provision focuses on damages from inaccurate, incomplete, or unlawfully obtained personal data.

Both provide a right to compensation for harm from data protection violations, but the Sri Lanka rule grants the Authority power to direct compensation as an administrative remedy rather than establishing a direct private right of action as in the Philippines DPA.

Both the Indonesian UU PDP and the Philippine DPA grant individuals the right to civil compensation for data protection violations, but the Indonesian law also adds the right to file a complaint with a national supervisory authority, and differs in scope, drafting, and procedural context.

Both grant individuals a right to compensation for damages from data protection violations, but the Philippine rule specifies particular types of data inaccuracy/misuse while Tanzania's provision is broader, covering any contravention of the Act by controller or processor.

Both require compensation to data subjects for harm caused by data processing violations, but Jordan's rule limits liability to gross negligence or misconduct by the controller, whereas the Philippines rule covers a broader range of data quality failures without requiring gross negligence.

Both grant individuals a right to seek compensation/indemnification for data protection violations, but the Pakistan PDPA additionally includes an explicit right to file a complaint with a supervisory authority (the PDPA Authority), combining regulatory complaint and civil redress in one provision, whereas the Philippine DPA rule focuses solely on indemnification for specific data quality violations.

Both establish a right to compensation for harm resulting from data protection violations, but the Philippine rule specifies indemnification for particular types of data inaccuracy/misuse while Ethiopia's provision broadly covers material and non-material harm from any violation of the Proclamation, and the two laws differ significantly in scope and drafting context.

Both grant individuals a right to complain to a data protection authority and seek civil compensation for damages from unlawful personal data processing, but the Philippine rule specifies the basis (inaccurate, incomplete, outdated, false, or unlawfully obtained data) while the Mexican rule is broader and routes complaints through INAI specifically with ordinary civil courts for compensation.

rule_text: Lawful heirs and assigns of a data subject may invoke the data subject's rights after death or during incapacitation.
rule_text_technical: The lawful heirs and assigns of the data subject may invoke the rights of the data subject to which they are entitled after the data subject's death or when the data subject is incapacitated or incapable of exercising the rights.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).
Both provisions allow heirs or successors to invoke data protection rights on behalf of deceased persons, drafted differently but substantively equivalent.
Both allow successors or heirs of deceased persons to exercise data subject rights including access, rectification, and deletion over the deceased's personal data.

Both extend data subject rights (access, copy, correction, deletion) to next of kin after death or incapacitation, though PIPL limits the scope to relatives of the deceased and specifies the particular rights covered.

Both address exercise of data subject rights by proxies when the data subject is incapacitated, but Zimbabwe's version specifically addresses child data subjects exercised by parents or legal guardians while the Philippines' rule covers heirs after death or during incapacitation.
Both allow a nominated or designated person to exercise data subject rights upon death or incapacity, drafted independently with different terminology.

Both address posthumous and representative exercise of data rights, but Mexico's 2025 rule additionally covers designation of a living representative for automated processing contexts and is broader in scope than the Philippine provision limited to heirs after death or incapacitation.

Both address the exercise of data subject rights by others upon death or incapacity, but India's rule frames it as a prospective nomination right exercised by the individual during their lifetime, whereas the Philippines rule automatically vests rights in lawful heirs and assigns without requiring prior nomination.

Both address rights exercised by a representative after the data subject's death or incapacitation, but the Bangladesh rule specifically frames this as a nominated representative right including for posthumous protection, while the Philippine law addresses lawful heirs and assigns.

rule_text: Your security measures must include safeguards for computer networks, a documented security policy, a process for identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, and regular monitoring for security breaches.
rule_text_technical: The determination of the appropriate level of security must include: safeguards to protect computer networks against accidental, unlawful or unauthorized usage; a security policy with respect to processing; a process for identifying and accessing reasonably foreseeable vulnerabilities and for taking preventive, corrective and mitigating action; and regular monitoring for security breaches.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: Your employees and agents involved in processing must hold personal information under strict confidentiality, which continues even after they leave employment.
rule_text_technical: The employees, agents or representatives of a personal information controller who are involved in the processing of personal information shall operate and hold personal information under strict confidentiality if the personal information are not intended for public disclosure. This obligation shall continue even after leaving the public service, transfer to another position or upon termination of employment.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).
Both require persons involved in processing to maintain confidentiality of personal data, including after their employment or relationship with the controller ends.
Both impose a confidentiality obligation on persons involved in personal data processing, with similar substantive requirements though independently enacted in different jurisdictions.

Bahrain Art. 9(2) prohibits those with access to personal data from using it for personal benefit and extends the obligation beyond employment, matching the confidentiality obligation in Philippines DPA s.20(e).
Both require confidentiality obligations for those processing personal data that continue even after the processing relationship ends, independently drafted.

rule_text: Government agency heads must secure all sensitive personal information they maintain using the most appropriate standard recognized by the ICT industry, and are responsible for compliance with security requirements.
rule_text_technical: All sensitive personal information maintained by the government, its agencies and instrumentalities shall be secured, as far as practicable, with the use of the most appropriate standard recognized by the information and communications technology industry. The head of each government agency or instrumentality shall be responsible for complying with the security requirements.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: Government employees may not access sensitive personal information on government property or through online facilities unless they have received a security clearance from the head of the source agency.
rule_text_technical: No employee of the government shall have access to sensitive personal information on government property or through online facilities unless the employee has received a security clearance from the head of the source agency.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: Sensitive personal information may not be transported or accessed off government property unless approved by the agency head, limited to no more than 1,000 records at a time, and encrypted using the most secure standard recognized by the Commission.
rule_text_technical: Sensitive personal information maintained by an agency may not be transported or accessed from a location off government property unless a request is approved by the head of the agency, subject to: a 2-business-day approval deadline (unanswered requests deemed disapproved); limitation to not more than 1,000 records at a time; and mandatory encryption using the most secure encryption standard recognized by the Commission.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: You cannot, through negligence, allow access to personal information; doing so is punishable by 1–3 years imprisonment and PHP 500,000–2,000,000 fine, or 3–6 years and PHP 500,000–4,000,000 for sensitive personal information.
rule_text_technical: Accessing personal information due to negligence shall be penalized by imprisonment of one (1) to three (3) years and a fine of PHP 500,000 to PHP 2,000,000. For sensitive personal information, the penalty is three (3) to six (6) years and PHP 500,000 to PHP 4,000,000.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

Both impose criminal penalties on data controllers/processors for breaching data protection obligations, but the Malaysian law sets a fine up to RM1,000,000 for contravening data protection principles, while the Philippine law imposes imprisonment plus fines for negligent access to personal information, differing in scope, threshold, and penalty structure.

rule_text: You cannot improperly dispose of personal information; doing so is punishable by 6 months–2 years and PHP 100,000–500,000 fine, or 1–3 years and PHP 100,000–1,000,000 for sensitive personal information.
rule_text_technical: Improper disposal of personal information shall be penalized by imprisonment of six (6) months to two (2) years and a fine of PHP 100,000 to PHP 500,000. For sensitive personal information, the penalty is one (1) to three (3) years and PHP 100,000 to PHP 1,000,000.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: You cannot conceal a security breach involving sensitive personal information; doing so is punishable by 1.5–5 years imprisonment and PHP 500,000–1,000,000 fine.
rule_text_technical: Concealment of security breaches involving sensitive personal information shall be penalized by imprisonment of one and a half (1½) to five (5) years and a fine of PHP 500,000 to PHP 1,000,000.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: You cannot maliciously disclose unwarranted or false information about a data subject; doing so is punishable by 1.5–5 years imprisonment and PHP 500,000–1,000,000 fine.
rule_text_technical: Malicious disclosure shall be penalized by imprisonment of one and a half (1½) to five (5) years and a fine of PHP 500,000 to PHP 1,000,000.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

Both prohibit unauthorized disclosure of personal data with criminal consequences, but Brunei's rule focuses on organizational/agency context and uses 'unauthorised disclosure' framing, while the Philippine rule covers malicious disclosure of unwarranted or false information with specific imprisonment/fine ranges.
Both criminalize unauthorized disclosure of personal data for personal gain or to harm others with imprisonment, but differ in penalty ranges and specific framing of the offense.

rule_text: If you commit a combination or series of prohibited acts under this Act, you face 3–6 years imprisonment and PHP 1,000,000–5,000,000 fine.
rule_text_technical: The combination or series of acts otherwise enumerated in Sections 25 to 32 shall be penalized by imprisonment of three (3) to six (6) years and a fine of PHP 1,000,000 to PHP 5,000,000.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: The maximum penalty in the applicable scale shall be imposed when personal information of at least 100 persons is harmed, affected, or involved.
rule_text_technical: The maximum penalty in the scale of penalties respectively provided shall be imposed when the personal information of at least one hundred (100) persons is harmed, affected or involved as the result of the violation.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: If a public officer commits an offense under this Act, an accessory penalty applies: disqualification from public office for double the term of the criminal penalty imposed.
rule_text_technical: If the offender is a public officer, as defined in the Administrative Code of the Philippines, in the exercise of their duties, an accessory penalty consisting in the disqualification to occupy public office for a term double the term of criminal penalty imposed shall be applied.

first_instance.law_name: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Philippines Data Privacy Act 2012 (Philippines, 2012-08-15).

rule_text: When you process sensitive data, you must inform the data owner that providing such data is optional and you cannot condition any product or service on its provision unless reasonably justified.
rule_text_technical: Where sensitive data processing is permitted, controllers must inform owners that responses to questions about sensitive data are optional, must specify which data is sensitive and the purpose of processing, and may not condition activities, goods, or services on the provision of sensitive data.

first_instance.law_name: Ley Estatutaria 1581 de 2012 — Proteccion de Datos Personales

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Colombia Personal Data Protection Law (Colombia, 2012-10-17).

Both require prior consent before processing sensitive personal data, but APPI specifies acquisition of sensitive data with limited exceptions while Colombia's rule focuses on informing data owners and non-conditioning of services.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request that incomplete or outdated personal data be updated.
rule_text_technical: Data owners may request the update of partial, inexact, incomplete, fractioned, or misleading data.

first_instance.law_name: Ley Estatutaria 1581 de 2012 — Proteccion de Datos Personales

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Colombia Personal Data Protection Law (Colombia, 2012-10-17).

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request a copy of the authorization granted to the controller for processing their personal data.
rule_text_technical: Data owners may request and obtain from the controller proof of the authorization granted for processing, except in cases excluded as a requirement for processing under Article 10.

first_instance.law_name: Ley Estatutaria 1581 de 2012 — Proteccion de Datos Personales

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Colombia Personal Data Protection Law (Colombia, 2012-10-17).

rule_text: The SIC must determine and publish which countries provide an adequate level of data protection.

first_instance.law_name: Ley Estatutaria 1581 de 2012 — Proteccion de Datos Personales

rule_text: The Autorité de Régulation des Télécommunications/TIC de Côte d'Ivoire (ARTCI) is designated as the supervisory authority for personal data protection, with powers to receive declarations, investigate complaints, issue opinions, and impose administrative sanctions.
rule_text_technical: ARTCI exercises data protection supervisory functions alongside its telecommunications regulatory role, including receiving declarations and prior authorization requests, investigating complaints and conducting ex officio investigations, issuing opinions and recommendations, imposing administrative sanctions, and referring matters for criminal prosecution.

first_instance.law_name: Côte d'Ivoire Law No. 2013-450 on the Protection of Personal Data

rule_text: You must have a valid legal basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, or legitimate interest) before processing personal data.

Both establish consent and other lawful bases (contract, legal obligation, legitimate interest) as prerequisites for processing personal data, but are drafted independently with different enumerations and scope.
Both require a valid legal basis (including consent) before processing personal data, though LGPD enumerates more bases and is a binding statute while the Côte d'Ivoire rule is similarly structured.

Both require a lawful basis (including consent) for processing personal data, but Brunei's rule focuses specifically on consent or deemed consent as the gateway, while the Côte d'Ivoire rule lists multiple alternative bases including contract and legitimate interest.

Both require a valid legal basis (including consent) for processing personal data, but PIPL provides a more detailed enumeration of lawful bases specific to China's legal framework.

Both rules require a valid legal basis (including consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests) before processing personal data, but the UAE law enumerates these bases in a single article while the Côte d'Ivoire law uses slightly different framing and structure.

Both require a valid legal basis for processing personal data, but the Sri Lanka Act adds layered schedule requirements for special categories and cross-border transfers, making it more granular than the Côte d'Ivoire provision.

Both require a valid legal basis (including consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, and public service/legitimate interest) before processing personal data, but are drafted independently under different jurisdictions.

Both require a lawful basis before processing personal data and list consent as the primary basis, but Jordan's rule frames consent as the default requirement with enumerated exceptions, while Côte d'Ivoire lists multiple equal legal bases.
Both require a valid legal basis (including consent, contract, legal obligation, or legitimate interest) before processing personal data, independently drafted but substantively equivalent.

Both establish a multi-basis lawful processing framework (consent, legal obligation, vital interests, etc.), matching the same substantive structure though drafted differently and in different jurisdictions.

Both require a valid legal basis (including consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest, or legitimate interest) for processing personal data, but are independently drafted in different jurisdictions with different phrasing.

Both enumerate substantially the same set of lawful bases for processing personal data (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest, legitimate interest), drafted independently in different jurisdictions.

rule_text: You may process personal data where necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject.
rule_text_technical: Processing is lawful where necessary to protect vital interests of the data subject.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ivory Coast Personal Data Protection Law 2013 (Ivory Coast, 2013-06-19).

rule_text: You must, as the responsible party, ensure that all conditions for lawful processing of personal information are complied with at the time of determining the purpose and means of processing and during the processing itself.
rule_text_technical: The responsible party must ensure that the conditions set out in Chapter 3, and all measures giving effect to such conditions, are complied with at the time of the determination of the purpose and means of processing and during the processing itself.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: You may only process personal information that is adequate, relevant, and not excessive given the purpose for which it is processed.
rule_text_technical: Personal information may only be processed if, given the purpose for which it is processed, it is adequate, relevant and not excessive.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to withdraw their consent to processing at any time, without affecting the lawfulness of processing before withdrawal.

rule_text: You may only process a child's personal information with prior consent of a competent person, where necessary for legal rights/obligations or international public law, for historical/statistical/research purposes with safeguards, or where the information has been deliberately made public by the child with consent of a competent person.
rule_text_technical: The prohibition on processing personal information of children does not apply if processing is carried out with the prior consent of a competent person; necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of a right or obligation in law; necessary to comply with an obligation of international public law; for historical, statistical or research purposes (with public interest, necessity, and sufficient guarantees); or of personal information deliberately made public by the child with consent of a competent person.

Both require parental or guardian consent before processing children's personal data, but LGPD adds the 'specific and highlighted' consent standard while POPIA also includes alternative bases such as legal rights and international obligations.

Both rules require parental/competent-person consent before processing a child's personal data, but Kenya's § 33(1) adds a 'best interests of the child' standard not explicitly present in POPIA § 35(1).

Both require consent from a parent or guardian before processing a minor's personal data, with Paraguay also allowing consent from a capable minor themselves, while South Africa's rule additionally covers legal rights/obligations and international agreements as alternative bases.
