Both rules require consent through a legal representative for minors, but Ecuador's Art. 24 introduces specific age thresholds (under 12, 15-17 with graduated autonomy) whereas South Africa's POPIA applies a broader 'competent person' consent requirement without the same age-graduated autonomy for adolescents.

Both require parental or guardian consent to process a minor's personal information, with PIPL setting the threshold at under 14 and additionally requiring specialized handling rules, while POPIA uses the broader concept of 'competent person' consent.

Both require parental/competent-person consent for processing children's personal information, but Quebec specifies a 14-year age threshold whereas POPIA does not set a specific age cutoff in the same way.

Both require parental or guardian consent before processing children's personal data and impose heightened restrictions, though Rwanda's rule additionally references behavioral profiling and commercial use of children's data.

Both require guardian/competent-person consent before processing a child's personal data, but Oman adds a 'best interest' exception while POPIA references legal rights/obligations and international agreements as exceptions.

Both require substitute consent from a guardian or competent person for those unable to consent themselves, but Tanzania's rule extends beyond children to also cover persons of unsound mind and others unable to consent, and specifies a broader list of authorized consent-givers.

Both rules prohibit processing a child's personal data without prior parental/competent-person consent, though India's DPDPA uses 'verifiable parental consent' and does not list the additional exceptions that POPIA includes for legal rights or international obligations.

Both require substitute consent from a representative when the data subject lacks legal capacity, but Jordan covers all persons lacking legal capacity via parent/guardian/court-approved rep, while POPIA focuses specifically on children.

Both require prior parental/competent-person consent before processing children's personal data, with Pakistan specifying under-16 and age verification mechanisms while POPIA focuses on a 'competent person' standard.

Both require parental or guardian consent before processing children's personal data, but Ethiopia's rule adds an explicit age verification requirement while POPIA focuses on consent from a 'competent person' and specific lawful bases.

Both require parental/guardian consent for processing children's personal data, but Bangladesh sets the age threshold at under 18 for most purposes, whereas South Africa's POPIA sets it at under 18 with narrower enumerated exceptions rather than a broad 'most purposes' qualifier.

rule_text: As an information officer, you are responsible for encouraging compliance with conditions for lawful processing, dealing with requests under the Act, working with the Regulator on investigations, and ensuring overall compliance.
rule_text_technical: An information officer's responsibilities include the encouragement of compliance, by the body, with the conditions for the lawful processing of personal information; dealing with requests made to the body pursuant to this Act; working with the Regulator in relation to investigations conducted pursuant to Chapter 6; otherwise ensuring compliance by the body with the provisions of this Act; and as may be prescribed.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

Bahrain Art. 10(1) assigns the Data Protection Guardian duties to assist the controller, liaise with the Authority and verify compliance, similar to POPIA's information officer role in s.55(1), but Bahrain's role also includes notifying both controller and Authority of violations.

Both establish accountability for private-sector/responsible party data protection through a designated officer, but Quebec's rule combines the accountability principle with a designation requirement while POPIA focuses on the information officer's specific compliance functions.

Both assign the data protection/information officer responsibility for compliance with the Act, handling data subject requests, and liaising with the supervisory authority, independently drafted but substantively equivalent.

rule_text: Information officers may only take up their duties under this Act after the responsible party has registered them with the Regulator.
rule_text_technical: Officers must take up their duties in terms of this Act only after the responsible party has registered them with the Regulator.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

Both require registration with a data protection authority before commencing certain processing activities, but the Turkish rule applies broadly to all natural or legal persons processing personal data registering with a Data Controllers' Registry, while the South African rule specifically concerns information officers registering with the Regulator.

Both rules require registration of a data protection officer/information officer with the supervisory authority before they can act in that role, but Bahrain uses a dedicated 'Data Protection Guardians Register' while POPIA requires registration of information officers with the Regulator as a general condition of taking up duties.

Both require registration with a data protection authority before acting as a data controller/processor, but Kenya's rule applies to data controllers and processors generally (subject to thresholds) while South Africa's rule specifically concerns registration of information officers.

Both rules require registration with a supervisory/regulatory authority (Rwanda's NCSA vs. South Africa's Regulator), but Rwanda's rule covers data controllers broadly whereas South Africa's rule specifically concerns the registration of information officers before they may act.

Both require registration of certain data controllers/officers with a data protection regulator, but Nigeria targets 'controllers of major importance' with annual fees while South Africa targets information officers who must be registered before taking up duties.

Both rules establish a registry or registration mechanism overseen by a supervisory authority covering data protection roles (controllers/processors/DPOs), but Jordan's rule is broader in scope and assigns registry administration to a dedicated Unit under Council instructions, whereas POPIA focuses narrowly on information officers registered with the Regulator.

Both require registration of a data protection officer/information officer with the supervisory authority, but Ethiopia additionally requires the DPO to possess adequate data protection expertise, whereas South Africa's rule focuses solely on the registration prerequisite before duties commence.

Both rules require registration with a data protection authority before operating, but India's rule is specific to Consent Managers with detailed eligibility criteria (Indian incorporation, minimum capital of INR 2 crore), whereas South Africa's rule concerns registration of information officers by responsible parties.

rule_text: You may not carry out processing notified to the Regulator under prior authorisation rules until the Regulator has completed its investigation or notified you that no detailed investigation will be conducted.
rule_text_technical: Responsible parties may not carry out information processing that has been notified to the Regulator in terms of subsection (1) until the Regulator has completed its investigation or until they have received notice that a more detailed investigation will not be conducted.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: You may not process personal information for direct marketing by electronic communication (including automatic calling machines, faxes, SMS, or email) unless the data subject has given consent or is an existing customer.
rule_text_technical: The processing of personal information of a data subject for the purpose of direct marketing by means of any form of electronic communication, including automatic calling machines, facsimile machines, SMSs or e-mail is prohibited unless the data subject has given his, her or its consent to the processing; or is, subject to subsection (3), a customer of the responsible party.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: You may only process existing customers' personal information for direct marketing if you obtained their contact details in the course of a sale, the marketing concerns your own similar products/services, and the customer has been given a free and easy opportunity to object both at collection and on each subsequent communication.
rule_text_technical: A responsible party may only process the personal information of a customer in terms of subsection (1)(b) if the responsible party has obtained the contact details of the data subject in the context of the sale of a product or service; for the purpose of direct marketing of the responsible party's own similar products or services; and if the data subject has been given a reasonable opportunity to object, free of charge and in a manner free of unnecessary formality, at the time when information was collected and on the occasion of each communication.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

Both address notifying data subjects of direct marketing opt-out rights, but Bahrain requires proactive pre-processing notification while POPIA's rule focuses on the conditions under which existing customers may be marketed to.

rule_text: You must give data subjects a reasonable opportunity to object free of charge, or to request verification, confirmation, or withdrawal of their information from a directory.
rule_text_technical: A data subject must be given a reasonable opportunity to object, free of charge and in a manner free of unnecessary formality, to such use of his, her or its personal information or to request verification, confirmation or withdrawal of such information if the data subject has not initially refused such use.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).
Both require the controller to honour a data subject's objection to direct marketing free of charge; Bahrain adds a specific 10 working-day compliance deadline not specified in POPIA.

rule_text: The prohibition on solely automated decisions does not apply where the decision is taken in connection with conclusion or execution of a contract (with the data subject's request met or appropriate safeguards in place) or is governed by a law or code of conduct specifying appropriate measures.
rule_text_technical: The provisions of subsection (1) do not apply if the decision has been taken in connection with the conclusion or execution of a contract, and the request of the data subject in terms of the contract has been met, or appropriate measures have been taken to protect the data subject's legitimate interests; or is governed by a law or code of conduct in which appropriate measures are specified for protecting the legitimate interests of data subjects.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

Both address automated decision-making rights but GDPR Art. 22(1) establishes a broad right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal/significant effects, while POPIA 71-2 describes an exception to that prohibition for contract-related decisions, covering different aspects of the same concept.
Both permit automated decisions where necessary for a contract or authorized by law with appropriate safeguards, independently drafted with the same substantive exceptions.

Both provide exceptions to the prohibition on solely automated decisions, but Zimbabwe's version allows exceptions for consent or legal provision while POPIA's exception is limited to contract-related decisions.

rule_text: Any person has the right to submit a complaint to the Regulator alleging interference with the protection of a data subject's personal information.
rule_text_technical: Any person may submit a complaint to the Regulator in the prescribed manner and form alleging interference with the protection of the personal information of a data subject.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).
Both grant individuals the right to file a complaint with a supervisory authority regarding personal data processing, with the Saudi PDPL specifying SDAIA as the designated body.
Both provide individuals the right to file a complaint with the national data protection supervisory authority, with Rwanda specifying the NCSA as the designated body.
Both grant individuals the right to file a complaint with a supervisory/regulatory body regarding non-compliant processing, though the designated body differs (Ministry vs. Regulator).
Both grant individuals the right to file a complaint with the data protection regulator, with Nigeria specifying the NDPC and South Africa specifying the Regulator.
Both grant individuals the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory/regulatory authority regarding data protection, differing only in the name of the authority.
Both establish the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection regulatory authority, independently drafted for different national supervisory bodies.

rule_text: The Regulator may impose administrative fines up to R10 million by infringement notice on responsible parties alleged to have committed offences under this Act.
rule_text_technical: If a responsible party is alleged to have committed an offence in terms of this Act, the Regulator may cause to be delivered by hand to that person an infringement notice. The notice must specify the name and address of the infringer; particulars of the alleged offence; the amount of the administrative fine payable, which may not exceed R10 million; and inform the infringer of options to pay, arrange instalments, or elect trial.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

Both empower the data protection authority to impose administrative fines on data controllers/processors, but Kenya sets fines up to 5 million shillings or 1% of annual turnover for undertakings, while South Africa sets fines up to R10 million.

Both empower a data protection authority to impose financial penalties on organisations for contraventions, but Brunei caps penalties at 10% of annual turnover or a fixed amount (whichever is higher) for intentional or negligent contraventions, while POPIA caps fines at R10 million without a turnover-based ceiling.

Both rules authorize financial penalties for data protection violations (security safeguards and breach notification), but differ significantly in penalty amounts (INR 250 crore / INR 200 crore vs. R10 million), the enforcing authority, and the specific violation categories covered.

rule_text: When determining the amount of an administrative fine, the Regulator must consider the nature of the personal information, duration and extent of contravention, number of affected data subjects, public importance, likelihood of substantial damage or distress, preventability, failure to conduct risk assessments or operate good policies, and prior offences.
rule_text_technical: When determining an appropriate fine, the Regulator must consider: the nature of the personal information involved; the duration and extent of the contravention; the number of data subjects affected or potentially affected; whether the contravention raises an issue of public importance; the likelihood of substantial damage or distress, including injury to feelings or anxiety; whether the responsible party or third party could have prevented the contravention; any failure to carry out a risk assessment or operate good policies, procedures and practices; and whether the responsible party has previously committed an offence.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

Both require the data protection authority to consider factors such as nature, gravity, duration of violation, number of affected data subjects, degree of responsibility, and remedial measures when determining administrative fine amounts.

Both require the supervisory authority to consider factors such as nature, gravity, duration, number of affected subjects, harm severity, and mitigation when determining penalty amounts, though drafted independently under different legal systems.

Both require the data protection authority to consider nature, gravity, duration, and mitigation factors when determining penalty amounts, though drafted independently with different specific factor lists and institutional contexts.

rule_text: You must, when acting on behalf of or under direction of the Regulator, treat as confidential the personal information that comes to your knowledge in the course of official duties, both during and after employment, except where communication is required by law or proper performance of duties.
rule_text_technical: A person acting on behalf or under the direction of the Regulator, must, both during or after his or her term of office or employment, treat as confidential the personal information which comes to his or her knowledge in the course of the performance of his or her official duties, except if the communication of such information is required by law or in the proper performance of his or her duties.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).
Bahrain Art. 37(1) prohibits Authority staff from disclosing information submitted under the Law without prior consent, matching the confidentiality obligation on Regulator personnel in POPIA s.54.
Both require confidentiality over personal data (not from public sources) even after activities end, independently drafted with similar scope.

Both independently impose a duty of secrecy/confidentiality on persons acting under the authority of the data protection regulator regarding personal data and confidential matters encountered in that capacity.

rule_text: Failure to comply with an issued code of conduct is deemed a breach of the conditions for the lawful processing of personal information and is enforceable under Chapter 10.
rule_text_technical: If a code issued under section 60 is in force, failure to comply with the code is deemed to be a breach of the conditions for the lawful processing of personal information referred to in Chapter 3 and is dealt with in terms of Chapter 10.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: You must bring all processing of personal information into conformity with applicable data protection standards within one year of this policy's effective date, with possible extension of up to three additional years by regulatory authority.
rule_text_technical: All processing of personal information must within one year after the commencement of this section be made to conform to this Act. The period of one year may be extended by the Minister, on request or of his or her own accord and after consultation with the Regulator, by notice in the Gazette in respect of different class or classes of information and bodies by an additional period which period may not exceed three years.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).
Both laws provide a one-year transition/compliance period, though Egypt's period runs from issuance of Executive Regulations rather than from commencement of a specific section.
Both rules provide a one-year transition period for existing data handlers to bring operations into compliance after the law's enactment, independently drafted with the same substantive obligation.

Both provide a one-year transition/compliance period for existing entities to bring their practices into conformity with the new data protection regulation, though the Kuwait rule refers specifically to reconciling status with CITRA regulations rather than bringing processing into conformity with data protection principles.

Both establish tiered compliance transition periods after commencement, but Bangladesh's Ordinance differentiates by enterprise size (large/significant vs. medium vs. small) with 12/18/24-month windows, whereas South Africa's POPIA provided a single one-year transition period for all entities.

rule_text: When the Regulator authorises processing of children's personal information, it may impose conditions including allowing competent persons to review processed information and refuse further processing, providing notice on the nature and processing of children's information, prohibiting actions encouraging children to disclose more information than necessary, and maintaining procedures to protect integrity and confidentiality.
rule_text_technical: The Regulator may impose reasonable conditions in respect of any authorisation for processing children's personal information, including conditions with regard to how a responsible party must: upon request of a competent person provide a reasonable means to review the personal information processed and refuse to permit its further processing; provide notice regarding the nature of the personal information processed, how it is processed, and any further processing practices; refrain from any action intended to encourage or persuade a child to disclose more personal information than reasonably necessary; and establish and maintain reasonable procedures to protect integrity and confidentiality of personal information collected from children.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: You may only process personal information concerning a data subject's health or sex life if you are subject to an obligation of confidentiality by virtue of office, employment, profession, legal provision, or written agreement, and must treat such information as confidential.
rule_text_technical: In the cases where processing of health or sex life information is permitted under subsection (1), the information may only be processed by responsible parties subject to an obligation of confidentiality by virtue of office, employment, profession or legal provision, or established by a written agreement between the responsible party and the data subject. A responsible party that is permitted to process such information and is not subject to an obligation of confidentiality by virtue of office, profession or legal provision, must treat the information as confidential.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

Both impose additional safeguards on sensitive personal data, but Qatar's rule specifies explicit consent, strict need-to-know, enhanced security, and a prohibition, while POPIA's rule focuses on confidentiality obligations for health and sex life data.

Both require heightened protections for sensitive personal data categories, but Uganda's Act frames the obligation more broadly as a general security/confidentiality standard rather than tying it to specific professional confidentiality obligations.

rule_text: A code of conduct must incorporate all the conditions for lawful processing of personal information (or set out functionally equivalent obligations) and prescribe how those conditions are to be applied or complied with given the particular features of the relevant sector.
rule_text_technical: A code of conduct must incorporate all the conditions for the lawful processing of personal information or set out obligations that provide a functional equivalent of all the obligations set out in those conditions; and prescribe how the conditions for the lawful processing of personal information are to be applied, or are to be complied with, given the particular features of the sector or sectors of society in which the relevant responsible parties are operating.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

Both involve a supervisory authority approving or issuing codes of conduct for data processing, but Zimbabwe's rule also includes ethical guidelines for data controllers whereas South Africa's focuses on lawful processing conditions.

Both rules require the adoption of standards/codes of conduct binding on controllers and processors, but Jordan's provision is a Council mandate in a new data-protection law while South Africa's is a sectoral code-of-conduct mechanism under POPIA, differing in governance actor, scope, and legal mechanism.

rule_text: Organizations adopting codes of conduct must specify safeguards for data matching programs, protections for individuals subject to automated decisions, and procedures for regular review and expiration of the code itself.
rule_text_technical: A code of conduct must also specify appropriate measures for information matching programmes if such programmes are used within a specific sector or for protecting the legitimate interests of data subjects insofar as automated decision making, as referred to in section 71, is concerned; provide for the review of the code by the Regulator; and provide for the expiry of the code.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: You must inform individuals of their right to request correction of their personal information when you provide them with access to their data.
rule_text_technical: If, in response to a request in terms of subsection (1), personal information is communicated to a data subject, the data subject must be advised of the right in terms of section 24 to request the correction of information.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: Where processing of personal information has been restricted, you may only process it (other than for storage) for purposes of proof, with the data subject's or competent person's consent, for the protection of rights of another natural or legal person, or where processing is in the public interest.
rule_text_technical: Personal information referred to in subsection (6) may, with the exception of storage, only be processed for purposes of proof, or with the data subject's consent, or with the consent of a competent person in respect of a child, or for the protection of the rights of another natural or legal person or if such processing is in the public interest.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: If you have used a record of personal information to make a decision about a data subject, you must retain the record for the period required or prescribed by law/code, or if no such requirement, for a period that allows the data subject a reasonable opportunity to request access.
rule_text_technical: A responsible party that has used a record of personal information of a data subject to make a decision about the data subject, must retain the record for such period as may be required or prescribed by law or a code of conduct; or if there is no law or code prescribing a retention period, retain the record for a period which will afford the data subject a reasonable opportunity, taking all considerations into account, to request access to the record.

first_instance.law_name: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Africa POPIA (South Africa, 2013-11-26).

rule_text: You must deliver a requested credit report in a clear, complete and accessible manner within five working days of the request, with optional secure internet platform access.
rule_text_technical: The SIC must deliver a credit report in a clear, complete and accessible manner within five (5) working days from the date of request; the data holder may optionally request secure access through an internet platform.

first_instance.law_name: Dominican Republic Law No. 172-13 on the Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Dominican Republic Data Protection Law 2013 (Dominican Republic, 2013-12-15).

Both grant individuals the right to know whether a credit information database holds information about them and to access it, but the Dominican Republic provision adds a five-day delivery deadline and secure delivery option not present in Paraguay's rule.

rule_text: You cannot operate as a Credit Information Company in the Dominican Republic without authorization from the Monetary Board, processed through the Superintendence of Banks.
rule_text_technical: To operate in the country, all SIC must obtain authorization by the Monetary Board, with applications processed through the Superintendence of Banks, and shall be subject to the Superintendence's inspection and surveillance.

first_instance.law_name: Dominican Republic Law No. 172-13 on the Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Dominican Republic Data Protection Law 2013 (Dominican Republic, 2013-12-15).

Both rules require authorization from a financial/banking authority before operating as a credit information company, but Paraguay specifies the Central Bank while the Dominican Republic specifies the Monetary Board via the Superintendency.

rule_text: You may refuse to suppress data when suppression would harm rights or legitimate interests of third parties or where there is a contractual or legal obligation to preserve the data.
rule_text_technical: Suppression does not proceed when it could cause harm to rights or legitimate interests of third parties, or when there is a contractual or legal obligation to preserve the data; in the case of deceased persons, the right is exercised by their successors.

first_instance.law_name: Dominican Republic Law No. 172-13 on the Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Dominican Republic Data Protection Law 2013 (Dominican Republic, 2013-12-15).

rule_text: During a habeas data process, the registry or database must clearly state in any reports that the challenged information is subject to judicial process or habeas data challenge.
rule_text_technical: During the habeas data process, the registry or database must settle or publish reports indicating that the challenged information is subject to a judicial process or challenge of habeas data.

first_instance.law_name: Dominican Republic Law No. 172-13 on the Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Dominican Republic Data Protection Law 2013 (Dominican Republic, 2013-12-15).

rule_text: You cannot use or provide an SIC credit report for the commission of a crime; doing so carries correctional imprisonment of six months to two years.
rule_text_technical: Any individual who uses or provides a credit report from a SIC with the purpose of committing a crime shall be liable to correctional imprisonment from six (6) months to two (2) years.

first_instance.law_name: Dominican Republic Law No. 172-13 on the Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Dominican Republic Data Protection Law 2013 (Dominican Republic, 2013-12-15).

rule_text: You must implement adequate measures, as determined by the Personal Data Protection Board, when processing special categories of personal data.
rule_text_technical: Adequate measures, as determined by the Board, shall be implemented in the processing of special categories of personal data.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

Both rules require implementation of adequate security measures when processing sensitive personal data, but Egypt's rule specifically assigns this obligation to a designated Data Protection Officer, whereas Turkey's rule places the obligation on processors generally and ties it to Board-determined measures.

rule_text: You cannot transfer personal data without the data subject's explicit consent, unless a specific lawful basis applies such as legal obligation, contract necessity, vital interests protection, public task performance, or legitimate interests with appropriate safeguards.
rule_text_technical: Personal data shall not be transferred without the data subject's explicit consent, except upon the existence of one of the conditions in Article 5(2) or Article 6(3) (provided sufficient measures are taken for special categories).

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

Both require explicit/express consent for processing sensitive personal data with limited exceptions, but Qatar's rule specifies vital interests and legal proceedings as exceptions while Turkey's rule cross-references distinct statutory lawful bases; the two are independently drafted.

Both prohibit transferring/providing personal data to third parties without the data subject's prior explicit consent, with limited statutory exceptions, though drafted under different legal frameworks.

Both require explicit/written consent for processing sensitive data, but Zimbabwe's rule specifically mandates written consent as the default requirement for sensitive data processing, while Turkey's rule addresses domestic transfer of personal data and permits alternatives under specific statutory bases.

rule_text: You must notify the Personal Data Protection Authority of any standard contract used for international data transfer within five business days of its signature.
rule_text_technical: The standard contract shall be notified to the Authority by the data controller or data processor within five business days following its signature.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

Both require notification to the data protection authority within a short timeframe of a specific event (appointment vs. standard contract), but the Bahrain rule concerns notifying of a DPG appointment within three working days while KVKK concerns notifying of international data transfer contracts within five business days.

Both require notifying a data protection authority about safeguards used for international data transfers, but Turkey's rule specifically concerns standard contracts and requires notification within five business days, while Brazil's LGPD Art. 36 requires communicating any changes to safeguards more broadly without a specific deadline.

Both require notification to a data protection authority regarding international data transfers, but Indonesia's UU PDP Art. 56(4) also mandates ongoing protection of transferred data at the destination, while Turkey's KVKK Art. 9(5) focuses narrowly on filing standard contracts within five business days.

rule_text: You must ensure that the protections under this Law continue to apply to onward transfers of personal data already transferred abroad and to transfers to international organizations.
rule_text_technical: Data controllers and data processors shall ensure that the safeguards established under this Law and the provisions of Article 9 also apply to onward transfers of personal data that have been transferred abroad and transfers to international organizations.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: You may transfer personal data abroad in cases where the interests of Türkiye or the data subject would be seriously harmed only with Board approval and after obtaining the opinion of the relevant public institution.
rule_text_technical: Without prejudice to international convention provisions, personal data may be transferred abroad only with the approval of the Board and after obtaining the opinion of the relevant public institution or organization, in cases where the interest of Türkiye or the data subject would be seriously harmed.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: Individuals have the right to make requests regarding the implementation of this Law to the data controller in writing or by other means determined by the Board.
rule_text_technical: The data subject shall make the requests relating to the implementation of this Law to the data controller in writing or by other means to be determined by the Board.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: You must either fulfill or refuse the request with justified grounds and communicate the response to the data subject in writing or by electronic means; if the request is due to your fault, any fee must be refunded.
rule_text_technical: The data controller shall act on the request or refuse it together with justified grounds and communicate its response to the data subject in writing or by electronic means. If the request is accepted, it shall be fulfilled by the data controller. If the request is made due to fault of the data controller, the fee is refunded to the data subject.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

Both require controllers to respond to data subject requests within a reasonable time and provide a complaint mechanism to a supervisory authority, but Qatar's law specifies the Ministry as the complaint body while KVKK references the data protection board.

Both require a substantive response to data subject requests within a set timeframe; LGPD specifies 15 days and requires a clear declaration including origin, criteria, and purpose, while KVKK sets 30 days and focuses on fulfillment or justified refusal.

Both require controllers to establish mechanisms for handling rights requests and to provide reasoned explanations when rejecting them, with PIPL additionally mandating convenient access to those mechanisms.

Both require written responses to data subject requests including reasons for refusal, but Sri Lanka specifies a 21 working-day deadline and an option to indicate partial compliance, while KVKK sets a 30-day deadline without the same tiered response options.

rule_text: You must send the information and documents demanded by the Board (other than state secrets) within fifteen days and, where necessary, allow on-the-spot examination.
rule_text_technical: Except for information and documents having the status of state secret, the data controller shall send the information and documents demanded by the Board related to the subject of examination within fifteen days, and shall enable, where necessary, on-the-spot examination.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

Both establish a supervisory authority's power to receive complaints, conduct inspections, and issue compliance orders for personal data violations, but Qatar's law bundles these powers together with administrative penalty authority while Turkey's KVKK separates them into distinct articles with specific procedural requirements.

Both require compliance with supervisory authority orders to produce documents and information, but Kenya's provision also covers attendance and access to electronically stored information, while Turkey's sets a 15-day deadline and allows on-site inspection.

Both require controllers to enable supervisory authority inspection and provide compliance evidence, but Egypt's rule focuses on enabling the Center to inspect and prove compliance while Turkey's KVKK specifies document production timelines.

Both require controllers/processors to cooperate with the supervisory authority and provide requested information/documents, but the Turkish law specifies a 15-day deadline and on-site inspection rights, while the Oman provision is open-ended.

rule_text: You must implement Board decisions identifying infringements without delay and at the latest within thirty days after notification.
rule_text_technical: Where the Board determines an infringement following an examination upon complaint or ex officio, the relevant data controller must remedy the identified infringements; this decision shall be implemented without delay and within thirty days at the latest after notification.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

Both rules empower a data protection authority to order cessation of violations, but Bahrain's Art. 55(1) also allows withdrawal of authorization, while Turkey's Art. 15-5 focuses on implementation of Board decisions within 30 days.

Both require regulated entities to comply with orders and recommendations from the data protection authority to cease violations or take corrective measures, but APPI Art. 148 is Japan-specific with its own procedural framework, while KVKK Art. 15(5) requires implementation within 30 days of notification.

Both require compliance with supervisory authority orders within a set timeframe, but the Sri Lanka PDPA adds a specific risk-mitigation/cessation dimension and does not specify a fixed deadline, whereas Turkey's KVKK requires implementation within 30 days of notification.

rule_text: The Board has the power to order you to halt the processing of personal data or international transfer where there is a risk of damages difficult or impossible to compensate, or in cases of explicit infringement of the law.
rule_text_technical: The Board may decide to stop the processing of personal data or transfer of personal data abroad in the case of damages which are difficult or impossible to compensate, and in the event of explicit infringement of the law.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: Organizations must inform individuals about data processing activities or face administrative penalties.
rule_text_technical: An administrative fine of 5,000 to 100,000 TL shall be imposed on those who fail to fulfil the obligation to inform as stipulated in Article 10.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: Organizations that fail to implement adequate data security measures are subject to administrative fines proportionate to the severity and scope of the failure.
rule_text_technical: An administrative fine of 15,000 to 1,000,000 TL shall be imposed on those who fail to fulfil the obligations related to data security as stipulated in Article 12.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: Organizations that fail to comply with regulatory board decisions must pay administrative penalties proportionate to the violation's severity and the organization's size.
rule_text_technical: An administrative fine of 25,000 to 1,000,000 TL shall be imposed on those who fail to comply with the decisions issued by the Board as stipulated in Article 15.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: Failure to register with the data controllers' registry or provide required notifications is subject to administrative fines.
rule_text_technical: An administrative fine of 20,000 to 1,000,000 TL shall be imposed on those who act contrary to the obligations for registry with the Data Controllers' Registry and for notification as stipulated in Article 16.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: You must notify parties to standard contracts as required; failure to do so may result in administrative fines.
rule_text_technical: An administrative fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 TL shall be imposed on those who fail to fulfil the obligation to notify as stipulated in Article 9(5).

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: The obligations to inform (Art. 10), most rights of the data subject (Art. 11, except compensation), and registration with the Data Controllers' Registry (Art. 16) do not apply to processing necessary for crime prevention/investigation, public data, supervisory/disciplinary functions of public bodies, or protection of state economic/financial interests.
rule_text_technical: Provided it is in compliance with and proportionate to the purpose and fundamental principles of this Law, Articles 10, 11 (excluding the right to claim compensation), and 16 shall not apply where personal data processing: (a) is necessary for crime prevention or investigation; (b) is carried out on data made public by the data subject; (c) is necessary for performance of supervisory or regulatory duties and disciplinary investigation by authorized public bodies; (ç) is necessary for protection of economic and financial interests of the State concerning budget, tax and financial matters.

first_instance.law_name: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu (Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698), as amended by Law No. 7499/2024

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Turkey KVKK (Law No. 6698, as amended 2024) (Turkey, 2016-03-24).

rule_text: Individuals have the right to obtain from controllers confirmation of the existence of automated decision-making (including profiling) concerning them, along with meaningful information about the logic involved and its significance and envisaged consequences.
rule_text_technical: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

Both grant individuals the right to request review of decisions based solely on automated processing that affect their interests; LGPD covers effects on interests broadly while GDPR specifies profiling and links to Art. 22 safeguards.

Serbia's Law on Personal Data Protection mirrors GDPR Art. 22 on the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal effects, independently drafted but substantively equivalent to the GDPR provision.

Both address rights around automated decision-making and profiling that produce legal or significant effects; GDPR Article 15(1)(h) covers the right to obtain information about such processing while ADGM's rule more broadly covers the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions.

Both grant individuals the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling that produces legal or similarly significant effects; the UAE Art. 19 is independently drafted but substantively mirrors GDPR Art. 22.

Both establish a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions including profiling, but Zimbabwe's version mirrors GDPR Article 22 more closely with the 'legal effects or similarly significant' threshold, while the existing matched rule covers the right to information about such processing.

Both grant individuals the right to challenge or require reconsideration of decisions based solely on automated processing, though Tanzania's § 36(2)(b) frames it as requiring the controller to reconsider while the GDPR provides a broader right not to be subject to such decisions.

instances.citation: LFPDPPP (2025) - Right not to be subject to automated decisions
instances.notes: Both address rights against solely automated decision-making with significant effects, but the GDPR rule focuses on the right to information about such processing while Mexico's 2025 revision establishes a broader right not to be subject to such decisions at all, more closely paralleling GDPR Art. 22 than Art. 15.

Both concern rights regarding automated decision-making, but the existing rule covers the right to obtain information about such decisions while this UK rule specifically grants the right to make representations about solely automated significant decisions, a narrower and distinct procedural right.

rule_text: Profiling is defined as any form of automated processing of personal data that uses such data to evaluate personal aspects relating to a natural person, particularly to analyse or predict performance, economic situation, health, preferences, behaviour, location, or movements.
rule_text_technical: 'Profiling' means any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person's performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

The Serbia PDPA definition of profiling is a near-verbatim transposition of GDPR Article 4(4), defining profiling as automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects including analysis or prediction.

Both define profiling as automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects, but the Swiss revDSG formulation is independently drafted with slightly different phrasing and examples compared to GDPR Art. 4(4).

Both rules define automated processing/profiling concepts for data protection law purposes, but China's PIPL Art. 73 additionally defines 'personal information handler' (analogous to GDPR 'controller') and 'automated decision-making' as a distinct defined term, whereas GDPR Art. 4(4) focuses solely on defining 'profiling' as a subset of automated processing.

Both rules define 'profiling' as collection/use of personal information to assess characteristics of a natural person (work performance, economic situation, etc.), but Quebec's formulation is independently drafted and uses slightly different phrasing from the GDPR's definition.

Both rules address data processing constraints within EU law, but NIS2 Art. 2(14) specifically limits personal data processing to what is necessary for cybersecurity purposes and cross-references GDPR, whereas GDPR Art. 4(4) defines profiling as a form of automated processing — different subject matter but both operate within the same GDPR framework with meaningful differences in scope and obligation.

rule_text: Biometric data is defined as personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics that allow or confirm unique identification of a natural person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data.
rule_text_technical: 'Biometric data' means personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to the physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a natural person, which allow or confirm the unique identification of that natural person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in GDPR (Article 22) (European Union, 2016-04-14).

Both define sensitive/special categories of personal data to include racial/ethnic origin, religious beliefs, political opinions, and health data, consistent with the international standard for special category data, though drafted independently with different phrasing.

Serbia's definition of sensitive data covers biometric data for unique identification, genetic data, health data, and special categories (racial origin, political opinion, etc.), substantively matching GDPR Article 9 sensitive categories and Article 4(14) biometric data definition, but drafted as a single combined provision rather than split articles.

Both rules establish special/sensitive categories of personal data requiring heightened protection, and both include biometric and genetic data, but the Indonesian UU PDP's list also distinctly includes health data, criminal records, child data, and personal financial data as a unified 'specific personal data' category, whereas the GDPR defines biometric data separately and has its own broader Article 9 special categories list.

Both rules define a category of sensitive/special personal data requiring heightened protection including biometric, health, genetic, racial/ethnic origin, and religious data, but Pakistan's provision is broader in scope (adding financial and criminal records) and is a standalone statutory definition rather than a narrower biometric-specific GDPR definition.

Both define special/sensitive categories of personal data including biometric, genetic, racial/ethnic origin, religious, and political data, but Bangladesh's definition also explicitly lists trade union membership and frames biometric data specifically as data used for unique identification, closely tracking GDPR Article 9 categories.

rule_text: You must ensure data collected is adequate, relevant, and not excessive in relation to the purposes for which it is collected.
rule_text_technical: Data collected must be adequate, relevant, and not excessive in relation to the purposes for which it is collected.

first_instance.law_name: Law No. 13 of 2016 on the Protection of Personal Data Privacy

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Qatar Personal Data Privacy Protection Law (Qatar, 2016-11-01).

Both rules require that personal data be adequate, relevant/sufficient, and not excessive relative to the collection purpose, but are drafted differently and come from independently adopted data protection laws in different jurisdictions.

Both rules require that personal data be adequate, relevant, and not excessive/limited to what is necessary, but are independently drafted under different data protection frameworks (Qatar PDPPL 2016 vs. Nigeria DPA 2023) with slightly different phrasing ('not excessive' vs. 'limited to what is necessary').

rule_text: You must obtain Ministry authorization to transfer sensitive personal data to countries lacking an adequacy determination.
rule_text_technical: Sensitive personal data is subject to stricter transfer controls, and transfers of sensitive data to countries lacking adequacy determinations require Ministry authorization.

first_instance.law_name: Law No. 13 of 2016 on the Protection of Personal Data Privacy

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Qatar Personal Data Privacy Protection Law (Qatar, 2016-11-01).

Both permit cross-border transfer to non-adequate jurisdictions under specified derogations including data subject consent, but Bahrain's Art. 13(1) applies to all personal data while Qatar's rule is limited to sensitive personal data, and Qatar requires Ministry authorization rather than relying on derogations.

Both require regulatory authority approval for cross-border transfers of sensitive personal data, though the Saudi law (SDAIA) also adds that the transfer must not conflict with national interests or regulations, a condition absent from the Qatari rule.
Both impose stricter controls and authorization requirements for international transfers of sensitive personal data, independently adopted under different national regimes.

rule_text: You cannot process personal data concerning criminal proceedings or judgments, except where carried out by competent public bodies, legal persons fulfilling legal objectives, persons pursuing their own litigation, attorneys serving clients, or for journalism or scientific research.
rule_text_technical: Processing of personal data concerning instituting and pursuing criminal proceedings or judgments therein is prohibited except: (a) by competent public bodies for their legal duties; (b) by legal persons for legally established objectives; (c) by any person as necessary to pursue litigation by or against them; (d) by attorneys for client interests; or (e) for journalism or scientific research.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

Both rules restrict processing of personal data in criminal contexts to authorized bodies with appropriate safeguards, but the Sri Lanka rule is broader (covering all criminal investigations) and frames the requirement as a permission with conditions, while the Bahrain rule specifically prohibits processing criminal proceedings/judgments data except by enumerated competent bodies.

rule_text: You cannot create or maintain a complete register of criminal cases and judgments unless you are the Public Prosecution, Military Judiciary, Military Prosecution, Ministry of Justice, or Ministry of Interior.
rule_text_technical: A complete register of criminal cases and judgments may be created and kept only by the Public Prosecution, Military Judiciary, Military Prosecution, Ministry of Justice, and Ministry of Interior.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

rule_text: You cannot carry out automated processing of sensitive personal data, biometric data for identification, genetic data, linked personal data files between multiple controllers, or visual surveillance recording without obtaining the Authority's prior written authorization.
rule_text_technical: Prior written authorization from the Authority is required before: (a) automatic processing of sensitive personal data per Article 5(2); (b) automatic processing of biometric data used to verify identity; (c) automatic processing of genetic data, except by physicians/specialists in licensed medical establishments for preventive medicine, diagnosis, healthcare or treatment; (d) automatic processing involving linkage between personal data files of two or more controllers processed for different purposes; or (e) processing involving visual recording used for surveillance purposes.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

Both restrict processing/transfer of sensitive/biometric data and allow narrow exceptions, but Panama Art. 13 focuses on transfer with explicit authorization and specific humanitarian/legal exceptions, while Bahrain art. 15-1 prohibits automated processing with a different scope of exceptions.

Both rules restrict processing of sensitive/biometric personal data and require specific authorization, but Egypt's rule requires a license from a regulatory Center plus explicit written consent, whereas Bahrain's rule prohibits automated processing of such data outright with different framing and scope.

Both Oman's Art. 5 and Bahrain's PDPL Art. 15-1 prohibit processing of special categories including biometric and genetic data, but differ in scope, permitted exceptions, and the specific categories enumerated (Oman adds ethnic origin, sexual life, political/religious opinions, and criminal data explicitly).

rule_text: Individuals have a non-waivable right to receive specific information about how their data is processed and used, and they cannot give up this right or the right to move their data between services.
rule_text_technical: No exercise of any right under Paragraph (1) of Article 17 or Article 20 shall be considered a waiver of any rights prescribed pursuant to this Section by the Data Subject.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

Both prohibit advance waiver of data subject rights; the Bahraini rule covers a broader set of rights under Articles 17 and 20, while the Swiss rule focuses specifically on the right to information under Art. 25.

rule_text: Board members must disclose in writing any personal interest, direct or indirect, in matters before the Board and may not participate in deliberations or vote on such matters.
rule_text_technical: If the Board considers a matter of direct or indirect personal interest to a member that conflicts with post requirements, the member must notify the Board in writing as soon as aware, and may not participate in deliberations nor vote on the matter.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

rule_text: The Chief Executive and Authority employees cannot have direct or indirect interests conflicting with their post requirements and must immediately report any such interest in writing.
rule_text_technical: The Chief Executive and any Authority employee shall not have direct or indirect interest conflicting with post requirements in the Authority's field of work; each must immediately report in writing any interest arising during the period of holding the post.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

Both rules impose confidentiality obligations on members and officials of a data protection authority, but Japan's rule covers divulgence and misappropriation of confidential information while Bahrain's focuses on conflicts of interest and disclosure requirements.

rule_text: You cannot transfer personal data outside Bahrain in violation of Articles 12 and 13; doing so is punishable by imprisonment up to one year and/or a fine of BD 1,000 to BD 20,000.
rule_text_technical: A person who transfers personal data to another country or territory in contravention of Articles 12 and 13 shall be liable to imprisonment up to one year and/or a fine of BD 1,000 to BD 20,000.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

Both impose imprisonment and/or fines for violating cross-border data transfer conditions, but Egypt specifies EGP 500,000–5,000,000 fines with at least 3 months imprisonment while Bahrain specifies up to 1 year imprisonment and BD 1,000 fine.

rule_text: You cannot process personal data without first notifying the relevant regulatory authority; violations are subject to criminal penalties including imprisonment and substantial fines.
rule_text_technical: A person who processes personal data without notifying the Authority in breach of Article 14(1) shall be liable to imprisonment up to one year and/or a fine of BD 1,000 to BD 20,000.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

rule_text: You cannot process personal data without obtaining prior authorization from the Authority where required; doing so is punishable by imprisonment up to one year and/or a fine of BD 1,000 to BD 20,000.
rule_text_technical: A person who processes personal data without obtaining prior authorization from the Authority in breach of Article 15 shall be liable to imprisonment up to one year and/or a fine of BD 1,000 to BD 20,000.

first_instance.law_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Bahrain PDPL 2018 (Bahrain, 2018-07-12).

rule_text: If you obtained consent and need to share personal data with other controllers, you must obtain specific consent from the data subject for that sharing, unless an exemption applies.
rule_text_technical: The controller that obtained consent and needs to communicate or share personal data with other controllers must obtain specific consent from the data subject for such purpose, except in the cases of consent waiver provided in this Law.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

Both require consent for international/cross-entity personal data transfers and allow legal exceptions, but Panama's rule applies to all cross-border transfers with a 'prior, informed, and unequivocal' consent standard, while Brazil's rule specifically addresses sharing with other controllers and requires specific consent for that sharing.

Both require consent before processing or transferring personal data, but Paraguay's rule is a broader general prohibition on any processing or transfer without free, express and conscious consent, while Brazil's rule specifically addresses sharing with other controllers when original processing was consent-based.

Both require notification/consent when sharing personal data with third parties, but PIPL mandates detailed prior notification to the individual (not just specific consent for sharing) and covers a broader set of disclosure elements.

Both require consent before communicating/sharing personal information with third parties, but Quebec's rule additionally mandates express consent for sensitive information and applies within a private-sector enterprise framework, while Brazil's rule focuses specifically on sharing between controllers.

Both require consent before disclosing personal data to third parties for certain purposes, but Kuwait's rule specifically targets marketing purposes unrelated to the original transaction, while Brazil's rule addresses sharing with other controllers more generally.

rule_text: If consent is provided in writing, it must appear in a clause distinct from other contractual clauses.
rule_text_technical: Where consent is provided in writing, it must be contained in a clause highlighted from the other contractual clauses.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

Both require written consent for sensitive data processing, but the Saudi PDPL applies this as a general requirement for all sensitive data consent, while LGPD art. 8-1 specifically addresses written consent appearing in a distinct clause from other contractual clauses.

rule_text: You bear the burden of proving that consent was obtained in compliance with the law.
rule_text_technical: The controller bears the burden of proof that consent was obtained in conformity with this Law.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

Both rules place the burden of proof for consent on the data controller/responsible party, but the Paraguay law frames it specifically in terms of the data subject's consent to use of personal data, while Brazil's LGPD frames it as proving consent was obtained in compliance with law.

Both require the controller to be able to demonstrate that consent/agreement for processing was obtained, though LGPD focuses specifically on consent while the Kuwait rule broadly covers any agreement by the data owner.

rule_text: When processing of personal data is a condition for providing a product, service or exercising a right, you must prominently inform the data subject of this fact and the means to exercise their rights.
rule_text_technical: When processing of personal data is a condition for the supply of a product or service or for the exercise of a right, the data subject must be prominently informed of this fact and of the means by which they may exercise the rights listed in Art. 18.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

Both address the obligation to inform data subjects about processing of their personal data, but Panama's rule specifically classifies failure to inform as a serious infraction and focuses on data not obtained directly from the subject, while Brazil's rule addresses disclosure when processing is a condition for a service.

rule_text: When you rely on legitimate interest as legal basis, you may only process personal data strictly necessary for the intended purpose.
rule_text_technical: When processing is based on the controller's legitimate interest, only personal data strictly necessary for the intended purpose may be processed.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

rule_text: When relying on legitimate interest, you must adopt measures to guarantee transparency of the data processing.
rule_text_technical: The controller must adopt measures to guarantee the transparency of data processing based on its legitimate interest.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

rule_text: You must produce a data protection impact report on legitimate-interest-based processing if requested by the national authority.
rule_text_technical: The national authority may request that the controller produce a personal data protection impact report when processing is based on its legitimate interest, observed commercial and industrial secrets.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

rule_text: You cannot share or communicate sensitive health data between controllers for economic advantage, except for portability requested by the data subject or for transactions in the provision of healthcare services.
rule_text_technical: Communication or shared use among controllers of sensitive health data with the purpose of obtaining economic advantage is prohibited, except in cases related to healthcare, pharmaceutical assistance and health services to permit: data portability when requested by the data subject; or financial/administrative transactions resulting from such services.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

rule_text: Private health insurance operators cannot use health data processing for risk selection in contracting any modality, or in contracting and excluding beneficiaries.
rule_text_technical: Operators of private healthcare plans are prohibited from processing health data for the practice of risk selection in contracting any modality, as well as in the contracting and exclusion of beneficiaries.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

rule_text: Research bodies conducting public health studies must process personal data exclusively within the body in a controlled and secure environment, applying anonymization or pseudonymization whenever possible.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

rule_text: You cannot use personal data referring to the regular exercise of rights by the data subject to their detriment.

rule_text: Public bodies processing personal data must publish clear and updated information on the legal basis, purpose, procedures and practices used, preferably on their websites.
rule_text_technical: Legal entities of public law processing personal data must inform the hypotheses in which they perform processing, providing clear and updated information on legal basis, purpose, procedures and practices used, in easily accessible vehicles, preferably their electronic websites.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

rule_text: You must keep public sector data in interoperable and structured format for shared use, public service delivery, decentralization and dissemination.
rule_text_technical: Data must be kept in interoperable and structured format for shared use, with a view to executing public policies, providing public services, decentralizing public activity, and disseminating and accessing information by the general public.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

rule_text: Public authorities cannot transfer personal data from their databases to private entities except in narrow specified cases (decentralized public activity, publicly accessible data, legal authorization, fraud prevention).
rule_text_technical: It is forbidden for public authorities to transfer to private entities personal data contained in databases to which they have access, except: decentralized execution of public activity for that specific purpose; publicly accessible data; where there is legal provision or contracts/agreements; or transfer aimed exclusively at preventing fraud and irregularities or protecting safety/integrity of data subjects.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brazil LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) (Brazil, 2018-08-14).

rule_text: Communication or shared use of personal data from public to private entities requires the data subject's consent and notification to the national authority, except in specific listed cases.
rule_text_technical: Communication or shared use of personal data from a public legal entity to a private entity shall be reported to the national authority and shall depend on the consent of the data subject, except: in cases of consent waiver under this Law; for shared use with publicity per Art. 23(I); or under exceptions in Art. 26 § 1º.

first_instance.law_name: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018
