first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Covered participants must disclose all positions and appointments, both domestic and foreign, including titled academic, professional, or institutional appointments whether or not paid and whether full-time, part-time, or voluntary.
rule_text_technical: Agencies shall require disclosure of positions and appointments, both domestic and foreign, including affiliations with foreign entities or governments, including titled academic, professional, or institutional appointments whether or not remuneration is received, and whether full-time, part-time, or voluntary (including adjunct, visiting, or honorary).

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Within 12 months, heads of federal research funding agencies must establish policies requiring disclosure consistent with the tiered table (Tier I: PIs, program officers, intramural recipients must disclose all four categories; Tier II: peer reviewers and advisory members must disclose affiliations, other support, and positions, but not talent program participation).
rule_text_technical: Within 12 months of the date of this memorandum, and consistent with applicable law, heads of United States research funding agencies shall establish policies requiring disclosure of the information reflected in the tiered table, with Tier I (PIs/key personnel, program officers, intramural funding recipients) required to disclose affiliations/employment, other support, foreign government-sponsored talent recruitment program participation, and positions/appointments; and Tier II (peer reviewers, advisory committee/panel members) required to disclose all categories except talent program participation.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Agencies must require initial disclosures upon hire, assignment, or proposal/award, and updates at least annually or more frequently, and must ensure individuals have reasonable recourse to correct or address inaccurate or incomplete information.
rule_text_technical: Consistent with applicable law, agencies shall require initial disclosures and updates to disclosure reporting; relevant agency employees and contractor personnel should provide initial disclosure when hired or assigned relevant duties; funding applicants should provide initial disclosure as part of the proposal or award process; updates should occur annually, or more frequently where appropriate. Agencies should ensure that individuals have reasonable recourse to correct or address inaccurate or incomplete information.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Within 1 year, funding agencies must establish policies requiring individual researchers supported by or working on any federal research grant to be registered with a service that provides a digital persistent identifier.
rule_text_technical: Consistent with applicable Federal laws and statutory authorities, within 1 year of the date of this memorandum, funding agencies shall establish policies regarding requirements for individual researchers supported by or working on any Federal research grant to be registered with a service that provides a digital persistent identifier for that individual.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Central government oversight bodies shall coordinate with relevant agencies to standardize AI disclosure processes, definitions, and forms across government institutions to the extent practicable, integrating digital persistent identifiers where appropriate.
rule_text_technical: Agencies shall standardize disclosure processes, definitions, and forms across funding agencies to the extent practicable. The Director of OMB shall work with OSTP, the Office of Government Ethics, and other agencies to coordinate the standardization of policies and forms related to disclosure of conflicts of interest and commitment, and where appropriate agencies should standardize forms for initial disclosures and annual updates, integrating digital persistent identifiers wherever appropriate and practicable.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Agencies must work with Inspectors General, General Counsel, law enforcement, university security officers, and the private sector to strengthen mechanisms to identify and investigate disclosure violations, sharing disclosure information consistent with privacy laws.
rule_text_technical: Agencies shall, as appropriate, work with their Inspector General, General Counsel, law enforcement, university program offices and security officers, and the private sector to strengthen mechanisms and capabilities to identify and investigate potential violations of agency disclosure requirements. Funding agencies or their Inspectors General shall cooperate and assist with administrative and law enforcement investigations, including sharing information from disclosure statements, consistent with privacy laws and other legal restrictions.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Agencies must ensure appropriate and effective consequences for violation of disclosure requirements, which may include termination of employment/grants, ineligibility for review panels, suspension or debarment from federal funding, suspension of Title IV funds, and civil or criminal penalties.
rule_text_technical: Agencies shall ensure appropriate and effective consequences for violation of disclosure requirements and engagement in other activities that threaten research security and integrity, which may include termination of Federal employment or contract; termination of a grant, cooperative agreement, contract, or award; preserving the award but barring the individual from work under it; ineligibility for U.S. Government review panels; suspension or debarment of eligibility for Federal funding; suspension or denial of Title IV funds; and civil and criminal penalties under Federal and State laws as applicable.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Agencies must have policies and processes to control and track access to and utilization of U.S. Government research facilities, including controlling physical access, vetting and securely hosting foreign visitors, and evaluating research partnerships with outside entities.
rule_text_technical: Heads of agencies shall ensure that their respective agencies have policies and processes to control and track access to and utilization of United States Government research facilities, consistent with applicable law and appropriations, including processes for controlling and tracking physical access, vetting and securely hosting foreign visitors, and evaluating research partnerships or contracts with outside entities.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Within 12 months, agency heads must establish policies prohibiting federal personnel who are participants in the U.S. R&D enterprise from participating in foreign government-sponsored talent recruitment programs, with disclosure requirements still applying to any exempted personnel.
rule_text_technical: Within 12 months of the date of this memorandum, and consistent with applicable law, heads of agencies shall establish policies, or clarify existing policies, that prohibit Federal personnel currently employed by their respective agencies who are also participants in the United States R&D enterprise from participating in foreign government-sponsored talent recruitment programs. Agency heads may extend this prohibition to contractor personnel and may grant exemptions, notifying the President through the APNSA within 30 days of any establishment of or change in exemption criteria; disclosure requirements in section 4(b) shall still apply to exempted personnel.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: The responsible minister overseeing immigration and visa matters must ensure immigration officers may collect and consider relevant information—including employment history, financial support, education history, research affiliations, participation in talent recruitment programs, field of study, and expected work locations—when adjudicating visa applications for study or research purposes.
rule_text_technical: The Secretary of State shall continue to apply a risk-based process to vet visa applicants seeking to study or conduct research activities in the United States and shall take such steps as are necessary to ensure consular officers may collect and consider, where relevant: employment and employment history; sources of financial support; education history including academic institutes, degrees, and research advisors; current and prior R&D affiliations and projects; current and pending participation in foreign government-sponsored talent recruitment programs; program of study and/or research; and facility/facilities and locations of expected work.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Within 3 months, the lead government ministry responsible for immigration and border security must assess what regulatory and technical changes are needed to require educational institutions to report equivalent information about foreign students and researchers in the national student tracking system and to provide annual or more frequent updates.
rule_text_technical: The Secretary of Homeland Security shall assess, within 3 months of the date of this memorandum, any regulatory and technical updates necessary to require relevant institutions to report the information specified in section 4(d)(i) in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) for foreign students and researchers subject to reporting in that system, and to provide updates in SEVIS annually or more frequently where appropriate; within 3 months of completion the Secretary shall provide an implementation plan to the APNSA.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Defense and security agencies, in coordination with relevant foreign affairs authorities, must assess the feasibility of including visa-applicant information in a searchable centralized database capable of flagging connections to sanctioned or restricted organizations, completing this assessment within one year.
rule_text_technical: The Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State, shall assess, within 1 year of the date of this memorandum, the feasibility and utility of including the information specified in section 4(d)(i) in a searchable centralized database, which should provide the capability to flag any disclosed or otherwise identified connections to organizations listed in the Department of Commerce's Entity List.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Government science funding agencies must share information about violators of disclosure or related policies across publicly-funded research institutions and with law enforcement and defense/security agencies, consistent with applicable data protection law, and shall include funding terms requiring such information sharing.
rule_text_technical: To strengthen the effectiveness of response measures, heads of agencies shall share information about violators across Federal funding institutions and with Federal law enforcement agencies, DHS, and State, to the extent consistent with privacy laws and other legal restrictions, and not interfering with law enforcement or intelligence activities. Heads of agencies should consider providing notice to other Federal funding institutions where significant concerns have arisen but no final determination has been made, consistent with due process and privacy. Funding agencies shall include within grant terms and conditions provisions that allow for such information sharing.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Heads of funding agencies must ensure federal personnel conducting R&D or allocating R&D funding receive research security training, including initial orientation for new personnel and annual refresher training.
rule_text_technical: The heads of funding agencies shall ensure that Federal agency personnel conducting R&D activities or participating in the process of allocating Federal R&D funding receive research security training, including risks to the U.S. R&D enterprise, individuals' responsibilities related to research security and integrity, and circumstances and behaviors that may indicate risk. Training programs shall include an initial orientation for new personnel and annual refresher training.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Within 12 months, heads of funding agencies must require research institutions receiving more than $50 million per year in federal science and engineering support to certify that they have established and operate a research security program covering cyber security, foreign travel security, insider threat awareness, and (as appropriate) export control training.
rule_text_technical: Within 12 months of the date of this memorandum, heads of funding agencies shall require that research institutions receiving Federal science and engineering support in excess of $50 million per year certify to the funding agency that the institution has established and operates a research security program. Institutional research security programs should include elements of cyber security, foreign travel security, insider threat awareness and identification, and, as appropriate, export control training.

first_instance.law_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy) (United States, 2021-01-14).

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request and receive a copy of their personal data and processing information within one month, extendable to three months in complex cases.
rule_text_technical: Data subjects may exercise the right of access to obtain a copy of their personal data and information regarding processing within one month of the request, with a permitted extension to three months in complex cases.

first_instance.law_name: Abu Dhabi Global Market Data Protection Regulations 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021 (ADGM (Abu Dhabi Global Market), 2021-02-14).

Both grant individuals the right to confirm whether their personal data is processed and receive a copy, but the ADGM rule specifies a one-month (extendable to three-month) response window while the UAE Federal Decree-Law Art. 13 does not specify a timeline in this provision.

Both concern enhanced rights of access to personal data and processing information, but Mexico's 2025 rule specifically targets automated processing details including profiling categories, which is more specific than the ADGM general access right.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request deletion of their personal data where it is no longer necessary, where consent has been withdrawn, or where data has been unlawfully processed.
rule_text_technical: Data subjects may request erasure of personal data where the data is no longer necessary for the purposes for which it was collected, consent has been withdrawn, or the data has been unlawfully processed.

first_instance.law_name: Abu Dhabi Global Market Data Protection Regulations 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021 (ADGM (Abu Dhabi Global Market), 2021-02-14).
Both grant a right to erasure on grounds including no longer necessary, consent withdrawal, and unlawful processing, with similar but independently drafted grounds and scope.
Both provide a right to deletion of personal data on similar grounds (processing violation, unnecessary, purpose fulfilled), with Ecuador adding detail on exceeding retention or consent withdrawal.

Both require deletion of personal information upon specified triggers (purpose achieved, consent withdrawn, etc.), with PIPL additionally imposing a proactive deletion obligation on handlers rather than only upon request.

Both grant the right to deletion on grounds including data no longer necessary, consent withdrawn, or objection; the UAE Federal Decree-Law and ADGM rule share the same jurisdiction and similar GDPR-influenced grounds but are separately drafted instruments.
Both provide a right to erasure where data is no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or processing is unlawful, reflecting standard GDPR-derived erasure grounds adopted independently.
Both grant the right to request deletion of personal data with exceptions; Oman's exception is specific to national archiving and documentation, while ADGM lists broader grounds.

Both provide a right to erasure of personal data on similar grounds (processing contravenes obligations, consent withdrawn), but Sri Lanka's law specifies grounding in sections 5–11 of its own Act and differs in procedural and jurisdictional framing.
Both grant the right to erasure where data is no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or processing is unlawful, drafted independently under different national frameworks.
Both provide a right to erasure on grounds including necessity lapse, consent withdrawal, and objection, independently drafted with slightly different enumeration of grounds.

Both require erasure of personal data, but India's DPDPA ties erasure specifically to withdrawal of consent or end of processing purpose, while the ADGM rule covers broader grounds including necessity and unlawful processing.
Both grant individuals the right to request erasure of personal data, with Jordan adding 'concealment' as an alternative remedy and tying it to specified conditions under the law.
Both provide a right to erasure on similar grounds (no longer necessary, consent withdrawn, objection upheld, unlawful processing), independently drafted under different legal systems.

Both establish a bundle of data subject rights including access, correction, deletion, and restriction, but Kuwait's rule is broader in scope, combining multiple rights (access, correction, deletion, restriction, objection, portability) into a single mechanism obligation.
Both establish a right to erasure on substantially similar grounds (no longer necessary, consent withdrawn, objection upheld, or unlawful processing), drafted independently.
Both establish a right to erasure on substantially the same grounds (no longer necessary, consent withdrawn, unlawful processing), independently drafted.

rule_text: You must ensure the DPO has expert knowledge of data protection law and performs duties including advising on compliance, monitoring DPR adherence, cooperating with the ADGM Registration Authority, and serving as a contact point for data subjects.
rule_text_technical: The DPO must have expert knowledge of data protection law and practice, and is responsible for advising on compliance, monitoring adherence to the DPR, cooperating with the ADGM Registration Authority, and serving as a contact point for data subjects.

first_instance.law_name: Abu Dhabi Global Market Data Protection Regulations 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021 (ADGM (Abu Dhabi Global Market), 2021-02-14).

Both require appointment of a qualified DPO with operational independence, but the Saudi law adds a registration requirement with SDAIA and conditions the obligation on processing sensitive data at large scale, creating a narrower scope than the ADGM rule.

Both require designation of a Data Protection Officer with advisory and compliance roles, but Ecuador's rule specifies additional triggering criteria (public sector, large-scale processing, special categories) similar to GDPR Article 37 scope.
Both require the DPO to have expert knowledge, advise on compliance, monitor adherence, liaise with the data protection authority, and conduct audits, though from different UAE sub-jurisdictions.

Rwanda's DPO appointment requirement covers public authorities and large-scale monitoring/processing similarly to ADGM and GDPR frameworks, but the precise thresholds and triggering criteria may differ from the ADGM rule.
Both require DPOs to have expert knowledge and specified qualifications in data protection law and practice, independently enacted.
Both require the DPO to monitor compliance with data protection law and perform advisory/documentation duties, though Jordan's formulation is more specific about documenting procedures.

Both require DPO appointment, but Ethiopia's Proclamation specifies triggering criteria (public authority processing at large scale, or large-scale regular/systematic monitoring or sensitive data processing), whereas the ADGM rule focuses on DPO qualifications and duties rather than appointment thresholds.

rule_text: You may rely on specific derogations (such as consent, contract, legal claims, or vital interests) for cross-border transfers, but these must be narrowly construed.
rule_text_technical: Derogations from cross-border transfer requirements for specific situations — including consent, contract, legal claims, and vital interests — are available but must be narrowly construed.

first_instance.law_name: Abu Dhabi Global Market Data Protection Regulations 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021 (ADGM (Abu Dhabi Global Market), 2021-02-14).

Both allow international transfers in the absence of adequacy via appropriate safeguards such as binding corporate rules, but the UAE Federal Decree-Law applies nationwide while the ADGM rule applies only in the Abu Dhabi Global Market free zone.

Both permit cross-border data transfers without adequacy protection under specific derogations including consent, contractual necessity, and legal claims, independently drafted with similar enumerated exceptions.

Both rules allow cross-border transfers where necessary to perform a contract with the data subject, as a derogation from adequacy requirements, though the Saudi rule is more narrowly focused on contract performance.

rule_text: You must make records of processing activities available to the ADGM Registration Authority on request.
rule_text_technical: Records of processing activities must be made available to the ADGM Registration Authority upon request.

first_instance.law_name: Abu Dhabi Global Market Data Protection Regulations 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021 (ADGM (Abu Dhabi Global Market), 2021-02-14).

Both require maintaining records of processing activities, but the Saudi PDPL rule specifies the content of those records (purposes, categories, recipients, transfers, retention periods, security measures) while the ADGM rule focuses on making records available to the supervisory authority on request.

Both rules require maintaining records of processing operations, but the Oman law specifies retention according to defined periods and procedures set by Regulation, while the ADGM rule focuses on making records available to a supervisory authority on request, reflecting different emphases on retention duration versus accessibility.

Both rules require maintaining records of processing activities including controller/processor contact details and processing purposes, but the Kuwait rule specifies additional elements (DPO details, representative information) and is a standalone retention obligation rather than an availability-to-regulator requirement.

rule_text: The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA) is designated as the regulatory authority responsible for issuing implementing regulations, receiving complaints, investigating, and enforcing the PDPL, with eventual transfer of certain responsibilities to the NDMO and coordination with the NCA on cybersecurity.
rule_text_technical: SDAIA is the regulatory authority primarily responsible for the PDPL during an initial period, with subsequent transfer of certain responsibilities to the National Data Management Office (NDMO) under SDAIA and coordination with the National Cybersecurity Authority (NCA) on security-related aspects.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19 of 1442H)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Saudi Arabia PDPL (Royal Decree M/19) (Saudi Arabia, 2021-03-16).

Both rules establish a dedicated supervisory authority for personal information/data protection, but Japan creates the Personal Information Protection Commission while Saudi Arabia designates SDAIA, and they differ in scope, jurisdiction, and institutional structure.

Both rules designate a specific authority to oversee personal data/AI regulation and develop specialized standards, but China's PIPL assigns rule-making coordination to the CAC specifically for small-scale handlers and new technologies including AI, whereas Saudi Arabia's PDPL designates SDAIA as the general regulatory authority for personal data protection with broader implementing regulation powers.

Both rules establish a national data authority with regulatory, investigative, and enforcement powers over personal data protection, but the UAE Data Office is a distinct institution from Saudi Arabia's SDAIA, which also covers AI, and the two laws differ in scope, jurisdiction, and specific powers granted.

Both rules designate a national authority as the supervisory body for data protection enforcement, but Rwanda designates the National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA) while Saudi Arabia designates the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA), reflecting different institutional structures and scope.

Both rules designate a national authority as the competent supervisory body responsible for implementing a data protection law, but Oman assigns this role to the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology while Saudi Arabia designates SDAIA, a dedicated data and AI authority with explicit rule-making powers.

Both establish a national data protection/AI authority with regulatory and oversight functions, but Pakistan's Authority is under the Ministry of IT whereas Saudi Arabia's SDAIA has broader AI and data mandates, and the scope and independence levels differ meaningfully.

Both designate a single national authority (SDAIA vs. INAI) as primary regulator with enforcement powers over data protection including AI-related processing, but Mexico's 2025 revision explicitly expands INAI's mandate to cover AI-specific compliance and algorithmic transparency, which goes beyond SDAIA's general data protection mandate.

rule_text: SDAIA may conduct inspections, require production of information, issue compliance orders, suspend processing, and impose administrative fines, with appeal rights to SDAIA and judicial review before the administrative courts.
rule_text_technical: SDAIA is empowered to conduct inspections, require production of information, issue compliance orders, suspend processing, and impose administrative fines; enforcement decisions are subject to appeal before SDAIA, with judicial review before the administrative courts.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19 of 1442H)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Saudi Arabia PDPL (Royal Decree M/19) (Saudi Arabia, 2021-03-16).

Both rules grant the national data protection authority powers to inspect, require information, issue compliance orders, suspend processing, and impose fines, but drafted independently under different legal frameworks (Rwanda NCSA vs. Saudi SDAIA).

Both give the supervisory authority powers to warn, order correction/deletion, suspend processing, and impose fines, but the Oman law is narrower in scope and the Saudi PDPL includes inspection powers and higher fine ceilings.

Both grant the national data protection authority broad enforcement powers including conducting investigations, requiring production of information, issuing compliance notices, suspending processing, and imposing administrative fines, independently drafted with similar scope.

Both grant the data protection authority broad investigatory and enforcement powers including inspections, document production, compliance orders, and processing suspension, but Pakistan's PDPA is a distinct statutory instrument with different institutional structure and scope from Saudi Arabia's PDPL.

Both grant a data protection authority powers to inspect, require information production, issue compliance orders, suspend processing, and impose administrative fines, but are independently drafted under different national frameworks.

rule_text: Violations of general PDPL obligations — including processing without lawful basis, failure to honor data subject rights, inadequate privacy notices, or failure to appoint a DPO — are subject to administrative fines up to SAR 5,000,000.
rule_text_technical: For violations of the Law's general obligations — including processing without lawful basis, failure to honor data subject rights, inadequate privacy notices, and failure to appoint a DPO where required: fines up to SAR 5,000,000.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19 of 1442H)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Saudi Arabia PDPL (Royal Decree M/19) (Saudi Arabia, 2021-03-16).

Both establish lower-tier fines for general/minor data protection violations, but Rwanda sets a specific RWF 10,000,000 ceiling for procedural failures while Saudi Arabia uses SAR-denominated amounts for a broader category of general violations.

Both establish tiered administrative fines for data protection violations with the highest penalties for cross-border transfer violations, but the Oman fines (up to 500,000 OMR) differ in amount and currency from Saudi fines and the penalty tiers are structured differently.

Both establish tiered administrative fines for general data protection violations with a revenue-based cap for organizations, but Nigeria's Act specifies ₦10M or 2% of global gross revenue while Saudi Arabia's PDPL uses different thresholds and currency.

Both establish tiered administrative fines for data protection violations scaled by severity, but Pakistan uses PKR-denominated thresholds (up to PKR 25,000,000 for serious violations) while Saudi Arabia uses SAR-denominated amounts, and the specific violation categories and amounts differ meaningfully.

rule_text: Violations involving sensitive data, unauthorized cross-border transfers, serious security breaches, and breaches of specific prohibitions are subject to administrative fines up to SAR 10,000,000.
rule_text_technical: For violations involving sensitive data, unauthorized cross-border transfers, serious security breaches, and violations of specific prohibitions: fines up to SAR 10,000,000.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19 of 1442H)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Saudi Arabia PDPL (Royal Decree M/19) (Saudi Arabia, 2021-03-16).

Both create a mid-tier penalty for serious violations including processing without lawful basis and ignoring data subject rights, but Rwanda specifies RWF 50,000,000 while Saudi Arabia has different currency thresholds and a broader enumeration of serious violations.

Both establish aggravated/higher penalties for violations involving sensitive data categories such as health, biometric, and children's data, but Nigeria's Act has distinct penalty thresholds and categories from Saudi Arabia's PDPL.

Both rules impose sanctions for unauthorized cross-border personal data transfers under Saudi Arabia's PDPL/SDAIA framework, but the new rule is specifically scoped to the 2025 Transfer Regulation's cross-border restrictions rather than the broader PDPL penalty provisions covering sensitive data and other serious violations.

rule_text: Repeat violations within three years of a final enforcement decision are subject to doubled fines up to SAR 20,000,000, and up to SAR 50,000,000 for the most serious repeat violations.
rule_text_technical: For repeat violations (committed again within three years of a final enforcement decision): fines doubled, up to SAR 20,000,000, and in some circumstances up to SAR 50,000,000 for the most serious repeat violations.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19 of 1442H)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Saudi Arabia PDPL (Royal Decree M/19) (Saudi Arabia, 2021-03-16).

Both address repeat violations with escalated consequences including processing suspension and referral for criminal prosecution, but Rwanda also includes public censure as a distinct remedy while Saudi Arabia focuses on doubled fines.

rule_text: Willful violations for personal gain or to cause harm are subject to imprisonment and/or criminal fines, with legal persons liable through their officers.
rule_text_technical: Criminal penalties apply to willful violations for personal gain or to cause harm: imprisonment and/or fines determined by the competent criminal court; legal persons may also be held criminally liable through their officers.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19 of 1442H)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Saudi Arabia PDPL (Royal Decree M/19) (Saudi Arabia, 2021-03-16).

Both impose criminal penalties (imprisonment and fines) for willful or serious data protection violations, but the UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 specifies up to one year imprisonment and fines up to AED 20,000,000 for repeat/serious violations, while Saudi PDPL focuses on personal-gain or harm-motivated violations with different penalty amounts and legal-person liability rules.

Both impose criminal penalties including imprisonment and fines for willful unauthorized data processing with corporate officer liability, but Rwanda specifies up to two years' imprisonment while Saudi Arabia does not specify a fixed term.

Both impose criminal penalties including imprisonment for willful violations involving sensitive personal data for personal gain or malicious purposes, but Nigeria's Act focuses specifically on unauthorized disclosure while Saudi Arabia's PDPL covers broader willful violations.

Both impose criminal penalties (imprisonment and/or fines) for willful personal data violations committed for personal gain or to cause harm, but Pakistan specifies up to 3 years imprisonment and PKR 5,000,000 fine for unauthorized acquisition/use/disclosure, while Saudi Arabia's criminal provisions are structured differently.

rule_text: You must develop a process to receive and respond to complaints arising from the application of this Order.
rule_text_technical: An organisation shall develop a process to receive and respond to complaints that may arise with respect to the application of this Order.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).
Both require establishment of complaint-handling mechanisms, though Jordan additionally requires publication on the official website.
Both require developing internal systems or processes to receive, respond to, and manage complaints or reports regarding data protection breaches or violations.

rule_text: You must communicate your data protection policies and practices to your staff.
rule_text_technical: An organisation shall communicate to its staff information about the organisation's policies and practices referred to in section 7(1)(e)(i).

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You must make information about your policies, practices, and complaint process available on request.
rule_text_technical: An organisation shall make information available on request about the policies and practices referred to in section 7(1)(e)(i) and the complaint process referred to in section 7(1)(e)(ii).

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You cannot obtain consent through false, misleading, or deceptive information or practices.
rule_text_technical: No organisation shall obtain or attempt to obtain consent for collecting, using or disclosing personal data by providing false or misleading information with respect to the collection, use or disclosure of the personal data, or using deceptive or misleading practices.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

Both address the quality and clarity of consent solicitation, but Jordan frames it as a positive requirement for clear, simple, unambiguous language, while Brunei frames it negatively as prohibiting false or deceptive practices.

rule_text: Before relying on deemed consent by notification, you must conduct an assessment that the proposed collection/use/disclosure is unlikely to have an adverse effect on the individual and take reasonable steps to inform the individual of the intent, purpose, and opt-out period.
rule_text_technical: For the purposes of section 12(1)(a), the organisation shall, before collecting, using or disclosing any personal data, conduct an assessment to determine that the proposed collection, use or disclosure is not likely to have an adverse effect on the individual; and take reasonable steps to bring information about the intention, purpose, and a reasonable opt-out period to the attention of the individual.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: In conducting the deemed consent assessment, you must identify any likely adverse effects and implement reasonable measures to eliminate, reduce, or mitigate them.
rule_text_technical: The organisation shall, in respect of the assessment mentioned in section 12(3)(a), identify any adverse effect that the proposed collection, use or disclosure is likely to have on the individual; identify and implement reasonable measures to eliminate, reduce the likelihood of, or mitigate the adverse effect; and comply with any other prescribed requirements.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: On receipt of a withdrawal notice, you must inform the individual of the likely consequences of withdrawing consent.
rule_text_technical: On receipt of the notice referred to in section 13(1), the organisation concerned shall inform the individual of the likely consequences of withdrawing his consent.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You cannot prohibit an individual from withdrawing consent to collection, use or disclosure of personal data.
rule_text_technical: No organisation shall prohibit an individual from withdrawing his consent to the collection, use or disclosure of personal data about the individual.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You must inform the individual of any further purpose for use or disclosure not previously notified, before such use or disclosure.
rule_text_technical: An organisation shall inform the individual of any other purpose of the use or disclosure of the personal data of which the individual has not been informed under paragraph (a), before the use or disclosure for that purpose.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: On request, you must provide the business contact information of a person able to answer the individual's questions about the collection, use or disclosure of their personal data.
rule_text_technical: On request by the individual, the organisation shall provide the business contact information of a person who is able to answer on behalf of the organisation the individual's questions about the collection, use or disclosure of the personal data.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: Before collecting personal data from another organisation without the individual's consent, you must provide that other organisation with sufficient information about the purpose to allow it to determine whether disclosure complies with this Order.
rule_text_technical: An organisation, on or before collecting personal data about an individual from another organisation without the consent of the individual, shall provide the other organisation with sufficient information regarding the purpose of the collection to allow that other organisation to determine whether the disclosure would be in accordance with this Order.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You cannot inform an individual that their personal data has been disclosed to a prescribed law enforcement agency where the disclosure was made without consent under this Order or other law.
rule_text_technical: No organisation shall inform any individual under section 18(1)(b) that the organisation has disclosed personal data to a prescribed law enforcement agency if the disclosure was made without the consent of the individual under this Order or any other written law.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: When providing partial access, you must notify the individual of the exclusion of any personal data or information requested.
rule_text_technical: Where an organisation provides an individual with the personal data or other information requested, the organisation shall notify the individual of the exclusion of any personal data or other information so requested under subsection (2) or (3).

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: When notified by another organisation of a correction, you must correct the personal data in your possession or control unless reasonable grounds exist not to do so.
rule_text_technical: When an organisation is notified under section 19(2)(b) or (3) of a correction of personal data, the organisation shall correct the personal data in its possession or under its control unless the organisation is satisfied on reasonable grounds that the correction should not be made.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: Where you have reason to believe a data breach affecting personal data in your possession or control has occurred, you must conduct a reasonable and expeditious assessment of whether the breach is notifiable.
rule_text_technical: Where an organisation has reason to believe that a data breach affecting personal data in its possession or under its control has occurred, the organisation shall conduct, in a reasonable and expeditious manner, an assessment of whether the data breach is a notifiable data breach.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You cannot take any action to re-identify (or cause re-identification of) the individual to whom anonymised information relates without the authorisation of the organisation or public agency holding it.
rule_text_technical: If an individual takes any action to re-identify or cause re-identification of the individual to whom anonymised information in the possession or under the control of an organisation or a public agency relates; the re-identification is not authorised; and the individual does so knowing or reckless as to whether the re-identification is unauthorised, the individual is guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding $5,000, imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years or both.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You must retain records relating to a Authority investigation for one year after the conclusion of the investigation, or any longer period specified by the Authority.
rule_text_technical: An organisation shall retain records relating to an investigation under this section for one year after the conclusion of the investigation or any longer period specified in writing by the Authority.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You cannot make an access or correction request under sections 18 or 19 in respect of another individual's personal data without that individual's authority.
rule_text_technical: Any person who makes a request under section 18(1) to obtain access to personal data about another individual; or makes a request under section 19(1) to change personal data about another individual, without the authority of the individual, is guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding $5,000, imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or both.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: Where you collect, use or disclose personal data without consent under the vital interests basis, you must notify the individual of the collection, use or disclosure and its purpose as soon as practicable.
rule_text_technical: Where the organisation collects, uses or discloses personal data about the individual under sub-paragraph (1) (vital interests), the organisation shall, as soon as is practicable, notify the individual of the collection, use or disclosure and the purpose for the collection, use or disclosure.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: Before relying on the legitimate interests basis, you must conduct an assessment to confirm legitimate interests outweigh adverse effects, identify and implement measures to eliminate/reduce/mitigate adverse effects, and provide the individual with reasonable access to information about your collection, use or disclosure.
rule_text_technical: For the legitimate interests basis, the organisation shall conduct an assessment before collecting, using or disclosing personal data; provide reasonable access to information about the collection, use or disclosure; identify any adverse effects; and identify and implement reasonable measures to eliminate, reduce the likelihood of, or mitigate the adverse effects.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: In a prospective business asset transaction, you and the counterparty must enter into an agreement requiring use or disclosure of personal data solely for purposes related to the transaction.
rule_text_technical: If X is a prospective party to the business asset transaction, X and Y shall have entered into an agreement that requires X to use or disclose the personal data solely for purposes related to the business asset transaction.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: For collection or disclosure under business improvement purposes between related corporations, you must be bound by a contract, agreement, or binding corporate rules requiring the recipient to implement and maintain appropriate safeguards.
rule_text_technical: For business improvement purposes, X and Y are bound by any contract or other agreement or binding corporate rules requiring the recipient of personal data about P to implement and maintain appropriate safeguards for the personal data.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You may use personal data without consent for research purposes only if it cannot reasonably be accomplished without identifiable data, there is clear public benefit, results will not be used to make decisions affecting the individual, and any published results do not identify any individual.
rule_text_technical: The use of personal data about an individual for a research purpose including historical or statistical research is permitted only if the research purpose cannot reasonably be accomplished unless the personal data is used in identifiable form; there is clear public benefit; the results will not be used to make any decision affecting the individual; and published results do not identify any individual.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: You may disclose personal data without consent for research purposes only if it cannot reasonably be accomplished without identifiable data, it is impracticable to seek consent, there is clear public benefit, results will not be used to make decisions affecting the individual, and any published results do not identify any individual.
rule_text_technical: The disclosure of personal data for research purposes is permitted only if the research purpose cannot reasonably be accomplished unless disclosed in identifiable form; it is impracticable to seek consent; there is clear public benefit; the results will not be used to make decisions affecting the individual; and published results do not identify any individual.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

rule_text: When relying on legitimate interest as your lawful basis, you must process only strictly necessary data, ensure transparency to the data subject, and may be required by the Authority to provide a risk assessment report.
rule_text_technical: Legitimate interest processing requires: (a) only strictly necessary data for the purpose; (b) transparency for the data subject; (c) the Data Protection Authority may require a risk report verifying no concrete threats to legitimate expectations and fundamental rights of data subjects.

first_instance.law_name: Ecuador Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (LOPDP) 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ecuador LOPDP 2021 (Ecuador, 2021-05-26).

rule_text: You cannot require data subjects to waive in advance, through mass adhesion contracts, their right not to be subject to automated decisions, and you must explicitly inform them of this right.
rule_text_technical: Renunciation of the right against automated decisions cannot be required in advance through mass adhesion contracts. The right must be explicitly informed by any suitable medium no later than the first communication regarding a decision based solely on automated assessments.

first_instance.law_name: Ecuador Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (LOPDP) 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ecuador LOPDP 2021 (Ecuador, 2021-05-26).

Both grant individuals a right to refuse or opt out of solely automated decisions with significant effects, though the Chinese PIPL also adds an explicit right to explanation and is framed as a positive individual right rather than a prohibition on waiver clauses.

Both rules permit automated decision-making under specified bases (contract, legal requirement, consent) and require informing individuals and providing protective measures, but Indonesia's UU PDP frames the obligation as informing and providing means of recourse rather than Ecuador's focus on prohibiting advance waiver and mandating safeguards.

rule_text: You must keep health data confidential, ensure secure processing, and obligations of confidentiality persist even after the relationship with the controller/processor ends.
rule_text_technical: Health data processing by the National Health System and health professionals is subject to duties of confidentiality, secure processing including protection against unauthorized/unlawful processing, loss, destruction, or accidental damage. Confidentiality obligations are complementary to professional secrecy and persist after termination of the relationship.

first_instance.law_name: Ecuador Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (LOPDP) 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ecuador LOPDP 2021 (Ecuador, 2021-05-26).

Both restrict health data processing to qualified health professionals and allow exceptions with consent, but Zimbabwe's rule adds the alternative ground of national law and is framed as a processing condition rather than a confidentiality obligation.

rule_text: You must, as a controller, comply with all enumerated obligations including implementing safeguards, conducting risk analyses, signing confidentiality contracts with personnel and processors, registering with the National Registry, and designating a DPO when applicable.
rule_text_technical: Controllers must: (1) process per principles/rights of this Law; (2) apply administrative/technical/physical/organizational/legal requirements; (3) implement periodic verification processes; (4) implement protection policies; (5) use risk analysis methodologies; (6) perform pre-processing security adequacy evaluations; (7) take preventive/corrective measures; (8) notify breaches; (9) implement protection by design and default; (10) sign confidentiality contracts with processors and personnel; (11) ensure processor offers sufficient mechanisms; (12) register and update the National Registry; (13) designate a DPO where applicable; (14) permit/contribute to audits; (15) comply with other obligations.

first_instance.law_name: Ecuador Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (LOPDP) 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ecuador LOPDP 2021 (Ecuador, 2021-05-26).

rule_text: You cannot record or intercept communications content as a telecommunications provider except by judicial order; unauthorized recording or interception triggers application of this Law.
rule_text_technical: Telecommunications service providers must guarantee secrecy of communications and security of personal data. Only by judicial order may providers use equipment, infrastructure, and installations recording communications content as ordered. Unauthorized recording or interception triggers application of this Law.

first_instance.law_name: Ecuador Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (LOPDP) 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ecuador LOPDP 2021 (Ecuador, 2021-05-26).

rule_text: You must specify the purpose of use of personal information as much as possible when handling it.
rule_text_technical: In handling personal information, the business handling personal information must specify as much as possible the purpose for which it uses that information (the 'purpose of use').

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: When acquiring personal information through business succession (e.g. mergers), you cannot handle it beyond the pre-succession purpose of use without prior consent.
rule_text_technical: If a business handling personal information acquires personal information by succeeding to the business of another business handling personal information due to a merger or other circumstances, it must not handle that personal information beyond the scope necessary for achieving the pre-succession purpose of use without obtaining the identifiable person's consent in advance.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You cannot acquire personal information by deception or other wrongful means.
rule_text_technical: A business handling personal information must not acquire personal information by deception or other wrongful means.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You must exercise necessary and appropriate supervision over employees who handle personal data to ensure security.
rule_text_technical: When having an employee handle personal data, a business handling personal information must exercise the necessary and appropriate supervision over the employee to ensure the security management of the personal data.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).
Both require training programs for staff handling personal data, though Japan's provision focuses on supervision while Jordan's mandates the DPO to organize training.

Both require that persons handling personal data (employees and contractors) be informed and supervised regarding data protection obligations, though the Kuwait rule extends explicitly to third-party contractors.

rule_text: You must prepare and retain records when providing personal data to a third party, in accordance with Personal Information Protection Commission rules.
rule_text_technical: A business handling personal information that provides personal data to a third party must, as prescribed by Personal Information Protection Commission rules, prepare a record of the date of provision and other matters specified by Commission rules.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).
Both require controllers to maintain records of data transfers including recipient, purpose, and consent, though Jordan's law is more explicit about documenting consents.

Both require maintaining records of cross-border personal data transfers, but the Saudi rule is broader in specifying detailed record content (legal basis, categories, recipient) and applies specifically to cross-border transfers, while the Japanese rule covers third-party provision records more generally.

rule_text: When receiving personal data from a third party, you must confirm the third party's identity and the circumstances under which they acquired the data, and prepare records.
rule_text_technical: A business handling personal information that receives personal data from a third party must, as prescribed by Personal Information Protection Commission rules, confirm the name and address of the third party and the circumstances of acquisition by the third party, and prepare a record of those matters.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: When providing 'information related to personal information' to a third party who is expected to acquire it as personal data, you must confirm that the identifiable person has consented.
rule_text_technical: A business handling information related to personal information must, when providing information related to personal information to a third party who is anticipated to acquire it as personal data, confirm in advance that the identifiable person has consented to the third party's acquisition of the information as personal data identifying that person.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You must make available to identifiable persons information about the personal data you hold, including your name, purposes of use, and procedures for requests.
rule_text_technical: A business handling personal information must place the following matters in a state where identifiable persons can know them: the business's name/address, the purposes of use of all retained personal data, the procedures for responding to requests, and other matters prescribed by Cabinet Order.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You must endeavor to explain the reasons when wholly or partly refusing a data subject's request or taking different measures than requested.
rule_text_technical: When a business handling personal information notifies an identifiable person of a measure that is wholly or partially different from what was requested or that no measure will be taken, the business must endeavor to explain the reason therefor.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You must endeavor to appropriately and promptly process complaints about your handling of personal information and establish necessary internal systems to do so.
rule_text_technical: A business handling personal information must endeavor to appropriately and promptly process complaints concerning the handling of personal information, and must endeavor to establish a system necessary for achieving this purpose.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: When preparing pseudonymized personal information, you must process personal information by deleting identifiers or individual identification codes per Commission rules so that specific individuals cannot be identified without collation with other information.
rule_text_technical: A business handling personal information that prepares pseudonymized personal information must process personal information in accordance with the standards prescribed by Personal Information Protection Commission rules, by deleting part of the descriptions or all individual identification codes, so that the specific individual cannot be identified unless collated with other information; and must take security measures regarding deletion information.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You cannot provide pseudonymized personal information to third parties except as permitted by law (e.g. legal basis, entrustment, joint use), and you cannot collate it with other information to identify the individual.
rule_text_technical: A business handling pseudonymized personal information must not provide pseudonymized personal information to third parties except in cases based on laws and regulations or where Article 27(5) applies; and must not collate pseudonymized personal information with other information for the purpose of identifying the identifiable person.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: When preparing anonymized personal information, you must process personal information per Commission standards so the specific individual cannot be identified and the original information cannot be restored.
rule_text_technical: A business handling personal information that prepares anonymized personal information must process personal information in accordance with standards prescribed by Personal Information Protection Commission rules so that specific individuals cannot be identified and so that the personal information cannot be restored, and take security measures regarding processing methods and other related information.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: When providing anonymized personal information to a third party, you must publicly disclose in advance the categories of information provided and the method of provision.
rule_text_technical: A business handling anonymized personal information must, when providing anonymized personal information to a third party, publicly disclose in advance the categories of information about the individual contained in the anonymized personal information to be provided and the method of provision, in accordance with Commission rules.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You cannot collate anonymized personal information with other information for the purpose of identifying the individual to whom the original personal information related.
rule_text_technical: A business handling anonymized personal information must not collate the anonymized personal information with other information or take any action prescribed by Commission rules for the purpose of identifying the specific individual relating to the personal information used to prepare that anonymized personal information.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You must take security management measures for anonymized personal information and endeavor to handle complaints regarding it.
rule_text_technical: A business handling anonymized personal information must take necessary and appropriate measures for the security management of anonymized personal information, and endeavor to take measures necessary to ensure the proper handling of anonymized personal information including complaint processing, and publicly disclose the content of those measures.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: Certified personal information protection organizations cannot use information acquired in the course of their certified business for purposes other than that business.
rule_text_technical: A certified personal information protection organization must not use information obtained in connection with the certified business for purposes other than the certified business.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: Administrative entities cannot use or provide personal information they hold beyond the purpose of use except in limited statutory circumstances.
rule_text_technical: Administrative entities must not use personal information they hold for purposes other than the purpose of use, or provide it to persons outside the entity, except in cases based on laws and regulations or other circumstances prescribed in Article 69.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: Administrative entities must give advance notification to the Personal Information Protection Commission of personal information files they hold and prepare/publish a personal information file register.
rule_text_technical: The head of an administrative entity must, in accordance with Article 74, give advance notification to the Personal Information Protection Commission of prescribed matters concerning personal information files to be held, and pursuant to Article 75 must prepare and publish a personal information file register.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: Employees and former employees handling anonymized personal information of administrative entities cannot disclose or use it for wrongful purposes.
rule_text_technical: Employees of administrative entities or persons formerly engaged in such work who have handled anonymized personal information held by administrative entities must not disclose or use the information acquired in the course of that work for wrongful purposes.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: The Personal Information Protection Commission may provide information to foreign enforcement authorities to assist in their performance of duties equivalent to the Commission's.
rule_text_technical: The Personal Information Protection Commission may provide information that is recognized as useful for the performance of duties by a foreign authority that performs duties equivalent to those of the Commission under foreign law, subject to conditions ensuring the information is used appropriately.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You cannot illegally collect, use, process, transmit, sell, buy, provide, or disclose other persons' personal information, nor engage in personal information handling that harms national security or public interest.
rule_text_technical: No organization or individual may illegally collect, use, process, or transmit other persons' personal information, or illegally sell, buy, provide, or disclose other persons' personal information, or engage in personal information handling activities harming national security or the public interest.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China PIPL (AI provisions) (China, 2021-08-20).

rule_text: When transferring personal information due to mergers, separation, dissolution, or bankruptcy, you must notify individuals of the recipient's name and contact, and the recipient must continue to fulfill handler duties.
rule_text_technical: Where personal information handlers need to transfer personal information due to mergers, separations, dissolution, or bankruptcy, they shall notify individuals of the receiving party's name and contact method; the receiving party shall continue to fulfill handler duties and must obtain renewed consent if changing the original purpose or method.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China PIPL (AI provisions) (China, 2021-08-20).

rule_text: You cannot disclose personal information you handle, except where you have obtained the individual's separate consent.
rule_text_technical: Personal information handlers may not disclose the personal information they handle; except where they obtain separate consent.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China PIPL (AI provisions) (China, 2021-08-20).

rule_text: You may handle personal information already disclosed by the person or otherwise lawfully disclosed within a reasonable scope, unless the person clearly refuses; and you must obtain consent where such handling has a major influence on the individual.
rule_text_technical: Personal information handlers may, within a reasonable scope, handle personal information already disclosed by the person or otherwise lawfully disclosed, except where the person clearly refuses; where handling already-disclosed personal information has a major influence on individual rights and interests, consent must be obtained.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China PIPL (AI provisions) (China, 2021-08-20).
